#6305. NASA’s Swift telescope will face a fiery demise after a failed rescue

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

During more than 22 years, the Swift Observatory made itself indispensable

This artist’s rendition shows NASA’s Swift Observatory in orbit around Earth.

NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab

For two decades, when the high-energy universe called, NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has answered. But now, the spacecraft’s science tenure is ending, just when its skills might be more valuable than ever. The Swift spacecraft is falling uncontrollably, destined to burn up in Earth’s atmosphere in just a few days.

The telescope launched in 2004, tailored to reveal the secrets of gamma-ray bursts. These outbursts are the most powerful kind scientists have ever seen, but they often faded before earlier telescopes could respond. Swift took its name from its ability to jump to work when a flash went off. That talent both illuminated these elusive bursts and made the observatory a cornerstone of modern astronomy for far longer than scientists ever dreamed.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“This was designed to be a two-year mission,” says astrophysicist Brad Cenko of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md. “We’re coming up on year 22. We are so fortunate to have had the opportunity to do all the things that we have.”

Over the decades, the spacecraft has lost about half its original altitude as it constantly slammed into molecules in the atmosphere. Those minuscule impacts infinitesimally slowed the observatory, pushing it closer to Earth. The sun’s relatively high activity in recent years has accelerated the process, leaving the spacecraft unable to continue into the 2030s as engineers hoped. A spacecraft commissioned by NASA to loft Swift out of danger launched in early July, but by late August, technical issues made a boost attempt impossible.

Swift is doomed — with nothing lined up to replace its unique capabilities.

When scientists dreamed up the Swift mission, the massive energy and elusive nature of gamma-ray bursts made them one of the most tantalizing phenomena out there. Astronomers desperately wanted to understand how they worked.

Swift was equipped with three instruments. Its Burst Alert Telescope gave scientists eyes on gamma-ray emissions from up to half the visible sky, with the resolution to pinpoint where light is coming from. The agile spacecraft could then swing itself and its other instruments — one tuned to X-rays and the other to visible and ultraviolet light — to quickly give scientists a view of a patch of sky across a swath of types of light. It was a combination unlike any observatory before or since.

“It’s such a unique telescope,” says astrophysicist Wen-fai Fong of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill., who is not part of the mission team. “It has all these views of the universe, all in one observatory, which by itself is rare, but it can also rapidly point any of these instruments.”

Swift’s roster of accomplishments speaks to the power of that recipe. “Almost immediately after launch, Swift started discovering things,” says astrophysicist Lynn Cominsky of Sonoma State University in Rohnert Park, Calif. That’s not an exaggeration: One record-breaking observation, taken just the month after launch, revealed that stellar corpses with powerful magnetic fields undergo outbursts that create a distinct kind of gamma-ray signature.

Goddard Space Flight Center Conceptual Image Lab/NASA

That observation pushed back against scientists’ existing categorization of gamma-ray bursts. Before Swift, the bursts fell into two buckets. Long gamma-ray bursts lasted as long as minutes, and scientists believed they stemmed from exploding stars triggering supernovae. Short gamma-ray bursts, in contrast, lasted less than two seconds and were believed to originate in merging neutron stars, the superdense remains of a star large enough to explode but too small to create a black hole.

Swift confirmed this basic sketch, but also complicated it by finding bursts that didn’t cleanly fit into this binary. “The more data you get, the more confused you get,” Cominsky says. Other notable bursts the telescope observed included the brightest (gamma-ray burst) of all time, nicknamed BOAT, the highest-energy photons from such a burst, and multiple claimants to the title of most distant burst.

Notably, all of Swift’s data was public right away, even as team scientists were still working to understand what the telescope had seen. “That was very new,” Fong says, crediting the mission with inspiring other observatory teams to follow suit.

As other astronomers heard about Swift’s work, they realized how powerful the observatory might be for their own interests as well. As Swift’s tenure unfolded, astronomers started asking to borrow the nimble observatory to study a whole range of objects changing on the sky.

“With scientists, if you give them a tool to do something, they will other find other things that you can do with that tool,” says astrophysicist Phil Evans of the University of Leicester in England. In its later years, Swift observed between five and 10 “targets of opportunity” most days, tallying hundreds or even thousands in a year.

Perhaps its most ground-breaking collaborations were partnerships with observatories hunting for ghostly neutrinos that travel nearly as quickly as light but don’t interact often, and for gravitational waves, the ripples in spacetime triggered by massive objects. In 2017, Swift participated in back-to-back discoveries: the unique explosion caused by two neutron stars merging, then the first neutrino traced back to its origin.

Since then, all efforts to observe light affiliated with a neutrino or gravitational-wave signal have come up empty. “We had these two really close together and then nothing since,” Evans says. “Which is frustrating, but also kind of fun.”

A range of current and future observatories will be able to take over some of Swift’s work, but not all of it. Even during the six months this year when Swift paused operations to prepare for the boost attempt, scientists felt its loss, says astrophysicist Judith Racusin of NASA Goddard. Racusin worked with Swift during its early years before turning her focus to NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, which launched in 2008 but boasts different strengths than its colleague. “We’re going to miss out,” she says of Swift’s loss. “Not just on the common events we have thousands of, but the really rare, unusual ones, which are often the ones we learn the most from.”

Mission personnel had Swift cram in as much science as possible as its demise approached. After the boost attempt was called off, the team turned Swift’s instruments back on for a scientific swan song. That included technical observations to ensure the utility of all its recent data, as well as indirect observations of Earth’s atmosphere at lower altitudes than many spacecraft are able to withstand. Swift even caught glimpses of a comet in its final weeks.

And, of course, there were gamma-ray bursts. One particularly intriguing burst came in late September and was rather far away but remarkably energetic.

“It feels a little bit like a last hurrah of Swift,” Racusin says of the event. “It’s a burst that we’ll be studying for some time, so I’m really glad we got Swift data on it while we could.”

#6304. Mountains are eroding fastest where you least expect it

Scientists have discovered why some gentle mountain landscapes erode faster than steep rocky slopes, revealing hidden effects on Earth's carbon cycle.

Every mountain range is, in geological terms, falling apart. Rivers cut downward, slopes shed material, rock weathers into soil and sediment and eventually finds its way to the sea.

Geologists have been measuring this process – denudation – for decades, using a clever trick involving cosmic rays.

When high-energy particles from exploded stars hit quartz grains at the surface, they create a rare isotope, beryllium-10, at a known rate.

The longer a grain sits exposed, the more ¹⁰Be it accumulates. Measure it, and you get an erosion rate.

The problem is that this has always worked better on some rocks than others. In granite, sandstone, and other coarse-grained rocks, quartz grains are large and easy to isolate.

In shale – one of the most common sedimentary rocks on earth, soft, fine-grained, and widespread across mountain landscapes – the quartz is too small and dispersed to extract cleanly using standard techniques.

As a result, shale has often been left out of erosion measurements, creating a significant gap in our understanding of how mountain landscapes change.

A team led by Eyal Marder at the University of Massachusetts Amherst has now fixed that. Their study describes a new method for extracting ¹⁰Be from fine-grained sedimentary rocks.

The researchers applied this method to the East River watershed in the Elk and West Elk mountains of Colorado.

This is a 465-square-kilometer catchment where resistant igneous rock and Cretaceous Mancos Shale sit side by side, subject to the same climate and the same tectonic forces.

“Shale’s erodibility is three times that of the harder rocks in the East River Watershed,” Marder said.

The shale catchments in the study erode at rates ranging from 0.05 to 0.38 mm per year, with a median of 0.11 mm per year. The intrusive igneous catchments erode at 0.03 to 0.07 mm per year.

That gap, on its own, is not surprising: geologists have long assumed weaker rock erodes faster. What the measurements reveal is the consequence of that contrast playing out over millions of years.

When weak and strong rocks sit next to each other in a landscape, they don’t erode in sync. The shale comes down faster while maintaining comparatively gentle, subdued topography.

The harder rock develops steeper slopes and higher relief as it adjusts more slowly. The result is that the fastest erosion in a mountain range is happening in the rounded, lower-relief shale terrain.

“When we look at landscapes, we are only seeing a snapshot in time,” Marder said. And that snapshot is misleading.

A steep cliff face of hard granite looks like where the action is. The quiet shale valley is where the ground is actually disappearing.

Shale and igneous rock don’t just erode at different rates. They also have opposite effects on atmospheric CO2.

Intrusive rocks like granite and monzonite undergo silicate weathering, a process that draws CO2 out of the atmosphere and locks it into dissolved carbonate.

Shale, by contrast, can contain pyrite and organic carbon, whose weathering can contribute to CO2 release.

In the East River watershed, chemical weathering accounts for roughly 10 to 70 percent of the total denudation rate.

Because the shale is eroding three times faster than the igneous rock, it is contributing disproportionately to CO2 release.

The landscape evolution modelling in the study suggests this imbalance persists for millions of years.

The models suggest that shale continues to erode faster than harder rock over extended periods, sustaining the difference in their contributions to the carbon cycle.

The cumulative CO2 implications are large.

“Scale our work up from the Elk and West Elk mountains to all the mountainous regions of the world, and getting erosion rates and their equivalent impact on CO2 release right has a marked impact on what we know about biogeochemical global cycles and climate change,” Marder explained.

Model simulations predict that the watershed could release approximately 85 teragrams of CO2 over 2.6 million years of continuous landscape adjustment.

That could potentially rise to 135 Tg if repeated glacial topographic resetting drives repeated transience cycles.

These are first-order estimates, and they exclude CO2 from oxidative weathering of fossil organic carbon in shale, which would push the numbers higher still.

The deeper lesson of the study is about what topography alone cannot tell you. Slope, relief, and channel steepness are the standard proxies geologists use to assess erosion rates and landscape equilibrium.

The steeper the terrain, the assumption goes, the faster it’s eroding. That assumption holds when the rock type is uniform.

Where it isn’t, the fastest erosion is hidden in the gentlest terrain. Models that ignore lithological contrasts will systematically misread both the erosion and the carbon flux.

The new ¹⁰Be technique for fine-grained sediments should allow researchers to fill in those gaps across other mixed-lithology mountain belts – the Appalachians, the Alps, the Himalayas.

There, shale and weak sedimentary sequences are common and their contribution to erosion and chemical weathering has been poorly constrained.

Getting that accounting right matters for anyone trying to understand how mountains regulate Earth’s carbon cycle over geological time.

The study is published in the journal Science Advances.

#6303. A diving pioneer found a Roman wreck off Portofino in 1959, then it vanished until police divers found it again 66 years later

Carabinieri divers training off Punta Chiappa, Italy, found 9 Roman wine amphorae at a Roman wreck first reported in 1959 and lost since 1960.

On November 7, 1959, the Italian diving pioneer Duilio Marcante went down off Punta Chiappa, near Camogli in northwest Italy. At about 150 feet (45 meters) he found Roman amphorae jammed between the rocks, the first sign of a Roman wreck.

Six months later the pile he had described was gone. Nobody found the site again for 66 years.

During a recent training dive, Carabinieri divers came across an intact amphora at the spot. Italian heritage officials said on October 22, 2026, that it is Marcante’s lost wreck. The announcement mentions no remains of the hull.

The divers belong to the Nucleo Carabinieri Subacquei of Genoa, the diving unit of Italy’s military police. During the exercise they spotted a complete Dressel 1 amphora, a standard Roman wine-jar type, at more than 130 feet (40 meters).

The spot lies inside the Portofino Marine Protected Area, a very busy diving area. The divers reported it at once to the regional heritage office, the Soprintendenza for Liguria.

Follow-up dives were run with the office’s own diving unit, the Servizio Tecnico di Archeologia Subacquea (S.T.A.S.). The first map counted nine amphorae in a small area along cracks in the cliff.

The jars are hard to spot because they are fused to the rock under a thick coralligenous crust, a hard pink layer built mainly by calcareous algae.

According to the official press release, the team lifted the two most exposed jars of the nine, because large numbers of divers pass over the area.

Marcante (1914-1985) ran the Centro Subacqueo Mediterraneo and a spearfishing school in Genoa. In 1958 he had joined the first campaign on the Roman ship of Spargi, in Sardinia.

On his 1959 dive he saw two amphorae stuck to the rocks by stony coral and calcareous algae. He swam around the area and saw more jars nearby. At the foot of the cliff there seemed to be a mound, covered by muddy sediment.

On Monday, November 9, the team dove again and brought up two intact jars. They feared looters would take them. The next day Marcante reported the site to the heritage office and to the underwater archaeology center in Albenga.

The difficulties of the season prevented an immediate follow-up. Nino Lamboglia, who directed the Albenga center, later wrote that the depth and steep seabed also argued against sending the ship Daino, then in its first year of work.

On May 8 and 9, 1960, Gianni Roghi went back with Marcante and the Carabinieri. Roghi worked for the Albenga center, run by Lamboglia (1912-1977), a founder of Italian underwater archaeology.

The mound in the mud was gone. They found one amphora tied with a thin line, ready to be carried off by looters. Three broken jars were still locked in the crust.

Lamboglia described the case at an underwater archaeology congress in Barcelona in September 1961. He wrote that the site had probably not stayed “immune from clandestine hoarders.” After that, nobody found it.

Simon Luca Trigona, who heads S.T.A.S. Liguria, said the survey and a first look at the jars confirm that this is Marcante’s site.

The amphorae form a uniform cargo of Dressel 1A wine jars from the Tyrrhenian side of Italy. The type dates them to between the late second century BCE and the first decade of the first century BCE.

Trigona tied the cargo to the years just after Rome conquered southern Gaul. Genoa and the other Ligurian ports were then important for Roman trade.

A second wreck from the same period was found off Pegli, on the western side of Genoa, in the early 1950s. It has not been located since either.

Other cargoes from the Roman era have survived in very different places, from a ship off Adrasan in Turkey with its plates still stacked to intact goods in Lake Neuchâtel.

The heritage office says the site now needs regular checks and rules for divers. Colonel Samuele Sighinolfi, who commands the Carabinieri naval and diving group, said it is under constant surveillance.

Major Alessandro Caprio leads the Genoa unit of the Carabinieri heritage command. He said his officers watch auctions, websites and illegal markets for the work of “tombaroli del mare,” or sea tomb robbers.

Tips from divers have mattered elsewhere in Italy, as when off Sardinia a diver alerted authorities to a hoard of about 50,000 Roman coins. Busy dive sites carry risks too, and a study that tracked more than 700 divers found that most reef damage is accidental.

Superintendent Vincenzo Tiné said the find shows how much work remains, “even in areas that we consider well studied.” He noted that thousands of divers visit them every year.

Giovanni Anelli, the mayor of Camogli, hopes the jars can one day go on display. Guglielmo Caversazio, president of the marine protected area, offered to help protect the site.

So far the divers have recorded only jars. No timber from the ship has been reported. The release does not say how many amphorae the vessel carried.

“Difficult to imagine the size of the vessel,” Trigona said. Only the more detailed surveys planned for the near future can confirm other remains, he added.

The release also does not say where the two jars raised in 1959 are today. Nor does it explain what became of the mound at the base of the cliff.

Alessandra Cabella, an art historian on the S.T.A.S. Liguria diving team, put the story in three words. “Discovered, lost, rediscovered,” she said. Carabinieri divers were there in 1959, and again for the rediscovery.

The information was obtained from the Soprintendenza Archeologia, Belle Arti e Paesaggio per la Liguria.

#6302. 11 Taos Airbnbs That Embody the Soul of the Southwest

From the first time my parents’ car crested the last hill on New Mexico State Road 68 en route to Taos, and the depths of the Rio Grande Gorge emerged in view, I was hooked. As a New Mexican, I’ve spent more than 30 years visiting the northern New Mexico town of Taos, where I enjoy dining on local cuisine, browsing contemporary art galleries, hiking the peaks around Taos Ski Valley, and rafting the Rio Grande rapids. As time has passed, the town’s unique charm has remained, but its popularity has only grown.

Indigenous peoples have inhabited the lands here since time immemorial, and today, the residents of Taos Pueblo welcome visitors to a stacked-adobe village whose architecture is synonymous with the Southwest. Creatives have long felt called to this area, from the likes of Ansel Adams, who turned his lens on the wide buttresses of St. Francisco de Assisi Mission Church, to Georgia O’Keeffe, who first visited in 1929.

One of the best ways to take in the local culture and enjoy the architecture is by staying in a Taos Airbnb. In this way, travelers get the chance to embrace elements of the town’s character, from its regional design to its counter-culture scene captured in the sustainable Earthships dotting the vast sagebrush mesa beneath mountain peaks. Whether you’re following your creative muse, want to embrace the desert landscape, or are eager to get a taste of Southwestern living, these are the best Taos Airbnbs to visit right now.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Set on 30 acres of private land and adjacent to Taos Pueblo acreage, this home offers a secluded stay that’s still just a short drive from the attractions of Taos Plaza. Daytime views unfold over the sagebrush mesa and southern Rocky Mountain peaks. Ready to find your muse? This former home of the Southwest painter Charles Henry Reynolds (1902–1963) is true to its nature, offering an artistic, historic feel. The thick-walled adobe house features all the hallmarks of Southwestern architecture, including viga ceiling construction, hand-carved beams, Saltillo tiles, and original fixtures and antique furnishings throughout. #6301. The Sky Today on Saturday, October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Let’s send off spooky season on a high note this Halloween with M74, also known as the Phantom Galaxy.

The best time to catch this ghostly galaxy is after darkness falls but before moonrise. Located in eastern Pisces, M74 reaches an altitude of 45° in the east by 9 P.M. local daylight time. You can find it just over 1° northeast of 4th-magnitude Eta (η) Piscium, or by skimming 6.6° southwest of  brighter 3rd-magnitude Beta (β) Arietis, also called Sheratan.

Ninth-magnitude M74 spans roughly 11’ in diameter — that’s quite big, because this galaxy is so nearby, just 24 million light-years away. Because it is so large, its light is spread out over a significant area, lowering its overall surface brightness and making this galaxy harder to spot than its magnitude would imply — hence its “phantom” moniker.

Once you do find it, you’ll see that M74 is a lovely face-on spiral with a bright core wrapped in fainter arms, the latter of which are best seen in 8-inch and larger scopes. The arms are mottled with bright regions of star formation, and a nebula filter can help improve the view. You may also notice the arms are not quite symmetric: the western arm is much longer than the stubby eastern one.

Sunrise: 7:28 A.M.Sunset: 5:59 P.M.Moonrise: 11:08 P.M.Moonset: 1:33 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (58%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time on November 1, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early on the 1st, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6300. Your brain follows bad advice even when you know better

A new study reveals why people continue to follow unreliable information even when they know it could be misleading.

Knowing that information is unreliable doesn’t necessarily stop us from believing it.

A new study found that even when people were warned that certain clues were no more accurate than a coin toss, they still allowed those clues to influence their decisions.

Even more surprisingly, participants recognized that the unreliable clues were influencing their decisions.

It shows that simply being aware of a bias doesn’t always stop it from affecting our choices.

Keiji Ota, an assistant professor at the University of Tsukuba in Japan, carried out the research with Lucie Charles of Queen Mary University of London. Both also work with the UCL Institute of Cognitive Neuroscience in London.

The pair tested people’s choices in a simple color-guessing game. It wasn’t a test of real news, but the findings raise questions about how much a warning label alone can do.

The study involved 140 adults in the United Kingdom, who played one of five versions of an online game.

In each round, a computer chose red or blue as the correct answer, and players scrolled at their own pace through six colored squares that predicted it.

A percentage above each square showed its chance of being right, so a 65% square gave the right answer about two-thirds of the time.

The instructions described a 50% square as “as reliable as if the square’s color had been determined by flipping a coin” and told players to ignore it.

Some clues were wrong more often than right. A 35% square could still help, but players needed to reverse its answer, much as they might do with advice from someone who usually lies.

After seeing all six clues, players chose a color and immediately learned whether they were right.

Each person played close to 300 rounds, without a time limit, while the five versions used different mixes of clues.

Players did fairly well overall, choosing the right color in 58% to 64% of rounds, depending on the version. Guessing alone would give an average of 50%.

A player who used the percentages perfectly would ignore every 50% square. Yet in all five versions, people chose blue more often when more of those random squares showed blue.

The researchers built a computer model of each person’s choices to measure the effect.

The model estimated that players treated these squares as though they were right about 54% to 62% of the time.

That was more trust than the clues deserved, but it rarely made much difference to scores. In only one version did people who relied more on the random clues perform noticeably worse.

A clue that’s wrong 65% of the time can tell you just as much as one that’s right 65% of the time. You just have to use the opposite answer, and players found that harder.

In the version with only reversed and random clues, volunteers got 58.2% of answers right. In a matching version with trustworthy clues, they reached 64.4%.

Players also gave the last clue more weight than the first, especially when most clues needed reversing.

The researchers suggest that earlier clues may have faded from memory as new ones appeared.

Mentally flipping each answer could add to that strain. The extra effort might leave people with less ability to remember the clues they had already seen.

In two versions, players answered a question after each choice about one randomly selected kind of clue. They moved a slider to show whether they had followed its color, ignored it, or chosen the opposite.

Their ratings matched patterns in their choices: when more squares of a given kind agreed with their final answer, they reported more influence from that kind.

The most informative clues drew the strongest ratings, whether players needed to follow or reverse them.

The random clues showed the same pattern, suggesting that participants could recognize how unreliable information affected their choices.

People who relied most on a kind of clue also generally felt most influenced by it, although this did not hold for every kind in both versions.

A second model compared how likely a player was to choose an answer with and without a clue.

The difference matched people’s ratings and was closely tied to confidence, according to the authors.

The researchers offer several possible explanations for the bias. Seeing the same color repeatedly may make it feel like the right answer, an idea psychologists call the mere exposure effect.

People may also expect whoever provides information to be trying to help. That expectation could make it difficult to accept that a clue contains nothing useful.

Or players may have turned to random clues when the useful ones left them almost evenly split between red and blue. In that case, a useless clue could serve as a tiebreaker.

Ignoring those clues might also take more work than it was worth. Since the bias barely hurt scores, the authors suggest that players had little to gain by resisting it.

Reliability labels already appear alongside social media posts, product reviews, and health advice. Research on whether they reduce misinformation has produced mixed results.

Some studies found that star ratings for news sources reduced people’s willingness to believe and share false stories.

A 2022 study, however, found little average improvement in the quality of news people read and no reduction in mistaken beliefs.

The volunteers’ awareness also differs from earlier research in which people often missed influences on their choices, including the order of search results.

Those studies used cues that weren’t spelled out, while this game clearly stated how reliable each clue was.

Colored squares are much simpler than real headlines, and each version of the game used only three reliability levels.

The slider used to measure people’s awareness is also new and needs testing with other wording, labels, and instructions.

The questions asked about kinds of clues rather than their place in the sequence. That means the study couldn’t show whether players noticed how much more they relied on the last clue.

Fact-checking labels aim to limit the influence of false information, but this experiment cannot tell us exactly how people respond to them online.

Still, the findings reveal something important about human decision-making: Knowing that information is unreliable doesn’t necessarily stop us from using it. Recognizing a bias and overcoming it may be two very different things.

The study is published in the journal PLOS Computational Biology.

The Cat's Head Nebula shows its ghostly insides and sinister red eye in rival views from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In space, nobody can hear you scream — or meow, for that matter. This was as true for Félicette — the stray Parisian tuxedo cat who safely completed the world's first (and only) suborbital feline flight, in 1963 — as it is for the gargantuan Cat's Head Nebula, which is featured in stunning new images from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes.

Rising from the cloudy Carina Nebula some 7,500 light-years from Earth, the Cat's Head Nebula is a column of star-sculpted gas and dust that vaguely resembles a feline sitting with its back to us, coyly turning its head to show off a single red eye. That eye is a young star that's embedded deep within the dust and possibly transforming it before our eyes.

Nebulas like these occur when the radiation from active young stars lights up and erodes the material around them. They are beautiful and easy to find; if this cosmic cat gets bored staring at us, it can just waltz over to the other side of the Carina Nebula and crawl into a similar globule of gas that looks exactly like a box with an open lid. (Cats will be cats, after all.)

In honor of Halloween, the European Space Agency (ESA) shared three competing views of the Cat's Head Nebula — one from the Hubble Space Telescope, which captures optical light, and two from the infrared instruments aboard the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The three views, shown below, reveal different features of the nebula in different wavelengths of light, getting progressively spookier as more color drains out of the scene.Take a look at all three images — and cast your vote for the spookiest in the poll at the end.

The Hubble Space Telescope's optical light view of the Cat's Head Nebula.

Observing the nebula in the same visible wavelength range that you could see through a strong backyard telescope, Hubble highlights the dark pillar of dust that has survived the ultraviolet assault of nearby stars. The wispy edges at the right of the column show where starlight is evaporating the gas around it, slowly whittling it away to nothing.

The glow of blue, yellow, orange and red light around the dust pillar mark where starlight is interacting with different gas molecules, including oxygen, hydrogen and sulfur, according to ESA. The process is similar to how different molecules in Earth's atmosphere produce different-colored auroras when excited by solar radiation — just on a much grander scale.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in near-infrared light.

Switching to light human eyes cannot see, JWST's Near-Infrared Camera cuts through the wispier outer layers of dust to show the densest material at the column's center. Countless additional stars and galaxies appear in the field of view as their infrared glow penetrates the surrounding material.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Here we see a more complex, turbulent column, showing how stellar radiation is carving up the inside of the cat's head as well as its edges. JWST's view also illuminates a disembodied, hand-like structure to the left of the cat, reaching out as if to pet its cosmic companion.

The James Webb Space Telescope's view of the Cat's Head Nebula in mid-infrared light.

The final view, taken with JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, cuts to the ghostly core of the nebula, showing little more than smoky, bluish light. According to ESA, these are the emissions of molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons — typically colorless molecules of carbon and hydrogen related to combustion.

While most starlight disappears in this view, a strange new bright spot emerges to the right of the cat's head. This orange speck is a true mystery, according to ESA, and its relationship to the rest of the nebula is unknown.

#6298. November 2026: What’s in the Southern Hemisphere sky this month?

Although Venus has dominated the evening sky since last summer, its long apparition came to an end at inferior conjunction in late October. That leaves Saturn as the only naked-eye planet visible as the sky darkens this month. The ringed planet glows at magnitude 0.5 as it edges westward relative to the background stars of northwestern Cetus the Whale.

Saturn reached opposition and peak visibility in early October, but the distant world’s appearance changes so slowly that you’ll find it nearly as impressive through a telescope as it was last month. In mid-November, the planet measures 19″ across its equator while the ring system spans 43″ and tilts 6° to our line of sight. Any telescope reveals Saturn’s brightest moon, 8th-magnitude Titan, and a 10-centimeter instrument brings in Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, which all glow at 10th magnitude.

November’s morning sky offers a bevy of treats. A few hours after midnight, you’ll see two planets forming an attractive trio with 1st-magnitude Regulus, the brightest star in the constellation Leo the Lion.

During the month’s first half, Mars rises first with Jupiter following close behind. The Red Planet moves eastward against the backdrop of western Leo, passing both Jupiter and Regulus during November. The ruddy world slides 1.2° north of Jupiter on the 15th and 1.8° north of Regulus on the 24th. Mars glows at magnitude 0.7 at midmonth, slightly but noticeably brighter than Regulus. Compare the orange-red color of the planet with the star’s blue-white hue.

Mars’ appearance through a telescope grows a bit more interesting during November. The planet spans 7″ at midmonth, large enough to show some subtle surface detail during moments of good seeing.

Jupiter steals the show in this part of the sky, however. Shining at magnitude –2.1 and with a disk measuring 37″ across, it easily bests its planetary companion in both brightness and telescopic splendor. The gas giant features a series of alternating atmospheric bands, with bright zones and darker belts running parallel to one another. Even under mediocre seeing conditions, the central Equatorial Zone and its neighboring belts stand out.

The approach of dawn brings the final two naked-eye planets into view. Venus appears first. It rises less than an hour before sunrise in early November but more than two hours before the Sun at month’s end. You won’t mistake the brilliant planet for any other object. It brightens from magnitude –4.2 on the 1st to magnitude –4.9 at month’s end.

A telescope reveals impressive changes to Venus during November, though its large crescent remains a treat all month. On the 1st, you’ll see a disk that measures a whopping 1′ across but is only 3 percent lit. By the 30th, the planet spans 40″ while the Sun illuminates 27 percent of its Earth-facing hemisphere.

Mercury passes between the Sun and Earth on Nov. 4 and slowly climbs into view after midmonth. The shallow angle of the ecliptic — the apparent path of the Sun and planets across the sky — to the eastern horizon before dawn at this time of year means the planet never gains a lot of altitude. On the 30th, it stands 5° high 30 minutes before sunrise.

Still, the innermost planet shines brightly at magnitude –0.7 and should be visible in the twilight. Point you telescope at Mercury that morning and you’ll see a disk 6″ in diameter and 83 percent lit.

A waning gibbous Moon occults Regulus on Nov. 30 Universal Time. Residents in New Zealand can watch the event in the early morning hours of Dec. 1 local time. From Auckland, the star disappears behind the Moon’s bright limb at 13h24m UT and reappears from behind the dark limb at 14h23m UT.

Look high in the south on any November evening and the relatively dim constellation Tucana the Toucan comes into view. Tucana’s brightest star, Alpha (α) Tucanae, glows at 3rd magnitude. The easiest way to find the constellation is to look just southwest of magnitude 0.5 Achernar, the brightest star in Eridanus the River. Tucana does possess two deep-sky treasures, however: the Small Magellanic Cloud and the stunning globular star cluster 47 Tucanae.

The origin of the constellation’s name remains a source of confusion. Sixteenth-century Dutch navigators Pieter Dirkszoon Keyser and Frederick de Houtman devised the constellation in the late 16th century. Flemish astronomer Petrus Plancius first placed Tucana on a celestial globe in 1598.

Yet Keyser and de Houtman observed the sky from what we now know as the East Indies after visiting Madagascar, and the toucan is not native to that part of the world. The brightly colored bird resides in Central and South America, which lies about 180° in longitude from the East Indies.

In 1603, De Houtman published Malay and Madagascan Vocabulary, which included a star catalog. He headed his entry for the constellation Tucana “The Indian Magpie, named by the Indians Lang.” On the line below, he included the subhead “Tucana.”

This is where Keyser comes back into the story. He once visited South America and likely had observed toucans. It seems plausible that the confusion arose because the toucan bears some similarity to the oriental pied hornbill of the East Indies.

The map below portrays the sky as seen near 30° south latitude. Located inside the border are the cardinal directions and their intermediate points. To find stars, hold the map overhead and orient it so one of the labels matches the direction you’re facing. The stars above the map’s horizon now match what’s in the sky.

The all-sky map shows how the sky looks at:

11 p.m. November 110 p.m. November 159 p.m. November 30

Dr. Martin George is an astronomy speaker and writer who currently serves as Chair of International Development and Elections at the International Planetarium Society.

#6297. Einstein had a packed schedule in Pittsburgh in 1934, but he made time for a group of amateur astronomers

In 1934, Albert Einstein visited a Pittsburgh astronomy exhibit organized by a plumber, highlighting his respect for amateur scientists and their work.

In December 1934, Albert Einstein came to Pittsburgh with a tight schedule. One stop he made a point of keeping was an exhibition by the city’s amateur astronomers.

The group’s co-founder, Leo J. Scanlon, was a plumber. Four years earlier, he had built a backyard observatory topped with a homemade aluminum dome for about $428.

Einstein was in town to give a lecture. The amateurs had invited him to see their display at the Mellon Institute, in Pittsburgh’s Oakland neighborhood.

In June 1929, Scanlon, who lived from 1903 to 1999, and Chester B. Roe founded the Amateur Astronomers Association of Pittsburgh.

In 1930, Scanlon and a group of friends traveled to the Stellafane convention of amateur telescope makers, which drew just under 100 registered guests. He kept a 41-page journal of the trip.

Back home, Scanlon built the Valley View Observatory beside his house on Van Buren Street. He ordered about 415 square feet (38.6 square meters) of sheet aluminum for the dome.

Its curved panels, called gores, were joined with an external double-turned seam. On November 15, 1930, with finishing touches still to come, the dome was lifted into place.

A dedication followed on November 23. The observatory without its dome cost $250, and the dome itself cost $178, according to Scanlon’s journal entries shared by the Springfield Telescope Makers.

A plaque near the site calls Valley View the first known astronomical observatory with an aluminum dome. Its shiny metal dome became a model for later observatories worldwide, the plaque adds.

In 1934, a national science convention met in Pittsburgh, with exhibits in the unfinished Mellon Institute building. Scanlon collected telescope-making materials from amateurs around the country for a free booth there.

He also wrote to Einstein, saying that a visit would encourage amateurs. Einstein answered that he would come if his schedule allowed.

“It would be my pleasure to examine the exhibit of the Amateur Astronomers,” Einstein wrote.

On December 28, 1934, Einstein, author of the general theory of relativity, lectured at the Carnegie Institute of Technology, now Carnegie Mellon University. His topic was mass-energy equivalence, the idea summed up as E = mc².

“People clambered to see Einstein’s lecture because he was one of the world’s first rock-stars,” said Gregg Franklin, a physics professor at the university.

A foggy photo taken from a balcony of the Little Theater is the only known picture of Einstein with a variant of that equation.

After his lecture in a nearby hall, Einstein asked the audience where the astronomers were, according to the club’s account. A professional astronomer in the room stood up.

“No, no,” Einstein replied. “I want to meet with the amateur astronomers.”

He reached the booth with a group of 40 or 50 people and stayed about 20 minutes. The display held equipment, material samples and photographs from telescope builders in eight states.

Scanlon’s brother Frank was working at a noisy grinding table. Scanlon showed Einstein the Foucault knife-edge test, which reveals tiny bumps and hollows on a telescope mirror.

On a 6-inch (15-centimeter) mirror, Scanlon pressed five fingertips to the glass. The test then showed five “hills” about one wavelength of light high, raised by the heat of his hand.

“I’m a plumber,” Scanlon replied when Einstein asked about his profession near the end of the visit. “Good,” Einstein answered, before asking him where the bathroom was.

David Topper, a Pittsburgh native, is a historian of science at the University of Winnipeg and the author of several books about Einstein.

“He had a thing about amateurs, whom he respected as much as professionals,” Topper said.

Another club member photographed Scanlon thanking Einstein at the booth. Scanlon kept Einstein’s written reply to his invitation.

“It is a letter that I still treasure,” Scanlon recalled many years later.

Steve Hill, a citizen scientist, showed that he could map Jupiter’s atmosphere with special color filters and a backyard telescope.

He then joined Patrick Irwin at Oxford University, whose team had studied Jupiter’s clouds with the MUSE instrument on the Very Large Telescope.

Their combined study concluded that the upper clouds are most likely ammonium hydrosulfide mixed with smog, not frozen ammonia, the European Southern Observatory reported in January 2025.

Clouds of ammonia ice may form only occasionally, when strong vertical convection carries ammonia to the top of the atmosphere.

Dan Caselden, a volunteer with the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 citizen science project, co-discovered the cold brown dwarf W1935, the American Museum of Natural History announced in April 2024.

The James Webb Space Telescope later detected methane emission from W1935, a possible sign of aurorae.

The information was obtained from the Amateur Astronomers Association of Pittsburgh

#6296. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:

#6295. November 2026: What’s in the sky this month?

Saturn is already visible as darkness falls; some challenging transits of its moons occur this month. Neptune is a binocular object close to Saturn, while Uranus is an easy target in Taurus. A Full Moon courses in front of the Pleiades in late November. Mars and Jupiter dominate the early-morning sky, and in the hour before dawn, look also for Venus and Mercury.

Neptune and Saturn are well placed for observation after sunset. They’re about 7° apart all month, with Neptune in southern Pisces and Saturn just across the border in Cetus. Only Saturn is visible to the naked eye, shining at magnitude 0.5. Neptune, at magnitude 7.7, requires binoculars to spot.

Swing 7×50 binoculars one field of view west of Saturn and look for a parallelogram of 4th- and 5th-magnitude stars: 27, 29, 30, and 33 Piscium. Neptune is within 3° northeast of 29 Psc all month. A waning gibbous Moon hangs 5° northwest of Neptune’s location on the 19th. The following night, Saturn is 6° south of the Moon.

As the month opens, Saturn is 24° high in the east an hour after sunset, reaching 50° by 9 p.m. local time following its opposition last month. It’s observable overnight and by the end of November sets by 2 a.m. local time. The rings are angled 6° to our line of sight and reveal their southern side. The planet spans 19″ through a telescope and the disk exhibits a pale yellowish hue. Atmospheric details are tricky to spot unless you have very good conditions.

Titan, Saturn’s brightest moon (magnitude 8.3), sits closest to the planet Nov. 8 and 24 (north), and Nov. 16 (south). Tenth-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea orbit closer in. Dione and Tethys transit Saturn’s disk this month. These transits and shadow transits are extremely challenging. They’re good targets for advanced observers with video imaging experience. Visit Astronomy.com for more details on the timing of their transits if you’d like to try for them.

Iapetus reaches greatest eastern elongation Nov. 10, when it stands 9.4′ east of Saturn. The moon’s darker face is turned earthward, dimming it to magnitude 11.9. It’s hard to find but as the month progresses, Iapetus brightens nearly a magnitude by the time it reaches inferior conjunction early on the 30th, 1.7′ due north of Saturn.

Uranus remains midway between Aldebaran and the Pleiades (M45). This position makes the planet easier to find than in previous years. It reaches opposition Nov. 25, visible from dusk to dawn. From 1.71 billion miles away, its disk spans 4″. Uranus shines at magnitude 5.6, within easy range of binoculars and potentially visible to the unaided eye from the darkest skies.

To find Uranus, look between Aldebaran and M45 for two stars: 37 and 39 Tauri (4.5° southeast of M45). Brighter 37 Tau glows at magnitude 4.4. On Nov. 1, Uranus is 1.6° southeast of 37 Tau, and by the end of November stands 1.5° due south of this star. Another star, some 2.7° southeast of 37 Tau, shines at magnitude 5.5. This is 43 Tau; in mid-November, Uranus is halfway between the two stars.

The Full Moon crosses the Pleiades early on Nov. 24, setting up a series of occultations of the northern part of the cluster just before dawn across the western half of the U.S. You’ll need a telescope — plan for higher magnification so you can place the brilliant Moon largely out of your field of view. Fifth-magnitude Celaeno is the first of the cluster’s brighter stars to be occulted, around 6 a.m. CST. Both visibility and timing heavily depend on your location, so set up at least 30 minutes before the event starts. You can download timings for the brightest occultations from 40 major North American cities from the International Occultation Timing Association at http://www.lunar-occultations.com/bobgraze/index.html.

Mars and Jupiter rise close together in Leo. They meet in a conjunction midmonth not far from Leo’s brightest star, Regulus. Mars rises first, soon after midnight on the 1st, followed by Jupiter about 30 minutes later. Jupiter shines at magnitude –2.0 and Mars at 0.8. They’re hard to miss.

On Nov. 1, Jupiter stands midway between Mars and Regulus, each just over 5° from its neighbor. A waning gibbous Moon sits in Cancer only a few degrees west of M44, the Beehive star cluster. On the 2nd, Mars and the Moon are 1.5° apart, and by the 3rd the Moon lies less than 2° from Regulus as they rise in the Midwest. Mars and Jupiter close in on each other, and by the 15th Mars is 1.2° due north of Jupiter.

Mars continues eastward, reaching a point 1.7° due north of Regulus on the 25th. By the 30th, Mars is just over 2° northeast of Regulus and is rejoined by the waning gibbous Moon, just southwest of Regulus. Through a telescope at the end of November, Mars has reached 8″ in diameter and its magnitude has increased to 0.4.

Home to the most visibly dynamic atmosphere in the solar system, Jupiter has a lot to offer through a telescope. The planet shows off a 36″-wide disk on the 1st, which grows to 39″ by the 30th. The hour before dawn can hold remarkable views if there is steady seeing. Look for the occasional appearance of the Great Red Spot.

Jupiter’s moons and their shadows often transit the planet or are eclipsed by it. Nov. 8 finds Io and Callisto transiting Jupiter’s disk along with Io’s shadow. Soon after, Europa exits from an occultation. East Coast observers will see the whole event; the Pacific Coast, only the latter half. It begins as Io’s shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb at 1:29 a.m. EST, followed 24 minutes later by the reappearance of Europa from behind Jupiter. Callisto’s transit begins at 2:07 a.m. EST. Io approaches the eastern limb, passing due north of Europa at 2:23 a.m. EST and beginning its transit 19 minutes later. Because of Io’s faster orbital speed compared with Callisto, it overtakes the larger moon within half an hour. Io’s shadow exits the disk at 3:45 a.m. EST, and Io itself ends its transit 74 minutes later. Callisto’s transit ends at 5:51 a.m. CST, as the sky is growing light in the Midwest.

Ganymede’s huge shadow crosses Jupiter’s face Nov. 11. The start of the transit at 12:27 a.m. EST is visible from the Eastern time zone; it ends at 4:03 a.m. EST, visible across the U.S. Ganymede begins to transit at 5:29 a.m. EST.

Ganymede, Europa, and Io orbit in resonance, so similar events recur, although they are not always observable. On Nov. 15, Io’s shadow begins a transit at 3:22 a.m. EST. Europa reappears at 4:27 a.m. EST, with Io close to the limb. They pass north-south just seven minutes later. Io’s transit begins at 4:36 a.m. EST. Its shadow leaves at 5:38 a.m. EST, and Io departs at 5:52 a.m. CST (in daylight for EST). Ganymede’s shadow transits again three days later, Nov. 18, from 4:25 a.m. EST to 6:01 a.m. MST (note the time zone change).

On Nov. 22, Io and its shadow are already transiting by the time Europa reappears. Io’s shadow transit starts at 5:15 a.m. EST; Io follows at 5:29 a.m. CST, with the sky very bright along the East Coast. Europa reappears at Jupiter’s eastern limb at 6:00 a.m. CST, as twilight begins in the Midwest and visible in darkness farther west.

To cap off the month, watch Ganymede reappear from behind Jupiter Nov. 29 at 5:53 a.m. CST (minutes before sunrise in EST), followed by Io’s shadow transit starting a few minutes later, at 6:08 a.m. CST. Io is due north of Ganymede at 6:49 a.m. CST, seen in twilight in the Midwest.

Mercury is at inferior conjunction Nov. 4, then moves into the morning sky. Northern Hemisphere observers gain good views in the second half of the month. Look for it Nov. 13, when it’s magnitude 0.5. An hour before sunrise, it is 4° high in the eastern sky, nearly 13° to the lower left of Venus. Swing binoculars toward Mercury to spot 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis 0.9° north of the planet.

Mercury reaches its greatest western elongation 20° from the Sun late on Nov. 20. The next morning, it shines at magnitude –0.5 and stands 7° high an hour before sunrise, easy to spot with a clear eastern horizon. Mercury displays a 62%-lit globe when viewed with a telescope, though it spans only 7″, so you’ll need steady air to see the phase. That phase grows to 84% by Nov. 30.

On Nov. 4, look for Venus 2° south of 1st-magnitude Spica, Virgo’s brightest star. A 25-day-old crescent Moon stands high above the pair. Three days later, on Nov. 7, Venus, Spica, and the Moon lie close together in the morning sky. Venus is 1.3° from Spica, with the waning crescent Moon about 2° below Venus, a stunning view in the brightening twilight. Venus rises about 100 minutes before the Sun and the trio is 11° high at 6 a.m. local time.

Venus reaches a stationary point Nov. 11. From the 10th to the 12th, Venus appears not to move in right ascension relative to Spica, as the planet slides due north to stand 1.2° due west of Spica on the 10th.

Check out Venus with a telescope. The bright planet becomes easier on the eyes as twilight grows, reducing the contrast. It’s already dazzling at magnitude –4.2 on the 1st, when its disk is 3% lit. By Nov. 15 it is 14% lit and magnitude –4.8, and reaches its greatest illuminated extent Nov. 29 at magnitude –4.9 and 27% lit. If you’re under Bortle 1 or 2 skies, can you see your shadow? Venus rises more than three hours before the Sun, so you’ll have a dark sky for an hour or so to check.

Much of the Moon’s history is encapsulated in one feature: the crater Schickard, way down in the lunar southwest. Protective measures are necessary to comfortably carry out this observation. Screw in a dark filter, mask off part of your scope’s aperture, or pump up the magnification to reduce the glare of an almost full lunar disk.

Start on the evening of the 21st, when the rays of sunlight strike the flooded crater at a glancing angle, highlighting the differences in height of the smaller features. This is an old crater, its rounded rim pounded down across the ages. The splatter of smaller craters across the smooth floor sport the classic sharp edges of relative youth. The western wall, steep at the instant of formation, slumped abruptly down into terraces that remain visible to this day. Shadows disappear over the next two evenings as the climbing Sun almost erases these features.

During the following nights, Schickard transforms into a two-faced striped crater, an unusual swath of lighter gray painted across the middle of this time-worn feature. The 130-mile-wide depression was carved out some 4 billion years ago as bombardment was ending. Lava soon welled up and covered its central peaks. Then the giant Orientale impact event to the west sprayed the whole region with lighter-hued material. A final surge of lava managed to cover the northern and southern portions, but did not rise enough to erase the lighter stripe.

This year’s annual Leonid meteor shower is active from Nov. 6 to 30 and peaks Nov. 17/18. A nine-day-old gibbous Moon sets right around midnight on this night, favoring the best time for meteor observing, which is after midnight. That’s when we’re on the leading hemisphere as Earth plows into the meteoroid stream.

Leo is also rising around local midnight and the radiant, located in the Sickle asterism, climbs to more than 60° in altitude by dawn. But don’t look at the radiant — meteors come head-on from that direction. Longer trails occur 40° to 60° away from Leo.

Rates are predicted to be 15 meteors per hour if the radiant were overhead. If you get more than a half-dozen per hour, you’re doing well. If you want a change, spend some time with Jupiter (also in Leo) through a telescope — Ganymede’s shadow is transiting the morning of the 18th.

The Leonids are known to be swift and some leave glowing, persistent trains, which are fascinating to experience. The shower is associated with Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which last reached perihelion in 1998.

Comet 10P/Tempel is floating halfway between Fomalhaut and Beta (β) Ceti. It’s about 10th magnitude, but historically has had post-perihelion outbursts, which could help it shine through the thicker air near the ground.

Meanwhile, Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS is higher and in a more interesting sky as darkness settles.

The Moon-free window closes after the 14th but reopens on the 27th. To see this 10th-magnitude fuzzy, a site well away from city lights is needed. Despite Earth’s increasing distance, the comet is sunward bound for perihelion Nov. 27, so its magnitude is fairly constant.

The short, broad fan should sport a circular green coma that looks great on images as it floats across the rich Milky Way north of Altair. At month’s end, Hartley-IRAS lies within 3° of the Coathanger asterism. Visually, a 4-inch scope can pull it in, but a larger one will show more detail, especially the sharp south flank where the solar wind pushes away the expelled dust in a bow shock.

Discovered in 1983, the comet returns every 21.5 years. Next month will be our last chance for a good look until two revolutions down the road, in 2069.

With five minutes of dark adapting, it’s easy to follow a main-belt asteroid along a retrograde curve. Saturn leads the way to 4 Vesta in the midevening sky — just drop down 9°, two binocular fields, to 25 Ceti, a magnitude 5.4 candle compared to the other nearby 8th- to 9th-magnitude stellar points. None of those will get confused with the brighter asteroid.

Use 25 Ceti and the more northerly 20 Ceti (closer to Saturn) to anchor a sketch or your memory. Watch a simple hockey stick pattern morph every three nights or so into a golf club, and then become a vertical line.

Spanning about 320 miles, Vesta is the second-largest body in the main belt. It was initially thought to be a chunk of the “missing” world astronomers expected between Mars and Jupiter. We now know it is an unfinished building block left over from the formation of the solar system, a rocky mantle surrounding an iron core.

The map below portrays the sky as seen near 35° north latitude. Located inside the border are the cardinal directions and their intermediate points. To find stars, hold the map overhead and orient it so one of the labels matches the direction you’re facing. The stars above the map’s horizon now match what’s in the sky.

The all-sky map shows how the sky looks at:

9 p.m. November 18 p.m. November 157 p.m. November 30

Martin Ratcliffe is a planetarium professional with Evans & Sutherland and enjoys observing from Salt Lake City. Alister Ling, who lives in Edmonton, Alberta, is a longtime watcher of the skies.

#6294. Microplastics can make toxic metals less dangerous, study finds

Scientists discover that sunlight-aged microplastics can transform toxic heavy metals into less harmful forms, revealing surprising new chemistry.

A recent study has found that, under the right conditions, microplastics can detoxify heavy metals.

The research was led by scientists at the Northeast Normal University. They found that polystyrene microplastics, after sitting in sunlight long enough, become chemically active in a specific and surprising way.

The particles start converting hexavalent chromium, a toxic industrial pollutant, into a far less dangerous form.

The researchers emphasize that this discovery does not make plastic pollution beneficial. Instead, it reveals an unexpected way that plastic can influence water chemistry.

It ultimately suggests that the standard picture of microplastics as passive, chemically inert contaminants is incomplete.

Chromium-6 can enter waterways through waste from metal finishing plants.

It dissolves readily in water, travels easily, and is toxic enough to be classified as a hazardous substance in China’s pollutant lists. It was also the contaminant at the center of the Erin Brockovich case in the United States.

In the environment, it exists alongside a much less dangerous cousin, chromium-3. This form tends to bind with other substances and become less mobile in water.

Getting from Cr(VI) to Cr(III) is a detoxification reaction, and natural organic matter in sunlit water already drives it to some degree.

The question is whether microplastics, which are accumulating in aquatic environments faster than anyone is cleaning them up, participate in that chemistry too.

The experiments showed that they can, particularly after prolonged exposure to ultraviolet light.

A fresh polystyrene microplastic is smooth, spherical, and unreactive. Leave it under UV light and the story changes.

The benzene rings that give polystyrene its structure absorb radiation and start breaking down.

Chemical bonds break, creating reactive molecules called free radicals, while oxygen-containing groups accumulate on the surface.

What builds up are environmentally persistent free radicals. These are reactive chemical species that, unusually, don’t vanish in milliseconds the way most radicals do.

They stay stable on the particle surface and remain available for electron transfer reactions.

The team aged polystyrene particles under UV light for 0, 6, 12, 24, 48 and 96 hours, then put them in chromium solutions.

Fresh particles reduced 38 percent of the Cr(VI) under UV irradiation. Ninety-six-hour-aged particles reduced nearly 90 percent.

Without UV light, the reaction barely happened at all.

To understand how the reaction works, the researchers ran parallel experiments under normal air and pure nitrogen.

The nitrogen blocked one of the two pathways, allowing the researchers to examine their contributions separately.

The direct route is the aged particle surface itself. Persistent free radicals transfer electrons straight to Cr(VI) molecules, reducing them on contact.

A chemical analysis confirmed that after the reaction, over 90 percent of the chromium on the particle surface had converted to Cr(III).

Removing oxygen reduced the reaction’s overall efficiency by about 20 percent, suggesting that direct electron transfer from the aged plastic surface plays an important role.

The second pathway involves chemicals released as the plastic breaks down.

Aging microplastics continuously shed dissolved organic matter into the surrounding water – fragments, additives, small aromatic breakdown products.

Under UV irradiation, this microplastic-derived dissolved organic matter generates superoxide radicals, which reduce Cr(VI) through a separate chemical chain.

That indirect pathway accounts for about 78 percent of what the dissolved fraction contributes on its own.

“Our findings suggest that microplastics are not simply passive carriers of pollutants. As they age under light exposure, they can become chemically active participants in environmental processes,” said senior author Jiunian Guan from the Northeast Normal University.

“Understanding these reactions is important for evaluating how plastic pollution may alter the behavior of heavy metals in aquatic ecosystems.”

Because the experiments took place under controlled laboratory conditions, researchers still need to determine whether similar reactions occur in natural waterways.

What happens at the pH, ionic strength and organic matter concentrations found in actual rivers is unknown.

Polystyrene’s aromatic structure makes it unusually susceptible to radical formation. Polyethylene and polypropylene, which are far more abundant in the real world, may behave differently.

Microplastics are already known to carry pollutants, break into even smaller particles, and provide surfaces where microorganisms can grow.

Now, researchers have shown that sunlight can also turn certain microplastics into active participants in chemical reactions that influence the behavior of toxic metals.

Whether these reactions make contaminated waterways safer or introduce additional environmental risks remains uncertain.

For now, the discovery offers another reminder that plastic pollution doesn’t simply sit in the environment.

It continues to change, interact with surrounding chemicals, and influence ecosystems in ways scientists are only beginning to understand.

The study is published in the journal Environmental and Biochemical Processes.

#6292. Birds that are supposed to be completely safe from extinction are actually losing their genetic diversity very quickly

Sixty-two common songbirds lost nearly half their genetic diversity in 50 years, and the most abundant species lost the most.

A songbird you can find on almost any hillside seems like it would be part of an abundant bird species with nothing to worry about in terms of population decline. In the Gaoligong Mountains of southwestern China, the bigger a songbird’s population, the faster it has been losing genetic diversity.

Across all 62 species the researchers compared, genetic diversity fell by an average of 43% to 49% in about 50 years. Every one of those species is listed as Least Concern, the lowest level of extinction risk.

Ri Liu, Feng Dong and their colleagues at the Kunming Institute of Zoology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, sequenced DNA from birds collected in the 1960s and 1970s. Then they compared it with DNA from birds sampled in the same mountains since 2000.

Only songbirds were sampled, and only in this one range. Birds have lost more genetic diversity than any other major animal group worldwide, so the team expects other animals here to be losing some too.

Genetic diversity is the sum of the small differences in DNA across a population. A species with a lot of it has more ways to adapt when conditions change.

The team measured that diversity two ways. Across a whole population, variation fell by an average of 48.8%, with species ranging from 18.1% to 77.2%.

Within a single bird, variation between the two copies of its genome fell by 42.9%, ranging from 21.8% to 80%. Not one of the 62 species held steady.

By either measure, that’s a far steeper fall than earlier work had suggested. A 2019 analysis of 91 species, which used short repeating stretches of DNA rather than whole genomes, estimated a loss of about 6% over roughly a century. The Gaoligong birds lost more than that every decade.

The losses do match the steepest theoretical forecast. A 2021 projection, built on the 73% drop in monitored vertebrate populations since 1970, predicted that genetic diversity could fall by more than half in 50 years.

The team then asked which traits went with the biggest losses. Several did. The unexpected one was the size of a species’ population worldwide.

In an interview with Earth.com, Dong said the direction of that result surprised the team. “We expected large populations to buffer against genetic erosion,” he said.

“Instead, we found the opposite: the more abundant a species was, the more genetic diversity it lost over the past five decades.”

The reason, in Dong’s account, is that a large population only stays genetically rich because birds keep moving and breeding across one continuous stretch of habitat.

Cut that habitat into pieces and a big population becomes many small, isolated ones, each losing variation on its own. “So the very species we assumed were safest turn out to be experiencing the heaviest genetic erosion,” Dong said.

Population size was a minor factor, though. It accounted for less than a tenth of the variation between species in how much they lost. And the population figures are global estimates, which may not match how many of each bird actually live in these mountains.

When people clear a forest, two things happen to the birds. Some habitat disappears outright, so fewer birds fit in what’s left, and what remains breaks into patches, so birds in one patch stop meeting birds in the next.

If the problem were outright loss, species that produce few young should suffer most. If it were isolation, strong fliers should suffer least, because they can still cross the gaps.

Strong fliers lost the least. The team scored each species’ ability to travel from its wing shape, and the better travelers lost less diversity per generation.

Clutch size, adult survival, and breeding elevation made no measurable difference. The only stronger predictor was the size of a species’ recent population decline.

Forest patches across the Gaoligong range have multiplied more than tenfold in recent decades, and the average patch is now under a tenth of its old size.

The worst breakup is at low to middle elevations, and that matters because rivers and steep terrain already isolate the range. The lowlands are the routes birds use to move between neighboring mountains.

Conservation planning “should treat connectivity – not just population size or protected area coverage – as a core conservation target,” Dong told Earth.com. In practice, he said, that means keeping and rebuilding low-elevation corridors between otherwise isolated populations.

The old birds came from a museum. The Kunming Natural History Museum of Zoology holds specimens collected across the Gaoligong Mountains in the 1960s and 1970s, and the team extracted DNA from them.

The modern DNA came from tissue samples taken between the 2000s and 2020s and stored in a tissue bank for wild species in Kunming.

Each species was represented by four or five birds per era. That’s a small number, and the team cites earlier work showing it is enough to capture how much variation a population holds.

The median collection year was 1973 for the old birds and 2022 for the new ones. For these small birds, 49 years is about 20 generations.

And those museum specimens were collected before forest fragmentation here intensified, so they show what the birds’ genomes looked like beforehand.

On the IUCN Red List, all 62 species are in the lowest-risk category, Least Concern, and Yunnan province’s own red list rates them about the same. The range itself already has formal protection.

The Gaoligong Mountains lie where the eastern Himalayas meet the mountains of Indo-Burma and southwest China, and they are part of a World Heritage site. They hold nearly a tenth of the world’s songbird species on about 0.02% of Earth’s land.

The losses are also larger than the world’s biodiversity agreement treats as tolerable. The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, set a 10% loss of genetic diversity as the limit for a species to keep its ability to evolve. The Gaoligong songbirds are already well past it.

Dong said conservation groups should stop treating “Least Concern” as a synonym for “genetically safe,” and that genetic monitoring should extend to common species rather than stopping at the rare ones.

The study ruled out mutation rate and elevation as explanations for the losses. It can’t say whether past hunting, climate change, or invasive species added to the damage alongside fragmentation.

The oldest birds in the comparison date from the 1960s, and the authors wrote that their figures may still understate the true historical loss.

The bigger open question is whether other animals and plants in the same mountains are losing diversity the way these songbirds are. The team expects they are, to a lesser degree, and hasn’t measured it.

Dong said genomic monitoring should start where the gap between a species’ official status and its actual genetic health is likely to be widest.

That means biodiversity hotspots with rapid recent fragmentation, and common, widespread species that go unmonitored because they aren’t listed as threatened. Low-elevation corridors in mountain hotspots, where connectivity loss is most severe, would be among the priority regions, he said.

Genetic indicators have been proposed for the global biodiversity framework, but they aren’t yet part of routine monitoring. The baseline for that monitoring, Dong said, already exists in museum collections like the one in Kunming.

The full study was published in the journal Science.
