#6291. Scientists discover hidden genetic clues that may help explain autism

Scientists have discovered overlooked DNA sequences that may help explain autism, revealing genetic changes missed by conventional testing.

Scientists have linked hundreds of genetic changes to autism, yet genetic testing can identify a cause in only about 15 percent of cases.

A new study suggests that some of the missing answers may be hiding in overlooked stretches of DNA.

Benjamin Blencowe of the University of Toronto‘s Donnelly Centre co-led the work with Quaid Morris of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Blencowe also works at King’s College London and the Francis Crick Institute.

The results are computer predictions checked against thousands of family genomes, and there’s no clinical test yet.

A gene isn’t read straight through. Cells copy it into a working message, then cut out some pieces and keep others, so one gene can make slightly different proteins in different tissues.

Some of these retained pieces, called microexons, are only three to 27 DNA letters long. Despite their tiny size, they can influence how proteins function in the brain.

Neurons use microexons much more than other cells do, and the same ones show up across vertebrates. Blencowe’s lab had already found that the brains of autistic people often use them incorrectly.

Mice with only one working copy of the main switch for them show autism-like behavior.

What nobody had was a full list. Most earlier searches used whole brain tissue, which can miss a fragment that only certain kinds of neurons use.

Guillermo Parada, a postdoctoral fellow in Blencowe’s London group and co-lead author, built a tool that scans RNA data, the working copies of genes, for microexon-shaped pieces.

He ran it over more than 100 terabytes of public data. He also included data from single cell nuclei, so a piece that only one kind of neuron uses could still show up.

The scan covered 4,790 human tissue samples and 47,380 single nuclei from the cortex.

It turned up 1,514 human microexons that no catalog had listed, and 292 of them are used differently in nerve cells than elsewhere. A matching search in mice found another 1,115.

Many of the new pieces, more often than known ones, insert a stop signal that makes the cell destroy the message instead of altering a protein. That gives neurons a way to turn a gene down.

The next question was what tells a neuron to keep a microexon included when editing the message for making a protein.

Parada and co-lead author Hannes Bretschneider worked with Morris to train a machine learning model on about 1,800 known neuronal microexons and 91,920 look-alike stretches that cells don’t use.

It reads 300 letters on each side of a fragment and scores how likely a neuron is to use it.

The team then changed every letter in those windows on the computer and recorded how the score changed.

The positions that mattered most matched the DNA that evolution has kept the same across vertebrates.

“What surprised me was that the sequences the model identified as important closely matched those conserved throughout vertebrate evolution,” Parada said.

The model also flagged a short pattern just upstream of some fragments as a signal to leave the piece out. In mouse cells, lowering the protein that binds there, QKI, made those microexons show up more often.

With their model in place, the researchers could investigate how genetic changes found in autistic people might disrupt the way neurons use microexons.

Working with Stephen Scherer and Brett Trost of The Hospital for Sick Children, they applied it to whole genomes from three large collections.

Two of them together held 2,666 pairs of siblings in which one is autistic and the other isn’t.

Rare changes, those seen in under 1 percent of reference genomes, had larger predicted effects than common ones. The same subset of microexons turned up as affected in all three collections.

“Using our model, we were able to show that rare genetic variants generally have the largest predicted effects on the splicing of neuronal microexons,” Blencowe said.

The results showed that autistic siblings carried more predicted genetic disruptions than their non-autistic siblings.

The three collections together held 25,132 people from 7,391 families, and in that group 72 of the genetic variants were tied to an autism diagnosis.

They turned up in 2.5 percent of the autistic participants and in none of their unaffected siblings.

Although these variants appeared in only a small percentage of autistic participants, they offered potential explanations for cases in which previous genetic testing had found no cause.

Of the people carrying those variants, 82 percent had no previously identified genetic cause.

The affected genes cluster at synapses, the junctions where neurons pass signals, and several were already on autism gene lists.

Nearly all of this is prediction. The team tested a few of the flagged variants in lab-grown human neurons, and those did change how the microexon was used.

A flagged variant isn’t a diagnosis, either. More than a third of everyone in the study, autistic or not, carries at least one change predicted to affect a microexon. The ones tied to autism were the rare few with large predicted effects.

The model learned its rules from known microexons, and only 59 of the new human pieces followed them, so others may obey a code it doesn’t yet have.

And only 12 percent of the new brain-specific human pieces have a clear match in mice, which limits what mouse experiments can check.

How a disrupted microexon changes the proteins a neuron builds is the open question.

“In terms of future work, it will be important to understand how disrupted microexons affect interactions between proteins that are important for nervous system development and function,” Blencowe said.

The team has published its prediction for every variant it scored, so other groups can run new genomes against it.

That includes genomes from people with schizophrenia or epilepsy, where microexons may also be disrupted.

The findings suggest that some of autism’s missing genetic explanations may lie not within genes themselves, but in overlooked DNA sequences that help determine how those genes are used.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

October 31: Glimpse the ghostly Phantom Galaxy

Daylight saving time ends at 2 A.M. local daylight time this morning, when clocks fall back one hour to 1 A.M. local standard time.

Early this morning, the waning gibbous Moon is in Cancer, just west of the naked-eye Beehive Cluster (M44). The cluster might be hard to catch today without optical aid due to the nearby light of our satellite, but should show up nicely in binoculars or even your telescope’s finder scope. Its stars are spread so widely — across nearly 100’ of sky — that observing them through a telescope at higher magnification only shows the cluster’s central regions.

East of the Moon, Mars and Jupiter shine brightly in western Leo, to the upper right of the bright star Regulus. Brighter Jupiter should be particularly easy to spot, located halfway between the Red Planet and the blue-white star.

The Moon will reach Last Quarter phase this afternoon at 3:28 P.M. EST.

#6289. Why people with ADHD struggle to stop watching short videos

In a survey of 302 adults, people with ADHD more often lost track of time while using short-video apps, and felt regret and guilt afterward.

A short-video feed never ends. Swipe past one clip on TikTok, Instagram Reels or YouTube Shorts and the next one is already playing, chosen to match what you’ve watched before.

In a survey of 302 adults, people with ADHD said those picks matched what they’d opened the app for just as well as they did for people without ADHD.

What set them apart was everything else: more trouble stopping, more lost time, and more regret once the app was closed.

The problem, the researchers wrote, isn’t bad recommendations. It’s a feed with no built-in place to stop.

The work comes from Elisabeth Lex and colleagues at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz) in Austria.

The research was released as a preprint ahead of ASSETS 2026, a computing accessibility conference held in Portugal in late October.

Earlier studies have tied heavy social media use and short-video habits to attention problems, but few have put numbers on how these feeds affect people who have ADHD.

The team recruited 302 adults through Prolific, a website that pays people to take part in research.

Of those 150 participants, 65 reported a formal ADHD diagnosis, while 85 identified themselves as having ADHD. This allowed the researchers to compare responses between the two groups

Splitting the ADHD group this way let the team check whether a formal diagnosis changed the answers. Participants ranged from young adults to people in their 70s.

YouTube Shorts was the most popular app, ahead of Instagram Reels and TikTok.

Each person rated 15 statements about their own viewing on a scale of 1 to 7, such as “Once I start watching short-content videos, I find it difficult to stop.”

The whole questionnaire took a typical participant under five minutes.

Participants with ADHD agreed more strongly that they often watched longer than they meant to and found it hard to stop once they’d started.

Asked how hard it was to pull away from the feed, the typical person with ADHD answered 5 on the 7-point scale. The typical person without it answered 3.

People with ADHD were also more likely to say they lost track of time while watching. Researchers call that time blindness – losing the sense of how many minutes have gone by.

Lex’s team named the pattern the engagement trap.

“By the ‘engagement trap,’ we mean a situation in which (video) recommendations are, on the one hand, perceived as highly relevant, but, on the other hand, people find it very difficult to tear themselves away from the screen and consciously control their own behavior,” Lex said.

The differences continued after people closed the app. Participants with ADHD more often said they regretted the time they’d spent, felt it hadn’t been valuable, and had put off things they meant to do.

They also reported lower mood after a long session than before it, and more guilt.

The biggest gap of all was frustration with their own difficulty disengaging. Even so, the differences were modest – small to medium by standard statistical yardsticks.

The team found no statistically reliable difference between people whose ADHD had been diagnosed by a doctor and people who identified it themselves.

“Our findings show that recommender systems optimized for engagement place a disproportionate emotional and behavioral burden on people with ADHD,” Lex explained.

Earlier research from a team led by Thomas Mildner found that people with ADHD were better than others at spotting manipulative design on social media.

Lex’s team wrote that a short-video feed works differently. There’s no deceptive visual element to spot, only a stream with no end.

With nothing to tell a viewer when to quit, stopping depends on self-control and a sense of how much time has passed. Those are the same abilities ADHD tends to strain, the authors wrote.

This may contribute to hyperfocus, a state of intense concentration that can make it difficult to disengage without an outside cue.

The survey also described seven possible app features, none of them built yet. They ranged from a gentle usage reminder to a mode that turns off the feed entirely.

None of them would require people to step away from the apps altogether.

People in every group liked the ideas, giving a typical rating of 5 on the 7-point scale. A fixed number of videos per session and an enforced break after a set time scored highest.

“To redress this imbalance, we must move away from optimization focused purely on engagement towards human-centered design practices that explicitly support users’ sense of time and their intentional control,” Lex said.

Everyone reported on their own habits from memory, and no one’s screen time was measured.

People with ADHD may also experience more guilt about scrolling, potentially influencing how negatively they describe their viewing habits.

The researchers did not independently verify ADHD diagnoses or ask about medication use, which may have influenced participants’ ability to stop watching.

The authors want future studies to compare how long people think they watched with how long they really did, using recorded watch time.

Whether a fixed video limit or a forced break actually cuts viewing time will take working versions of those features to find out.

The full study has not been published in a journal yet and is available as a preprint on arXiv.

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

#6287. Late-night snacking may be putting your liver at risk

A study of nearly 200,000 people links late-night eating to higher risks of fatty liver disease and cirrhosis, even after accounting for diet and weight.

When people think about the health effects of late-night snacking, they usually focus on calories. But new research suggests that when you eat may matter just as much.

Now, a 16-year study involving nearly 200,000 nurses and other health professionals has linked late-night eating to an increased risk of fatty liver disease.

People who said they ate after dinner or after bedtime went on to develop fatty liver disease and cirrhosis more often than people who didn’t.

That gap stayed after weight, diet quality and alcohol were taken into account. The authors can’t say the late eating caused the damage.

What they can say is that meal timing was linked to liver disease on its own, apart from how much or how well people ate.

Robert Wilechansky, a liver specialist at Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), led the analysis with colleagues at OHSU and Massachusetts General Hospital.

Andrew McHill, a sleep and circadian physiologist at OHSU who studies the body clock, was a co-author of the study.

In an interview with Earth.com, McHill said the point of the study is broader than any one snack.

“It is not only what or how much you eat, but also the timing of when you eat that matters for your health,” he noted.

The data came from three long-running American health surveys.

These were the Nurses’ Health Study, its younger sister study, and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study.

Together they contributed 199,155 people with no liver disease at the start. Most were women and the median age was 59. At the start, 22 percent had obesity and 5 percent had diabetes.

Every two to four years, participants reported what they ate and when.

Anyone who said they usually ate after dinner or after bedtime counted as a late-night eater. About 29 percent of the participants were in this category.

The surveys also asked whether people skipped breakfast and how many times a day they ate.

Participants also reported whether a doctor had diagnosed them with liver disease during follow-up surveys.

Over a median of 16 years, 4,492 people developed fatty liver disease, in which fat builds up in liver cells. Another 315 developed cirrhosis, the scarring that follows years of damage.

Late-night eaters developed fatty liver disease at a rate 36 percent higher than everyone else, and cirrhosis at a rate 28 percent higher.

Those figures already account for age, body mass index, daily calories, diabetes, cholesterol, smoking, exercise, alcohol and a standard score of diet quality.

Skipping breakfast and eating fewer or more meals a day looked risky at first. Those links disappeared once the same factors were counted, and only the late eating survived.

When the team also accounted for night-shift work, the cirrhosis link grew stronger rather than weaker, to 49 percent higher.

Setting aside anyone diagnosed in the first four years barely moved the numbers either, which argues against disease that was already under way.

McHill told Earth.com the team had expected a link, but not one that size.

“I think we were somewhat surprised by the strength of the relationship,” he said, especially after accounting for body weight, poor diet and drinking.

The liver has its own internal clock. Earlier research has shown that the timing of meals influences how the liver processes nutrients.

“We know the liver is very much in tune with the body’s circadian rhythms,” Wilechansky said.

Eating most of the day’s calories in the evening has been linked to obesity and poorer metabolic health.

A 2026 study found that in people with fatty liver disease, the liver was more resistant to insulin at night than in people with obesity alone.

McHill said eating when the body clock is promoting sleep makes the body less efficient at processing food.

He added that animal studies have shown the liver to be one of the organs most sensitive to a mismatch between eating and sleeping.

Asked by Earth.com what a habitual late snacker should take from this, McHill drew a line between a treat and a habit.

A dessert now and then is unlikely to hurt the liver, he said. A nightly habit, kept up over years, may carry health risks that a person doesn’t notice.

The people in these surveys were mostly white, well-educated health workers. They had lower rates of obesity and diabetes than the country as a whole, and lower rates of liver disease too.

The researchers had no liver scans or blood tests to confirm the diagnoses or assess how severe the disease had become.

Eating times were asked about in only a few survey rounds, so some late eaters were probably counted as early ones.

The authors said that kind of error tends to shrink a real link rather than invent one.

Wilechansky said only a small fraction of people with fatty liver disease go on to serious forms such as cirrhosis.

Whether moving dinner earlier would change anyone’s liver is the question the surveys can’t answer.

That is the next study. McHill said his team is recruiting people for a trial that will record meal times with photographic food diaries and track the liver with hospital imaging.

The trial could help answer a question that years of observational research cannot: Can changing when we eat actually protect the liver?

The full study was published in the journal Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology.

#6285. This Halloween, amateur astronomers may be in for a dwarf planet treat

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Astronomers also have their eyes on objects near Neptune that may be solar system building blocks

This 3-D view of the solar system shows the orbit of the dwarf planet candidate 2026 ED138 in the location it held on May 8, 2026. It is among the largest and brightest objects discovered beyond Pluto, but had gone unnoticed until now.

NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/R. Proctor

The outer solar system is yielding its secrets to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Less than five months into the observatory’s decade-long survey of the sky, a potential new dwarf planet has already popped up in its data, astronomers reported this week at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division of Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Another team reported a handful of new Neptune Trojans, icy objects that share an orbit with Neptune, at the meeting and in the Astrophysical Journal Letters. The findings are filling in astronomers’ picture of the Kuiper Belt at the solar system’s frigid fringes.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“It feels a little bit like we’re replicating the 1800s and early 1900s, discovering what the solar system even looks like in general,” says Sam Deen, an amateur astronomer based in Simi Valley, Calif. “We’re finding out what there even is in the first place that makes up most of the Kuiper Belt.”

Perched on a mountaintop in Chile, the Vera Rubin Observatory is on a mission to map the entire southern sky every couple of nights, searching for faint and fast-moving cosmic objects. The observatory took its first images in June 2025 and officially began a decade-long survey in June 2026.

Even before the official survey started, Rubin had detected the motion of an object orbiting billions of kilometers beyond Pluto. Rubin observed the object 30 times on 20 nights from March 4 to July 11. But no one knew it was there until October 13, when astrophysicist Matt Holman of the Smithsonian Astronomical Observatory in Cambridge, Mass., ran a search for moving dots of light in the data.

The object, called 2026 ED138, appeared to be about 47 times as far from Earth as Earth is from the sun. Its brightness suggests it’s between 600 and 1,500 kilometers wide, potentially as large as other dwarf planets like Ceres and Makemake. That’s probably big enough to be spherical, making it a dwarf planet.

“It’s really big. It’s damn huge,” Deen says. “No matter what you call it, it’s still the biggest thing we’ve found in the entire solar system in 19 years.”

When Holman realized what he had found, he was thrilled but doubtful. “It’s quite an exciting thing,” Holman said in a news briefing at the meeting on October 27. “But one of the things that you need to do when you discover something potentially of this size is to try to verify that it’s true.”

Holman and colleagues were able to find observations of the same object in archived data from the Dark Energy Camera, located on an adjacent mountaintop in Chile, taken in 2016.

Deen was able to trace it back even farther, to photographic plates taken as part of a sky survey at Palomar Observatory in California in 1954. Other amateur astronomers independently found the same sightings.

“They took an image from Palomar in 1954, and another about half an hour after the first one, that both by pure chance happen to point at where ED138 is,” Deen says. “And it’s really obvious. If you know it’s supposed to be there, it’s not particularly faint.”

So why didn’t anybody notice it until now? It’s partly because ED138 practically crawls across the sky, orbiting the sun once every 280 years. It was also moving against a dense background of Milky Way stars, where it blended in.

By combining observations spanning decades, astronomers can calculate the object’s orbit with more precision.

Deen is hoping to observe the potential new dwarf planet pass in front of a distant star on Halloween. That sort of observation, called an occultation, can help reveal more details of the putative dwarf planet’s size and shape, and even whether it has moons or rings. Usually, it takes years to understand an object’s orbit well enough to predict an occultation, Deen says. “Getting to do it immediately is like being a kid in a candy shop, really.”

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

Caltech, Space Telescope Science Institute

A crop of newly spotted Neptune Trojans were masked by the Milky Way, too. These asteroids gather in the same orbit as Neptune, but offset from the planet at 60 degrees. Astronomers think they were some of the original building blocks of the solar system and contain an ancient record of planetary formation and evolution.

Other planets have Trojans, too. Jupiter has thousands. Astronomers think Neptune has many more, but so far they have seen only 30 in the cluster of space objects that orbit ahead of Neptune, and just two in the cluster behind it.

“We would expect these [groups of Trojans] to be symmetric in numbers, so you have to get more than two,” planetary scientist Meg Schwamb said in a news conference at the meeting on October 28.

The trailing cloud happened to have been moving in front of the Milky Way from the perspective of Earth for the last 15 years. Spotting individual Trojans against that crowded background was “like finding a needle in a sequined dress,” said Schwamb, of Queens University Belfast in Northern Ireland.

Schwamb and colleagues examined Vera Rubin data taken from the commissioning phase — the period when engineers were testing the telescope. In this early data haul, the team found two more trailing Trojans, plus one candidate. They seem to be similar in composition to the leading ones, which matches theories of how the solar system formed.

“It just kind of got lucky,” Schwamb said. “These objects photobombed the commissioning survey.”

“This is really the appetizer for what Rubin Observatory is going to do in its mission for the next ten years,” she added. “There’s hundreds more of these objects likely to be found.”

Some of the excitement about these discoveries is dampened by fears of losing observations to bright satellites crisscrossing the telescope’s field of view, says astronomer Sam Lawler of the University of Regina in Canada.

“I have to put in the constant downer of how the increasing numbers of satellites will make these discoveries harder,” Lawler says. “There are one hundred new satellites launching every week, and they keep getting bigger and brighter. These discoveries will be hindered by that.”

But even with the satellites, Lawler anticipates many more cool discoveries from Rubin.

“Just finding a dwarf planet so quickly, maybe we’ll find something even bigger,” she says. “There could be something the size of Mars out there. And then we’d have the whole planet debate all over again. It would be fun.”

#6283. What Happens If Your Passport Expires While You're Abroad?

Most countries don't allow international travelers to enter their territory unless they have at least six months left before their passport expires. That might sound like an unnecessary ask for a week-long vacation, but the rule is in place for good reason.

That's because if you do find yourself in a scenario when your passport expires while you're abroad—say due to an unexpected medical issue or trip delay, for example—you could be facing a major bureaucratic headache.

However, although it might feel like a crisis, having your passport lapse while traveling is not the end of the world. There are procedures that travelers can follow to obtain a renewed document and get their trip back on track. Here’s a look at what happens if your passport expires while you’re abroad.

Many countries do not allow international tourists to visit unless they have a certain amount of validity left on their passport. A common rule of thumb that many nations observe is the six month rule: there must be at least six months before your passport expires in order to enter the country.

In some countries, including many popular destinations in the EU, your passport is required to be valid for an additional three months after your intended departure date. Before you board an international flight, airlines will verify your passport expiration and usually will not let you board the plane if your passport doesn’t meet the validity requirements. It's important to note that some airlines and cruise lines might have their own passport validity policies that differ from the country's official requirements, so be sure to check both.

Sometimes, it’s possible to enter a different country and stay past your passport’s expiration date. If that's the case, the protocol you’ll need to follow is similar to when a passport is lost or stolen abroad.

First, you’ll need to contact the nearest US embassy or consulate for assistance. If you’re not sure where the nearest embassy or consulate might be, you can use the search tool on the State Department’s website. You’ll need to then visit the embassy or consulate location in person in order to have them issue you a new passport. Keep in mind this could mean you need to travel to a different city within the country you’re visiting.

When you arrive, you’ll essentially need to apply for a new passport. That means you’ll need to bring:

“Even if you cannot present all these documents, consular staff will do their best to help you get a new passport quickly,” the State Department’s site says.

US citizens abroad who have urgent travel plans are usually issued an emergency passport, which is valid for up to one year. However, it’s also possible to get a full-validity passport that doesn’t expire for 10 years. It will depend on the specifics of your situation.

Replacement passports are usually issued by the next business day, according to the State Department.

If you’re a US citizen living overseas for an extended period of time, you might qualify for routine passport renewal by mail through the nearest US embassy or consulate. Processing times for renewal by mail are usually about four to six weeks, not including shipping time. Visit the website of the local embassy or consulate in your area and follow their instructions for passport renewal.

This Roman glass cup can change from jade green to ruby red, and it features a mythical king who tried to banish Dionysus.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Roman-era Lycurgus Cup has a color-changing effect depending on the light source.

The Lycurgus Cup is a Roman-era glass goblet that changes color from jade green to ruby red depending on if a light is shining on its front or back. But experts are unsure where the cup was found, where it was made, or whether the glassblower who made it created the color-changing effect on purpose.

In 1958, the British Museum acquired the cup from the Rothschild banking family, which had owned the artifact since the mid-19th century. Known colloquially as the Lycurgus Cup for its depiction of the mythical king who angered the god Dionysus, the glass is about 6.3 inches (15.9 centimeters) tall and weighs around 1.6 pounds (700 grams).

The glass is a remarkably well-preserved example of a Roman "cage-cup," according to a 1959 study of the artifact by archaeologists D. B. Harden and Jocelyn Toynbee. Only a handful of cage-cups still exist, and experts believe the goblets were made by cutting and grinding decoration into thick glass. Because small bridges were left to ensure the decoration remained on the glass, the overall effect is like a cage. Harden and Toynbee estimated that the Lycurgus Cup was manufactured in the fourth century, likely in Italy, but they noted that the bronze frame that forms the stem and rim of the goblet is probably a 19th-century addition.

Depicted on the cup is the myth of the punishment of Lycurgus, king of the Thracian tribe called the Edoni (also called the Edonians). Lycurgus did not approve of the worship of Dionysus and banished the god into the sea with an ax. But one of Dionysus' priestesses, Ambrosia, decided to fight Lycurgus. Ambrosia changed herself into a vine and wound herself around Lycurgus, who was unable to escape. The other priestesses thronged around them and tormented Lycurgus. Given that Dionysus was a god of wine and merriment, the depiction of Lycurgus' punishment may have been particularly appropriate for this goblet. Additionally, the change in color from green to red may have been meant to mimic the ripening of grapes on the vine.

Color-changing cups, also called dichroic cups, were mentioned in ancient Roman historical records. For example, a second-century letter possibly penned by Emperor Hadrian to his brother-in-law mentions a gift of two dichroic cups to use during banquets. But very few fragments of this mysterious type of glass survive today, a 2007 study noted.

For decades, experts have been working out how ancient Romans produced dichroic cups, and some have even replicated the Lycurgus Cup's color-changing effect. A 1963 study confirmed that the key seems to be the addition of microscopic nanoparticles of gold and silver during glassblowing that produce the appearance of milky-green glass when lit from the front and nearly translucent red glass when lit from behind. The metal nanoparticles are smaller than grains of sand and interact with light, creating the perception of a color change.

A replica of dichroic glass made by Corning Glassworks in the 1960s went from green to amethyst in the light, the 2007 study reported, and in 2020, researchers included silver and gold nanoparticles in 3D printing to replicate the color-changing properties of the glass.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

More recently, experts at the University of Sheffield in the U.K. reproduced the dichroic glass by reverse-engineering the "recipe" from the original Lycurgus Cup. The team then commissioned a glass artist to create a Lycurgus-inspired design from the replica.

But because so few examples of dichroic glass exist, experts are still unsure whether Roman artisans created the color-changing effect on purpose or whether traces of gold, which would have been available in an ancient craft studio, slipped into the molten glass and made a rare and unusual material that mystified even the most skilled glassblowers.

#6281. Melting permafrost has birthed a new type of large landslide

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Wildfires and water underneath the ground could dislodge large chunks of frozen earth

In 2018, an immense landslide in Canada’s Mackenzie Valley dammed the Redstone River (shown) and created a 3.5-kilometer-long lake. Researchers say the event was a new type of large landslide called a permafrost detachment slide.

In 2018, a strange and enormous landslide occurred in Canada’s Northwest Territories. A slab of earth roughly equivalent in volume to seven Great Pyramids of Giza suddenly began sliding downhill, leaving behind a barren scar in the forested landscape. But what puzzled scientists was that the slide had initiated in frozen ground that had been glued in place for years.

An analysis of the event reveals that it represents a new class of catastrophic landslides called permafrost detachment slides, researchers report in the Sept. 28 Geophysical Research Letters. The slides may be set in motion by wildfires that occurred decades earlier, destabilizing the ground and opening cracks through which water infiltrated deep underground. Over time, that water may have thawed the frozen layer from below, eventually unleashing the entire frozen layer in a catastrophic slide.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Large landslides don’t normally mobilize so much still-frozen material, and when they do begin in thawing layers they usually move slowly, says Dmitry Nicolsky, a geophysicist studying permafrost at the University of Alaska Fairbanks who was not involved in the study. But he says this new research suggests scientists need to better study what’s occurring beneath the surface in permafrost regions, because “we don’t know how [the ground] will move — it might go slowly or it might go catastrophically.”

The inspiration for the research manifested in 2019, when permafrost geologist Joseph Young, based at the University of Alberta in Edmonton, Canada, at the time, was helicoptering to a field site in the Northwest Territories to assist a colleague’s research. In some of the valleys out there, the slopes were “just collapsing with landslides everywhere,” says Young, who is now at an engineering firm in Edmonton. That was surprising because they were in an area where the permafrost — ground that has been frozen for at least two consecutive years — shouldn’t have been thawing much.

Once on the ground, more puzzling details emerged. “Traditionally with permafrost, it melts from the top down, and that releases this slurry of muddy material,” Young says. But at some of the landslide sites, large blocks of still-frozen ground seemed to have been moved hundreds of meters, he says.

Young and his colleagues studied two of the largest slides in the region that had moved big chunks of permafrost. These were the 2018 slide, which mobilized 18 million cubic meters of earth and dammed the Redstone River, and another event in 2017 that moved 4.5 million cubic meters of material.

Field observations revealed that both events had initiated along flat sliding surfaces roughly 20 meters underground, where the permafrost layer’s base was identified. Meanwhile, satellite observations showed that the ground at both sites had been gradually moving meters each year for decades.

Young and his colleagues hypothesized that climate warming and wildfire had somehow played a role in causing the slides. They set up instruments nearby that tracked ground temperature from 2020 to 2022, focusing on spots either with undisturbed forest or where wildfire had burned about 25 years earlier.

They then plugged that data into computer simulations to estimate how the ground would have evolved in the decades after a fire. Based on the results, the researchers concluded that wildfire and extreme summer temperatures can warm and weaken the frozen ground surface, causing it to start creeping and form tension cracks. As these cracks grow, water can penetrate deeper into the frozen ground and eventually reach beneath the permafrost layer, causing it to thaw from below and eventually detach.

More than 150 other slides in the region, identified via satellite observations, may also have been permafrost detachment slides, Young says. This could occur wherever there’s a relatively thin and warm permafrost layer and a rapid warming event to set things in motion, he says.

Permafrost is thawing in cold regions around the world, and these huge slides are very visual manifestations of that, Young says. “This is a direct reality of a changing climate.”

#6280. What is the physical size of a 1-billion-solar-mass black hole compared to the Sun?

When a supermassive black hole is measured as 1 billion solar masses, what would be its actual physical size relative to the size of our Sun?

The size of a black hole is generally taken to be the size of its event horizon. The event horizon is a mathematical boundary around the black hole that marks the “point of no return” — anything that crosses this boundary is trapped inside and becomes part of the black hole forever.

The size of the event horizon can be calculated from Einstein’s field equations, and it depends on (1) the mass of the black hole, and (2) how fast the black hole is spinning. For a nonspinning black hole that has the same mass as our Sun, the radius of the event horizon (also called the Schwarzschild radius) would be about 1.8 miles (3 kilometers). A nonspinning supermassive black hole that is a billion times more massive than our Sun would have an event horizon radius that is a billion times larger, or 1.8 billion miles (3 billion km). This is 4,300 times larger than the radius of the Sun, or about the typical distance between the Sun and Uranus. However, if a billion-solar-mass black hole is spinning very rapidly, then the radius of the event horizon would shrink by about 30% (to around 1.3 billion miles or 2 billion km) because of the way the black hole distorts and drags space around it.

It is important to note, however, that while the event horizon is considered the outer boundary of the black hole, the mass inside the black hole has likely collapsed into a much smaller size under its own self-gravity, often referred to as a singularity. But we don’t actually know if the mass has collapsed into an infinitely small point in space, and, unfortunately, we can’t really say more than that because our understanding of physics breaks down under the extreme conditions that are present inside a black hole. So we use the event horizon as a convenient reference for the black hole’s size, because everything inside the event horizon is part of the black hole.

Misty BentzProfessor of Physics and Astronomy, Georgia State University, Atlanta

#6279. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Monday, November 2The Moon slides 1.1° south of Mars at 9 A.M. EST, then passes 0.5° south of Jupiter at 6 P.M. EST. Some parts of the world will see these planets disappear behind the Moon, although this is not visible from North America. Instead, we’ll focus on the trio’s appearance before this in the early-morning sky, where they dominate in the hours before sunrise.

By 5 A.M. local time, western Leo is more than 50° high in the southeast. The Moon lies just to Mars’ upper right, roughly 1.5° southwest of the Red Planet’s position and 6.3° west-northwest of Jupiter.

This view offers a great opportunity to see just how far the Moon travels through our sky in a day. By tomorrow morning at the same time, Luna will have moved some 14° to the east, passing close to Regulus and standing southeast of the star in the early-morning sky at the same time.

Sunrise: 6:30 A.M.Sunset: 4:56 P.M.Moonrise: —Moonset: 1:41 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (36%)

Tuesday, November 3The Moon now passes 0.8° south of the bright star Regulus in Leo at 4 A.M. EST. Some regions of the world will see our satellite pass in front of Regulus in an occultation, but again, the event is not visible from North America.

The pair rises together shortly after midnight on the 2nd. By 5 A.M. local time on the 3rd, the Moon-star pair is nearly 50° high in the southeast. The waning Moon has shrunk from roughly 43% lit yesterday morning to 33% lit today. It is just under a week from New phase, which occurs on the 9th.

Sunrise: 6:31 A.M.Sunset: 4:55 P.M.Moonrise: 12:34 A.M.Moonset: 2:07 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (26%)

Wednesday, November 4Venus sits 2° south of Virgo’s brightest star, Spica, in the early-morning sky. The pair is joined by a lovely crescent Moon just over 20% lit, high above them in Leo.

Sunrise: 6:32 A.M.Sunset: 4:54 P.M.Moonrise: 1:44 A.M.Moonset: 2:30 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (17%)

Sunrise: 6:34 A.M.Sunset: 4:53 P.M.Moonrise: 2:50 A.M.Moonset: 2:53 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (10%)

Sunrise: 6:35 A.M.Sunset: 4:52 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 A.M.Moonset: 3:16 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

Live Science spoke with psychiatrist Anand Kumar about the next edition of the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual Of Mental Disorders", which will include biological factors like genetics in studying and diagnosing psychiatric conditions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For decades, psychiatrists and other mental health professionals have used the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders," or DSM, to diagnose patients with conditions such as major depression, anorexia and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To reach diagnoses, mental health practitioners identify symptoms via interview, case history, questionnaire, or observation to paint a clinical picture.

But for the next version of this "psychiatry bible", the DSM-6, scientists are planning to add other factors into the diagnostic criteria.

Dr. Anand Kumar, a psychiatrist who served for two years on the DSM Strategy Committee, says one of the most important potential changes is the introduction of biological factors into the diagnostic framework. While Kumar, the head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois Chicago, no longer serves on the committee, he was influential in discussions about how biology could be incorporated into the DSM-6. Some of these biological factors include data from genome-wide association studies of hundreds or thousands of genes that each increase the risk of a mental disorder by a tiny amount. Other biological factors include signs of inflammation or immune-system dysfunction that may show up in blood tests or brain scans.

Live Science spoke to Kumar about how this update to the DSM could change the way mental disorders are understood and potentially help improve treatment.

Dr. Kumar is the Lizzie Gilman Professor and Head of the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Illinois at Chicago. Dr. Kumar's research focuses on late-life depression and mental disorders of the elderly, including Alzheimer's disease. He has served as Treasurer, Program Committee Chair, and President of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry (2004-2005). Dr. Kumar is Associate Editor of the American Journal for Geriatric Psychiatry and has served as reviewer for numerous NIH review committees.

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry: How is the DSM-6 going to be different from the DSM-5?

Anand Kumar: Up to this point, the distinctions between the different major groups — who has clinical depression, or what we call major depression; who has an eating disorder; who has PTSD, etc. — have been based exclusively on clinical grounds: You meet certain criteria, and you fall into this category. If you meet some other criteria, you fall into another category.

An attempt that's being made now, one of the major attempts for the next DSM, is to introduce biological factors into the manual.

The idea is not new. It's been discussed in the past, but it was difficult to get a consensus on what goes in and what should not go in. That's still going to be tricky, but at least there's a broad acknowledgement that the time is ready to start introducing biology into the DSM.

It's very likely that, at the end of it, there will be meaningful changes in a positive kind of way. It's not going to make everyone happy. There are going to be gaps, but the idea is to incrementally improve this and make it more modern as we go along.

KHC: What sort of biological markers have you seen that we can actually correlate with these disorders?

AK: What the committee is doing is taking a more nuanced approach. Outside the realm of Alzheimer's disease, which I'll get into in a minute, there are no clear-cut diagnostic biomarkers — meaning no blood tests or brain scans that you can look at and say, "This person has a diagnosis of depression," or "This person has PTSD," or "This person has schizophrenia."

The committee talked about how, in addition to biological biomarkers, there's a concept of biological factors. What I mean by that is biological pathways and mechanisms that have a role in the development of a particular disorder, but the findings have not crystallized into a laboratory test.

For example, immunology — the study of the body's response to a variety of stresses, including infections and others — has been shown to be impactful in about 30% of cases of major depression. Yet there is no single biological laboratory test that is currently available that can be used [to diagnose immune-mediated depression] in clinical practice. So these come under the category of what we call biological factors.

In the Alzheimer's disease field there are clear-cut biomarkers. There are now blood tests for proteins called tau and amyloid that have been approved by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] as biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease. Meaning, if you have a clinical picture and a mental-status exam consistent with intellectual decline, you must have a positive biomarker test to be categorized as having definitive Alzheimer's disease.

And that's new. Ten or 15 years back, there were brain scans, and if you did a lumbar puncture, you could find these proteins in the spinal fluid. But those are invasive. Now you actually have a blood test.

A neuron, in blue, is surrounded by a plaque of amyloid-beta protein, in yellow, which causes the symptoms of Alzheimer's disease. Tests can be used to detect biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease.

But that degree of precision, for lack of a better term, is not available in the other branches of psychiatry. Nonetheless, there are clues that other pathways and mechanisms are involved.

I mentioned immunology as one. Another big elephant in the room is genetics.

Most people think of genetics as an abnormal gene or a mutation — meaning a gene switches or changes and confers increased risk — as one mutation causing one disease. That's how most people in the general public think about mutations: They cause disease.

But when you get into complex diseases like heart disease and diabetes, there are multiple genes involved. And diseases may or may not be caused by a gene. Abnormal genes may or may not cause the disease, but they increase risk.

With mental disorders, the situation becomes immensely more complicated. It's not just a few genes here and there. There are hundreds of genes, each increasing the risk for depression, schizophrenia and anxiety disorders by a small amount.

So while there is no single genetic test that can now be used, large numbers of genes have consistently been shown — and many of the recent studies are strong — to be associated with certain disorders. But because there's no single gene or small group of genes, we cannot walk away from the science. Complexity doesn't mean we throw our hands up and say, "Well, it's all too much."

It may seem overwhelming, but genetic profiles are better understood today than they were 20 years ago. So that's something else this committee is thinking about and I think should take into account going forward: to somehow incorporate that into the diagnostic categories.

KHC: Do you think there's any sort of risk with adding those biological factors into the DSM?

AK: I don't think so, because if you think about genetics, it's not going to be introduced as a biological test.

Most folks know that mental disorders, like other medical disorders, run in families. And genetics is the most plausible explanation for that. What this does, I hope, is introduce a degree of more comprehensive description of these disorders. So when a busy clinician looks at it, it confirms what they already suspected: There's a family history here, and family history means genetics.

It's complex, many genes are involved, and it produces a better characterization of this. The diagnosis is still going to remain clinical, but this provides a biological context, very much like, say, diabetes or heart disease.

Genes and environment cause a variety of medical disorders. With heart disease, there's no one gene. When cardiologists develop a risk profile for heart disease, it includes genes, other physiological factors such as BMI, which is the weight-height ratio, diet and a variety of environmental factors.

That degree of classification is missing today in mental health and psychiatry. We hope this is a first step in correcting, if you will, those conceptions about what causes these disorders.

KHC: How would you end up using this in a psychiatrist's office to guide treatment?

AK: I can give you one possible example. I'm reaching a bit.

There's a term commonly used in clinical psychiatry and psychology called comorbidity. What it means is that people who are diagnosed with depression also have anxiety, or people who are diagnosed with an anxiety disorder also have substance abuse or alcoholism in general.

That is not coincidental. It's not something that we just somehow find. A lot of these disorders share genes.

For example, about 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with a major mood disorder also have an anxiety disorder. And you flip that around: About 45%, roughly, of patients diagnosed with an anxiety disorder — it could be generalized anxiety disorder, what we call PTSD, or a phobia — also have a mood disorder.

Patients with anxiety may also be diagnosed with a mood disorder.

I think when clinicians classify them together, not as the same disorder but as sharing a lot of psychological as well as genetic risk, clinicians should be on the lookout for both. A patient with a mood disorder, for example, could either now or at some later point develop an anxiety disorder. Or someone with an anxiety disorder is at risk for substance abuse.

So treatments need to be tailored a little more broadly. I'm hoping that'll be something clinicians think about when they talk to patients and their families.

KHC: What do you think is the most unique aspect, from your perspective, of this upcoming DSM-6?

AK: My bias is the biology. I say this because a lot of the other things, the cultural factors, etc., are largely appreciated, and they'll be better characterized. Some things like cognitive changes, such as working memory and attention [tests], are not unique to any given disorder.

Biology will be qualitatively new when introduced into the DSM, and I hope it's done well. I hope that they do it appropriately, and I think they will [do it] correctly.

It's not going to be perfect, but it's going to be a first step. I think introducing the idea that genetics, immunology and other factors are very important in the causation of mental disorders, and explain some of the phenomena that we previously could not find an explanation for, is — I hate to use the word "leapfrog" — but that's kind of what it is.

It moves the field conceptually forward, and not as a slow, steady, gradual increase. For the DSM, it would be an important step forward.

This interview has been condensed and edited lightly for clarity.

#6277. Copenhagen is Opening a Stunning New Bathhouse Along Its Harbor This December—And It's Shockingly Affordable

Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Locals and visitors alike have taken her words to heart ever since.

In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbor after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts, and boaters, especially on hot summer days. In recent years, cold plunging has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health—nowadays, you can expect winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbor to have lengthy waiting lists.

The new bathing house was designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates and has been 8 years in the making.

The next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday, December 5: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbor.

Designed by the Japanese architectural firm Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 62,500 square-foot bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbor. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbor, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag.

Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 82-foot pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbor with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbor itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating.

This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools—known as "water culture houses"—where entry is typically under 100kr (about $10). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK ($150 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden.

Kai will open on Paper Island on December 5, 2026.

Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.”

The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbor from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen.

Copenhagen's harbor is the heart of the city's year-round swimming culture.

If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbor is the place to start—but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbor for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition.

Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area.

#6276. South Korea eyes rocket debut and China lines up four launches

On Monday, Nov. 2, Rocket Lab launched The Sea God Surveys on an Electron rocket from its Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula at 11:41 a.m. EST. Aboard was a QPS-SAR satellite for private Japanese company iQPS It marked Electron’s 10th flight for iQPS. The company is building out a fleet of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites with the goal of handing customers worldwide radar views in close to real time.

On Monday, Nov. 2, CAS Space — the commercial launch company founded by the Chinese Academy of Sciences — is targeting 7:10 p.m. EST for a Kinetica 2 launch from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, according to Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed, but the only prior Kinetica 2 launch carried a batch of SpaceSail satellites. SpaceSail, also known as Qianfan or “Thousand Sails,” is a Chinese broadband megaconstellation designed to beam internet service from low Earth orbit (LEO).

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-432 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 8:28 p.m. EST. After stage separation, the Falcon 9 first stage will aim for a landing on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You, stationed in the Pacific Ocean.

On Wednesday, Nov. 4, South Korea’s Agency for Defense Development (ADD) may attempt a demonstration flight of its Mir rocket from Jeju Island, off the country’s southern coast. That date comes from Next Spaceflight’s tracking; South Korean officials have said only that the launch will happen before the end of the year. ADD, the military research arm of South Korea’s defense ministry, has been developing the solid-fueled rocket since 2021. The military plans to use it to launch small military reconnaissance satellites into orbit. The demo was originally set for June 30 but slipped over safety concerns.

On Thursday, Nov. 5, China’s state-owned launch provider, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), has two launches scheduled, according to Next Spaceflight. First, a Long March 2C is slated to lift off from the Xichang Satellite Launch Center in southwestern China at 11:00 a.m. EST with an undisclosed payload. Then at 4:15 p.m. EST, a Long March 12 will launch from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island, also with an undisclosed payload.

On Friday, Nov. 6, Chinese commercial company Galactic Energy will launch a Ceres 2 rocket from Jiuquan at 6:35 p.m. EST, according to tracking from Next Spaceflight. The payload has not been disclosed. This will be the second test flight for the Ceres 2 after the rocket suffered a first-stage failure and fell short of orbit on its first flight in January.

On Tuesday, Oct. 27, SpaceX launched Starlink Group 15-16 from Vandenberg at 3:25 a.m. EDT, with the booster landing on Of Course I Still Love You.

On Friday, Oct. 30, the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the NVS-03 navigation satellite, also known as IRNSS-1L, aboard a GSLV Mk II rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota. The satellite joins NavIC, India’s regional satellite navigation system — the country’s homegrown counterpart to GPS.

SpaceX followed early Saturday, Oct. 31, with Starlink Group 15-18, lifting off from Vandenberg at 12:04 a.m. EDT. Its booster also touched down on Of Course I Still Love You.

No earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, United Launch Alliance (ULA) is targeting the launch of Amazon Leo (LV-01) on a Vulcan rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The flight will loft a batch of satellites for Amazon Leo, Amazon’s broadband constellation formerly known as Project Kuiper.

No earlier than Saturday, Nov. 14, Rocket Lab plans to fly The Mountain God Rises from Māhia — Electron’s 100th launch. The milestone flight goes to a familiar customer: another QPS-SAR radar satellite for iQPS, bound for a low Earth orbit.

#6275. Newborn survival improves when families receive financial support

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Rx Kids, a cash transfer program, boosted infants’ health in Flint, Michigan

Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield announces Rx Kids' Detroit debut in 2025. The program began in Flint, Mich., in 2024. “We know how to deliver this support efficiently and with dignity," pediatrician and Rx Kids director Mona Hanna told Science News.

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.
