Satellite radar and underground electrical scans have revealed a 2,600-year-old structure at Buto, one of ancient Egypt's most sacred cities. The real surprise wasn't the walls — but what was underneath them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Egyptian researchers have found a hidden 2,600-year-old structure the size of a football field after using satellites to peer below the ground. But what they found beneath the structure may be just as remarkable as the building itself.

The site they examined is known as Buto (modern-day Tell el-Fara'in), a sprawling mound of layered history in the northwestern Nile Delta. To the ancient Egyptians, it was the sacred home of Wadjet, the cobra goddess of Lower Egypt, and one of the most religiously important cities in the pharaonic landscape.

Archaeologists have excavated its upper layers for decades, finding remains from the rule of the Macedonian Ptolemaic dynasty (305 to 30 B.C.) and Roman era (30 B.C. to A.D. 395). But the deeper, older layers at the site — including a mound called Kom C, sitting below groundwater level in waterlogged delta clay — had stayed stubbornly out of reach. Kom C itself rises above the surface as a visible mound, but earlier excavations had reached only the Ptolemaic and Roman layers before hitting the water table.

Now, researchers have turned to noninvasive tools, including satellite imagery, to delve into the mysterious subterranean layers.

First, they turned to the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellite, which can produce radar images by beaming down microwave pulses from orbit and then measuring how they reflect back; the returning signals can reveal subtle differences in surface moisture, elevation and reflectivity that can hint at buried structures beneath the ground. After looking at these radar images, the team spotted a large oval-shaped anomaly buried beneath Kom C that was 420 feet long and 203 feet wide (128 by 62 meters).

The geological profile of Tell el-Fara'in (ancient Buto) and the surrounding Nile Delta, showing the layered sequence of river sands and flood-plain clays from the last ice age and the settlement mound above.

To learn more without disturbing the site, the team ran 15 parallel lines of electrical resistivity tomography (ERT) across an area of roughly 58,100 square feet (5,400 square meters). This technique reveals the underground landscape by passing electrical currents through the earth, measuring how they travel and creating a map that archaeologists can read.

The picture that came back was layered. Between the surface and 10 feet (3 m) down, the team found scattered Ptolemaic and Roman debris, including displaced mudbricks, pottery shards and broken limestone, which point to centuries of continued occupation and rebuilding on the site. Later residents dismantled older structures for reuse and left a scatter of displaced material behind.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment.

Deeper still, between 10 and 20 feet (3 and 6 m), the researchers found a large mudbrick structure from the 26th dynasty (688 to 525 B.C.), also known as the Saite period. They were able to date this discovery based on its layer, the unique shape of the mudbricks and other artifacts such as pottery, which the team dated by style and their archaeological layer, with carbon-14 dating applied to associated organic material. The large structure may be a tomb, a house for priests or a religious shrine, the team wrote in the study, published in March in the journal Acta Geophysica.

And below that, at 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) underground, the researchers unexpectedly found a thick, clean layer of sand.

That sand is the discovery within the discovery, the team wrote in the study.

The Nile Delta's clay is notoriously treacherous to build on. It absorbs moisture and swells, and then contracts and shifts as it dries — posing a slow-motion threat to anything heavy sitting on top of it. The Saite builders, it seems, knew this. Before laying the foundations to their structure, they packed a cushion of clean sand beneath it. This sand would have spread the building's weight, let groundwater drain through, and stopped the clay from creeping. It is the same logic behind modern load-distributing foundations — applied here more than two and a half millennia ago.

A 2D electrical resistivity scan aligned with a partially exposed mudbrick wall — the colored subsurface anomaly matches the location of the visible structure above ground.

"By combining satellite radar with deep ERT profiles, we didn't just map the walls of this massive Saite-era structure — we were also able to analyze the subsurface layers," study co-author author Abdelaziz Elfadaly, an associate research professor at Egypt's National Authority for Remote Sensing and Space Sciences, told Live Science. "The detection of a significant, clean sand foundation layer beneath the mudbrick walls explains how these heavy structures survived the high water table and shifting clayey soil of Buto."

The sand layer, in effect, acts as a barrier; it stops groundwater from wicking upward into the mudbrick, which would soften and dissolve it. The sand also lets water drain sideways instead of pooling against the foundation, according to Elfadaly.

A 3-by-3 foot (10 by 10 m) excavation trench that was around 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 m) deep confirmed the presence of thick mudbrick walls resting on that sand layer, and nearby, a spread of objects that hint at the site's sacred function. According to Elfadaly, these finds included ushabti and shawabti figurines — small servant statues typically placed in tombs to serve the deceased in the afterlife — and a limestone altar whose carved channels bore dried residues consistent with animal blood, pointing to offering rituals performed at the site. The study also noted a rarer find: a faience baboon figurine, the kind associated with Thoth, the god of wisdom.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

Layout of the ERT (electrical resistivity tomography) survey at Kom C. The blue lines mark one first set of profiles, and the red lines mark the second. Insets show the electrodes and cables deployed in the field, and a large mudbrick wall dating to the Late Roman period.

Image credit: Abouarab et al.,Acta Geophysica (2026); CC BY 4.0

A selection of artifacts recovered from the excavated square at Kom C, including small figurines and worked stone fragments from the Saite-era structure.

The Saite period was a moment of cultural revival. After generations of Assyrian and Libyan domination, Egyptian pharaohs retook the throne and poured resources into restoring Egypt's religious landscape, particularly in the Nile Delta, which had been their power base. Buto, with its deep ties to Lower Egyptian identity, was a natural focus. The Saite kings ruled from the nearby delta city of Sais, so restoring Buto reinforced their roots and their claim to the throne.

"A monumental building of this scale underscores the Saite pharaohs' intense commitment to glorifying the Delta region," Hussein Bassir, director of the Antiquities Museum at a cultural research center known as Bibliotheca Alexandrina who wasn't involved with the study, told Live Science in a WhatsApp message. "Using pure sand as a stabilizing cushion was a brilliant, deliberate tactic — the ancient builders profoundly understood their environment."

The team is planning a return visit, this time using wider-spaced electrical resistivity surveys to reach deeper layers, along with specialists who study ancient plants and also understand how geological features changed over time, which may help reconstruct what the landscape around Buto looked like when these walls were first laid.

Abouarab, M. a. R., Elfadaly, A., Elbehery, W., Wafa, O., Aboalkassim, I., Younes, A., Hiekl, A. M. A., Saada, S. A., Wilson, P., & Ibrahim, A. (2026). Multi-scale detection of buried archaeological elements across different occupation phases: an integrated approach using radar satellite imagery and electric resistivity tomography at Buto, northwestern Nile Delta of Egypt. Acta Geophysica, 74(2). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11600-026-01809-4

She specializes in archaeological conservation and ancient Egyptian material culture, and brings firsthand field experience from Egyptian archaeological sites. Her work has been published on Ancient Origins and Medium, where she focuses on making Egypt's rich archaeological record accessible to global audiences.

#6273. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6272. The Best Islands in the World: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best cities in the world as voted by you, our readers.

View all of the the Readers’ Choice Awards winners for 2026 here.

The six islands of the Bazaruto Archipelago—Bazaruto, Benguerra, Magaruque, Santa Carolina, Bangue, and Shell—are a protected conservation area and national park off the eastern coast of Africa. Nicknamed the Pearl of the Indian Ocean, the islands have only seen the arrival of big-name resorts within the past decade, like the impeccable andBeyond Benguerra Island in 2015.

Pro tip: This is one of the few habitats of the endangered manatee-like dugong, which sailors sometimes mistook for mermaids.

Getting there: Fly to Vilanculos on the coast of Mozambique; from there, take a seaplane to your final destination.

Instagram and Pinterest have created renewed interest in this island in the Indian Ocean, thanks to its so-called underwater waterfall—a visually stunning runoff of sand and silt best viewed from above. Roughly 550 miles east of Madagascar, Mauritius may also be home to a lost continent hiding beneath the waves.

Pro tip: Don’t trust the scales on Mauritius: The island has a stronger gravitational field, causing things (and people) to weigh more.

Getting there: The island’s Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam International Airport is your link for flights to other cities in Africa, as well as to major cities in Europe, Asia, and Australia.

With its white coral sand beaches, turquoise waters, and laid-back island vibe, few destinations offer a sense of escapism quite like Zanzibar. Add to that plenty of sunshine and consistently pleasant temperatures, and it’s easy to see its appeal. For the history buffs among us, don't skip historic trade center Stone Town, famous for its meandering lanes, minarets-crowned buildings, and the 19th-century House of Wonders where the Sultan used to live.

Pro tip: Visit the island during the dry season from June to October, when temperatures average out at 77 degrees. This time range also overlaps with the high season for safari, should a two-for-one trip be of interest.

Getting there: To get to Zanzibar, fly directly to Abeid Amani Karume International Airport (ZNZ), or arrive by ferry from Dar es Salaam in Tanzania.

Our readers aren’t the only ones who consider this African nation one of the best islands in the world: Prince William and Kate Middleton and Victoria and David Beckham spent their honeymoons on the North Island of the Seychelles. Yet some stretches of sand are so deserted that parts of the movie Castaway were filmed here. The ultimate draw, however, is the nature—the white beaches here are so beautiful that visiting them borders on a religious experience.

Pro tip: Seychelles is one of the best spots in the Indian Ocean for snorkeling. Head to the islands of La Digue and Félicité for the best variety of sealife.

Getting there: Air France, Air Seychelles, and Turkish Airlines have regular flights that connect to Seychelles International Airport (SEZ), just south of the capital of Victoria.

A chain of 26 atolls and more than 1,000 islands in the Indian Ocean, the Republic of Maldives is one of the most sought-after tropical destinations in the world. It’s dense with villas and overwater bungalows, and the diving is unreal (though, sadly, some of the coral has been threatened by bleaching). Still, there’s a dive for all skill levels at Ari Atoll, where you can swim with rays and, deeper down, reef sharks.

Pro tip: Cheval Blanc Randheli, the number one resort in the Indian Ocean (per this year’s reader survey), has 45 luxe villas—some tucked among the coconut groves, some jutting out directly over the water.

Getting there: Fly into Malé’s international airport and transfer there to the appropriate resort or atoll.

If your idea of the perfect vacation involves three-day beach parties, Koh Pha Ngan is the Thai island for you. Famous for its full-moon parties at the Haad Rin peninsula's Sunrise Beach, this island is for hardcore partygoers and the anything-goes crowd. During peak season, the island can see upwards of 20,000 visitors dancing and cavorting on the white sands under a full moon. If you can't make it at the right time of month, don't worry—there are half-moon and black-moon parties in intervening weeks, too, and there's action every night of the week at the island's beach and cocktail bars.

Pro tip: There are secluded beaches far from the crowds (like local favorite Bottle Beach, arguably one of the best beaches in Thailand), and plenty of spas where you can check yourself in for an afternoon of recovery, from the basic to the deluxe (such as the Ayurvana Spa at Santhiya Resort on Thong Nai Pan Noi Beach in the north of the island).

Getting there: From Koh Samui, take the ferry or a high-speed boat from a nearby pier like Maenam or Bangrak to Thong Sala Pier or Haad Rin Pier.

India's Andaman Islands are chock-full of beaches for thrill seekers looking to snorkel among sea life and peer through shipwrecks, as well as relaxing sandy stretches for more meditative types who prefer their quiet strolls backgrounded by sherbet-hued sunsets alike. Whether you're enjoying Havelock Island's serene Radhanagar Beach or Elephant Beach, whose shores are a veritable water sports arena, these islands provide 365 days of sun, sand, and fun.

Pro tip: Beyond the beaches, hike through the Baratang Limestone Caves' striking natural corridors through one of the most renowned natural wonders of these islands.

Getting there: Direct flights to Port Blair's Veer Savarkar airport fly from Kolkata, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Delhi, and Vizag. Alternatively, travelers may also choose to arrive at Port Blair via ferry from Kolkata or Chennai.

The Phi Phi Islands lie in the cozy cradle between Phuket and the Straits of Malacca off Krabi Province. Each of the six islands—Ko Phi Phi Don, Ko Phi Phi Le, Bamboo Island, Mosquito Island, Bida Nai, and Bida Nok—have their own charms to offer. From silky soft white sand to dramatic limestone cliffs, the beaches found on these islands are among Southeast Asia's finest.

Pro tip: For a feel of local life, stop by Ko Phi Phi Don, the largest and most populated island of the group. If flopping in solace is more your speed, pop over to Ko Phi Phi Le, which lays claim to some of the island's most stunning vistas and coastal stretches.

Getting there: As there are no airports on any of the Phi Phi Islands, visitors will have to arrive via ferry from ports such as Phuket or Krabi.

Phuket is not exactly a hidden gem, but that's because it's such a magical place to vacation, whether you want a busy immersion in city life or a quieter experience. Since it’s the biggest island in Thailand, you’re sure to find something to fit your desired itinerary. In general, though, we recommend skipping the overcrowded west coast and heading to quiet corners like Cape Panwa, where you’ll find luxury accommodations and rum distilleries that feel a bit more removed from the oft-touristed track.

Pro tip: Phuket Town receives far fewer tourists than the western beach areas. Here you can sample colorful spices at markets, visit aging Taoist temples, and snap photos of the colorful street murals.

Getting there: There are more than a dozen daily flights from Bangkok to Phuket, with most trips clocking in at an hour and 20 minutes.

Nowhere on the planet offers the same combination of surfing, spirituality, and sun-kissed pleasure as Bali. The island has sadly become synonymous with the concept of overtourism, but there are still enclaves of hidden cultural treasures and undiscovered gems—if you know where to look. For a primer on everything Insta-famous and off-the-beaten-track, check out our list of the best things to do in Bali.

Pro tip: The shoulder months of April-May and September-October are the best times to visit Bali. Not only can you enjoy lower airfares and hotel rates during the low season, but you’ll also have the rare ability to see the island without its usual crowds.

Getting there: Many airlines fly directly from the United States to Bali, including Singapore Airlines, Delta, and American.

Thailand’s second-largest island is famous for its palm-lined beaches, buzzing nightlife scene, and luxurious hotels. AVANI+ Samui Resort was voted one of the best resorts in Thailand by our readers, though the hillside villas at Four Seasons Resort Koh Samui and floor-to-ceiling bookshelves at The Library are also worth checking out. In terms of beaches, be sure to visit the five-mile Chaweng Beach, lined with coconut trees and surrounded by a natural reef. Just note that the northern end of the beach is party central.

Pro tip: If you are looking for parties, check out Green Mango, one of Koh Samui’s oldest and most famous clubs.

Getting there: You can fly directly from Bangkok to Koh Samui. A more budget-friendly option may be to fly to Surat Thani and then catch a ferry to Koh Samui—it will add a couple of hours to your travel time, but the views are pretty spectacular.

Located off the northwestern coast of Malaysia, the Langkawi archipelago has pristine beaches, coral reefs, and lush mountains—plus that famous Sky Bridge you’ve definitely seen pictures of. This collection of 99 islands is also a foodie wonderland (eating is the unofficial national sport here), with spicy peanut satay skewers and macheted coconuts sold everywhere from high-end hotels to sidewalk stands.

Pro tip: The Ritz-Carlton, Langkawi was voted the best resort in Asia by our readers this year—chalk it up to a world-class spa, multiple beachfront restaurants, and a location in a 10 million-year-old rainforest.

Getting there: Take a one-hour flight from the Malay capital of Kuala Lumpur.

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6271. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

Chemical signatures found in a Brazilian dinosaur bone may be preserved red blood cells, a new study suggests, but not all experts agree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Red blood cells found in a 115 million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Brazil are the oldest chemical evidence of blood-related material in a dinosaur fossil, a new study claims.

However, not everyone agrees with the research team's conclusions, with some experts saying the shape doesn't match those of reptilian red blood cells.

In the new research, published Monday (Nov. 2) in the journal PNAS, the scientists said they identified microscopic structures resembling red blood cells alongside chemical signatures of heme, the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin.

The new findings come from limb bones of a roughly 10-foot-long (3 meters) dinosaur called Aratasaurus museunacionali. While previous research has detected blood in dinosaur fossils, this is the first study to use chemical processes to identify heme-based signatures in dinosaur bones.

"Traditionally, fossils give us information through bones, teeth, shells and morphology. But exceptionally preserved fossils may contain another archive of information: microscopic structures and molecular traces of the original organism," study co-author Kliti Grice, a professor in the School of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Curtin University in Australia, told Live Science via email. "That opens the possibility of asking questions about ancient biology that skeletal anatomy alone cannot answer."

The team was not originally looking for traces of dinosaur blood, Grice said. Her research was driven by a broader question: How much of an ancient organism's original biology can survive fossilization?

To investigate, Grice and her team studied the limb bones of A. museunacionali, an extinct species of small theropod that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in Brazil. Theropods were a group of mostly meat-eating dinosaurs that walked on two legs. They included famous predators such as Tyrannosaurus rex and Velociraptor.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Using microscopic and chemical analysis on the theropod's limb bones, the researchers found numerous microscopic structures within vascular canals, channels that once carried blood vessels through the bone. Their shape, size and location were consistent with red blood cells, the team said.

"We combined microscopy, mineralogical analyses and molecular geochemistry," Grice said. "Critically, we investigated the chemistry in situ [in the bone itself], so we could relate the chemical signals to the microscopic structures in their physical context within the fossil. That is much stronger than simply extracting molecules from a piece of fossil and assuming where they originated."

The team's chemical analyses detected preserved heme-related compounds associated with these structures, providing more chemical evidence to support the idea that the finding could be traces of dinosaur blood, as heme is the iron-containing, ring-shaped molecule that forms a key part of the molecule hemoglobin in red blood cells.

Grice and the team think the conditions the theropod dinosaur was buried in could have helped preserve the vascular structures and the red blood cells within them. They suggested that the animal was rapidly covered by sediment in a low-oxygen environment containing microbial mats ‪—‬ thin biofilms made of microorganisms. These conditions may have altered the normal process of decomposition, helping to preserve the microscopic structures and associated chemical signatures.

An illustration of a microbial mat covering A. museunacionali's bones after it died.

"The red-blood-cell-like structures were mineralised with hausmannite, a manganese oxide mineral (Mn₃O₄)," Grice said. "We think early mineralisation helped stabilise or replicate microscopic biological structures before they were completely destroyed, while aspects of the associated chemistry also survived in altered form."

The fossil also contained preserved amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein found in bone.

While blood has been found in dinosaur fossils before, not everyone agrees that these latest findings are truly red blood cells.

"I very much appreciate this team bringing rigor to the study of deep time fossils," said Mary Schweitzer, a molecular paleontologist at North Carolina State University who was not involved in the study but has previously studied soft tissues from the dinosaur age. "I am in agreement that endogenous [produced within the body] molecules can persist over geological time in some form, and that there is much these can teach us. However, I am not convinced that the images they figure are remnant RBCs [red blood cells] for several reasons."

For one, the structures do not convincingly match the expected appearance of red blood cells in nonmammalian animals, Schweitzer said. Unlike mammalian red blood cells, which lose their nuclei during development, those of birds and reptiles retain their nuclei. This typically produces a characteristic nuclear bulge in the shape of the cell.

According to Schweitzer, the latest findings show the microstructures having more of a concave shape with no nuclear bulge. The structures also were smaller than most non-mammalian red blood cells, "so morphological similarity is not met," Schweitzer said.

"I appreciate these authors bringing technological innovations to the study of dinosaur fossils," she said. "I am excited to see that this team and others are moving forward with a molecular approach to ancient fossil remains."

Editor's Note: This article was updated at 5:44 p.m. E.D.T. to remove an outside comment that suggested the study did not include resonance Raman spectroscopy. The team did perform that analysis.

O., Demore, J., Saraiva, A. a. F., Rickard, W. D. A., Ohkouchi, N., Sayão, J. M., . . . Kellner, A. W. A. (2026). Heme signatures in mineralized red blood cells within vascular canals of a 115-million-year-old dinosaur bone. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 123(0), e2614248123. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2614248123

#6269. Where to Stay in Big Sky, Montana, When You’re Dreaming of the Wild West

I’ve visited Big Sky, Montana, a handful of times over the past six years, and I’m still completely smitten. This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. Winter ski days beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak give way to summer rafting trips and fly-fishing on the Gallatin River, while fall brings horseback rides that sprawl across open ranchlands, and spring offers hikes through wildflower-strewn meadows. The iconic Yellowstone National Park is about an hour south too, putting geysers, steaming hot springs, and roaming bison within day-tripping distance.

The city itself is a quaint yet buzzy collection of restaurants, shops, and watering holes, all adding a welcome dose of small-town charm to all that wilderness. And lately, the destination’s hospitality scene has been booming, with a new wave of stylish hotels and mountain retreats bringing some fresh takes to the city’s rugged Western roots. From luxe resorts with front-row views of the towering peaks to authentic dude ranches and design-forward Airbnbs with cozy fireplaces, there’s an accommodation for every style of Big Sky getaway on the list below. Read on for the best places to stay in Montana’s sweet mountain hub.

A peek at Big Sky's small but mighty town center, where the mountains and Main Street look great together.

Stay at Lone Mountain Ranch, just five minutes from the town center, for a dreamy dude ranch retreat.

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: Mountain access, gorgeous standalone cabins, private hot tubs, spa and wellness facilities (with indoor-outdoor lap pool, heated onsen soaking tub, cold plunge, steam room, and sauna)

Famed for its sumptuous yet tasteful resorts in far-flung destinations like Mauritius, Rwanda, and Malaysia, One&Only’s 2025 Moonlight Basin opening was the brand's American debut, as well as its first foray into the outdoor adventure space. A luxury alpine retreat like this requires a specialized type of hospitality, and the team here—a crew who can do everything from book your activities to whisk you between buildings on a side-by-side ATV—knows exactly what they’re doing. Guests get a direct line to the slopes via the One&Only gondola, as well as access to plush locker rooms, tuning equipment, and gear rentals that will impress even members of Yellowstone Club (the famously tiny private ski community next door).

Moonlight Basin is worth visiting outside of ski season too. Situated on 240 secluded acres within the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, the resort links two sections of protected wilderness in southwestern Montana’s Rocky Mountains, providing critical migration routes for species like moose and bobcats, which means you're in for some exceptional wildlife sightings. Add fly-fishing, stargazing at the on-site observatory, and unwinding at the 17,000-square-foot spa, and even the most discerning ski bums will find themselves spoiled rotten. —Hannah Towey

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Lone Peak, Madison River Valley, Big Sky Mountain, Madison Base Area

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: White-glove service, buzzy après bar, full spa, on-site activity center, ski-in/ski-out location

Montage Big Sky has always been more rugged than refined, but the buzz around this slopeside resort has Aspen and Jackson Hole loyalists rethinking their next ski vacation. The first five-star resort in Big Sky ushered in a whole new era of luxury for this mountain destination, with an 11,000-square-foot spa (the first true spa in the region), a buzzy bar scene, and stellar restaurants.

Most of the 139 rooms, suites, and residences have terraces and balconies with mountain views, and gas fireplaces turn on with a flip of a switch. Head to Beartooth Pub & Rec for a menu of comfort foods, like Wagyu nachos and oversized hot pretzels served alongside cold-smoked beer-cheese dip. —Jen Murphy

Neighborhood: Spanish PeaksThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Ousel Falls Trail, Lone Peak, Beehive Basin Trail, Gallatin and Madison Rivers

Number of guests: VariesBed and bath: VariesWhy we love it: True dude ranch experience, tasteful cabin design, horseback riding experiences for all levels, easy access to town

Lone Mountain Ranch, one of Montana’s longest-standing dude ranches, has plenty going for it: a wonderfully attentive staff, character-filled cabins, and a calendar of special events that draw in both longtime regulars and first-time horseback riders. The on-site wranglers are happy to work with riders of all levels one-on-one, even if that means helping you get past a few preexisting fears before climbing into the saddle. The ranch’s roots reach back to the early days of Yellowstone, with its owners involved in conversations around Big Sky’s formation and the region’s ranching, logging, and wilderness preservation. Yet unlike many of Montana’s more remote ranches, it’s conveniently less than a 10-minute drive from town.

You may still find little reason to leave: Set among towering aspens, the 150-acre guest ranch has 25 restored historic cabins, each with its own Wild West–inspired name and one to six bedrooms. And then there are the signature experiences, including Cowgirl Up, a weeklong retreat that brings women from around the world together to experience ranch life and release their inner cowgirl.

Neighborhood: Lone MountainThings to do nearby: Big Sky Town Center, Ousel Falls Trail, Moonlight Basin, Gallatin River, Big Sky Resort

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s (iconically named) Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s hiking and wildlife spotting in the warmer months. It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to look elsewhere. A big plus? The town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Neighborhood: Cowboy HeavenThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Lone Mountain, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, in-unit washer and dryer, indoor wood-burning fireplace, fully equipped kitchen, patio with outdoor furniture, longer stays allowed

With three floors and two separate living areas, this Big Sky rental gives small groups room to spread out between outings. And there’s plenty to get out for: Big Sky Resort is about 1.2 miles away, Beehive Basin Trailhead is roughly 2.6 miles, and Ousel Falls Park is another nearby option for low-key but scenic walks.

Inside the light-filled abode, fun Western touches are everywhere. In true Big Sky fashion, you’ll find everything from hanging longhorns and antlers to framed photographs of bison and horses. Through a wall of windows, you can look past the cozy fireplace into the hilly woods—the towering trees are gorgeous year-round. Do note this base might be best for four, rather than six, despite what the listing says. There are two generously sized bedrooms, but two sofa beds in the living room.

Neighborhood: Moonlight BasinThings to do nearby: Big Sky Resort, Beehive Basin Trailhead, Gallatin River, Lone Mountain, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, firepit, spacious design, game room, fully equipped kitchen, patio space with seating and grill, proximity to Yellowstone National Park

For a fun departure from the usual cabin-in-the-woods vibe, this modern mountain retreat sleeps up to eight and puts you in a handy spot for mountain treks, foodie-forward itineraries, and all the trips in between. It’s incredibly spacious, with a large patio for grilling local ingredients, warming up around the fire, and stargazing. In winter, take advantage of the trails practically right next to the property for snowmobiling; you're also in a prime position for skiing at Moonlight Basin, Big Ski Resort, or Bridger Bowl ski area (a bit further north). According to the listing, a sauna is set to open on the property—check in with the hosts to see if it will be set up by the time you visit.

It’s worth noting that this is the closest Airbnb to Yellowstone on this list. You can drive to the West Yellowstone entrance in around 45 minutes.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: Gallatin River, West Yellowstone, Lone Indian Peak, Buck Ridge Trailhead, Crown Butte, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Private hot tub, shared firepits and sauna, board games and books, kid-friendly amenities

This gem of a rental is high on my Big Sky bucket list for more reasons than one. To start, the tastefully designed home is all about panoramic views of misty, moody Ramshorn Ridge. With heaps of walking paths and a mountain-facing hot tub under string lights, guests will be almost poetically connected to Montana’s wide-open landscape. But you won’t be too far from the mountain town’s buzz: This home is part of Aspects, a 10-home village set in a ryegrass field in the Gallatin Valley, meaning you’ll have access to the community’s saunas and two firepits, which you can share with like-minded travelers.

Downtown Big Sky is just a five-minute drive away, while hiking trails branching from Yellowstone are within 15 minutes of the home. Along with its great location, I’m personally captivated by this home’s aesthetic design touches—from the light wood walls that warmly envelop the dining space to the vibrant art that brings fun, unexpected pops of color throughout the home.

Neighborhood: Gallatin ValleyThings to do nearby: The Riverhouse BBQ, West Yellowstone, Downtown Big Sky, Cinnamon Mountain, Gallatin River

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Unique design, minutes from Big Sky Resort, sauna, private walking/biking trail from the property

A little off-grid, a bit otherworldly, and just a couple of miles from Big Sky Resort, this Earthship Airbnb is a unique kind of Montana hideaway. Set on 20 private acres in Michener Meadows, the solar-powered house is designed to bring the outdoors in, with its own potable spring water and a private walking and biking trail winding around the property.

Neighborhood: Michener MeadowsThings to do nearby: Ousel Falls Park, Dudley Creek Trailhead, Table Mountain, Horn and Cantle, Big Sky Town Center

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Walkable to Big Sky Town Center; patio with grill; indoor fireplace; fully equipped kitchen; shared access to indoor pool, hot tub, and sauna

For those in search of an easy, breezy Big Sky stay, this convenient condo is a boon. Tucked just outside of the city’s small but mighty town center, you’ll be within walking distance of cozy cafés, outdoor gear and gift shops, and hyper-local pubs and restaurants. Back at “home,” your launchpad is as design-friendly as it is inviting. There’s a snug living room with an electric fireplace, a raised patio with a barbecue, string lights, and a table for enjoying meals made in your fully equipped kitchenette. It’s pretty spacious for a condo—each of the bedrooms boasts a king bed, and there’s a bathroom for each duo.

You’ll also be a short drive to the ski resort and practically right next to Big Sky Golf Course, where you can enjoy an award-winning 18-hole expanse and Nordic skiing, depending on the season. A plus for those chasing the snow? There’s an in-unit washer and dryer for all your ski gear, so it’ll be clean and dry for more mountain fun the next day.

Neighborhood: Meadow VillageThings to do nearby: Big Sky Golf Course, Big Sky Resort, Big Sky Town Center, Lone Mountain Trail, Blue Moon Bakery, Historic Crail Ranch, The Reflector Trail Loop

#6268. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.

It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.

That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.

For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.

Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!

Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.

Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.

What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.

How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.

Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.

Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.

Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. They are the moments where you did something.

Global Work & Travel makes doing something deep accessible in a way that genuinely wasn’t available a decade ago. If you’ve been thinking about doing something like this but the logistics have felt too complicated, check them out and use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a $100 discount on your trip.

#6267. Planning Your First Trip to New Zealand? Here's Where to Go

Living in Sydney, I’m guilty of thinking of New Zealand as somewhere I can always go next month. It’s close enough for a skiing trip, which is usually my first excuse to book. I love Queenstown for that, but what I’ve particularly enjoyed discovering on my travels is how naturally New Zealand brings together its spectacular outdoors and a tradition of luxury hospitality, in every season.

Aotearoa is easy to admire from a car window, but I’ve found that the places I remember most are those where I’ve stopped and spent a little more time. Wellington is overdue for another visit, and Fiordland is somewhere I'd like to explore properly. Then there are the lodges, each with its own character and reasons to return: Huka Lodge for its history, Cabot Lodgefor its working-farm roots, and many others worth discovering.

Below are the five places I’d build a trip around, leaving enough room in the itinerary to linger a little longer wherever I find myself wanting to stay.

I’d start with Queenstown if you’re coming for the mountains, with time allotted for Arrowtown and a few days in Fiordland National Park. For the North Island, Auckland is a useful starting point before heading towards Rotorua for its geothermal landscapes and Māori culture, then Lake Taupō. If food is your priority, I’d make Wellington part of the trip. My main advice is to choose a few places you’re interested in and give each at least a few days.

It can be, although a luxury lodge and a helicopter aren’t compulsory parts of an itinerary. I’d spend on a stay I really wanted, then balance it with somewhere simpler, ideally with a kitchen so you can cook some of your own meals. Skiing and guided activities can take a sizable bite out of the budget, so decide which matter most before booking everything else. If you’re considering a camper van, compare the total hire cost, including fuel and campsite fees, with a car and accommodation. I’d also leave room on the budget for eating out and wine tasting.

Seven days is sufficient for a trip, but I wouldn’t try to cover both islands in that time. On the South Island, you could spend the week around Queenstown and Arrowtown, adding Te Anau if Milford Sound is a priority. Or drive from Christchurch to Lake Tekapo and spend time in the Mackenzie region. On the North Island, Rotorua and Taupō work well together.

I always prefer to spend an extra night somewhere than keep repacking. Leave some flexibility, too: if you’ve come for stargazing and the sky clouds over, you’ll appreciate having another evening available.

Arrowtown, 20 minutes from Queenstown, is an idyllic place to visit.

Queenstown is great for the skiing, but I’d make time for nearby Arrowtown even if it meant losing a day on the slopes. I love the old cottages and shopfronts, and how much of its gold-mining history is still visible. The partially restored Chinese miners’ settlement beside Bush Creek is worth walking through before lunch.

Food is another reason to stay. At Aosta, northern Italian cooking makes good use of Central Otago produce. Nearby Ayrburn occupies a former 150-acre farm, with restaurants spread across its restored buildings. Billy’s, in the original homestead, serves modern Chinese food. I’ve visited both Arrowtown and Ayrburn, and would happily organize another Queenstown trip around eating here, with some skiing fitted in.

Where to stay: Arrowtown House is a small boutique hotel in town, making walking to dinner easy. Millbrook Resort, nearby, has more of a resort feel, with apartments as well as rooms and a spa for sore ski legs.

I still think about the water outside Huka Lodge. The Waikato River is this extraordinary emerald color, and I could have spent much of my stay watching it. Huka also got me interested in New Zealand’s lodge history: it began as a fishermen’s camp in 1924. There’s something appealing about discovering that a place has been welcoming people for the same reason for more than a century.

You don’t have to stay there to spend time beside the river. Follow the riverside walks towards Huka Falls, where the water forces its way through a narrow rock channel. I’d also get out on Lake Taupō, with a boat or kayak trip to the Ngātoroirangi Mine Bay Māori rock carvings. Created by Matahi Whakataka-Brightwell and his team, they’re a striking example of contemporary Māori art.

Where to stay: Huka Lodge has a certain stateliness, with its manicured grounds beside the Waikato River and a history of royal guests. I have dreams of running away to Poronui Safari Camp, in the wider Taupō region. Its two canvas tents sit beside the Mohaka River, with hot showers and food supplied by the kitchen. It’s booked exclusively for up to four people.

The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges on crystalline Lake Tekapo

I visited Dark Sky Project while reporting on quiet destinations for Traveler and loved having someone explain what I was looking at. The indoor experience brings Māori astronomy and science together, and houses an enormous restored 19th-century telescope. It gives you a way into the subject even if your astronomical knowledge is limited. For nighttime stargazing, book the Summit Experience at Mount John Observatory, within the Aoraki Mackenzie International Dark Sky Reserve. I’d arrange it early in the stay, leaving another night available if the weather doesn’t cooperate.

There’s plenty to look at during the day, too. Lake Tekapo gets its milky turquoise color from fine glacial rock flour floating in the water. It’s a good place to spend a few days on a South Island drive from Christchurch, with time for the Southern Alps and a separate excursion into Aoraki/Mount Cook National Park.

Where to stay: The Cairns Alpine Resort’s Alpine Lodges take their inspiration from musterers’ huts. Inside, there are two bedrooms and a kitchen, with timber-lined rooms and a wood-burning fireplace. After a late night stargazing on Mount John, you can have a lie-in and cook breakfast whenever you’re ready.

The city of Wellington, a great place to visit for good eating and galleries.

New Zealand received its first Michelin restaurant selection in 2026, although you hardly need the guide to eat well here. For me, Wellington would be a few days of galleries and restaurant bookings, with enough time between them to walk around and see what’s changed since my last visit some years ago City Gallery’s reopening has moved it up my list and is the sort of thing I’d build a weekend around. I’d leave plenty of time for eating, though.

Puffin is on my list for a glass of natural wine. I’m also keeping an eye on Rita, a small restaurant in an Aro Valley cottage known for its changing set dinners. The team is also opening a daytime deli called Super Rita, expected to open in early next year.

Where to stay: The Intrepid Hotel is the one I’d book: 18 rooms in Te Aro, near Cuba Street, with Puffin downstairs. I like the idea of a nightcap in a locals-filled wine bar and a short walk upstairs to bed.

The Cabot Lodge, a working farm, is an intriguing stay in Fiordland

Milford Sound and Doubtful Sound are still on my list, and I’d like to give Fiordland a trip of its own. I’d stay around Te Anau rather than make the long journey out and back from Queenstown. There are glowworm caves across Lake Te Anau, while nearby Manapouri is the starting point for the most direct land-and-water route to Doubtful Sound: a boat across Lake Manapouri, followed by a coach over Wilmot Pass to the fjord.

I also have a shopping recommendation for the journey. At The Key, on the approach to Te Anau, Davaar sells knitwear (that has a cult following) made from wool grown on the family’s working sheep station, Davaar Station. Founder Kate Macdonald is the fifth generation, and her sister Anna runs the food caravan next door. I bought a jumper a few years ago when she had a pop-up in Arrowtown that I still love. It’s exactly the sort of place I want to find when traveling: a homegrown product with a family story; make the best souvenirs.

Where to stay: Cabot Lodge interests me because it’s on a working farm overlooking Lake Manapouri, and near Doubtful Sound departures. For a night at Milford itself, Milford Sound Lodge has chalets overlooking the river and rainforest. I’d decide which sound I wanted to spend more time exploring before choosing where to stay.

#6266. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.
