#6250. Can You Pack Power Banks in Checked Luggage? 2026 Airline Battery Rules Travellers Need to Know

Most travellers now fly with several battery-powered items: a phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones, smartwatch, portable charger or vape. But packing one of them in the wrong bag can cause real problems at the airport.

In 2026, aviation safety authorities are warning travellers to pay closer attention to lithium batteries after reports that millions of batteries are still being packed incorrectly. The biggest mistake is simple: power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not go in checked luggage.

They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat, smoke or catch fire. This matters even more when your carry-on gets taken away at the gate and sent underneath the plane.

No. Power banks, portable chargers and spare lithium batteries should not be packed in checked luggage. They belong in your carry-on bag or personal item, where they can be reached quickly if they overheat.The same goes for loose camera batteries, spare laptop batteries, rechargeable battery packs, vape devices and phone battery charging cases. If your carry-on bag is taken away at the gate and checked underneath the plane, remove all power banks and spare batteries before handing it over.Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras with batteries installed are treated differently from spare batteries, but the safest habit is still to keep valuable battery-powered electronics in the cabin whenever possible. If an airline allows a device to be checked, it should be completely powered off, protected from damage and prevented from turning on accidentally.

The safest habit is simple: power banks, spare batteries and removable batteries stay with you. Valuable electronics are usually better in the cabin too.

Power banks are not allowed in checked luggage because they contain lithium batteries that can overheat if damaged, poorly packed, overcharged, exposed to heat or affected by a defect.

In rare cases, lithium batteries can enter thermal runaway. That means the battery heats faster than it can cool itself down. It may swell, smoke, burn or ignite.

If that happens in the cabin, passengers and crew can spot the problem quickly. Cabin crews are trained to respond to battery incidents. If the battery is hidden inside a suitcase in the cargo hold, it is much harder to access.

That is why this rule is not just airport red tape. A small charger in the wrong bag can become a serious safety issue.

Before you check a suitcase, look for anything with a loose, spare or removable lithium battery.

These items should stay in your carry-on or personal item:

You should also think carefully before checking valuable electronics with installed batteries, including:

Some airlines may allow certain devices with batteries installed in checked luggage if they are completely powered off and protected from damage. But for most travellers, the smarter choice is to keep electronics in the cabin.

Checked bags get dropped, delayed, searched and occasionally sent on their own little vacation. Your laptop does not need that character-building experience.

This is where the rules confuse a lot of travellers.

A spare battery is any battery that is not installed inside the device it powers. A power bank also counts because it is an external battery used to charge other devices.

A battery installed in a device is different. This includes the battery built into your phone, laptop, tablet, camera, headphones or smartwatch.

If the battery is loose, removable or used to charge something else, do not check it. The FAA’s lithium battery guidance says power banks and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage, not checked luggage.

Gate-checking is one of the easiest ways to accidentally break the battery rule.

You may pack your power bank correctly in your carry-on at home. Then you reach the gate, the overhead bins are full and the agent tags your carry-on to go underneath the plane.

At that moment, your carry-on has become checked luggage.

The easiest system is to keep all power banks and spare batteries in one small pouch inside your personal item. If your roller bag gets gate-checked, you can remove the pouch in seconds instead of digging through your suitcase while the boarding line gives you the collective death stare.

Airlines measure lithium-ion battery size in watt-hours, written as Wh.

Most standard phone power banks are under 100 Wh and are usually allowed in carry-on baggage. Larger batteries may require airline approval, and very large batteries are generally not allowed in normal passenger baggage.

The 100 Wh rule matters most for large laptop power banks, professional camera gear, video equipment and drone batteries.

A typical 10,000 mAh power bank is often around 37 Wh. A 20,000 mAh power bank is often around 74 Wh. Larger power banks can get close to the limit, so check before you pack.

According to CATSA’s battery packing guidelines, travellers should keep batteries and electronic devices containing batteries in their carry-on baggage, avoid damaged or recalled batteries, and protect spare batteries from short-circuiting.

Look for the Wh rating printed on the back, bottom or side of the power bank. Newer batteries often show this number clearly.

If the label only shows mAh and volts, you can calculate watt-hours with this formula:

Since 1,000 mAh equals 1 Ah, a 20,000 mAh power bank is 20 Ah.

That would usually fall under the 100 Wh carry-on limit.

If the label has rubbed off and the airline cannot confirm the battery rating, the item may be refused. Do not rely on guessing at the airport.

Laptops, phones and tablets have batteries installed inside the device, so they are not treated the same way as loose spare batteries or power banks.

However, airline rules vary. If an airline allows these devices in checked luggage, they should be completely powered off, protected from damage and packed so they cannot accidentally turn on.

That means fully powered off, not sleeping, hibernating or sitting there quietly planning to wake up mid-flight.

In practice, keep phones, laptops and tablets in the cabin whenever possible. They are valuable, easy to damage and often essential if your checked bag is delayed.

No. Vapes and e-cigarettes should not be packed in checked luggage because they contain batteries. They should travel in the cabin and must not be used or charged during the flight.

Rules for vaping products also vary by destination, and some countries restrict or ban them. If an adult is legally travelling with one, it still needs to follow airline battery rules.

If you are packing for someone else, check for these before closing a checked suitcase. A vape tossed into checked luggage can create the same battery issue as other lithium-powered devices.

Smart luggage can usually be checked only if the battery can be removed.

A smart bag is luggage with built-in charging, tracking or other battery-powered features. If the bag is going into the cabin and meets carry-on size limits, it may be accepted as a carry-on. If it has to be checked, the battery must usually be removed and brought into the cabin.

If the battery cannot be removed, the airline may refuse to accept the bag as checked luggage.

Before travelling with smart luggage, find the battery compartment at home. Do not wait until the check-in counter to discover that the “removable” battery requires a tiny screwdriver, a prayer and the patience of a saint.

The drone or camera body may be allowed in checked luggage by some airlines, but spare lithium batteries should be removed and carried in the cabin.

Spare camera batteries and drone batteries should be individually protected so the terminals cannot touch metal or each other. Use the original packaging, a battery case, a protective pouch or tape over exposed terminals.

If you travel with several batteries for photography or video work, check your airline’s quantity limits before you fly. Battery rules can be stricter for professional video gear and larger drone batteries.

Loose batteries should never be thrown into a bag with coins, keys, jewellery, cables or other metal objects. Battery terminals can short-circuit if they touch metal.

This is especially important for camera batteries, drone batteries and loose rechargeable cells.

Do not travel with a battery that is swollen, cracked, leaking, unusually hot, damaged or recalled.

A swollen power bank is not “probably fine.” It is a damaged battery and should be taken to an appropriate recycling or disposal location.

Before flying with an older power bank, check the model number and look for current recall notices from the manufacturer or your government recall site. Some recalled power banks may be prohibited onboard entirely.

If a battery looks questionable, leave it at home. Replacing a charger is cheaper than dealing with a safety incident at the airport.

If a battery or device becomes hot, starts swelling, smokes, sparks or smells strange during a flight, tell the cabin crew immediately.

Do not put it in the overhead bin. Do not hide it in a bag. Do not take it to the washroom. Cabin crew are trained to respond to battery incidents, but they need to know right away.

The goal is not to handle the problem yourself. The goal is to alert the people trained to deal with it.

Before leaving for the airport, do this quick check:

This takes less than two minutes and can prevent a pulled bag, confiscated item or airport delay.

Before you check a suitcase or hand over a carry-on at the gate, make sure:

Before you check any bag, open it and look for batteries.

Power banks, portable chargers, spare batteries and removable lithium batteries stay with you in the cabin. Phones, laptops, tablets and cameras are usually safer in your carry-on. If your carry-on gets taken at the gate, remove your battery pouch before the bag goes underneath the plane.

The goal is not to stop travelling with electronics. The goal is to stop packing them on autopilot.

A two-minute battery check before every flight can save your bag, your gear and possibly your travel day.

#6249. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

#6248. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6247. Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas.  You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

Basically, it takes everything in the Unlimited Plan (unlimited data, hotspot, phone number, 160+ destinations) and adds a a small travel insurance component that ib:

How much does it cost? Ultra is $90.95 a month if you pay monthly, $82.65 a month on the quarterly plan, or $73.41 a month if you pay yearly. For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. A single doctor visit abroad, or one session with a psychologist, nutritionist, or personal trainer, can easily cost more than that. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

Getting set up takes a couple of minutes, not a couple of hours:

If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. However, if you’re a frequent traveler who is in and out of multiple countries within a given month or a digital nomad who needs reliable, ongoing connectivity for work, not just casual browsing, then get Holafly Plans. It’s easier and will save you money in the long run.

****Holafly plans make life easier if you’re a long-term traveler. You don’t have to swap SIM cards, you get unlimited data, and you get a phone number. It’s the closest thing to a traditional phone plan that is out there but without any huge costs or data caps.

And, as someone who roams the world a lot and uses a lot of data, especially to stream video and use my phone as a hotspot, these plans save me a ton of money!

If you’re roaming the world and plan to be out of your home country for a while, this is the product to get!

Is Holafly Plans different from a regular Holafly eSIM? Yes. Regular Holafly eSIMs are one-off purchases for a single trip or destination (200+ available). Holafly Plans is an ongoing global subscription for people who are more or less always traveling.

Does Always On cost extra? No. It’s included automatically with every Holafly Plans subscription and keeps giving you 1GB of backup data a month across 150+ destinations even after you cancel.

Can I switch between Light and Unlimited? You’d need to cancel your current plan and purchase the other tier — there’s no in-place upgrade yet.

What if I don’t like it? Holafly backs Plans with a 6-month refund policy, which is more generous than most eSIM companies offer.

#6246. The Best New Restaurants in NYC Come in All Cuisines and Sizes

New York City has a new restaurant flinging its doors open seemingly every hour—and that's on top of the time-worn institutions, from old-school steakhouses and delis to bagel shops run by the same family for decades.

When it comes to the new, we're spoiled for choice: One week, it's a fabulous Korean small-plates bar with a commendable natural wine list downtown; the next it's an imported taverna from Argentina in the Village where the steaks are juicy as hell and, well, there's even more great wine to work your way through. To help you parse through all the opening news and find the buzzy spots worth fighting for a reservation at, our editors are eating out night after night, trying new Mexican mariscos joints and modern Indian fine-dining spots, to report back on the ones that stand out.

This is our Fall 2026 status report on the best of the new—the places to try your luck walking into, or commit to a Friday night dinner at, whether you're a NYC local or a visitor in town for just the weekend. These are the best new restaurants in New York right now.

The best new restaurants in New York City stretch across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Staten Island. Every business on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has personally tried the restaurant in question. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of the city. We’re always looking for standout dishes, a great location, and warm service—as well as serious sustainability credentials. In terms of how we define ‘new,’ we've chosen to focus on restaurants that have opened within a year of the publish date. When you work your way through the list, check back in: We'll update this guide regularly as new restaurants open in New York City.

Read our complete New York City travel guide here, which includes:

This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: Martini hour and Shrimp Voodoo

After around seven years of living in Williamsburg, I’ve finally found the moody, cozy refuge this pocket of the neighborhood was missing. Booth’s Extra Fine, which just opened on October 9, feels like a sexy little secret. Hidden behind discreet oxblood curtains, the space simulates a vintage 20th-century supper club with dark walnut, rich leather booths, and deep, amber, brain-massage-like lighting. The heart of the restaurant stems from chef Nick Pfannerstill’s grandfather, Booth—an effortlessly stylish Milwaukee car salesman whose 1920s-50s photos line the walls.

Lean into the nostalgia and splurge on the porterhouse steak for two (or three—it's massive), but don't skip the Caviar Royale or the chef’s-kiss Shrimp Voodoo appetizer, cooked and swimming in Creole garlic butter. Personally? I can't wait to return and try the dry-aged Extra Fine Burger and a nice martini. Speaking of martinis, look out for Booth's "martini hour" launching soon, putting $12 cocktails—gin or vodka—at your disposal. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

Neighborhood: Hudson Yards, ManhattanGo for: A standout egg curry

Indienne, a tasting-menu-driven Indian restaurant, comes from chef Sujan Sarkar, who has worked in kitchens across Mumbai, New York, and San Francisco and runs a Michelin-starred restaurant of the same name in Chicago. Sarkar’s shtick? In his words: he reimagines Indian cuisine by “blending classical Indian flavors with refined European technique.” Think: deconstructed and then reconstructed. It takes a couple of courses to get a feel for what Sarkar is doing. The dhokla, for instance, isn’t spongy; it’s cubed, dehydrated, crackly, and tinged with white chocolate. The zingy passionfruit pani puri arrives in the shape of an oyster shell over reindeer moss. But once you get past the initial surprises, things really pick up. The “egg curry”—a whole steamed egg sitting on top of curry foam encrusted with potato sev and topped with caviar, served with buttery babka pao and house-churned butter—is an absolute standout. Things get a little more traditional with the chicken makhani that my husband got: chicken, three ways (chicken breast topped with spiced chicken mince wrapped over malai mousseline), served with buttery dal and even butterier naan. I didn’t miss the meat for a second, being on the vegetarian tasting menu myself, because my celeriac kebab was smoky and melt-in-your-mouth. And then came another surprise: the ghewar, a traditional Indian sweet that arrived like a mini layer cake with edible gold leaf (there’s a lot of this) and a bouncy coconut foam. A Penicillin-adjacent drink made with apricot whisky, mead, and ginger kept me company along the way. As we left, we were shown Sarkar’s other venture in the same premises, the British-Indian chophouse Elder, that was busy on a Tuesday night. —Arati Menon, global digital director

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ribeye among many other things

From the man (Pablo Rivero) behind one of Buenos Aires's most iconic steakhouses (Don Julio) comes Graciela—an Argentine tavern on a cozy corner in the West Village, where the wine list is long and commendable, the food is fire-cooked, and the room is star-studded in that quiet, in-the-know way. All the hype made me suspicious, but if you're expecting a Corner Store or Carbone experience, this is not that. It's just fantastic cooking that is elevated and pristinely executed enough to be covetable, with an experience that stays focused on the food. And the space, with dried herbs hanging from the ceiling and heavy wooden furniture and warm, low light, feels both moody and inviting; cool yet welcoming.

It's easy to rack up a major bill here, because every corner of the menu is worth exploring—from a red pepper dip with wood-fired oven-made bread, to the sliced bondiola coppa with lemon zest and olive oil (a very true must), to, of course, the salty, sizzling steaks. (The iconic whole tomato starter has been lost to the turning of the seasons, but I am certain something autumnal will replace it.) Some flavors are more complex, but much of what you'll find are crowd-pleasers, like the milanesa neapolitana which our serve aptly described as being "like a pizza milanesa" which is impossible to complain about. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Roti, actually, to accompany the beef cheek panang curry

The preponderance of new restaurants in the West Village specifically should be studied—sometimes it feels like we could dedicate a whole list to that neighborhood alone. The best of them, like Hommali, take the cuisine of choice and present it in an eminently stylish, upscale dining room. Every time I asked general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin where something—the stemware, any number of the vividly colorful paintings on the walls—had come from, the answer was JJ Market, or Chatuchak Weekend Market, in Bangkok. It just looks good in there, I can't stress it enough. And then there's the matter of the food, which is buoyant, delightful, and oftentimes a wonderful introduction to Thai flavors for many Americans. I'm talking about a cold tom yum seafood cocktail, a heavily-spiced beef tartare on tripe cracker, and tao jiew lon, a fermented soybean-coconut dip scooped up with fried veggies. The mains are enormous and well-priced, and the best bite of the evening was not the beef cheek panang curry (although that was great on its own), but rather the piece of delicate roti used to scrape up the last remnants of sauce. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: SoHo, ManhattanGo for: sashimi and sake pairing

For this toro-obsessed tuna lover, Noury’s torotaku tartare topped with uni was love at first bite. As I greedily piled the pale-pink tuna belly, pillowing orange uni, and pickled yellow daikon radish with a dash of sushi rice onto a sheet of toasted nori to make a DIY handroll, I knew at once that I had reached appetizer ambrosia. And the saké pairing? Divine nectar.

I had high expectations for chef-and-sommelier duo Alex Chang and Lina Goujjane, who opened Kiko together in 2024, which I believe remains one of the city’s most underrated restaurants simply because of its isolated locale in so-called Hudson Square. Now, with Noury the pair finally has an address to match their ambitions in prime Soho, on Sullivan Street between West Houston and Prince.

While Kiko is cozy and chic, Noury is stylish and sexy. The restaurant is modeled after a Japanese “izakaya,” relaxed dining establishments that serve shareable plates and drinkable tipples. As such, small bites, raw seafood, and saké are the star, but the vibe isn’t so puritan as an omakase counter. In addition to the daily changing sashimi and futomaki, there are also non-fish entrees like the steak haché (not my favorite bite, but a popular crowd pleaser) and pork and cheese mille feuille katsu; plus a surprisingly addictive chrysanthemum salad. To pull it all together, Chef Alex tapped Joji Miwa as Noury’s chef de cuisine, whose career spans award winning restaurants like Sushi Sanshin in Osaka and Sushi Noz in New York. That’s where he first met Lina, the mastermind behind the beverage program, which includes both extremely rare and accessible sakes and a selection of shochu cocktails and refined spirit-free options. Like at Kiko, the service at Noury is knowledgeable and their hospitality kind. Come. Eat. Drink. Be merry. —Hannah Towey, news editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: ox tongue

Somssi, like Arthur, is new but doesn't feel it. It's a West Village restaurant with no flash or bombast, just a short and clever menu that jumps off from operator Ahris Kim's Korean origins and a casual, dimly-lit couple of dining rooms with lace accoutrements and eclectic hanging art giving the most comfortable feeling that you're at a friend's supper club rather than a sterling food and beverage operation. There's the semi-viral "Potato, Potato, Potato and Caviar" croquette, which is what it sounds like and will appeal to all, but more fun is to be had with things like the Grilled Ox Tongue, which comes undisguised as such on the plate with its uneven triangular shape atop romesco. I only gagged once while eating it, when my teeth came too close to my own tongue and I thought too hard about what I was eating, but then quickly continued my feast for love of the novel and tender dish. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Nolita, ManhattanGo for: crudo spotted with stracciatella and a late night

It was fitting that I ended up at Tashca just a few days after returning from Portugal, because I could fully appreciate how plucked-from-Lisbon this special spot in the LES is. Open only on Thursdays (the space is available for private events on other nights), this breezy little restaurant feels like being at a friend’s slightly chaotic but very endearing dinner party. Your table may or may not be ready when it’s supposed to be (we were given sparkling wine when ours took 30 minutes longer than planned, which is a trade I would have willingly made), and on that note, all reservations are made by Instagram DM (and you will need one; I saw several walk-in hopefuls turned away). But when you do flit through the open doors into the dining room, you won’t want to leave. Candles burn low throughout the night, and flowers hang from light fixtures—and the food, most importantly, sings, toeing the line between beauty and comfort, with distinctly Portuguese dishes that feature great seafood, bright produce, and a long list of tasty wines to pair. On the night I visited, there was a $95 prix-fixe made in partnership with visiting chef Joao Magalhaes Correia (who is usually in the kitchen at his Lisbon spots like Bar Alimentar). It featured a couscous bathed in squid ink and topped with a perfectly charred skewer of grilled octopus; melon draped in presunto ham; and a crudo topped with globs of stracciatella that I never could have imagined would work as well as it did. Come early, and plan to stay late. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: NoMad, ManhattanGo for: fried chicken, actually!

When the Jungsik team closed sleek offshoot Sea in NoMad in May, it wasn't to abandon ship. They worked with commendable quickness to open a new concept, Mūje, by July. Like Jungsik proper, Mūje serves a tasting menu. Unlike Jungsik proper, Mūje is casual and focused on Asian food more generally rather than Korean exclusively. It's also more affordable at $150 for eight courses (Jungsik will cost you $335 for 10). There's a lot of fun to be had here with such a premise, like the tender short rib that comes with four different wraps nodding to Chinese, Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese approaches, respectively. The best bite by a mile is the chicken wing, which is insane. It comes deboned and stuffed with pork, a Chinese technique, but is fried with the Korean Prinkle seasoning (a combination of cheese and onion and other good stuff) to create something really special. You only get one, so savor it. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Greenpoint, BrooklynGo for: an immaculate and affordable champagne list, plus the half chicken of the moment

I loved being at Arthur. With its lively and long dining room, buoyant soundtrack of soul music, and warm service, it's a place that feels like it's been around for a long time despite having opened in April. Food and drink are reasons to visit, in equal measure. Charlotte Mirzoeff's wine list is extensive and counts the French along with the Corsican and Portuguese, with a Champagne list 30-plus bottles deep (Mirzoeff is obsessed with the stuff, wants us all to be drinking more of it, and has two options for less than $100 to help make that happen.) Kevin Finch's food is rustic and comforting, the type you want to eat on the regular, but never boring—escargot comes grilled on a skewer beneath a bed of chives so ample it looks like a wig, for example. Two favorites: the kohlrabi with anchovy, herbs aplenty, and hazelnut (sop up the sauce with the pillows of housemade brioche) and the sasso chicken, with its crispy skin served atop crispier rice. Burgerheads take note: they've got an excellent one, with dijon, blue cheese, caramelized shallots, and a thick brisket patty between a sesame seed bun, but it's only available on Wednesdays. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Dumbo, BrooklynGo for: oysters broiled with bone marrow butter

Mexican food is back in the former Gran Electrica space on Front Street, a stretch of Dumbo real estate bustling with tourists moving to and from the Brooklyn Bridge vantage point. This time, the operation is run by Alan Delgado, the chef behind Fort Greene burrito spot Los Burritos Juarez, with drinks from bartender Ivy Mix. The great backyard garden patio remains, although I enjoyed my meal in the front dining room, which manages a moody mise en scène with its terracotta walls and glowing light despite lovely, huge windows overlooking the street and its passersby. Mix's beverages are stellar and inventive, in particular the rotating micheladas and frozen beverages that are tart and perfect. On the food front, the must-order comes first in the oysters, which are broiled a delicious brown color in bone marrow, and arrive bubbling. It's the perfectly decadent start. People talk about the fish tacos in particular, but I preferred the suadero, a confit brisket with guac on a corn tortillas rather than the flour Delgado is known for (and which can be purchased plain on the side, something I recommend.) There are flashier entrees, but the Chile Colorado—a braised pork shoulder with pinto beans and pickled onions that takes on a stew-like consistency, is subtly smoky, extremely filling, and something I'll be returning for. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

Neighborhood: Williamsburg, BrooklynGo for: potato bread, celery salad, and a breezy dining room

In the location of the former Llama Inn, a beloved modern Peruvian eatery in Williamsburg, the new Cafe Bar J.F. has arrived. Despite a name that feels designed to be confused and/or forgotten (both of which I keep experiencing), the space inside—and the food they serve—is an honorable replacement for Llama Inn. The concept, which comes from the Llama Inn team and is spearheaded by chef Francisco Castillo, is a “South American Tavern”. To me? It feels like eating at one of the many breezy, design-eyed restaurants I love to splurge at in Lima or Buenos Aires, with dishes that build on beloved foundations like ceviche and asado. Madrid-based Plantea Estudio has elevated the room from the plant-filled corner it once was to a more demure combo of dark-wood and metal furniture (and while the rooftop remains open, the interior is so lovely I chose to stay indoors). The prices will get ya if you don’t pay attention, but certain items—the potato bread and the celery salad, two surprising ones—really lingered. Go for a date night, or a celebratory dinner with a friend, and take the excuse to work through the satisfying cocktail menu. —Megan Spurrell, senior features editor

Neighborhood: The West Village, ManhattanGo for: Guinness, oysters, and whatever seafood special is on the chalkboard

My friend Sarah put it best. There we were—me leaning back in a booth, she perched on a stool—at Dean's, the lively new pub from King team leaders Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi, the windows flung open in celebration of one of spring's first sunny days, and she says, “This feels like what the Hamptons is supposed to be like.” The parts that make it so: a location in the Village and the according clientele, nautical stylings (lots of dark wood and blues of the navy variety), abundant seafood done the British way. All to say that, somehow, we felt as though we'd stumbled into something of a seafood shack. The halcyon weather won't be a constant, of course, but the place will do just as well comforting the cold in winter with its pies and beers—the stargazy pie, a hopefully perennial special, is strikingly fish-forward when it appears on your plate, head and tail of a milky-eyed mackerel protruding. Whether or not you eat its eyeballs, the rest of the dish beneath the buttery crust is basically chowder, not at all intimidating but very much delicious. It's also rather heavy, so if you want to try as many dishes as possible while also downing excellent Guinness pour after excellent Guinness pour, perhaps stick to such happy hits as the oysters, fish and chips, and scallops in malt vinegar. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6245. United Airlines CEO Accuses Boeing And Airbus Of Colluding To Avoid Building New Planes

Scott Kirby says Boeing and Airbus have quietly agreed not to develop new aircraft because neither faces enough competition to force its hand. I understand his frustration with the slow pace of aircraft development, but that is a substantial allegation, and the United Airlines CEO’s argument overlooks both an airplane his own airline ordered and the competition concerns he dismisses when discussing airline mergers.

I have already discussed Scott Kirby’s appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast with John Collison and Ben Thompson. The full conversation is worth a listen, even if I disagree with some of his conclusions. As always, Kirby offers a remarkably candid look at how he thinks about the airline business.

One exchange that deserves a closer look concerns Boeing and Airbus, the lack of an all-new Boeing 757 replacement, and whether the aircraft manufacturers have become too comfortable with their position in the market.

In the interview, Kirby argues that the Boeing–Airbus duopoly has weakened the incentive to invest in new aircraft. He says:

“I think the fundamental problem is Boeing and Airbus have a global duopoly, and they have quietly, not officially agreed, but they have quietly agreed: ‘Neither one of us will invest in new airframes.’”

He attributes that reluctance partly to investors and says he has spent more than two decades asking for a 757 replacement. His proposed remedy is another aircraft manufacturer to challenge the incumbents.

First, that is quite a serious accusation. Kirby does not present evidence of an agreement during this exchange. Two companies independently deciding that an expensive development program does not offer an attractive return is different from agreeing to avoid competing. I can accept that limited competition may reduce the urgency to invest. But that does not establish collusion.

There is also a rather large omission from this argument: Airbus has developed a functional replacement for the Boeing 757.

The A321neo family fills much of that commercial role, with the A321LR and especially the A321XLR extending it to longer routes. These are not identical aircraft with interchangeable capabilities in every operating condition and I concede that an A321XLR does not solve every requirement an airline might have for replacing both 757s and larger 767s.

But it is difficult to argue that Airbus simply refused to answer the 757 replacement question.

In fact, United announced its order for 50 A321XLRs in December 2019 specifically to begin replacing its Boeing 757-200 fleet. Its own announcement described the aircraft as an “ideal one-for-one replacement” for older aircraft on certain intercontinental routes.

Airbus advertises a range of up to 4,700 nautical miles for the XLR, opening longer routes with single-aisle economics (though it seems the actual range is much shorter…)

An aircraft does not have to be designed from scratch to represent innovation. Improving an existing platform’s efficiency and extending the routes it can economically operate can achieve the same goal. Kirby may want something substantially better–he mentioned the superior efficiency of delta wing design (a triangular wing shape) like the SR-71–I would welcome that too. But wanting a more ambitious airplane does not mean show collusion or that Airbus has not already offered a 757 replacement.

This debate also brought me back to two stories I wrote seven years ago.

In July 2019, I covered United’s push for clarity on Boeing’s proposed new midmarket airplane, commonly called the 797. I wrote:

“Boeing is still studying the business case for the NMA, but has shifted the bulk of its attention to the troubled 737 MAX program.”

That same story identified the A321XLR as Airbus’ answer to United’s replacement needs.

Two months later, I covered Delta’s interest in the proposed 797, including its substantial need to replace aging 757s and 767s. Boeing’s MAX crisis was already consuming attention and engineering resources. Meanwhile, Airbus was securing XLR orders.

“But Boeing’s pain has been Airbus’ gain.”

That sounds like competition to me, even if Boeing failed to offer the product its airline customers wanted.

There is ample room to criticize Boeing’s priorities. But a company struggling with its existing aircraft programs may lack the resources or appetite to launch another enormously expensive one. It may also conclude that the potential market does not justify the investment.

Neither explanation requires a quiet agreement with Airbus.

Finally, one more thought on competition.

Kirby recognizes that when United has fewer suppliers to choose from, those suppliers may feel less pressure to deliver the products United wants. Another competitor could force them to work harder for his business.

But when I apply similar reasoning to his proposed merger with American Airlines, Kirby wants us to focus on the benefits of a larger network and a better airline.

Aircraft manufacturing and airline operations have different economics. Adding a manufacturer is an immense undertaking, and combining airlines can create useful connections. I do not suggest that the two markets are identical.

Nevertheless, the underlying concern is common: customers lose bargaining power when credible alternatives disappear.

If United benefits from having another manufacturer compete for its aircraft orders, passengers can benefit from having American compete with United for their tickets. A larger route map does not eliminate that competitive pressure’s value.

Kirby is persuasive when explaining why he wants more choices as a customer. He is much less persuasive when explaining why we should accept fewer!

That said, I’d love to see Lockheed get back into the commercial airline business…coming soon, an L1011-800! 😉

I would welcome a compelling new aircraft that advances what airlines can offer passengers. Kirby is right to push manufacturers to do better. But the A321XLR demonstrates that development has not stopped, and Boeing’s failure to launch the 797 does not establish an agreement to suppress innovation.

More fundamentally, Kirby understands why a customer should worry about too few competitors. I wish he would give that concern equal weight when the customer is buying a United Airlines ticket!

#6244. Best Things to Do in Hamilton, Ontario

A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us. Dave’s dad was born and raised in Hamilton, and Dave spent much of his childhood visiting family in the city. We’ve watched “The Hammer” change from the Steeltown we knew as kids into one of Ontario’s most interesting places to visit.

Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.

Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something new therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.

The best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario, include visiting Dundurn Castle, chasing waterfalls at Webster’s Falls and Tews Falls, hiking the Dundas Valley, exploring the Royal Botanical Gardens, walking the Waterfront Trail, visiting the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum, attending James Street Art Crawl, and eating at local favourites like Born & Raised on James Street North.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

Hamilton has a deep industrial, military, and political history. These museums and historic sites help explain how the city shaped Ontario and Canada.

Dundurn Castle is one of the top attractions in Hamilton and a great place to start if this is your first visit as this grand 1830s villa was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, who served as Premier of the United Canadas.

The house has been restored to show what life looked like in the 19th century, with guided tours and period rooms that make the history easy to understand. Admission to Dundurn Castle is by guided tour only, and the City of Hamilton notes that admission includes access to the Hamilton Military Museum on the same property.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Leave time to walk the grounds and kitchen garden however even if you are not a big museum person, the views over the bay and the historic setting make this one of Hamilton’s must-see stops.

Tickets cost $16.75 for adults and $10 for children, with children under 5 allowed in for free.

Located beside Hamilton International Airport, the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum is a must for aviation and history lovers. It houses a major collection of Canadian military aircraft, including vintage planes connected to Canada’s wartime history.

The highlight is the Avro Lancaster, one of the museum’s most famous aircraft and if you time your visit right, you may even see vintage aircraft taking off.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the museum schedule before you go as seeing one of these historic aircraft in motion is far more memorable than only viewing it on the floor.

HMCS Haida is one of Hamilton’s most unique attractions. This floating museum sits on the waterfront and lets visitors explore a former Royal Canadian Navy destroyer.

Known as “Canada’s most fightingest ship,” HMCS Haida served during the Second World War, the Korean War, and the Cold War. Walking through the ship gives you a real sense of how tight, loud, and intense life at sea must have been for the crew.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear good shoes. You’ll be climbing steep ladders and moving through narrow spaces, which is part of what makes the experience feel so real.

When staying in Hamilton, a great choice is the Holiday Inn Express on Upper James Street it’s a 15 minute walk to TD Coliseum and near some of the best dining and nightlife in Hamilton.

Housed in the restorThe Hamilton Museum of Steam & Technology is housed in a restored 1859 waterworks building and tells the story of steam power and industrial innovation in Canada.

The massive steam engines are the star of the visit. They once helped supply water to the growing city and remain an impressive reminder of Hamilton’s industrial roots.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Try to visit during a live demonstration. Seeing the machinery in action makes the museum much more interesting.

The Battle of Stoney Creek was a key moment in the War of 1812, and the site preserves that history through Battlefield House Museum and the Battlefield Monument.

The house, grounds, and monument help visitors understand how important the area was during the conflict between British, Canadian, and American forces.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Climb the monument if it is open during your visit. The view helps you understand why this location mattered strategically.

The Erland Lee Museum in Stoney Creek is a meaningful stop for anyone interested in Canadian history and women’s history. This 19th-century farmhouse is connected to the founding of the Women’s Institutes, an organization that began locally and later spread around the world.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: This is one of Hamilton’s quieter historic sites, but the story is important. It is especially worth visiting if you like places with a strong local connection.

Hamilton sits along the Niagara Escarpment, giving the city one of the best natural settings in Southern Ontario. This is where Hamilton really surprises people.

Hamilton is often called the Waterfall Capital of the World, and chasing waterfalls is one of the best things to do in the city. The region is known for having more than 100 waterfalls, many of them tucked into forested escarpment trails and conservation areas. Tourism Hamilton highlights the city’s waterfalls as one of its major outdoor draws.

Some of the most popular waterfalls include:

Webster’s Falls is one of the most famous, while Tews Falls is one of the tallest. Albion Falls is another classic stop, with water cascading over wide rock shelves.

Important Tip: Access rules, parking, shuttle systems, and reservations can change, especially at popular waterfalls. Always check the Hamilton Conservation Authority before you go.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t only chase the famous waterfalls. Tiffany Falls is beautiful and easy to reach, making it a great stop if you want a short walk without committing to a long hike.

Spencer Gorge Conservation Area is one of the best places in Hamilton for scenery. It is home to Tews Falls, Webster’s Falls, and access to the Dundas Peak viewpoint.

Dundas Peak is especially popular in autumn when the valley turns colour. The view over Dundas and the surrounding forest is one of the best in Southern Ontario.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a weekday if you can. This is one of Hamilton’s most popular outdoor areas, and it can get very busy on weekends.

The Royal Botanical Gardens, often called the RBG, is one of the top attractions in the Hamilton area. It is Canada’s largest botanical garden and includes formal gardens, nature sanctuaries, walking trails, and seasonal blooms.

The RBG is huge, so it is best to pick one or two areas instead of trying to see everything in a single visit.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you only have time for one section, start with Hendrie Park or the Rock Garden. Both are beautiful and easy to enjoy without feeling rushed.

Hamilton is a great hiking city because the Bruce Trail passes right through the area. The Dundas Valley Conservation Area also has more than enough trails for a full day outside.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Start at the Dundas Valley Trail Centre if you want an easy introduction. From there, you can connect to several trails without overcomplicating the day.

Hamilton’s waterfront has changed dramatically over the years. What was once mostly industrial has become one of the city’s best recreation areas.

Bayfront Park is one of the best places in Hamilton for a relaxed afternoon. It has walking paths, harbour views, green space, a playground, and room for families to spread out.

It is also a great place to start if you want to walk or bike along the waterfront.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Bring a picnic or grab food nearby and spend some time watching the boats in the harbour.

The Hamilton Waterfront Trail connects parks, lookout points, and harbourfront paths. It is flat, scenic, and easy to enjoy whether you are walking, cycling, or visiting with kids.

This is one of the best low-effort ways to experience Hamilton outdoors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Rent bikes if the weather is nice. The trail is easy, and stopping for ice cream along the way is part of the fun.

A harbour cruise gives you a different view of Hamilton. You’ll see the city’s industrial history, waterfront redevelopment, and working harbour from the water.

This is a good choice for visitors who want to understand the city beyond the usual attractions.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: The narrated sightseeing cruise is more interesting than you might expect also Hamilton’s harbour tells a big part of the city’s story.

ThGage Park is one of Hamilton’s classic city parks. It has gardens, walking paths, open green space, a tropical greenhouse, and seasonal events.

The Tropical Greenhouse is especially nice in winter when you want a warm escape without leaving the city especially on a cold day, the greenhouse feels like a mini vacation. It is a great stop if you are visiting Hamilton outside of waterfall season.

Hutch’s is a Hamilton-area classic. This old-school spot near the waterfront has been serving fish and chips, burgers, ice cream, and milkshakes for generations.

We have a soft spot for Hutch’s because Dave used to come here as a kid because he lived just down the road in Burlington, and her dad would take the family there as a Sunday treat.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Expect a lineup on a sunny day and order the fish and chips, but don’t skip the milkshake.

Hamilton’s arts scene is one of the biggest reasons the city feels so different today since the city still has its industrial edge, but it now mixes that with galleries, music, theatre, sports, restaurants, and street festivals.

James Street Art Crawl is one of the best things to do in Hamilton if you want to feel the city’s creative energy.

Held on the second Friday of every month, Art Crawl transforms James Street North into a street festival with galleries, shops, restaurants, artists, vendors, music, and food. The event runs from around 5 p.m. until late, and from May to October, part of James Street North becomes pedestrian-only during the event.

This is the kind of event that shows how much Hamilton has changed. It feels local, creative, casual, and welcoming. You can browse galleries, listen to live music, grab food, shop from local makers, and make a full evening of it.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Plan your visit around the second Friday of the month if you can. Start with Art Crawl, then book dinner on James Street North so you don’t have to move the car or rush across town.

The Art Gallery of Hamilton is the oldest and largest art museum in Southern Ontario. Its collection includes historical and contemporary Canadian art, with works connected to some of the country’s most important artists.

It is a great indoor activity and a strong cultural stop if you are spending time downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Give yourself at least a couple of hours. The Canadian collection is the highlight. Please verify the current admission structure on their official website.

Hamilton is a football city, and seeing the Tiger-Cats play at Tim Hortons Field is one of the most local experiences you can have.

The CFL season usually runs from summer into fall, and the atmosphere at a Ticats game is loud, loyal, and very Hamilton.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear black and gold and join the “Oskee Wee Wee” chants, besides, even if you are not a huge football fan, the energy is infectious.

Located at Tim Hortons Field, the Canadian Football Hall of Fame celebrates the history of Canadian football and the CFL conversely it is a good add-on if you are already going to a game or visiting the stadium.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pair this with a Ticats game for the full experience.

Hess Village is one of Hamilton’s classic nightlife areas. The pedestrian-friendly cobblestone street is lined with bars, patios, restaurants, and live music spots and it is liveliest in summer when the patios are full.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Hess is great for drinks and nightlife, but for dinner we’d also look at James Street North or King William Street.

Theatre Aquarius is Hamilton’s main professional theatre company and a great option for a night out downtown.

The productions are polished, and it is a nice alternative to heading into Toronto for live theatre.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the schedule before your visit because a show here makes an easy culture-and-dinner evening.

Hamilton’s food scene has grown into one of the best in Ontario. You’ll find old-school classics, farmers’ market eats, pizza, cocktails, patios, and chef-driven restaurants.

Hamilton Farmers’ Market has been part of the city since 1837 and remains one of the best places to eat downtown.

You can find fresh produce, cheese, meat, baked goods, prepared foods, coffee, and international food stalls, plus it is a great lunch stop, especially if you are visiting the Art Gallery of Hamilton or exploring downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t just shop. Plan to eat here. It is one of the easiest ways to sample Hamilton’s food scene in one place.

Born & Raised is one of the best restaurants to pair with a visit to James Street North, as it is located right in the Art Crawl district, it is surrounded by galleries, shops, cafes, and the creative energy that makes this part of Hamilton so fun.

The restaurant was created by chef Vittorio Colacitti and focuses on bold flavours, Italian-inspired dishes, pizza, and a lively neighbourhood atmosphere. It is a great choice for dinner after Art Crawl or a night out downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are visiting during James Street Art Crawl, make a reservation if possible because the street gets busy, and this is exactly the kind of place you’ll want to settle into after walking the galleries.

King William Street has become one of Hamilton’s best dining areas, with restaurants, patios, and cocktail spots packed into a walkable downtown strip especially if you want a more polished dinner, this is a good area to explore.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: King William is a great choice if you want to turn a Hamilton day trip into an evening out.

Hamilton is a great family day trip because many attractions are easy to combine. therefore good family-friendly stops include:

The key with kids is not to overpack the day. Pick one museum, one outdoor stop, and one easy food stop.

Hamilton can be a budget-friendly day trip if you plan it well.

Always check parking and reservation requirements before visiting waterfalls or conservation areas.

Yes, Hamilton is worth visiting because it combines waterfalls, hiking trails, museums, waterfront parks, restaurants, art galleries, and local culture in one easy day trip or weekend getaway. It has the outdoor appeal of the Niagara Escarpment, the history of an old industrial city, and the food and arts scene of a place that has reinvented itself without losing its character.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it is close enough for a full-day visit but different enough to feel like a real change of scenery. You can tour Dundurn Castle, hike to waterfalls, walk the waterfront, visit the Art Gallery of Hamilton, and end the day with dinner on James Street North.

Hamilton is best known for its industrial history, waterfalls, hiking trails, the Niagara Escarpment, arts scene, food scene, and waterfront. It is still called “Steeltown,” but today it is just as well known for outdoor adventure, creative neighbourhoods, and one of Ontario’s most underrated city breaks.

Spring, summer, and fall are the best times to visit Hamilton for waterfalls, hiking, gardens, patios, festivals, and James Street Art Crawl. Fall is especially beautiful in the Dundas Valley, while winter is better for museums, restaurants, theatre, the Royal Botanical Gardens, and indoor attractions.

A car is useful in Hamilton, especially if you want to visit waterfalls, conservation areas, Dundas, Stoney Creek, the Royal Botanical Gardens, or attractions outside downtown. Once you are downtown, areas like James Street North, King William Street, the farmers’ market, and the Art Gallery of Hamilton are much easier to explore on foot.

#6243. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…
