#6226. American Airlines Pilots Told Not To Eat The Tiramisu, Now Union Says Never Mind

UPDATE: The Allied Pilots Association has withdrawn its warning about tiramisu served in American Airlines crew meals in Phoenix. Following an investigation involving American’s safety team, Phoenix inflight staff, and the caterer, the union now says it was a false alarm.

Yesterday, APA ​Aeromedical was advised by the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office that ​a dessert ​included ​with ​some crew meals may ​have contained ​alcohol.

Out of ​an abundance of ​caution, APA issued an immediate ​advisory recommending that crewmembers ​not ​consume the dessert, ​specifically ​the ​tiramisu, ​until ​additional information ​could be obtained. ​Following coordination ​with ​AA ​Corporate ​Safety, PHX Inflight, ​the catering ​provider, and ​other ​involved ​parties, APA has confirmed ​that ​the desserts ​in question ​are safe ​to ​consume ​and ​do not pose a ​risk to ​aviation safety.

We appreciate the ​PHX ​Flight ​Office ​for promptly ​raising the concern and ​working with ​both American Airlines ​and APA to investigate the potential ​issue. The ​initial ​advisory ​was ​issued ​based on the information available ​at ​the ​time ​and ​with crew ​and ​flight ​safety ​as ​the priority. ​We appreciate your patience ​while additional fact finding ​was ​conducted.

For those pilots ​involved ​in a HIMS ​program ​we ​would like to ​use ​this ​as an opportunity to ​remind you that ​consuming ​certain ​food additives ​and extracts in large quantities may pose a ​risk to ​abstinence ​monitoring. Please consult ​the APA ​HIMS Subcommittee ​for additional ​information.

As ​always, ​please reach out to APA ​Aeromedical ​with any ​questions or ​concerns.

APA explained that its initial warning was precautionary, based on information available at the time…though I’m wondering what information

American Airlines pilots have been warned to skip the tiramisu in some crew meals out of Phoenix because it contains alcohol. That is an awkward ingredient to find in a meal provided to people who are supposed to be flying airplanes…

JonNYC shared a warning attributed to the Allied Pilots Association’s Aeromedical–HIMS Committee concerning meals supplied by American’s contracted caterer in Phoenix:

“The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays. Because the dessert is not cooked after the alcohol is added, alcohol may remain in the finished product.

“We recommend that no crew member consume this dessert.

“APA cannot determine the amount of alcohol contained in an individual serving or what effect consumption could have if a crewmember were subsequently required to undergo DOT alcohol testing.”

"PHX Crew Meal Alert – Tiramisu Containing Alcohol

The APA Aeromedical–HIMS Committee has been made aware of an issue affecting crews based in or transiting PHX.

The contracted catering provider has included tiramisu containing alcohol on some crew meal trays.…

The notice says the committee is coordinating with the Phoenix Flight Office to have the dessert removed and replaced. In the meantime, crews are advised to accept an incomplete meal rather than eat it.

Pilots who have already consumed the tiramisu and have concerns about their fitness to fly are instructed to contact their union domicile representatives immediately. The warning expressly tells them not to let schedule pressure influence that decision.

The notice does not establish that a serving would cause impairment or a failed alcohol test. The committee says it does not know the alcohol content or the potential testing consequences. But crews should not have to evaluate that uncertainty while eating an airline-provided meal!

The FAA explains that a confirmed alcohol concentration of 0.02 to 0.039 requires temporary removal from safety-sensitive duties, even though that result is not itself a federal testing violation. A confirmed result of 0.04 or greater carries more serious consequences.

American’s Phoenix caterer apparently supplied an alcohol-containing dessert in crew meals, prompting a union warning to leave it untouched while a replacement is arranged. I like tiramisu, but this is one setting where the alcohol-free version is the obvious choice. Pilots have enough to think about without wondering whether their crew meal could complicate an alcohol test…

#6225. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

#6224. We've Tested Dozens of Toiletry Bags—These Are Our Top Picks

If there's one travel truth I live by—and hold dear to my heart—it’s that a dream vacation deserves a dream toiletry bag. After all, what’s a perfectly packed carry-on without a designated home for your favorite lipstick, beloved serums, sunscreen, and all those little beauty essentials that somehow multiply before every trip? The best toiletry bags make room for the whole glam squad, without adding any more suitcase chaos to the packing equation.

On all of our worldly journeys, Condé Nast Traveler editors (myself included) have tested dozens of travel toiletry bags to find the ones worth your precious packing space, from streamlined makeup pouches for the less-is-more crowd to roomy, cleverly compartmentalized cases for those who believe in a 10-step skincare routine. It's no easy job finding the best ones: Some tear after just a few months of use, others have awkwardly sized compartments. Many are too big for a standard carry-on, while others have proven too small to fit the simplest of our travel necessities.

With wipe-clean linings and durable construction, plus smart pockets and ultra chic designs, the carefully selected, editor-tested toiletry bags that earned a spot on this list are the crème de la crème. Read on for our recommendations to keep your essentials organized and your travel beauty routine in check.

Tested by: Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? About a year now, and despite how much it’s melded to different parts of my suitcase, the leather has stayed nicely intact.

What is it best for? It's best for longer trips, when you need to carry full-size toiletries. That being said, it also works if you don’t have that much to pack, because the leather folds down however you’d like. I like that the products stay upright for the most part, so you don’t have to worry about bottles squeezing open. The shape makes it so that you can rifle through your things comfortably without dumping everything out.

How much does it hold? My entire skincare routine—cleanser, toner, moisturizer, sunscreen—plus my daily makeup. There’s even room for my vitamins too.

Tested by: Madison Flager, commerce director

How long have you been using it? I've been using this Peak Design toiletry bag for five or six years.

What is it best for? If you're in search of a toiletry bag to keep up with an extended itinerary, this is your solution: It's ideal for longer trips of five days and more. Sometimes I pack it on weekend trips too, but it's a bit bulky, so I find it better suited to checked luggage, or trips where I'll need a good amount of product.

How much does it hold? This is one of the toiletry bag's best features—it truly holds so much. Everything in my routine fits like a glove, each with a dedicated space. I usually bring along shampoo, conditioner, body wash, face wash, moisturizer, eye cream, contact solution, a toothbrush, toothpaste, and floss, plus smaller items like tweezers and nail cutters. There's an exterior pocket sized for a toothbrush, and one inside with a magnetic snap where I store a razor. Plus, there’s a hook on the outside, so you can hang it up in the bathroom.

Tested by: Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

How long have you been using it? This gem is a newer addition to my travel rotation. I've traveled with it for around two months now—and knew it had to be mine when I saw it came in a glazed dark cherry colorway. (That's now sold out, but there are loads of other fun colors to choose from in the same style.)

What is it best for? Given its spacious yet puffy, cloud-like design, the Luka bag is ideal for any trip where you have some extra room in your carry-on, or are bringing a checked bag. It's a bit bulky for a weekender or duffel bag, though I'd try to squeeze it in if I was packing light. For any of these trips, you can use the hanging clip for easy access.

How much does it hold? It's a bit deceiving just how much this toiletry bag holds—which is much more than it gives off at first glance! I bring all of my beauty products in here, from foundations to lipsticks and moisturizer galore. And though he packs way lighter than me, it can fit my partner's personal care items, too: a face buzzer, hair gel, a toothbrush, and so on. As well as the main pocket with a zippered enclosure, it has two convenient, grab-and-go side pockets as well as an enclosed compartment on the back.

Tested by: Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor How long have you been using it? I’ve had Away's large toiletry bag for just over two years now, and have been obsessed with it ever since.

What is it best for? This is my travel companion for holding my go-to skincare products and toiletries, and it comes with me on every trip. I do also keep all my everyday products in there at home, so it's proven to be always at my ready. It's so chic—especially because it has my initials embroidered on the front—and keeps everything contained. I love that it has so many interior compartments, both zippered and clear, to keep small objects like hair ties, jewelry, and Band-Aids separated from my bigger tubes and bottles.

How much does it hold? Full disclosure: I don’t travel light. But this bag truly holds so much. It fits my entire skincare routine, toothbrush case, deodorant, hair products, body wash, razor, and beyond with ease. The two halves make it easy to find a place for everything.

Tested by: Bridget Knowles, associate social media manager

How long have you been using it? Elizabeth Scarlett’s eponymous label is a London-based luxury accessories brand I discovered during a bout of retail therapy in East London eight years ago. I’ve never looked back since—it’s an unspoken “it-girl” possession.

What is it best for? For longer trips, the Wash Bag is really great to keep everything organized. It has a wipe-clean lining fit for all lotions and potions, and you can personalize it with monograms too, which makes for a great gift. For shorter trips and everyday use, I use the Everyday Pouch—which I strongly suggest adding to your cart. (It’s my life companion in many ways.)

How much does it hold? I put everything in the Wash Bag: daytime makeup, going out makeup (you get me), my nighttime routine, and my morning routine. It’s lined with pockets so you can easily organize brushes, and—I mean—my electric toothbrush even fits in it. That’s how good it is.

Tested by: Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

How long have you been using it? I've been using—and in love with—this toiletry bag for around two years now.

What is it best for? I promise, my adoration of this bag comes from more than just its good looks. I've been reaching for it nonstop to carry my very extensive skincare routine with me wherever I go—and it's made packing easier than ever. I think I've finally cracked the code to keeping my toiletries organized and ready to go whenever I am. The extra roomy toiletry bag is designed to be packed in your checked luggage, where you have more suitcase space and no restrictions on the amount of liquids you can have inside.

How much does it hold? I used to keep all of my reusable toiletry bottles and miscellaneous minis in a small storage bin underneath my bed. And when it was time to pack for a trip, I'd sift through it and decide what I needed for a particular trip. I decided to put all of my go-to toiletries inside The Kit, including cleanser, body wash, moisturizer, shampoo and conditioner, dry shampoo, tooth paste, floss, and even contact lenses. Now when it's time to travel I can easily grab the pre-packed kit and throw it right into my personal item. I don't even open it anymore to see what I need—it's already stocked up and ready to go.

Read a full review of the toiletry bag here.

How long have you been using it? I ordered this Calpak train case in unison with the aforementioned Luka toiletry bag—so around two months now.

What is it best for? With its boxy, clear, and haute look, the train case is best for extended trips where a checked bag is obvious. Otherwise, it's a superb makeup bag at home for those who don't love too many compartments, and like to have their ready products in view: The transparent panels let you quickly locate what you need without digging. (Not to mention, it looks super cute with the Luka, given the matching colorways. I'm obsessed!)

How much does it hold? When this bad boy arrived at my apartment, it was (luckily) bigger than I expected. It's tall, so it can easily hold my toner bottles, makeup brushes, and blending sponges.

At home, not only does it store my everyday beauty products, but a stock of my next-on-the-lists and just-in-cases—it's where my unopened moisturizers, different lip shades, and nail care products go. My favorite part? There's a hidden, dedicated interior organization pocket attached to the top compartment, which holds the products I wish to keep separate.

#6223. Introducing “Delta Disruptive” Class For Flights Within Florida (Hilarious SNL Skit)

Forget Delta One. Saturday Night Live has imagined another cabin for Delta Air Lines it calls “Delta Disruptive Class,” and this one addresses a problem even a lie-flat seat cannot solve: the passenger who makes everyone else’s flight miserable.

In a spoof commercial from its October 31 episode, Saturday Night Live introduces “Delta Disruptive,” a separate section for passengers whose behavior makes them particularly unwelcome elsewhere on the aircraft.

The premise is simple: instead of letting these travelers ruin the flight for everyone, put them together behind a thick plexiglass partition.

— Saturday Night Live (@nbcsnl), November 1, 2026

The fictional cabin accommodates everything from obnoxious personal habits to full-blown onboard meltdowns. There are passengers clipping toenails, fighting over seats, and shouting conspiracy theories. One customer offers a testimonial while duct-taped to her seat. A Tiffany Gomas character also makes an appearance..

Naturally, the airline presents all of this with the polished enthusiasm of a commercial announcing an exciting improvement to your travel experience.

“All Delta Disruptive flight attendants are the toughest, gayest, ex-Spirit Airlines employees who have seen much worse.”

I love how Kenan Thompson, who plays flight attendant “Kevin,” grabs an emotional support iguana and throws it off the plane. He also has a ring on every finger, lol.

The new cabin class is rolling out soon…on flights within Florida. Book now…

“Delta Disruptive” is a joke, but the desire to enjoy a flight without becoming an unwilling participant in someone else’s viral video is quite real. Part of me wishes that we could throw unruly passengers into padded part of the plane instead of diverting and costing everyone time and money.

As usual with SNL skits, the joke captures a frustrating truth about flying: as carefully as you may choose your airline seat, you cannot choose the person sitting nearby. One passenger can make an otherwise pleasant flight unbearable.

United Airlines is bringing its most premium plane to a city where it’s rarely spotted.

In January, the Chicago-based carrier will operate a few round trips between Las Vegas and Tokyo, and TPG has learned United plans to use one of its brand-new, luxe Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners on the route.

This is the posh plane United debuted earlier this year, featuring the “Elevated” interior, complete with its next-generation Polaris Suites and the extra-spacious Polaris Studios.

To score a seat on one of those aircraft, you typically have to be flying out of one of United’s major hubs like San Francisco or Houston. So far, the carrier has prioritized these planes — which have a whopping 99 premium seats — on routes to destinations where high-end seats are in high demand, like London, Singapore and Seoul.

But it will make a limited appearance on a route United doesn’t typically fly: Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Las Vegas to Narita International Airport (NRT) in Tokyo.

The occasion for the special route with the luxe plane is the 2027 Consumer Electronics Show, which is set to run in Vegas from Jan. 6 to Jan. 9.

It’s one of the biggest conventions in the city each year, which draws visitors from all over the world.

Airlines often add special temporary routes around major events — sometimes with planes fit for the occasion, such as when American Airlines sent its popular Airbus “A321T” to Sin City for the Super Bowl in 2024.

We also noted last month how carriers are leaning more heavily into major sporting events, with new and unusual routes focused on college and professional football games.

Caviar, lie-flat beds and a cool snack bar: 17 hours in United's swanky new Polaris suites

United’s 787 will certainly be a unique sight at LAS, but top rival Delta Air Lines is the U.S. airline that has historically made the biggest splash at CES.

Nearly four years ago, at that convention, Delta laid out its plans to make on-board Wi-Fi free for all SkyMiles members — a move that nearly every major U.S. carrier matched.

And in January 2025, Delta took over Vegas’ iconic Sphere for a keynote presentation by its CEO, Ed Bastian.

Delta, for its part, is also adding special routes centered around CES.

It’ll operate one-off services from Las Vegas to Hong Kong and Taipei, along with extra daily flights during the event to its hubs and its focus city, Austin.

As for United, its “Elevated” 787 service from LAS to NRT will run on three days toward the tail-end of CES: Jan. 9, 10 and 11.

United’s premium-configured 787-9 features:

Flights from Tokyo to Las Vegas (Jan. 3, 4 and 5) will be on an older Boeing 777-200ER.

#6221. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6220. Air Canada Launches 11 Long-Haul Boeing 787 Routes: See Full List Now

Air Canada is preparing to use its Boeing 787 Dreamliners on 11 routes from November 2026. Along with new destinations, the Canadian carrier will deploy the 787 on returning services and on routes currently served by other aircraft types.

Three cities will join the airline's network for the first time, namely Guangzhou (CAN), Sapporo (CTS) and Dubrovnik (DBV), while nonstop flights to Quito (UIO) will return from both Toronto and Montreal. Six routes will receive Dreamliner service during the 2026/27 winter season, with the remaining five changes to follow in May and June 2027.

Air Canada will operate the 787 from all three of its main hubs: Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and Vancouver International Airport (YVR). Its first change will be a temporary one, scheduling a handful of Boeing 787-8 flights between Toronto and Phoenix (PHX) for November only. The Dreamliner has served the route before, with the airline operating a daily 787-9 during the 2023/24 winter season.

December will then bring five additional 787 routes. From December 1, the airline's daily service between Vancouver and Cancun (CUN) will switch from the Boeing 737 MAX 8 to the 787-9, while Montreal–Quito and Toronto–Quito return with 787-8s on December 4 and 5, respectively.

Toronto–Barcelona (BCN), normally a summer route, was initially scheduled to receive three weekly 787-8 flights between December 16 and January 9. However, this will rise to up to a daily flight over the holiday period, using both the 787-8 and 787-9. Vancouver–Sapporo then launches on December 17 with three weekly Boeing 787-9 services.

The remaining five changes will take place during summer 2027. Vancouver–Guangzhou launches on May 4, followed by Montreal–Dubrovnik on May 11, with both routes operating three times weekly. Montreal–Tel Aviv (TLV) will also return with three weekly 787-9 flights in May. Toronto–Prague (PRG) and Toronto–Stockholm (ARN) will switch to the 787-9 in May and June, respectively.

At 6,340 miles (10,203 km), Vancouver–Guangzhou is the longest of the 11 routes and will become Air Canada's third destination in mainland China, joining Beijing and Shanghai. The carrier will become the only North American airline serving Guangzhou, although it will face competition from China Southern Airlines, which already flies between Guangzhou and Vancouver.

When announcing Vancouver–Sapporo, Air Canada said it would be the only nonstop connection between North America and Hokkaido. However, United Airlines has since announced it will launch a three-times-weekly 787-9 service from San Francisco on December 11, six days before Air Canada's first flight. Air Canada originally planned to use the 787-8, but its latest schedule update now shows the 787-9 operating every flight.

Dubrovnik will mark Air Canada's return to Croatia for the first time since summer 2019. The seasonal service will run until October 24, using the smaller 787-8. Meanwhile, Quito will rejoin Air Canada's network for the first time since March 2020.

The airline previously operated seasonal flights from Toronto using Air Canada Rouge Boeing 767-300s, but suspended the service at the start of the pandemic. It will become the only airline offering nonstop flights between Canada and Ecuador, flying from both Montreal and Toronto until March 2027.

They're all in Europe, Asia and South America. Find them all now!

Air Canada's Boeing 787-8 and 787-9 both offer three cabin classes, with Signature Class (business class), Premium Economy and Economy. The 787-8 has 20 Signature Class seats, 21 Premium Economy seats and 214 Economy seats, while the larger 787-9 increases capacity to 30 Signature Class, 21 Premium Economy and 247 Economy seats.

Signature Class features lie-flat business class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, giving every passenger direct aisle access. Premium Economy is set up in a 2-3-2 layout, while Economy is arranged in a 3-3-3 configuration. Air Canada currently operates 40 Boeing 787s, comprising eight 787-8s and 32 787-9s. It also has 14 Boeing 787-10s on order, with the first expected to arrive around the end of 2026.

#6219. United Airlines Adds Five Routes From San Francisco, Including Four Surprising Transcons

United Airlines is adding five routes from San Francisco next spring, including four transcontinental flights to smaller East Coast markets. The latest additions, Richmond and Norfolk, are particularly interesting because both will operate just twice weekly. United is also taking on Breeze Airways directly in Richmond.

Across two rounds of announcements in late October, United unveiled new or returning service from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) to Charleston, Hartford, Oklahoma City, Richmond, and Norfolk.

I had not yet covered the earlier additions, so let’s look at all five together:

The new routes were flagged by Ishrion Aviation.

The first round of additions, from SFO to CHS, BDL, and OKC were loaded on October 22–23.

Charleston International Airport announced its seasonal San Francisco route on October 22, listing Boeing 737-800/MAX 8 aircraft. The airport emphasized both travel to the Bay Area and connections beyond United’s West Coast hub.

Bradley International Airport followed with its announcement of daily, year-round Hartford service. Unlike Charleston’s limited weekly schedule, this represents a daily commitment to the Connecticut market.

A Boeing 737 MAX 9 will be used for Hartford and a SkyWest-operated Embraer E175 for Oklahoma City. The OKC flight will operate daily.

The newer announcements extend that expansion into Virginia. Interestingly, none of these five new routes were formally announced by United.

Richmond International Airport announced its twice-weekly service on October 30. Meanwhile, Norfolk International Airport confirms its new San Francisco flights begin March 31.

The twist on the RIC and ORF flights are the frequencies. Twice-weekly service is familiar territory for leisure-focused airlines but rather atypical of the daily-or-better schedule many passengers associate with a United hub route or that of another network carrier. That certainly suggests United is approaching these markets differently from Hartford. A Richmond traveler can choose a Thursday departure and Sunday return for a long weekend. Someone needing to travel on other days will still need a connection or another option.

The Richmond addition also creates a direct competitive overlap with Breeze Airways, which already offers nonstop service between Richmond and San Francisco.

Breeze is an annoyance to United at SFO and while Breeze is smart enough not to full Independence Air (ramping up at a major United hub too much, too fast, then going bust), I would be incredulous if Breeze did not influence United’s decision to launch this route, particularly given the twice-weekly schedule.

The bigger question is whether both airlines can make the route work over time. More competition is useful when it lasts.

Both Hartford and Charleston’s airport announcements explicitly promote those onward connections…that’s true for all five routes. Ultimately, this is just United trying to grow its network and dominance at its primary West Coast hub.

United Airlines will add or restore five San Francisco routes in March 2027, with daily service to Hartford and Oklahoma City, four weekly flights to Charleston, and twice-weekly flights to Richmond and Norfolk. Richmond brings direct competition with Breeze, while the broader expansion strengthens United’s reach into smaller domestic markets. These are less glamorous additions than another international route announcement, but quite useful as United also continues to rebuild its domestic network.

#6218. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Thatched Cottage Tucked Away in the Cotswolds

Choosing the perfect place to hole up for a weekend getaway is not always straightforward. But this spring, the decisions seemed to make themselves. After a relentlessly busy start to the year, I was looking for a place to escape. And the place needed to fit certain criteria: Somewhere my partner and I wouldn't have to speak to anyone but each other; somewhere we could sleep for 12 hours a night and take the days slow and easy without guilt; somewhere within a couple of hours’ drive from our home in northwest London; somewhere rural, where I wouldn’t be woken up by the neighbors’ bathroom light or the sound of the tube; and somewhere we could have the place to ourselves, but still be close to some nice pubs or restaurants, so we wouldn't have to hunt and gather our own dinners, God forbid.

An Airbnb in the Cotswolds was the obvious choice. Luckily, I remembered I’d saved a cozy-looking cottage on Instagram a few months prior to feeling the sudden urge to get away. I revisited my staycation wishlist and found Strawtop Cottages: two 16th-century thatched-roof cottages that sit side by side on a quiet street in the quaint little village of Adderbury. I booked one of them, Strawtop Two, for a long weekend in April.

We checked into Strawtop Two after a speedy drive from London on a Friday night. As we unlocked the front door, we found switched-on lamps casting a cozy glow across the beamed living room; kindling ready to be lit in the wood-burning fire. In the egg-yolk yellow kitchen, a fresh loaf of sourdough was sitting pretty on the chopping board for us; organic eggs and marmalade on the counter; Daylesford butter, bacon, and rosé in the fridge. My partner prepared a simple supper while I nosed around the rest of the cottage, discovering a sweet dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows and an enormous bunch of fresh flowers around the back, as well as a boot room with Barbour jackets, Wellies for stomps across the fields, and umbrellas (likely a requirement, considering we were visiting in April).

I learned that the sister properties are owned by local content creator Josie Irons (@Josieldn on Instagram) and her husband Charlie Irons (who manages the properties), who have been custodians here for just a small part of the cottages’ centuries-long history. Their meticulous renovations have restored the spaces beautifully, preserving all the Grade II-listed original features that make staying here feel like a journey back to a simpler, more peaceful time, while adding plush finishing touches that feel every bit as cosseting as those of the area’s top-of-class hotels.

I originally saved this cottage because of the kitchen, drawn in by sunshiny pictures and clips of its buttery-hued walls, vintage copper pans, and an old-school kettle whistling on the Aga stove. But as I nipped between the two bedrooms—one on the first floor with minty green walls, one folded into the eaves on the top floor with tongue-and-groove woodwork—I found there’s a lot more to love here, like the Bamford pillow mist left next to the beds, and the blackout blinds creating one of the darkest and quietest bedrooms I’ve ever drifted off in. Wrapped up in the bed linens, I snoozed more peacefully than I’d managed to in months.

After homemade coffee sipped while listening to the Roberts Radio on Saturday morning, we headed a few minutes up the road to The Yurt at Nicholsons restaurant. This was one of a handful of recommendations that Charlie had sent us ahead of time. Normally, I’m a stickler for doing my own research (read: a snob and a control freak), but in the name of keeping things as relaxed as possible, I decided to put my faith in his suggestions. I shouldn’t have hesitated: a gooey camembert croissant, cut through with umami bacon, and a full English breakfast with melty pork belly chop and smoky baked beans hit the spot.

Our supper, also recommended (and booked for us) by Charlie, at The Norman Knight was every bit as impressive. I ordered perfectly blushing steak frites and felt smugly like I’d uncovered a hidden gem. Our Sunday lunch at The Duke of Cumberland’s Head, where we shared bowls of cauliflower cheese and crispy potatoes, was one of the tastiest roasts I’ve had in a while. Trust me, having Charlie as a de facto concierge is one of the biggest unsung perks of booking a stay here.

Back at the house, we hibernated on the sofa, reading the paper and watching Netflix in the dinky living room. I took mental notes of my favorite design details: the antique coffee table laden with magazines, the books plopped into recesses in the stone chimney, the deep-green rainfall shower stocked with Bamford products, the Steamery steamer and Dyson hairdryer in the bedroom vanity, and the Soho Home robes. If I could make my London flat one-tenth as comfortable as this little countryside cottage, I’d be thrilled. For now, I’ll bookmark the cottage next door for my next escape.

A free flight is rewarding, but so is knocking $100 off your credit card bill. Cash back is less flashy, but far more straightforward: you can use it wherever your budget needs it most. The question is whether your purchases earn a forgettable 1% back or enough to make a noticeable dent in your next statement.

By matching cards to your spending and layering in welcome offers, bonus categories and card-linked deals, you can earn more cash back on purchases you were already planning to make.

Knowing how you spend your money is an important step before applying for a new cash-back credit card. Do you spend heavily on specific types of purchases, such as dining and travel? Or does your spending shift from month to month?

This is also a great time to consider what you want from your rewards credit card and how you would maximize cash-back rewards.

To understand your spending habits, take some time to review charges on any existing credit cards. Issuers like Chase assign categories to card charges, making it easy to identify what types of transactions dominate your budget.

Whether you're spending on ride-hailing services or on groceries, mapping out your spending habits will help you pick the best card.

Once you've identified how you spend, you can select a cash-back credit card that complements your typical spending habits. No single cash-back card will earn the highest rate on every purchase, but knowing this can help you compare options that coincide with your particular needs.

For those who enjoy cooking at home, a bonus-earning rate on groceries might be the best way to maximize cash-back rewards. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express is an excellent choice as it offers 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $6,000 per year; 1% cash back thereafter), all for a low $95 annual fee once the $0 introductory annual fee for the first year is up (see ).

Additionally, Blue Cash Preferred cardmembers also earn 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming services and 3% cash back on transit and at U.S. gas stations. Members receive cash back in the form of Reward Dollars that they can redeem as a statement credit and at Amazon.com checkout.

If your spending habits change from month to month, consider the Bank of America® Customized Cash Rewards credit card. Cardholders earn 6% back in the category of your choice for the first year (3% thereafter) and 2% back on grocery stores and wholesale clubs for the first $2,500 of combined bonus category and grocery spending per quarter; after hitting that threshold, you’ll earn 1% back on these purchases.

You can change your preferred choice category once per month for extra earning flexibility.

Related: Cash back vs. travel rewards: How to choose a credit card

A welcome offer can deliver a substantial chunk of cash back soon after you open a card. Before applying for any card, compare current offers and make sure the spending requirement fits the purchases you already plan to make.

The following cash-back credit cards are currently offering solid welcome bonus offers:

Customers with flexible spending habits may also want to look into cards with rotating rewards categories. These cards feature a new group of eligible merchants or spending categories each quarter. One quarter might include gas stations and electric vehicle charging, while another could feature restaurants.

The Chase Freedom Flex has no annual fee and earns a strong 5% cash back on purchases in activated bonus categories each quarter on up to $1,500 in purchases, then 1% after that. Similarly, the Discover it® Cash Back card earns 5% cash back on up to $1,500 in combined purchases each quarter in rotating bonus categories (activation required), and 1% cash back on all other purchases.

Both Chase’s rotating bonus categories and Discover’s quarterly bonus categories change throughout the year, with past lineups featuring popular merchants and spending categories such as Amazon, Target, grocery stores, drugstores and more.

Pairing a bonus-category card with a flat-rate cash-back credit card allows you to maximize your earnings where it matters most and still earn strongly on spending that falls outside of its categories.

Use a card that earns 2% cash back whenever your bonus-category card would earn less, like the Citi Double Cash. It offers 2% cash back on all purchases — 1% cash back when you make a purchase and 1% cash back as you pay for your purchases.

Many issuers offer shopping portals and card-linked deals that can stack with a card’s standard rewards.

Chase Freedom Unlimited® (see ) and Freedom Flex cardholders, for example, can access Chase's shopping portal, earning additional cash back on their purchases on top of standard rewards.

The stores on Chase's shopping portal vary and occasionally change, so it's worth checking which shop is offering a bonus and maximizing cash-back rewards.

Additionally, credit cards may provide targeted merchant offers. American Express, Chase, Capital One and Citi all have offers that can be activated via an issuer's mobile app or website to earn even more rewards. Generally, these offers have a limited redemption window, varying cash-back percentages and limits on how much cash back you can earn from each offer.

Cash back excels in its simplicity, and these strategies should provide big wins without any mental gymnastics.

Just don't skip the math entirely. Interest charges can erase months of cash back surprisingly fast, so the top strategy remains the most basic: pay your balance in full to ensure your earnings are truly a bonus.

#6216. Review: Emirates 777-300ER “Game Changer” First Class Dubai To Brussels

Seven years after my first flight in Emirates’ fully enclosed Boeing 777 first class suite, I returned to the same route and same flight, EK183, from Dubai to Brussels. The “Game Changer” suite remains extraordinary, but this flight demonstrated that even a superb seat cannot compensate for disappointing service, though perhaps my exceptions were too high? My latest review follows, with the original 2019 review preserved below for comparison.

I first reviewed this product in 2019 and came away impressed. Returning in 2026, I was curious whether it would feel quite as special after experiencing more of the world’s leading first class products. The suite certainly did. The experience around it was less consistent, especially compared with my excellent Emirates A380 flight from Mumbai to Dubai.

As I explained in the introduction to this trip report, I booked Mumbai–Dubai–Brussels for 102,000 Emirates Skywards miles and approximately $700 in taxes and fees. That included my A380 flight the day before and this flight to Brussels on a Boeing 777-300ER featuring Emirates’ “Game Changer” first class suites.

I took an Uber from my hotel to DXB. Emirates has a dedicated terminal for business and first class check-in and within area, there’s a posh first class check-in lobby.

However, with so many first class passengers, there is not the sort of personalized ground service you might experience with Air France or Lufthansa. After checking in, I was on my own to get through security, passport control, and to the lounge.

I visited both the Concourse A and Concourse B Emirates First Class lounges before my flight.

I reached the gate (further than I thought) about 30 minutes prior to scheduled departure and the flight had fully boarded, with a “final call” announcement from the gate agent and on the monitors.

I settled in onboard, noticing the cabin was booked full. What war?

The first class cabin has six suites in a 1-1-1 configuration with the middle suites having virtual windows (with a live feed of the world outside).

My suite, 1K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush “dentist” chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look…it’s just so odd that after all these years Emirates has only retrofitted nine jets with this product.

There’s also a flip-up cabinet with a mirror that houses the amenity kit skin products and a cool souvenir notebook and pen.

The suite has universal A/C, USB-A, and USB-C power (plus HDMI for those still living in 2012).

There are also plenty of lighting options.

Within the suite, you can customize your experience not only via adjusting the seat from upright to reclined to fully-flat, but you can adjust the temperature and lighting (even the color of the lighting).

I didn’t need to sleep on this daytime flight to Brussels, but I ended up taking a 4-hour nap: the bedding is superb and the 79-inch bed very comfortable in 180º lie-flat mode.

In terms of the hard product alone, this seats beats out the JAL A350-1000 suite. But of course a flight is about more than the seat, especially in first class….

Emirates’ “ICE” entertainment system includes hundreds of movies, TV shows, live TV, music, and games…more than enough for a journey around the sun, let alone a quick trip to Europe.

Noise cancelling headphones are from Bowers & Wilkins.

While this flight did not have Starlink Wi-Fi, the OnAir internet was complimentary and worked reasonably well, even if it felt more like dial-up than high speed.

It was also a lovely day just to look out the window, especially as we neared Brussels.

Upon boarding, I was offered a refreshing glass of Champagne and chose Dom Rosé 2010.

Menus were distributed prior to pushback, with a la carte breakfast and lunch choices available throughout the flight. along with an exceptional collection of wine and spirits plus a “movie snack bar” menu.

I thought the breakfast choices were limited. My omelet was fine, but I’ve had much better omelets on other carriers and even had a better one out of Mumbai on Emirates the day before.

Service began with fresh fruit, a cappuccino, orange juice (with ice cubes?), rhubarb yogurt, and delicious bakery items like a cinnamon bun and almond croissant.

The omelet had beans, potatoes, and cooked spinach with it…utterly forgettable.

After waking up from extended nap, it was time for the main feast. While my meal was being prepared, I was offered mix nuts and hydrated with some sparkling water.

The caviar course was excellent and I had more Dom Pérignon Rosé with it.

Next came fabulous Arabic mezze with humus, grape leaves, tabbouleh, falafel, kibbeh, and fattoush salad..everything was great.

With time running out, I skipped the soup and went right for my main course: pan-fried lamb loin and cutlet, served with olive caramel sauce, tomato fondue, beetroot jus, potato pavé with pistachio dukkah-crusted kale, and blanched sugar snap peas.

Sadly, it was so overdone that I did not finish it. However, I did enjoy some excellent garlic bread and red wine (a Bibi Graetz Colore 2015 from Tuscany) with it.

Lunch ended with a cheese course and chocolate truffle cake (with roasted hazelnuts and pistachios). The cheese included:

The “new” 777 has two lavatories in the front of the cabin, shared by crew. They are spacious, though not like upstairs on the A380:

I was never proactively offered an amenity kit. When we landed, I asked about it and was told, “They are on request only.” So be aware of that…

Slippers and pajamas (what Emirates class loungewear) was proactively offered. I took size medium, which fit me (I’m 6’1″) and was very comfortable.

As I mentioned above, skin products from Byredo were present in the suite.

I’ll repeat what I wrote in my first impressions of this flight.

After breakfast, my dishes sat for over 20 minute untouched. Not the service I was expecting.

I woke up a couple hours before landing for the meal and was totally ignored for almost 30 minutes (and my suite door was open). I realize that I could have just pressed the call button (and eventually did), but I don’t think that should be necessary in first class…I think that the FAs should have been far more proactive in monitoring the cabins.

When I did call the FAs to begin meal service, there was 90 minutes left in the flight, which in theory should have been time for everything. I provided the full order and the caviar came quick, but once again the crew was not attentive. I finished the caviar and waited. Finally, the mezze came and I finished it…and waited. I waited and waited for the main course and it came (having been left in the oven far too long).

I waited again. The captain announced our descent into Brussels. My glass was empty, my plate was pushed way, but no one was coming.

Do I really have to push the call button after I finish each course? That’s not the kind of first class service I like.

With 40 minutes left in the flight, I finally flagged a FA down and asked her to bring the cheese and dessert at once. She seemed very agitated, not in the hostile sense, but because she was so stressed…because it wasn’t only me trying to finish my lunch, but the other four in the cabin (it was booked 5/6).

She brought over the cheese and dessert and I ate it…it was fine…but I felt too guilty ordering coffee with so little time left…again, not a feeling I should have in first class. Drink refills were not offered.

The pre-arrival service could have been so much better executed. The service flow was so perfect on my A380 flight because the flight attendants took charge and proactively executed service. Not so on this flight and it wasn’t because the FAs were too busy: they were chatting in the galley.

So was it was the best flight ever? Nope. The A380 flight the day before was perfect…this one was not.

I think it’s always appropriate to mention here that I am incredibly grateful to fly first class on Emirates and this sort of “first world problem” is not meant to condemn Emirates or gripe so much as it is to offer an honest comparison between this and other premium cabin products. Comparatively speaking, Emirates fell short here.

Despite the questionable service, what a pleasure it was to fly on this product and enjoy the beautiful suite and multi-course meals. I look forward to doing this again. Next time, though, I think I’ll skip breakfast and just have one meal in the middle of the flight.

The review below was originally published on June 7, 2019, and covers my earlier flight from Dubai to Brussels.

I booked my ticket from Dubai to Brussels a couple night before the trip using Emirates Skywards. The points transfer on a 1:1 basis from American Express Membership Rewards and the trip cost 85,000 miles and about $420 in taxes/fees. The same trip would have been 75,000 miles with Qantas, which has now been added as an American Express transfer partner.

I began the day with a 4:00 A.M. cab ride to Dubai International Airport from the Park Hyatt. Although I tired to sleep, I was too excited for the upcoming journey. Pulling up to the Emirates premium class check-in area Dubai, a line of uniformed staff were waiting to assist with luggage, but today I was traveling only with hand baggage.

Inside, I  found myself the only passenger in a huge terminal…it felt a bit surreal. After checking in, I proceeded down a long hallway toward the security checkpoint and passport control.

After a couple hours in the first class lounge, I headed to the gate for boarding, which began ahead of schedule about an hour prior to takeoff.

B1 is used for aircraft departing from remote stands and passengers were being funneled down a single escalator and onto a waiting bus. I tried to board but was told to wait and that first class boarding would begin “soon”. So I waited. And waited. And waited. 25 minutes passed. I was getting antsy. So were the three other first class passengers. We were the only ones left in the gate area.

Finally, we were invited to head downstairs where our “first class” bus was awaiting. I don’t know if “first class” was the right word, but the bus was very comfortable. We soon began what turned out to be a 15-minute bus ride to the aircraft…which seemed to be parked in Abu Dhabi (I jest…). Upon reaching the aircraft, we were invited to carry our own bags up the fairly steep air stairs onto the 777-300ER that would shortly be departing for Brussels.

Onboard, three FAs were waiting at the door. After a warm welcome, one escorted me to my suite.

I was grinning ear-to-ear as I stepped into the beautiful six-seat cabin. Wow, this was spacious! The cabin is arranged in a 1-1-1 configuration with four window/aisle suites and two suites in the middle, one with an entrance on aisle one and the other with an entrance on aisle two.

My suite, 2K, included a large table, screen, closet, cabinet for hand luggage, and an oversized, plush chair. Sounds simple enough, but the accents were tremendous and I loved that Emirates’ latest first class cabin has ditched most (but not all) of the gold bling for a more refined look.

What I appreciated most about this new cabin was the attention to detail Emirates placed in making it practical. For example, my rollerboard carry-on fit perfectly in the cabinet, which was so much more convenient and aesthetically pleasing than having to leave it under the ottoman (like in Singapore or Etihad First Class) or store it in a closet (Lufthansa First Class) or overhead bin (Air France First Class).

There was also a closet that easily accommodated my garment bag and clothes on a hangar and smaller storage cabinets along the window.

A power port and USB charger was conveniently located within arm’s reach, as was a USB-C charger (which my laptop has…).

Adjacent to my seat was a touch panel that allowed for control of the lighting (including customizable mood lighting) and the temperature of the suite. The armrest also had a four-button seat control.

In addition the drink cabinet, there was a basket with snacks sitting on the table along with beautiful orchids:

But the attention to detail went even further. The careful stitching on the seat and embroidered Ghaf (prosopis cineraria) tree above the window further showed how much thought Emirates put into this cabin. And the overhead lights were shaped like diamonds.

Each suite had binoculars to look out. These were not souvenirs; FAs collected them as we approached Brussels.

The suite across the aisle from me stayed vacant, so I had a chance to check out the “fake” windows”. Kudos to Emirates for trying, but I was not impressed.

I structured the flight around a nap…not because I wanted to sleep through a pricey flight, but because I slept poorly the previous two nights and wanted to try out the bed and bedding.

Thus, shortly after my post-takeoff breakfast flight attendants prepared the bed for me while I changed into my pajamas. The bedding is simply tremendous, with a satin-like finish that was soft and so comfortable.

Window shades lower by button (sheer blinds and blackout) but Emirates also added real curtains. While I figured these were purely for aesthetic reasons, light seeped through one of my three windows so it turns out the curtains were quite practical.

The only annoying thing was that I could not figure out how to shut off the small band of blue light overhead:

I slept for about 3.5 hours, asking the FAs to shake me awake with about two hours to go until landing.

Prior to pushback, I was offered a drink of choice and chose orange juice, which was freshly-squeezed. Later on in the boarding process, I was also offered Arabic coffee and a choice of dates.

After takeoff, I examined the menu for today’s flight:

Having had steak for “breakfast” I was actually in the mood for some eggs, but only a light continental breakfast was offered. No problem…I wasn’t all that hungry. The purser, Ashwin, came by to introduce himself and took my breakfast order. I just wanted some fruit and yogurt along with a cappuccino. Almost immediately, my table was prepared by Tetiana and I was offered more orange juice along with a basket of warmed breakfast breads.

The table folds out from the console in front:

Mixed nuts were also offered and I enjoyed a glass of Dom Pérignon 2008 Champagne.

I do try to stay away from these fatty carbs, but the croissants smelled so good I ended up eating two of them…and some danish. So much for my light breakfast…

The fruit, yogurt, and cappuccino (notice the chocolate powder stencil art is the Emirates logo?) were all tasty and the whole breakfast service took only about 20 minutes. I still had plenty of time for sleep and a big feast prior to landing.

I was presented with a hot towel after my breakfast dishes were cleared.

After my nap, Tetiana again set up my tray table for lunch.

Hot bread from the oven and my favorite Isigny Sainte-Mère butter from France were offered.

I started the meal off with some more Dom, though this time some Dom Pérignon Rose 2006. It was served at the perfect temperature and was a spectacular accompaniment to the meal which would follow.

I began with caviar, admittedly more so for the trip report than because I felt like it. Still, I ate it and enjoyed it. I appreciated that Emirates warmed the blinis.

While I was eating my soup, Maria brought over my next course, a green salad with French dressing.

For my main course, I ordered a beef filet with asparagus and boiled potatoes. The dish was beautifully presented and the asparagus with truffle hollandaise sauce was spectacular…even better than Lufthansa First Class.

But the beef filet? Not so much…it was served beyond well-done and I ended up only nibbling at it. Such a shame that it was served overcooked. Tetiana was concerned that I did not eat and offered to bring me something else, but by this point I was already full and there were still two courses left.

As you can read in the menu above, the cheese course was quite extensive. I had a sample of each piece, but could not finish it.

Finally, I completed my meal with warm chocolate cake with raspberry sauce and another cappuccino.

Kudos to Emirates for an excellent dining experience in first class.

Emirates does not offer amenity kits on daytime flights. That said, there were several toiletries available in the lavatory and a box at each seat contained Byredo (Swedish) amenities like eye cream and skin toner. The amenities were “hidden” away in a cabinet along the table that folded up to reveal a mirror with lights. A leather-bound notebook and writing pen were also present.

Pajamas were available by request. Emirates uses “breathing” pajamas that are supposed to help the body stay ventilated. While that may just be a gimmick , I loved the soft pajamas and they have become my new favorite airline pajamas…my old favorites were also from Emirates.

Finally, the slippers were also quite comfortable and also large enough for my feet.

Ok, this is what surprised me the most. I knew the flight would have wireless internet, but like all (and I do mean ALL) my previous Emirates flights, I just assumed it would not work. Boy was I wrong. Not only was the internet functional and free (as a Skywards member), it was FAST!

Make sure your Skywards number is associated with your reservation in order to take advantage of the complimentary wi-fi.

On the other hand, the IFE was no surprise. I knew Emirates would offer a comprehensive library of movies, TV shows, live TV, games, and music and of course it did. There were even two cameras to allow for live views from outside.

What did impress me, however, was the wireless remote in the suite and the detachable tablet that served as a secondary IFE device, especially suited for games and music. When detached, it was totally wireless and also controlled the seat, could summon FAs via video conference for service, and easily controlled my customized soundtracks.

Newspapers were offered prior to takeoff.

Lastly, the Bowers & Wilkins noise-cancelling headphones were comfortable and worked very well.

Two first class lavatories were compact, but kept very clean and offered towels, Buglari toiletries, and other amenities like toothbrushes and combs. There were even little bars of soap like airlines used to offer decades ago.

Tetiana, Maria, and Ashwin provided excellent service from start to finish. Tetiana and Maria primarily took care of me and were not only lovely and charming, but highly polished. I appreciated how precisely the table was set, drinks were poured, and food served. I never had to wait long between courses and plates and utensils were always promptly cleared. Throughout the flight, I was addressed by last name.

Upon landing in Brussels I requested a picture of the flight crew and they happily obliged:

The only problem with this flight was that it ended so quickly. 6.5 hours was not enough time to fully enjoy the wonderful hard and soft product onboard. I was simply ecstatic throughout the flight…Emirates takes first class to a whole new level.

Was this my best first class flight ever? I don’t know if I’d go that far, but it was absolutely the best first class hard product (suite) I have ever experienced. While the old Emirates suite is still very nice, the new suite is even more spacious, even more comfortable, and even more cutting-edge.

Emirates has room for improvement with its first class ground product, but its in-air product is top-notch.

Awesome photos!!! That suite looked very spacious. I agree with you that 6.5 hours doesn’t seem to be that long. I hope EK will have this hard product on their A380s someday or at least have their 777 planes with the new F fly ultra longhaul on a regular basis.

You didn’t try the ’01 Mouton Rothschild? Epic fail!

The Rolex of wines – good quality and carefully made, but prices are sky-high because it’s collected by fanatics and therefore maintains a certain mystique. There are more interesting wines out there for less money.

Curious, why do you not like the video windows?

Thank you very much Matthew. I am overwhelmed seeing the great pictures you took on our flight. It was a pleasure having you as a guest on-board. I hope i’ll welcome you again soon on one of our trips again. Regards Ashwin.

These are great photos. Did you use a wide-angle? What camera?

Matthew my wife and I are travelling with Emirates from Brisbane to Madrid First Class. We are flying from Brisbane to Dubai on a 777-300ER are you aware if Emirates have upgraded their 777 from Brisbane. From Dubai to Madrid we are in an A380 in First Class we have flown in the A380 First Class before but not the 777. From your review we are hoping for the upgraded 777 experience.

Sadly, it looks like your 777 will have the old first class. It won’t be so bad, though. 😉

Hi Matthew Late posting but I wonder can you help? Flying from Singapore Dublin via Dubai on 10 March. Have a few options on that day to Dubai. Any new 777’s on the route? Also if I take the morning one I have 1.30 transfer time in Dubai. Do they offer any ground service? I’ve never had any help on the ground before but never had such a short transfer

Hi Annie, new first class does not operate to Singapore at this time. Ground services are lacking in Dubai. You’ll have lounge access, but no escort from flight to lounge to flight. If you are departing from a remote stand, you’ll have a private bus.

Matthew, Thanks for the comprehensive review…. notwithstanding the envy I have for your flight. My question is a very mundane item (although I consider it to have enough weight to differentiate EK’s new F suite), since the suite is totally enclosed and you are able to control the suite temperature… how cool and how warm can the suite be set? Regards

Michael, I prefer cool cabins (with heated seated if available…not here, unfortunately) and I noticed my suite was noticeably cooler than the aisle/lavatory.

Do they not board out of the lounge for the 777? When I took the A380 we boarded out of the lounge.

I’ve taken this flight twice and neither times has it boarded from lounge.

#6215. Alaska Airlines Unveils Surprising New 6-Hour Nonstop Route: See Map Now

Journalist – Aaron is an aviation and travel journalist with 14 years of experience in the travel and tourism industry. His background spans airport operations, aviation infrastructure, and travel consulting, having worked with global organizations across New Zealand, Europe, and North America. Combining industry expertise with firsthand travel experience across more than 52 countries and five continents, Aaron covers airlines, airports, aviation policy, and the wider travel sector. He is based in Canterbury, New Zealand. His work has been published in Simple Flying and featured by MSN, SAM CHUI Aviation & Travel, EIN News, Pakistan Defence, and Climate Depot.

Alaska Airlines will add another nonstop international route from its Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) hub, offering a direct link to Guadalajara International Airport (GDL). The route will operate up to three times a week starting March 18 and will be served by the airline's Boeing 737-800 aircraft.

Demand for travel to the Mexican state of Jalisco remains popular for West Coast travelers, and Alaska will become the third carrier serving the city pair. Volaris and Aeromexico already operate nonstop flights to Guadalajara from Seattle.

In mid-March, oneworld alliance partner Alaska will serve Seattle to Guadalajara for the first time. The airline has never operated to Guadalajara from Seattle before, and will join the incumbent Volaris, which has been operating the route since 2016.

Aeromexico also began serving the route in 2025, and will provide stiff competition for Alaska Airlines' three-weekly service. With Alaska joining the group of airlines on the city pair, this will mark the first time three airlines have all operated the route concurrently.

Guadalajara International Airport is the third busiest airport in Mexico, and will become Alaska Airlines' third route to the airport. The airline currently maintains year-round services from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), and seasonal services from Norman Y. Mineta San Jose International Airport (SJC). The new Seattle service is expected to operate year-round. Full list of these routes with competition below:

Tickets are already on sale, with the airline's website showing passengers able to book their next trip from Seattle to Guadalajara with round-trip fares in its Saver fare for $615 return.

Outbound flights from Seattle are scheduled to depart late evening, with a five-and-a-half-hour flight time. The nonstop flight arrives in the early morning at Guadalajara the next day. The return flight departs at noon, with a late afternoon arrival back in Seattle. Full schedule as below:

For travelers, these flight times will enable a full day in Seattle before departing for Mexico, and a modest noon departure time on the return flight avoids the early morning wake-up before heading to the airport.

The two carriers have added added 4.4 million more seats to/from the city this year. Find out more here!

As captured by Enilria, Alaska will also shelve two routes to Hawaii for the upcoming winter season. Alaska will terminate its Sacramento International Airport (SMF) to Lihue (LIH) service, which it has continuously operated since April. Services from Sacramento to Kailua/Kona (KOA) are also being axed.

These changes come as the airline continues to trim and reshuffle its West Coast network. This strategy is to eliminate those underperforming and low-demand routes and optimize overall capacity with Hawaiian Airlines. Continued high operational costs as a result of increasing fuel costs have seen the airline look to streamline routes, but also drop thinner routes that experience soft demand.

These changes come in the same week that the airline also announced plans to restore an international service from Alaska to Asia, with the carrier planning to operate from Anchorage International Airport (ANC) to Tokyo Narita Airport (NRT) starting next year.

Here in New York City, it's one of the absolute best weekends of the year: Halloween and the New York City Marathon. Last year, a team of TPG staff came out to the race to cheer me on while I ran, which was a very caring way for my work family to spend their free time.

And speaking of free time, Club Med recently commissioned a study of 2,000 Americans and Canadians to find how people actually feel about their free time — and what they do with it. One statistic in the report really resonated with me: 81% of North Americans miss the sense of wonder they had as kids more than the free time they had then.

So this week I'm sharing some hotel news that speaks to that sense of wonder we all apparently long for, like a chic new hotel at the very tip of Africa to a revamped, sky-high cocktail bar with views of the iconic Las Vegas strip.

Here's the hotel news you need to know about.

One of the most anticipated hotel openings of the year, The Cape Town Edition, is now open. Set on the V&A Waterfront, the stylish hotel is the brand's first outpost in Africa. At the property, guests can stay in one of 142 rooms and suites, enjoy art and design selected as "a reflection of Africa's creative landscape," and eat at numerous dining and bar outlets. And for people like me who love to relax, the hotel has a spa.

In November, New York's celebrity-loved hotel The Mark is getting its first spa: The Mark Wellness & Longevity Spa by Augustinus Bader. The Mark is already The Met Gala's fashion hot spot, plus home to caviar-loaded baked potatoes at Caviar Kaspia, so it only makes sense to have a luxe spa. The spa, the first Augustinus Bader-branded location in the U.S., will feature three treatment rooms, state-of-the-art and science-backed treatments, plus in-room massage services. The opening comes hot on the heels of The Mark's recent room updates, making the hotel as fresh — and relaxing — as ever.

In 2024, Marriott took over the former Delano hotel at Mandalay Bay and converted it into the W Las Vegas. Now, two years later, the W brand is really making the hotel its own with the relaunch of Skyfall Rooftop Bar & Lounge. Situated on the 64th floor and offering panoramic views of Sin City, Rockwell Group recreated the space with bold interiors accenting the floor-to-ceiling windows. In the hotel's lobby, the Living Room bar has also been reimagined.

"Together, these spaces sophisticatedly blend glamour, futuristic energy, and immersive nightlife to capture the true spirit of Las Vegas while embodying the bold, playful quality signature to a W hotel," W Las Vegas said in a statement shared with TPG.

Going back to how we spend our free time, Club Med's report also shared that 88% of people experienced at least one positive impact the last time they challenged themselves to try something new. If you want to feel that positive impact, it might be time to go ... to Delaware.

Hotel Du Pont in Wilmington has launched the Equestrian Escape Package, which comes with equestrian-centric loaner pieces, like riding boots and jackets, from The Frye Company; a private riding lesson at the 200-acre Carousel Park Equestrian Center; and a gourmet picnic from the hotel's Le Cavalier French brasserie.

We've all been patiently waiting for the 69-room Thompson Rome, the first property from the brand in Italy, to open its doors. Well, that day has finally come. The hotel, right near Piazza Venezia and other major attractions, features restored elements from the hotel's original building, a contemporary Mediterranean restaurant, a rooftop cocktail bar and a lobby bar.

#6213. My Favorite Airbnb: A Dreamy Cabin on a Vineyard Just 2 Hours From London

I'm always on the hunt for a new cabin stay in the British countryside. Having visited at least two a year since 2020, I'd now dub myself something of an expert. Living in East London, sometimes all I crave is solitude, and I find that a slightly rustic spot, kitted out with all the necessary amenities, can be more restorative than a jam-packed, buzzy hotel stay.

I don't drive (hey, I'm a Londoner), which can be a rather large obstacle when planning cabin stays. But Liba Vineyard, a luxury glamping site made up of three pod-style homes in Porton, just a 15-minute taxi ride from Salisbury station, presents no such problem. The pods are all bookable on Airbnb, and I scooped up the Hawthorn Pod for a stay this autumn, eager to hunker down and work on writing my upcoming book. Door-to-door from London, I managed to reach it in two hours, armed with enough books and food to last two nights.

Once I'd settled into the Hawthorn Pod, I realized the Wi-Fi was excellent, and I wouldn't need to leave at all during my stay. The pods are dotted along winding wood-chip paths, which branch off towards the three cabins: Hawthorn, Beech, and Elder. All sleep four people and have a wood-fired hot tub, although Hawthorn is slightly more snug than the other two and better suited to solo visitors and couples. Beech is best for anyone traveling with children, while for larger groups, renting all three would be a fun way to celebrate a birthday. It's a spot that can be both solitary and social, depending on what you're after.

Inside, the pods are neutral, bright, and cozy. Draped curtains add a sense of grandeur to the French doors, while the bathroom—the biggest test of any cabin—was a welcome sight. A flushing toilet and strong water pressure are unsung luxuries, and things I'm always relieved to find in a cabin. The kitchen has everything you'd need, but there's also an outdoor barbecue firepit, making cooking here a genuine joy.

Nearby, there are plenty of sightseeing opportunities, pubs, day trips, and activities: UNESCO World Heritage Site Stonehenge is just a 15-minute drive away, while Cranborne Chase National Landscape and the New Forest are both under a half-hour drive. The property itself is full of life as well, with alpacas grazing, chickens clucking, and a muster of peacocks running between hedgerows. On Mondays and Wednesdays, you can join a yoga class in a studio above the winemaking barn.

Each morning, I'd wake to the sound of peacocks, open the drapes to soft golden light trickling in, and breathe in the fresh air before lighting a fire to get breakfast started. Since returning home, I've longed for the calm of those mornings and the methodical mindfulness of cooking over a flame.

The owners have big plans in the works. Soon, wine will be available from the vineyard, which is expected to produce up to 10,000 bottles a year over the next few years. Chris Reynolds, who owns the land with his wife, Louise Marshall, gives every pod guest a tour, something that will become an even bigger selling point once wine is available to taste. Ahead of this, visitors can sponsor a vine through a subscription model in exchange for wine, pod stays, and events such as harvest parties. Liba is already certified organic and is working towards biodynamic certification within the next nine months.

Next summer, the 10-acre farm will be bookable for weddings, while early discussions are underway about an on-site café and additional activities to complement the existing yoga studio.

#6212. United CEO Hints at Potential Destinations

United is exploring potential new markets in a part of the world not served by any of its U.S. competitors.

CEO Scott Kirby told the hosts of the Cheeky Pint podcast that global network planning chief Patrick Quayle and his team were recently in Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan.

“We can’t fly there today because we can’t fly over Russia,” he said. “But he’s there. This could work down the road.”

Kirby did not elaborate on plans for the region but cited United’s seasonal service to Nuuk, Greenland, as evidence that unconventional destinations can work.

No U.S. airlines currently fly to Central Asia. Russia’s ban on Western airlines – enacted in the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war – would make the trip uneconomically long.

Historically, there was little demand among American travelers for connections to Central Asia, but that is changing. American arrivals in Uzbekistan, for instance, increased from around 17,000 in 2019 to more than 26,000 in the first seven months of 2026 alone. The newfound interest has been attributed to visa liberalization measures in Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and Kyrgyzstan, the relative affordability of the region, and trips by travel influencers.

In Kazakhstan, international airlines mainly serve Almaty, the country’s most populous city. In Uzbekistan, the main international gateway is Tashkent.

The only Central Asian carrier with flights to the U.S. is Uzbekistan Airways. The airline serves New York-JFK from Tashkent.
