#6211. 55 Thoughtful Gifts for Men Who Love to Travel

The holiday season will be here before we know it, which means it’s time to start thinking about gifts for the ones you love. When you’re shopping for a special guy in your life this year, skip the things he doesn’t actually need and go straight for the ones that count: thoughtful pieces he’ll put to good use on his next trip, upgrades to his everyday essentials, and a few small luxuries that make being on the road that much better. The best gifts for men, after all, aren’t necessarily the flashiest—they’re the ones that become part of his routine, whether that means packing them in a carry-on or enjoying them on a quiet Sunday morning at home.

I’ve hand-selected over 50 gift ideas for men who love to travel, featuring many talked-about favorites with a few less expected additions too. From a timeless leather weekender that’s perfect for a quick getaway to at-home accessories that will enrich any guy’s space, I've got you covered with plenty of options he’ll love. Read on for all of the best travel gifts for men or jump straight to the section you think will interest him most.

At Condé Nast Traveler, editors spend a lot of time debating, researching, testing, and re-testing all things travel accessories and luggage. If you’re looking for the best suitcase to buy your guy this holiday season, look here. But if you want something a little unique that will absolutely rock his travel routine for years to come, check out some of the gift ideas below. To make his next long-haul flight more comfortable, consider gifting him a comfy neck pillow, sleep mask, or a pair of compression socks. A ludicrously capacious leather weekender or a luxurious Italian notebook are smart upgrades he’ll cherish forever. And in case of emergencies, a good ol' fashioned flask will more than do the trick.

Here’s the thing about men: There’s a part of us that will always relish having a new toy to play with. This category is for those who will appreciate a wild card gift and savor the element of surprise. A perfect pair of travel-sized binoculars made from the best optical-grade crystal in the world? Jackpot! The latest generation of AirPods with top-notch noise-canceling technology? Bingo! A smart watch that can track his steps on the go? Perfect!

Clothes are a tough gift for the holidays. Everybody is different, every body is different, and a lot of guys are just downright picky when it comes to what they get dressed in everyday. That being said, there are a few tricks of the trade to consider here—when gifting clothes, don’t go too big, too outré, or too outlandish. The secret is to select timeless, quintessential pieces that travel well, age well, and can be styled into any wardrobe: a Barbour jacket, a crisp white shirt, or a navy suit that packs nicely into a suitcase. When in doubt, a pair of high-quality sunglasses in a classic silhouette is generally a win too.

Lovers of the great outdoors are a funny bunch to shop for. They typically have all of their most treasured gear ready to go already, so this is a demographic for whom you need to be on your A-game. Gifts for outdoorsy types need to be the newest of the new with smart details, category-leading engineering, and unassailable durability. Think a lightweight Norwegian cooler that keeps drinks cold without any ice (that’s right—no ice), or a comfortable running shoe that can handle endless wear and tear. Outdoorsy folks will say that they can never have too many puffy layer-type things—so go ahead and consider a thick blanket or the iconic Arc’teryx Atom insulated hoodie. And if all else fails you can get them a beautiful Stanley bottle to keep their favorite soups and beverages warm in even the most wintry conditions.

I hate to stereotype the genders—but a lot of self-care products out there are marketed more heavily toward women, leaving the average guy in the lurch. He may not know the benefits of investing in a Dr. Barbara Sturm skincare regimen, or how an Omnilux LED mask can help slow visible signs of aging. There’s a whole world of self-care products out there! Here, I’ve gathered some of the best items to kick-start his journey—sometimes all it takes is Dr. Dennis Gross’ miracle-working peel pads.

Food is one of my favorite ways to experience travel. If you’re not quite ready to gift someone a trip to sample authentic panettone straight from the oven in Italy, the good news is that the marvels of modern packing and shipping have made some of the world’s tastiest foods closer than ever. A sampler of high-quality spices will upgrade his at-home cooking. A $60 bag of beans is the perfectly fun gift for a coffee snob who might not buy it for himself. And a perfectly unassailable upgrade to his go-to sauté pan (if he even has one), or the investment of a proper stand mixer, are foolproof.

No matter what the recipient’s sense of style is, there are certain upgrades that are likely to fit into most any home. Beautiful linen sheets are always welcome, as is a great bathrobe or pair of slippers to remind him of a luxury hotel. When in doubt, the flourish of a Flamingo Estate candle hits just the right notes.

#6210. Hertz President’s Circle elite status is included with several top travel cards. I put it to the test to see if it delivers real value

I've kept the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card for several years now because it's been my favorite premium travel credit card for many reasons.

In all that time, I never once bothered to activate one of its perks: the complimentary Hertz President's Circle status.

Related: The best rental car loyalty programs in 2026

President's Circle is the top published tier of the Hertz Gold+ loyalty program, and earning it the traditional way means completing 15 rentals or spending $3,000 with Hertz in a calendar year.

The reason I overlooked it is that I rent a car maybe a couple of times a year and usually shop around for the best deal, with little brand loyalty.

But with a full day ahead of me recently to explore the spectacular Rocky Mountain National Park in Colorado, I wanted to put this elite status to the test to see whether it was a valuable credit card benefit.

President's Circle is the highest published elite tier in Hertz Gold+ Rewards, the rental company's loyalty program, which costs nothing to join. It sits above the entry-level Gold tier and the mid-tier Five Star elite status.

It's worth remembering that Ultimate Choice is available only at select Hertz airport locations, and you'll need to reserve a midsize or larger vehicle. The guaranteed upgrade requires a reservation made at least 48 hours in advance at a participating location, is capped at a full-size vehicle and does not apply to Manager's Special rentals or certain premium vehicle collections.

Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: Hitting the road on your vacation? Everything you need to know about rental car elite status

The following premium credit cards offer complimentary President's Circle status:

Related: The best credit cards for rental car elite status

To receive the President's Circle status benefits, it's important to follow the correct booking process, which is not onerous:

As a solo driver, there was no need for me to add a complimentary second driver, and I didn't need to call Hertz in advance, so I couldn't test the dedicated President's Circle line.

I received 1.5 Hertz Gold+ Rewards points per dollar spent on the rental, as advertised, but the real perks I was interested in were the pickup experience and the type of car I received.

When I arrived at the pickup location, my name was on the President's Circle board with a note to "see desk." This was my first Hertz Gold+ rental, and first-time members may need to verify their driver's license and payment card at the Gold desk before they can bypass the counter on subsequent rentals.

Make sure you go to the Five Star/President's Circle desk, rather than the main building desk. At larger locations like Denver International Airport (DEN), where I was, these are two separate buildings.

Being unsure, I went to the main building desk and had an utterly bizarre interaction with the staff there, who found my reservation, insisted my President's Circle status had expired, despite me only activating it a month earlier, refused to activate it and insisted that if I reactivated myself, I would have to cancel the booking and rebook if I wanted any status benefits, which would likely be much more expensive to do last minute. This is despite my showing them my live Hertz account, including the booking confirmation, and my President's Circle status level was clearly visible.

Fortunately, I sought a second opinion at the Five Star and President's Circle desk, where the staff could not have been more helpful, found my reservation, could immediately see my President's Circle status and had me on my way to the President's Circle lot within minutes.

This was the highlight of the day. More than 50 cars were waiting in the President's Circle section. I don't pretend to be an expert on cars (I don't currently own one), so I just chose the one that looked the most luxurious.

Walking up and down the rows and picking out exactly what I wanted to drive was great fun, and I settled on a shiny new 2026 Wrangler Sahara 4WD with just a few thousand miles on the clock, which I thought would be awesome for tackling the winding roads of the Rocky Mountain National Park.

Having originally booked a midsize-category Kia K4, driving off the lot in a Jeep Wrangler Sahara sure felt like a superior car, but I subsequently checked the sticker price for each car, new. At more than twice the Kia's retail price, the Jeep was definitely an upgrade.

With the keys already inside, I drove my chosen car to the exit, showed the attendant my receipt with the large "PC" status written on it and headed out the exit to the mountains.

Related: Delta adds Hertz status for all Medallion elites, revamps earning structure for rentals

After years of ignoring the Hertz President's Circle status that comes with my Venture X card, I'm a little sheepish about not using it sooner.

Despite the initial confusion at the main counter, Hertz ultimately delivered on the status benefits I valued most, and for someone who doesn't know much about cars, I felt like a television game show winner, wandering the lot and choosing any car I wished.

The rental wasn't the cheapest from any agency in the area, so if an upgrade doesn't interest you, you still may wish to shop around. Ultimate Choice is available only at certain locations, so a downtown Hertz branch may not have a President's Circle section at all.

It's probably not a perk I'd open a new credit card for on its own, but if you already hold one of the cards above, submitting the enrollment only takes a few minutes, and it turned what would have been a forgettable rental into one of the highlights of my trip. For special occasions like exploring one of the country's best national parks, I would definitely give my President's Circle status a spin again.

#6209. Inexpensive things to do in Alaska on a cruise

If you're used to cruising in the Caribbean, shore excursion prices on your Alaska cruise might surprise you.

Want to take a helicopter ride to the top of a glacier to enjoy a dogsled ride? It'll cost upward of $700 per person. Excited about an authentic Alaska fishing experience? That's a more than $400 tour. A nearly three-hour scenic train ride on the White Pass and Yukon Route Railroad starts at more than $150 per traveler.

Not only are tours so pricey because Alaska is a remote destination (where it costs more to fly in goods and materials), but also because Alaska is part of the U.S., where wages and tour insurance costs can be higher than in the islands. Plus, many Alaska excursions involve seaplanes, helicopters, specialized boats and other equipment that only add to the price of your onshore experience.

For many, an Alaska cruise is a once-in-a-lifetime trip, and many tours are worth the splurge. But you don't have to spend money hand over fist in every port. Whether you're trying to balance your budget with a few cheaper days or you simply don't have the resources to spend big every day of your vacation, you'll want to seek out cheap or free things to do in Alaska's cruise ports.

Luckily, you have plenty of options. I know because I've spent many a day exploring independently in Alaska's ports. Plus, I consulted with Alaska's tourism representatives to bring you a comprehensive list of free (and cheap) things to do in Alaska on a cruise.

Skagway is known for its gold rush history, but you don't need a pricey tour to immerse yourself in the town's storied past. Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park has four free museums open to visitors, including the Visitor Center Museum (with interactive exhibits), the Moore House Museum (former home of the first family to live in Skagway, with two restored Victorian-era rooms), the Jeff Smiths Parlour Museum (a former bar with a shady past) and the Mascot Saloon Museum (a restored gold rush saloon).

If you're fully embracing the old-timey vibe, you'll want to belly up to the bar at the Red Onion Saloon. Once, it was Skagway's signature bordello, but now it's the place to sling back an Alaska-brewed beer or snack on apps and pizzas named after former good-time girls. For a reasonable $20 a person, you can sign up for a Quickie Tour of the venue's supposedly haunted brothel museum. Ghost sightings don't cost extra!

One of my favorite things to do in Skagway is stretch my legs on a hike, and there are several trailheads within easy walking distance of your cruise ship. Options include the Upper and Lower Dewey Lake, Reid Falls and Gold Rush Cemetery, and Icy Lake and Upper Reid Falls trails. The National Park Service kindly lists its hikes by distance from Skagway's Historic District, as well as by level of difficulty. No guide is needed, and you don't have to pay to access the trails.

Related: Alaska cruise guide: Best itineraries, planning tips and things to do

Window shopping is a popular activity along the main streets by Juneau's cruise docks, but you might be tempted to blow your budget on souvenirs. (Look for sales, especially during end-of-season sailings, if you want to buy gifts for less.)

Typically, you can pay $60 for an all-day pass up and down Juneau's Goldbelt tram*, or if you're in good shape, you can hike from your ship to the top of the tram on the Mount Roberts Trail for free. I did this hike on my recent Alaska cruise, and while it's not technical, it is steep and can be muddy after a rainstorm. Make lots of noise just in case bears are on the trail.

At the top, you can visit the Chilkat Theater to watch a free movie about the region's Tlingit people. If you're too tired to hike back down, you can get a ride back on the tram for $20.

However, the Goldbelt tram has been closed since late April 2026 for maintenance. Visitors can still go to the base of the tram to watch Tlingit artists carve totem poles, weave ceremonial robes and perform cultural dances for no charge.

Other hikes accessible from your ship include the Gold Creek Flume Trail and the Perseverance Trail.

If a stroll through downtown is more your speed, self-guided tours of Juneau come free of charge. The Juneau Voices project features audio installations at 11 spots around town where you can learn about the city through the stories of Native Alaskans. Or grab a map from a tourist welcome center and follow this walking tour to see the city's highlights.

You can also find a PDF guide to Juneau's totem poles online.

If you prefer to get your history and culture indoors (not a bad plan in Alaska, given the temperamental climate), Juneau offers a few museums with modest admission fees that are worth checking out.

The Juneau-Douglas City Museum offers a mix of permanent and temporary exhibits on the area's history and art. Admission is $7, but you might need a cab if you're not up for a 20-minute walk. The museum also runs a free walking tour of the Alaska State Capitol Building.

Also, a 20-minute walk from the port is the Alaska State Museum, where you can learn about the cultures of the Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian peoples. Admission is $14. For more information on Native Alaskans and their cultures, visit the Sealaska Heritage Institute's Walter Soboleff Building ($10 admission) and its gift shop, which features local art. Don't miss the signature totem pole and handcrafted clan house.

If you're keen for a scenic uphill walk, head up Basin Road to the Last Chance Mining Museum ($5) to learn about the gold rush in a historic mining building.

*At the time of writing, Goldbelt tram is closed but has plans to reopen soon. Check availability and prices before you plan.

Related: Alaska cruise mistakes you never want to make

Ketchikan is best known for its Creek Street Historic District, built on a wooden boardwalk above the salmon-filled Ketchikan Creek. Stroll for free by its historic buildings, shops and restaurants, or pay $10 to stop into Dolly's House for a glimpse into the city's former red-light district.

Not far from Creek Street, the Tongass Historical Museum and Totem Heritage Center immerses you in the area's history for a modest $6 fee (children and military are free). From there, you can embark on a self-guided, 1 1/2-mile Ketchikan Salmon Walk to learn about the fish's impact on the town (and maybe even spot some, in season, at the Salmon Ladder). The walk will take you past the Totem Heritage Center (also $6, or get a combo ticket to both museums for $9), with its collection of 19th-century totem poles rescued from nearby islands.

If you're feeling adventurous, you can skip the tour and head out to the Saxman Native Village on your own. It's 2 miles south of Ketchikan, so it's walkable — but for a few bucks, you can take a city bus there instead. It costs just $5 to wander the park on your own and see the 25 replica totem poles, as well as Native carvers working on new poles using traditional techniques.

Icy Strait Point is a manufactured cruise port near the town of Hoonah. It was created to offer everything cruisers could possibly want in a port, so all the activities are planned to get you to part ways with your hard-earned cash. That said, there are still plenty of things to do in Icy Strait Point for free or cheap.

A free gondola ride transports visitors from one cruise pier area to the other, but if the line is long or you're afraid of heights, you can walk the same path on nature trails instead. Keep your eyes out for wildlife.

The port has tons of beach access, so you can wander Icy Strait's shores, stop for scenic photos and look for marine life free of charge. At the Hoonah Cannery building, you can browse the Hoonah Packing Co. Cannery Museum exhibits interspersed among the shops, or get tickets to the Native dance show for $20 per person at the on-site ticket booth.

From the cannery, it's a 1 1/2-mile (roughly 30-minute) walk to Hoonah, an actual town where many of Icy Strait Point's workers live and home to Alaska's largest Tlingit village. You can also take an affordable $10 shuttle to town, where you can admire the totem poles and sip a local beer at Icy Strait Brewing.

Related: The best Alaska cruise shore excursions — from heli-hiking to whale watching

Sitka offers a compelling mix of Native Alaskan and Russian history and culture, and a self-guided tour of the key sites in town won't cost you much (if anything at all).

You can get a free tour of the Russian Bishop's House, an example of 19th-century architecture during Russia's colonization of Sitka. Baranof Castle State Historic Site (Castle Hill) was occupied throughout the centuries by Tlingit people and later by Russian settlers, and it was the site chosen for the transfer of Alaska from Russia to the U.S. You can check out the views and the informative signs for free.

St. Michael Cathedral National Historic Landmark is an exact replica of the first Russian Orthodox church in the Americas. Because the site has an active congregation, visitors can view its collection of 17th-century religious artifacts for a limited time each day.

Museums with small admission fees include the Sitka History Museum (featuring exhibits on local history) and the Sheldon Jackson Museum (showcasing a collection of Alaska Native artifacts). If exploring old cemeteries is your thing, you'll want to stop at the more than 200-year-old Sitka Russian Cemetery, with gravestones made from the ballast of Russian ships.

The Sitka National Historical Park's visitor center and grounds (with walking trails and totem pole installations) are open to all, free of charge. It's a scenic spot for an easy nature walk, or you can come inside to learn more about Sitka's Russian and Tlingit cultures or join a ranger program.

You don't need a tour to gawk at eagles, hawks, owls and falcons at the Alaska Raptor Center. Admission is $16, though it is a bit of a walk from downtown. Watch injured birds relearn how to fly, and take a stroll through the center's forested grounds.

Finally, you can attend various dance performances at affordable ticket prices. The Alaska Storytellers dance show ($15) celebrates traditional and modern Russian dance, while the New Archangel Dancers' performances highlight Russian folk dances. Or, step into a Tlingit clan house to enjoy the music, costumes and choreography of the Naa Kahidi Tlingit Dancers.

You don't need to spend a fortune on tours to explore Alaska's culture and history or enjoy its natural splendor. You'll find plenty of free things to do in port on an Alaska cruise. However, I do encourage you to budget for a few tours, whether it's to travel beyond the port area into Alaska's wilderness or to immerse yourself in an activity, such as dog sledding, kayaking, fishing, or whale or bear watching. You won't regret spending the money on amazing experiences and memories.

Planning a cruise? Start with these stories:

You don’t need to plan free activities in Alaska in advance. Many are self-guided hikes and city walking tours or museums that are free to enter. Many of the low-cost museums, attractions and performances do not require you to purchase tickets far in advance, but some require you to purchase a timed ticket, either same day or in advance. You might want to have a general idea of what you’d like to do in port so you can pack and dress accordingly and plan your visit around opening hours.

It is very safe to explore Alaskan cities and towns on your own. Most of the main attractions are in areas popular with cruise ship visitors. As always, you should take reasonable precautions to protect valuables whenever you’re in a crowd. It is also safe to go hiking in Alaska on your own, but you do run the risk of encountering bears, so make sure you know what to do in that situation before you head out.

Sitka offers the best free options for cruisers on a budget, with a mix of Russian cultural heritage sites and the National Historical Park’s walking trails and Alaska Native cultural exhibitions.

#6208. Cruising to Alaska? Check if Your Next Port, Bus, or Lodge is Indigenous-Owned

The Huna Totem Corporation was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2026. Read the full list of winners here.

From April to October, cruise ships tower over downtown Juneau’s Marine Way, a coastal path that connects the port zone to downtown. Should a traveler pause for a moment between ship and souvenir store, they’ll notice Kaagwaantaan Kootéeyaa, a tall, intricately carved pole rising against a backdrop of forest and mountains. At its base, a panel explains that the cedar pole depicts five of the Kaagwaantaan Tlingit clan’s crests: a hat, person, orca, eagle and bear. It is an arresting introduction to the long-overlooked human history of this place.

Since 2023, totem poles have adorned this highly trafficked shoreline, part of Kootéeyaa Deiyí (“Totem Pole Trail”)—a city-wide project led by the Sealaska Heritage Institute (SHI) that represents the cultures of the Tlingit people who have inhabited Juneau for at least 10,000 years, as well as the Haida and Tsimshian who arrived a few hundred years ago. Visible evidence of the region’s Indigenous communities was previously limited, says SHI’s Ricardo Worl (Tlingit), who sees the trail as “an opportunity to reestablish our presence on our ancestral lands.” Noting that more than a million cruise ship passengers land in Juneau each year, Worl hopes the trail “is the beginning of their education about our culture.”

Alaska’s cruise industry has long invited travelers to experience the “Last Frontier” while relegating Indigenous peoples to the margins of the tourism economy. Now, a shift is occurring—one that goes beyond simply incorporating Indigenous culture into the cruise experience. Across Alaska, Native corporations are increasingly owning and shaping the tourism infrastructure itself, from cruise docks and terminals to ground transportation, giving them a greater stake in how destinations develop, and how visitors experience them.

I came to Alaska to see how Indigenous ownership is changing the experience on the ground, following a route that took me from whale watching at cruise ports on the coast to bear and moose spotting at a lodge deep in the Interior. At each stop, I saw how Alaska Native corporations are shaping the places that travelers pass through.

Created following passage of the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, Alaska Native corporations are for-profit companies run by and for Alaska Native shareholders. For Huna Totem, a Tlingit village corporation representing shareholders with ties to Hoonah and Glacier Bay, tourism is an important part of its economic development strategy. Its best-known development, Icy Strait Point in Hoonah, is Alaska’s first private cruise destination and has become a model for Alaska Native-owned tourism—creating local jobs, keeping economic benefits within the community and making Tlingit culture part of the visitor experience.

When Icy Strait Point opened in 2004, Huna Totem leadership was focused on “providing economic stability for generations, so the culture can be perpetuated,” says Ruth Banaszak, director of marketing and communications. Icy Strait Point has two cruise ship piers located about a half-mile apart and activity areas for 30 different excursions to distribute visitor flow around the site so that it never becomes overwhelming. To get around the vast site, I made use of the forested walking trails and two gondola systems, one of which took me to the summit of Hoonah Mountain, which I quickly and thrillingly descended via the ZipRider, a six-cable zipline. Walking around the museum exhibits housed inside a 1912 salmon cannery that closed when the fishing industry declined, I could connect tourism's present and future with its economic history. The cannery was once a symbol of loss; now it provides new economic opportunities. “We hire around 350 people for the season,” says Banaszak. “So, in a town of 950, anybody who wants to have a job in the community has one.” The model has also allowed local residents to build businesses of their own, including boat tours to Point Adolphus where, in just two hours, I spotted dozens of orcas, a few humpback whales and uncountable numbers of sea lions and sea otters. In each place, instead of being whisked onto an excursion operated by an outside company, I was experiencing a destination that had been shaped by the community whose ancestral home I was visiting.

“We’ve done this for our own community in Hoonah,” says Banaszak, “so now [we’re asking] how can we take what we’ve learned here and help other rural communities do the same thing?”

That thinking has led Huna Totem around Southeast Alaska and beyond. In Whittier, the corporation opened Glacier Gateway cruise terminal in 2024. Huna Totem and Doyon, Limited, another Alaska Native corporation, have also acquired Portage Glacier Cruises and Alaska Coach Tours, creating Native-owned touchpoints that extend from ship to shore and beyond. In Klawock, on Prince of Wales Island, Huna Totem partnered with Doyon and the local Alaska Native village corporation Klawock Heenya to develop a new cruise port in 2024. The destination uses a single-ship model, with development focused on Tlingit culture, local involvement and community values.

Back in downtown Juneau, Huna Totem is developing Áak’w Landing, a cruise dock and waterfront development targeting its first full season in 2028. The project is designed to improve how cruise visitors move through the city—including eliminating the need for tender boats at the site—rather than simply bringing in more ships. Reflecting its approach of being “culturally driven, community-centric, [and] business-focused,” says Banaszak, Huna Totem sees the project as both infrastructure enhancement and an opportunity to incorporate Alaska Native culture into the visitor experience—two poles from SHI’s Kootéeyaa Deiyí will be raised at the site.

The broader ambition is to create a network of Native-owned tourism businesses across Alaska. “So that Alaska Native tourism grows: culturally-led tourism as it should be done, people telling their own story themselves,” Banaszak says.

The cruise industry may seem an odd venture for Doyon, Limited, which is based in Fairbanks and represents the largely Dene people of the Interior, but, says Jordan Sanford, president of Doyon Tourism, “more than 60% of visitors come to Alaska by cruise, so [we realized] if we wanted to grow, we needed to be involved.”

Deep in Denali National Park, Doyon has operated Kantishna Roadhouse, the park’s only Indigenous-owned lodge, for 30 years. Arriving via a small plane from the park entrance—road access, closed for five years due to a landslide, will return in 2027—I spent blissful days backcountry hiking free from cell service. Evenings were spent listening to presentations by staff, such as an introduction to Dene beadwork and regalia; spotting wildlife including grizzly bears, moose, and caribou, then watching the setting sun light up the slopes of mighty Denali. Since 2004, in partnership with Aramark, Doyon has also operated bus tours, transit services, and campgrounds in the park. The partnership with Huna Totem gives Doyon an opportunity to diversify and grow, while responding to a recent shift in cruise passengers’ expectations: “They’re looking for more authentic experiences,” she explains. “We see that as our advantage. We put shareholders to work, and they share their culture,” she says. “There's a lot of businesses here that have been sharing the culture for so long, but from non-Alaska Natives,” she adds.

Next up is the restoration of the 1925 Chatanika Gold Camp near Fairbanks, which is scheduled to open in 2027 as a northern lights experience center, filling a critical infrastructure gap. Aurora viewing in Alaska today typically means pulling off the side of the road and drinking a hot chocolate, says Sanford. With Chatanika, “we're creating a space [with] cultural programming to make it more of an experience.”

It’s another link in an emerging network of Native-owned businesses across the state. The ultimate goal is “an Alaska Native-owned corridor, where [travelers] are visiting Alaska Native-owned businesses along the way,” says Sanford. For cruise passengers, that means more opportunities to encounter Indigenous culture, while knowing that Indigenous people are benefiting from the industry. And it means that your next Alaska cruise itinerary might begin at a Native-owned port, continue aboard a Native-owned bus, lead to a Native-owned excursion, and end at a Native-owned lodge.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6206. Most Versatile? Why Boeing Made The Iconic 747-400 Compatible With 3 Distinct Powerplants

In the late 1980s, as Boeing prepared to launch the definitive variant of its iconic jumbo jet, it handed airline customers an extraordinary level of operational control. Most other aircraft give global carriers a choice of just one or two engine manufacturers, but Boeing designed the 747-400 to seamlessly accommodate three completely distinct powerplants from three competing aerospace giants: General Electric, Pratt & Whitney, and Rolls-Royce. The tri-option compatibility allowed airlines to order the same four-engine widebody customized to their existing maintenance ecosystems, pilot type ratings, and regional manufacturer loyalties.

Integrating three radically different engine builds onto a single wing was a massive structural and financial undertaking. Each engine variant needed bespoke nacelle designs, flight deck indication logic, and expensive airworthiness certification flight tests. Why exactly did Boeing willingly absorb the staggering development costs required to certify three competing engines for a single aircraft program?

The biggest motivation behind offering three distinct engine options on the 747-400 was securing commercial market dominance by removing barriers to purchase. During the late 1980s, major long-haul carriers had fierce loyalty to specific engine manufacturers based on existing overhaul infrastructure and local supply chains. As highlighted by Simple Flying, ensuring that General Electric, Pratt & Whitney, and Rolls-Royce were all available on the airframe meant that engine preference never became a reason for an airline to look toward competing widebody designs.

Boeing certified the 747-400 with the Pratt & Whitney PW4056, the General Electric CF6-80C2B1F, and the Rolls-Royce RB211-524G/H. According to technical documentation from Aircraft Commerce, these modern turbofans produced between 56,500 lbf (251 kN) and 63,300 lbf (282 kN) of static thrust depending on the sub-variant, delivering vastly superior fuel efficiency and payload range over early-generation 747 powerplants.

This customer-first engineering philosophy was not born overnight. Instead, it was the natural culmination of two decades of operational feedback, market evolution, and rapid fleet expansion across earlier iterations of the Queen of the Skies. When Boeing initially launched the 747 program in the late 1960s, a single-engine approach was necessary to get the massive airframe off the ground efficiently. However, as international routes expanded and global competition intensified, airlines made it clear that airframe versatility was just as vital as raw lift capacity.

When the original Boeing 747-100 entered commercial service in 1970, it was powered exclusively by Pratt & Whitney’s JT9D turbofans. However, as international airlines expanded their long-haul networks throughout the 1970s, carriers operating mixed fleets demanded engine options that matched their existing equipment. As recorded by Airliner World, Boeing responded during the development of the 747-200 and 747-300 by integrating General Electric's CF6 and Rolls-Royce's RB211, establishing the multi-engine paradigm that would later define the 747-400 program.

The economic incentive for airlines to maintain engine commonality across their fleets was overwhelming. An airline already flying CF6-powered Douglas DC-10s or RB211-powered Lockheed L-1011 TriStars could seamlessly integrate the 747-400 without investing millions of dollars in duplicate ground support tooling, specialized mechanic training, or spare engine inventory. Historical fleet analysis from Boeing-747.com notes that this operational flexibility allowed flagship carriers like British Airways, Lufthansa, and Cathay Pacific to optimize their long-haul maintenance budgets while scaling up international routes.

In addition to the financial benefits of fleet commonality, the three powerplants offered on the 747-400 formed two different approaches to jet engine engineering. General Electric and Pratt & Whitney favored a traditional dual-spool design that prioritized mechanical simplicity and established maintenance procedures, whereas Rolls-Royce pursued a complex triple-spool design engineered for higher thermal efficiency and rapid throttle response. Boeing allowed international carriers to select not only an engine supplier, but the exact internal mechanical philosophy that best aligned with their long-term operational and engineering strategies.

Both of these engines power the Boeing 787 Dreamliner.

Moving to the internal engine design, the key differentiator between the engines is the two-spool versus three-spool design. The General Electric CF6-80C2 and Pratt & Whitney PW4056 used a classic two-spool configuration, where concentric shafts connect high-pressure and low-pressure turbine stages to their respective compressors and fan sections. As detailed in technical analysis from Aircraft Commerce, the two-shaft arrangement reduced the overall count of rotating bearings and internal seals, lowering initial overhaul complexity and offering a proven, highly reliable mechanical baseline for long-haul operators.

In contrast, Rolls-Royce equipped its RB211-524G/H with a unique triple-spool layout featuring three independent, concentric shafts rotating at different optimal speeds. According to information from Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University, splitting the compressor into low, intermediate, and high-pressure sections allowed each stage to operate closer to its peak aerodynamic efficiency across varying altitudes and flight regimes. The three-shaft design yielded superior surge margin protection, faster engine acceleration during go-arounds, and reduced overall blade stress, though it needed more specific shop tooling and unique maintenance procedures during heavy C and D checks.

The existence of these contrasting mechanical designs gave airlines unprecedented flexibility in structuring their engineering departments. However, beyond thermodynamic efficiency and spool counts, offering three competing powerplants provided airlines with a critical operational safety net against catastrophic fleet groundings.

In commercial aviation, an Airworthiness Directive (AD) or unforeseen safety issue targeting a specific engine family can instantly paralyze an airline’s widebody operations. If an airframe is built around a single exclusive powerplant, any fleet-wide grounding directive immediately halts long-haul schedules and costs carriers millions of dollars per day in lost revenue. As highlighted in Simple Flying coverage, the multi-engine compatibility of the 747-400 provided major international airlines with an invaluable operational insurance policy, allowing carriers to hedge their long-term fleet risk across multiple engine manufacturers.

For large global flag carriers operating massive long-haul networks, this risk mitigation strategy played out in several ways. Some carriers chose to split their total 747-400 orders between two distinct engine types, so that a technical fault or supply chain problem on one engine line would never completely freeze their international timetable. Other operators banked on their mixed-engine experience to negotiate better power-by-the-hour maintenance contracts and spare parts support, using competition between General Electric, Pratt & Whitney, and Rolls-Royce to drive down total operating costs across the entire lifecycle of the airframe.

The multi-engine paradigm defined the peak of widebody customer choice throughout the 1980s and 1990s. Despite this, as aerospace development costs soared and aerodynamic integration requirements grew ever more precise, Boeing's flexible manufacturing philosophy would ultimately vanish on the final iteration of the jumbo jet family.

The aircraft remains one of the most unique aircraft in commercial aviation history.

Despite the commercial success of offering three engine options on the 747-400, the multi-powerplant philosophy did not survive into the final generation of the jumbo jet family. Boeing launched the 747-8 in the mid-2000s, and it abandoned the tri-option strategy entirely, selecting General Electric as the exclusive engine supplier. As detailed by Simple Flying, the 747-8 was powered solely by the GEnx-2B, which was a decisive shift away from customer engine choice toward sole-source airframe-engine integration.

The transition to a single-engine provider was driven by the immense cost and aerodynamic complexity of modern widebody engineering. Designing, flight testing, and certifying three distinct engine nacelles, pylon structures, and digital bleed air systems for a modern airframe ends up totaling hundreds of millions of dollars in duplicate development capital. Furthermore, aerospace manufacturers realized that optimizing a wing structure for a single, tightly integrated engine casing offered far greater aerodynamic efficiency and fuel savings than designing multiple bespoke pylon structures and strut fairings to hang three competing engine geometries from the same wing box.

Boeing's shift away from multiple engine choices came from general trends seen across the entire commercial aviation industry. As sole-source engine agreements became the standard on flagship programs like the Airbus A350, the 747-400 stood out as the last grand monument to an era when airline preference dictated airframe design.

The 747-400, even today, is one of the most versatile and adaptable widebody airliners ever constructed, largely because Boeing allowed the needs of international carriers to shape its core engineering. The 747 accommodated two-spool designs from General Electric and Pratt & Whitney alongside the three-spool architecture of Rolls-Royce, fitting seamlessly into almost any global airline’s existing maintenance ecosystem. It gave operators total freedom over fleet planning, protective hedges against engine groundings, and strong negotiating power with overhaul providers.

In today's commercial aviation landscape, where exclusive sole-source engine deals dominate new aircraft development, the multi-engine legacy of the 747-400 feels like a distant golden age of customer flexibility. Modern airframers prioritize wing-nacelle aerodynamic integration and streamlined certification costs over engine choice, so that future long-haul jets will rarely offer three competing powerplants on the exact same wing assembly.

The remaining 747-400 passenger and freighter airframes are now gradually moving toward retirement, and they leave behind a unique industrial legacy. The Queen of the Skies demonstrated that an airliner could achieve global supremacy not by forcing carriers to adapt to a rigid factory baseline, but by offering the engineering versatility required to power international flight on an airline’s own terms.

#6205. TAP Air Portugal Launches New U.S. Route

TAP Air Portugal on Thursday began nonstop service between Lisbon and Orlando, Florida.

The transatlantic connection will operate three times weekly, on Mondays, Thursdays, and Saturdays, using Airbus A330 aircraft. Each flight has 34 Business Class seats, 12 Economy Prime seats, and 240 Economy Class seats.

“With the launch of the route between Lisbon and Orlando, TAP Air Portugal continues to invest in strengthening its network in North America, a market of enormous importance to the airline,” Renato Inácio, TAP’s chief financial officer, said in a news release. “This new route brings Portugal closer to one of the United States’ leading tourist and economic regions, whilst offering our customers opportunities for connections throughout Europe, Africa, and South America.”

Orlando is TAP’s second destination in Florida, behind Miami, and its ninth in the U.S. Its other U.S. destinations are New York-JFK, Newark, New Jersey, Boston, Washington Dulles, Chicago O’Hare, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.

#6204. AirBaltic Moves to Cut Around 300 Employees

Distressed Latvian flag carrier airBaltic plans to lay off around 300 employees as it continues restructuring, according to the Latvian Aviation Union.

The union, which represents pilots, cabin crew, aircraft technicians, office staff, and other workers in Latvia’s airline sector, said airBaltic expects to cut around 100 pilots and 200 flight attendants. The LAU strongly opposes the move and said it has not received the carrier’s assessment criteria for which workers will be let go.

“These are people’s careers, livelihoods, and futures,” the union said. “Decisions affecting hundreds of aviation professionals must not be made through a process that lacks transparency and agreed rules.”

The LAU also called on the Latvian government to intervene in the process.

AirBaltic filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the U.S. in September. It is facing serious financial headwinds from higher jet fuel prices and route disruptions caused by conflicts in Eastern Europe and the Middle East.

The carrier is continuing to operate its normal schedule while its bankruptcy case proceeds. It mainly serves destinations in Europe but also flies to North Africa, the Middle East, Turkey, and the Caucasus.

AirBaltic has secured a commitment for €350 million, or about $403.6 million, in debtor-in possession financing, which it said will be enough to support operations during the bankruptcy process.

#6202. Livery of the Week: Aer Lingus

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Aer Lingus’ standard livery is centered on the shamrock, a symbol that has represented the Irish carrier for more than 80 years. Although the airline has changed its aircraft appearance several times, the three-leaf emblem remains the most recognizable feature of its fleet.

The current design was unveiled on Jan. 17, 2019, during a ceremony at Dublin Airport. It marked Aer Lingus’ first major aircraft rebranding in more than two decades, replacing the predominantly green-and-white scheme introduced in the 1990s.

The redesign retained the shamrock but introduced a revised version with a slight tilt and more pronounced heart-shaped leaves. According to Aer Lingus, the changes were intended to represent movement and the airline’s Irish heritage while giving the logo a more contemporary appearance.

The most noticeable change was the shift away from the green upper fuselage used on the previous livery. The updated scheme features a predominantly white aircraft with a teal vertical stabilizer and engines. Large teal “Aer Lingus” titles appear along the forward fuselage.

The shamrock appears in several locations beyond the tail. Aer Lingus incorporated the emblem into the airline’s wordmark, near the aircraft’s boarding door and on the wingtips. The airline specifically positioned the wingtip design to make it visible to passengers looking out from the cabin.

The aircraft’s lower fuselage also received a teal treatment, making the color visible from below. The combination of white and teal replaced the darker green that had dominated much of the airline’s branding for decades.

Aer Lingus worked with global design consultancy Lippincott on the rebranding. The airline considered more than 50 shamrock designs before selecting the final version. The updated identity also included a new typeface, redesigned digital platforms and changes to other customer-facing materials.

Two aircraft were presented in the new colors during the January 2019 unveiling: an Airbus A330-300 named St Munchin and an A320 named St Schira. The A330 made its first scheduled flight in the updated livery the following day, operating from Dublin to New York.

Aer Lingus has also retained several connections to its earlier aircraft designs. Its 1960s-inspired retro livery, introduced in 2011 to celebrate the airline’s 75th anniversary, featured a darker green-and-white appearance that contrasted with the newer scheme.

More than seven years after its introduction, the 2019 design remains the standard appearance of Aer Lingus aircraft. The colors and placement of the branding have changed, but the shamrock continues to link the carrier’s modern fleet with its earlier history.

#6201. The Very Best Thai Food in New York City

There are several ways to describe delicious food in Thai: Aroy means delicious, while aroy mak takes it a step further to very delicious. But my favorite word is zaab (also spelled zabb or zab; แซ่บ), a term rooted in the Isan region of northeastern Thailand that conveys a bold deliciousness, often associated with the heat. In New York City, we’re spoiled for choice when it comes to food that delivers true zaab.

I’ve spent my life immersed in the world of Thai food. One of the joys of growing up in a Thai restaurant family is participating in one of our favorite hobbies: scoping out other Thai restaurants to see what’s good. Most summers, my aunts would close down their restaurant in Royal Palm Beach for two weeks, and they’d road trip from South Florida up to New York City to check out casinos and taste Thai restaurants along the way—when I was lucky, I got to join them. My grandpa, for his part, used to drive to the city weekly to get products for his grocery store in Washington, DC, and through his firsthand research, old friends, and the Internet, he created detailed restaurant guides to help me find footing when I moved to the city almost five years ago.

As I continue to eat my way through the city’s Thai restaurants, I feel spoiled for choice. More and more chefs are serving regional specialties of their hometowns and maintaining Thai food’s great balancing act between the spice, acid, salt, sweetness, and umami, while incorporating their own signature flair.

While the city’s established Thai spots, particularly out in Elmhurst, Queens, remain beloved, plenty of the most compelling and exciting bites can be found in various parts of the city. There has never been a more exciting time to eat Thai food in NYC, and these 14 restaurants best embody its golden era.

If you want an overview of the best dishes across Thailand without leaving the city, let your first stop in Queen’s Little Thai Town be Ayada. The beloved restaurant has familiar favorites like pad thai and tom yum, but let its expertise in other regional favorites be an excuse to try my dad’s favorite Yen Ta Fo, a bubblegum-pink soup with soft rice noodles and a savory tomato and bean curd sauce.

364 Grand Street, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Any of the fiery curries on the rotating menu

When the news of Ugly Baby’s closure last year hit my WhatsApp chat with my Thai friends, you would’ve thought that someone had died. In a way, it felt like we lost a family member. Ugly Baby was one of the rare spots in the city that didn’t hold back on heat like many in America do to appease Western palates and milder heat tolerances. But all was saved when the beloved restaurant announced its reopening in Williamsburg earlier this fall. It’s now a fun, lively two-floor restaurant with eclectic dishware and recipes from various Thai provinces, including brutally hot curries from Southern Thailand and Northeastern Isan cuisine.

Its menu is sorted from least spicy to most spicy—written out as “the laughs” to “the ugly” (dishes toward the latter end consist of a few menu items that will make you feel like you’re breathing fire). Luckily, waiters are standing by with large jugs of water, ready to refill at the sight of sweat dripping down your forehead.

Bangkok Supper Club makes a convincing case for the arrival of upscale Thai dining.

Order a la carte, or do the $150 tasting menu at Bangkok Supper Club.

641 Hudson St, New York, NY 10014 (Meatpacking District)

With an award-winning cocktail program by Suwincha "Chacha" Singsuwan and a menu from executive chef Max Wittawat, Bangkok Supper Club makes a convincing case for the arrival of upscale Thai dining. The drinks are as much of a draw as the food. I like to start my meal with a fish sauce cocktail, a savory, umami-forward drink that captures the depth of fish sauce while balancing it with sweet notes of floral pear. It’s unexpected, but feels just right, and is a lovely accompaniment to my other must-order: the pork jowl. These deep-fried pork cheeks arrive atop a fragrant, garlic-baked rice.

One of the best parts about eating in Thailand is getting food from restaurants and stalls that specialize in one singular dish. As my dad says, that’s how you know it’s good. Eim Khao Mun Kai is one such place. Its one dish, khao mun gai, is the Thai version of Hainanese chicken rice, served with a spicy, fermented bean sauce.

The $12 set meal includes tender steamed chicken thighs made with halal meat and gizzards, fragrant ginger rice that’s cooked with chicken droppings, and a savory broth-based soup made from the bones, with sides of cilantro and cucumber plus plenty of sauce. It’s a tight shop and cash-only. When my dad comes into town, it’s the first place we go to.

Must-order dish: Northern-style curry noodles

Since 1990, this institution has been serving what my friend calls “old-school auntie energy” with wooden accents, white tablecloths, and a sprawling menu. When I say sprawling, I mean it. You can flip through pages at SriPraPhai and can eat all the fried meats, papaya salads, curries, and noodle dishes your heart desires.

Zaab Zaab specializes in Northeast Isan cuisine, repping where both owners are from.

76-04 Woodside Ave, Queens, NY 11373 (Elmhurst)

208 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Zaab Zaab has locations in both Elmhurst and Williamsburg, and specializes in Northeast Isan cuisine from where owner Bryan Chunton and chef Aniwat Khotsopa hail. The restaurant’s signature dish, an herb-packed larb ped udon, features cilantro- and mint-packed ground duck, fried liver, and crispy skin; it’s served with a plethora of fresh lettuce, cabbage, extra herbs, and sticky rice. When I go with a group, though, I also make sure we order the pla neung manow, which comes steamed with a chili, garlic, and lime sauce that’s so flavorful, you’ll want to drink it like soup (luckily it’s served with little bowls so you can).

800 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Chor muang for an appetizer; pad kea mao seafood as a main

Focusing on 19th- century recipes from the royal consort court, Kaew Jao Jorm’s (named after the former King Rama V’s favorite flower) serves a regal menu in its intimate, 20-seat restaurant. The exterior is on an unassuming street in Williamsburg, but inside, it is the restaurant incarnation of Mary Poppins' bag: compact, but they manage to pack in far more than you’d expect.

Though the signature dumplings, chor muang—chicken and peanut filling encased in delicate butterfly pea flower dough—are the star, don’t overlook the noodle dishes, which are slurpable, expertly sauced, and so soft as to be almost buttery.

Thai Diner does diner favorites reimagined, like their beloved Thai Disco Fries.

Head to Thai Diner for brunch, lunch, or a vibey dinner.

If you have friends from out of town that you really want to impress and show how fun eating in New York City can be, go to Thai Diner and get an order of the Thai Disco Fries. I find that these crispy, crinkle-cut fries smothered in a peanutty massaman curry sauce are delicious enough to justify to out-of-towners how much you overspend on rent. Reservations can be hard to get, but they do take some walk-ins, so your best bet is to either arrive slightly before opening, or put your name down and wander around Nolita until your name is called.

The restaurant has a tropical dive bar feel, with plenty of diner favorites reimagined like a custardy Thai tea babka, French toast, and a signature Thai Diner egg sandwich made with Isan-style sausage wrapped in a plush roti. Co-owners Ann Redding and Matt Danzer also recently opened Mommy Pai’s, a fast Thai chicken takeout spot on the same block that’s a great lunch spot without the wait.

Dishes are meant to be shared family-style here—like a whole fish drenched in cliantro-lime broth.

661 Driggs Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11211 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Steamed fish with Thai herbs

Specializing in seafood dishes, Fish Cheeks focuses on the bright flavors of southern coastal Thailand. Dishes are meant to be shared family-style here, and though the menu features a few poultry, pork, and beef options, your best bet is trusting the name and going straight for fish. I recommend getting a whole steamed fish for the table—your dinnermates will relish in sharing the communal centerpiece and drenching rice in its cilantro-lime broth, or the coconut crab curry, which comes with rice noodles for soaking up every last bit of the creamy sauce.

Though its flagship Noho location can book out quickly, its equally delicious (and newer) spot in Williamsburg is a bit easier to secure a reservation at, for now.

New Flatiron restaurant LenLen is definitively cool.

The menu at LenLen includes crowd-pleasers and bolder dishes like a durian crab curry.

40 E 20th St, New York, NY 10003 (Flatiron)

If I had to describe LenLen in one word, it would be cool. This relatively new spot hit Flatiron earlier this year, bringing a fresh excitement to the Thai food scene in midtown. For me, the standout of the menu is the love-it-or-loathe-it durian crab curry. It’s earthy, fruity, and well worth the visit alone. While you’re there, order the wagyu beef boat noodles, too, which are served in a rich, dark broth that reminds me of the ones I’ve had in Ayutthaya, one of my favorite cities in Thailand (and the birthplace of boat noodles).

There are whispers of a speakeasy opening downstairs in the coming months, which gives the restaurant extra potential to become a go-to dinner spot that seamlessly transitions into a night out.

Ler Lers does classic Bangkok-style fare right.

From pad thai to grilled meats, Ler Lers does it all.

417 Tompkins Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11216 (Bed-Stuy)

Not to be confused with LenLen, Ler Lers is a newer spot in Bed-Stuy and does classic Bangkok-style fare right. Its ambiance is stylish and warm, with a mix of rattan and earthy tones, for a setting that makes sipping on a sweet iced Thai tea feel right even on a cold rainy day.

I’m pretty weary of ordering pad thai out in restaurants, just because the cuisine has so much else to offer. But a friend promised me that the pad thai topped with crispy pork belly was “awesome,” and after trying it for myself, I’ve started saying the same to friends and family. The rest of the menu has a lot of other familiar favorites like fried rice and grilled meats, and if you’re someone who enjoys a sticky tamarind sauce as much as I do, try the branzino, too.

Hommali is stylish in every sense of the word, from the plating to the space.

The Hommali cocktail menu is also expansive—go for the signature tomato option.

28 7th Ave S, New York, NY 10014 (West Village)

A newcomer to the West Village restaurant scene, this design-forward space has some serious pedigree with a menu curated by Bangkok-native Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, formerly of Eleven Madison Park. The restaurant is stylish in every sense of the word, with sage green tiles, oak accents, and warm lighting.

You can’t customize spice level here, so expect to get a little red from dishes like the prik larb beef tartare that comes with crispy tripe chips and is fiery with northern larb spices. The Hommali Five Spice dry-aged duck is also a standout and comes with fragrant rice that’s cooked in duck drippings. My opinion? The best order is getting the panang curry with tender beef cheek. It’s spicy, nutty, and you’ll want to order a side (or two) of roti to soak up that sauce.

The cocktail menu is also expansive—go for the signature tomato cocktail, which is vodka and rice wine-based with tomato extract, poblanos, and tamarind.

Soothr in the East Village specializes in noodles from all across Thailand.

204 E 13th St, New York, NY 10003 (East Village)

25-20 43rd Ave, Long Island City, NY 11101

Must-order dish: Sukhothai-style tom yum noodle soup

Thai noodle shop Soothr specializes in noodles from all across Thailand, and though the stir-fried variety is delicious, the soup noodles are the real standout. The Sukhothai-style tom yum noodle soup is a must-order, and encapsulates the best of Thai noodle soups with a deeply savory-acidic broth topped with bouncy fish cakes, meatballs, and rice noodles. Soothr has a new-ish Long Island City location that’s got a more nightlife vibe to it (and just as great noodles).

Kru in Williamsburg draws on Thailand’s vast culinary history, reimaging regional traditions through a contemporary lens.

90 N 14 St, Brooklyn, NY 11249 (Williamsburg)

Must-order dish: Lamb massaman curry pot pie

Named after the Thai word for “mentor,” chef Ohm Suansilphong honors the many teachers in his life through Kru. Here, he draws on Thailand’s vast culinary history, reimaging regional traditions through a contemporary lens. This looks like a crispy, massaman curry pot pie sprinkled with slow-cooked, pull-apart jackfruit, and tender lamb or tamarind-chili coated calamari that’s sweet, salty, and a little spicy. Chef adds and tweaks the menu seasonally, but I suggest the first thing you eat is always the Ma Hor, a savory bite of seasoned meat atop fresh fruit. The word means galloping horse, and it has enough warmth to open your tastebuds for the rest of the meal. Pay attention to the wine list: the restaurant is just as thoughtful about its award-winning program as it is the rest of the menu. Consider this a go-to as worthy of casual weeknight dinners as it is of special occasions.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6200. The 10 best places to visit in November 2026

November is peak shoulder season: The weather can be unpredictable (but you can get really lucky), crowds are small nearly everywhere and prices are often the lowest they'll be all year for many destinations. It is an ideal time to travel in many ways, if you're willing to risk less-than-ideal weather in some places.

Thanksgiving also takes place in the U.S., and if you are not obligated to visit family, you can enjoy a wonderful four-day vacation without missing any school or work. And for those who love Christmas markets and lights, several spots start their displays at the end of the month.

Here are 10 great destinations to consider for your November getaway.

This stunning desert and mountain region enjoys cooler weather in November that's ideal for hiking in the Atlas Mountains. Meanwhile, the nearby city of Marrakech is as vibrant as ever, with more people coming out in the less-than-scorching temps that linger all summer. Wander the souk, stroll the gorgeous gardens, and visit architectural highlights without breaking a sweat.

Nov. 18 is Morocco's Independence Day, and this year's Marrakech Coffee & Tea Festival will run Nov. 5-7, with more than 400 exhibitors and various workshops and classes. This year's Marrakech International Film Festival runs from Nov. 20–28.

Use points to stay at the Park Hyatt Marrakech, which opened in 2025 (rates from $594 or 25,000 World of Hyatt points per night), or check out the new Riad Beij, in the heart of the Medina (rates from $168 per night). To stay in the Atlas Mountains, you can use Virgin Red points at the luxe Virgin Limited Edition Kasbah Tamadot (rates from $577 or 140,000 Virgin Red points per night).

TPG tip: Marrakech has increased seasonal direct flight access, including a direct flight from Newark on United Airlines, which launched in 2024, and from Atlanta on Delta Air Lines, which debuted at the end of 2025.

Oaxaca's celebration of Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, is legendary, especially in Oaxaca City, where festivities and commemorations take place every year from Oct. 31 to Nov. 2. Expect elaborate costumes, parades, street festivals, cemetery and altar visits, and plenty of music, food and drinks.

After the city festivities, plan to stay at one of the region's design-forward hotels. Boutique hotel 7 Casa Laurel opened in April this year, and Casa Yati opened in Ventanilla on the beach last summer. La Valise Mazunte is a member of Small Luxury Hotels of the World with just six suites and a villa (rates from $400 or 130,000 Hilton Honors points per night).

TPG tip: You can fly directly to Puerto Escondido on United Airlines' Houston-to-Puerto Escondido route, which debuted in 2025. American Airlines launched its direct flights to Puerto Escondido from Dallas-Fort Worth in December 2025.

November is the very beginning of the dry season in Thailand, so it's a good time to beat the winter crowds and score good airfare and hotel pricing. Nov. 24 is Loy Krathong, the beautiful floating lantern festival that lights up the Bangkok waterways on the night of the full moon in the 12th month of the Thai lunar calendar. Various events happen along the Chao Phraya River, in public parks and at cultural landmarks.

The city, which has several new hotels this year, with something for almost every loyalist. Voco Bangkok Surawong opened in January 2026 (rates from 19,000 IHG One Rewards and $137 per night). Canopy by Hilton Bangkok Sukhumvit opened in August 2026 (rates from 45,000 Hilton Honors points and $170 per night). The long-delayed Fairmont Bangkok Sukhumvit finally opened, also in August, with LEED Gold certification, a jasmine-inspired spa, seven food and beverage outlets and 474 rooms (rates from 12,345 ALL Accor points and $278 per night).

TPG tip: Last year, United Airlines launched a new daily flight to Bangkok via Hong Kong from Los Angeles and San Francisco, making it the only domestic airline to offer a daily one-stop flight to Bangkok from the U.S.

Looking for an adventure? November is the last month of the dry season to visit the Amazon, so there's still time to squeeze in an adventure before the end of the year. If colorful birds, jaguars, river dolphins and caiman sightings aren't enough for you, the first-ever Global Citizen music festival in the Amazon, in Belem, is Nov. 1. Global Citizen Festival Amazonia brings Brazilian music stars Anitta, Seu Jorge and Gaby Amarantos and Coldplay's Chris Martin together with Indigenous leaders to amplify climate action campaigns.

TPG tip: Avianca flies to Belem via Bogota, Colombia, from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), and LATAM flies there through Sao Paulo/Guarulhos International Airport (GRU). Book a room at Ibis Styles Belem Batista Campos ($67 per night) or Grand Mercure Belem do Para ($474 per night). Both are members of Accor Live Limitless.

If you've dreamed of a vacation in St. Barts but thought you couldn't afford it, November may be the best time to visit the gorgeous Caribbean island. You'll enjoy warm weather, beat the winter crowds and enjoy better prices on hotels and flights. And while the French island is known for always having excellent food, November brings even more culinary star power to the isle.

The Saint-Barth Gourmet Festival is Nov. 9-15 and features five chefs from Michelin-starred restaurants, including chef Amaury Bouhours of Restaurant Le Meurice Alain Ducasse and Thibault Sombardier of Les Parisiens.

TPG tip: Getting to St. Barts can be a bit of a journey if you don't have a private jet (ahem), but Cape Air flies twice daily from well-connected St. Thomas.

Looking to the other hemisphere is always a good idea, and in Australia, they're experiencing the other shoulder season: spring. In Western Australia, this means gorgeous wildflowers and some excellent festivals worth traveling for.

Foodies should plan to attend the world-renowned Pair'd Margaret River Region food and wine festival (Nov. 19-22), which brings world-class wine, food and music to the Margaret River region. This year's lineup includes chefs Rodney Scott, Matt Abe, and Mindy Woods, as well as wine writer Erin Larkin.

TPG tip: Hyde Perth opened in March of this year (rates from $239 per night) as the first Hyde hotel in Australia, a brand from Ennismore (also behind the Hoxton, Mama Shelter, Delano, and 25Hours brands) that also has locations in London, Ibiza, Dubai, and Miami.

Some November trips require compromising on the weather, but not in the desert. Palm Springs in November is ideal: With a daytime high of 79 degrees Fahrenheit and a low of 52 degrees Fahrenheit at night, you'll still avoid its peak tourist months, which begin in January. It's also ideal weather to hike in nearby Joshua Tree National Park.

Though most Pride events occur in June, the Palm Springs Pride Festival is a fall event. This year, it runs from Nov. 6–8, with the big parade on the final day. Expect live music, comedy, local vendors and artists, and plenty of food and drink stands in several areas across the downtown area. The Sunset Music and Comedy Festival runs concurrently each night at the Agua Caliente Casino.

There are several new and improved attractions in the desert: The Palm Springs Air Museum recently completed a $2.5 million renovation, and reopened in September, featuring a turbine-inspired façade, new exhibits, and the Ronald M. Auen Learning Center, and DSRT Surf, a manmade surf lagoon that creates the perfect wave, every time, opened this summer in Palm Desert.

TPG tip: The iconic La Quinta Resort & Club celebrates its centennial in 2026, with special events and guest experiences all year long. It's now a part of Hilton's Curio Collection, so you can use and earn rewards points there (rates from 85,000 Hilton Honors points and $329 per night)

Florence in summer can be a hot, crowded mess, but come November, there are fewer crowds and mild weather (although rain is likely). It's also truffle-hunting season in Tuscany.

Film lovers should mark Oct. 31-Nov. 8 for the Festival dei Popoli, Europe's oldest international documentary film festival. And Nov. 29 brings runners from around the world to the Estra Firenze Marathon. Finally, most Christmas markets open around the city in the last week of November.

TPG tip: The city recently welcomed Borgo Pignano Florence, set on a 5-acre estate with 11 historic buildings and 32 rooms and is part of Relais & Chateaux. La Resérve Firenze opened Oct. 15 inside a restored 15th-century palazzo. If you want to use points, W Florence (rates from $507 or 70,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night) opened last year.

Rev your engines for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, when Formula 1 racing comes to Sin City from Nov. 19-21.

Outside the hugely popular event, you can find some hotel and flight deals this November. And there's still plenty to do in November beyond F1. At the Sphere, you can catch the 4D version of "The Wizard of Oz" daily throughout the month, or see Metallica Nov. 4-7, the Eagles Nov. 13-14 and 27-28.

Christmas also starts early in Vegas on Nov. 5, when the 3-acre Cactus Garden at Ethel M Chocolate Factory opens its annual lights show, and Nov. 14 at the Bellagio Conservatory, where they pull out all the stops to create a lit-up floral winter wonderland.

Foodies should also be excited: Taylor Swift favorite and NYC hotspot The Corner Store is opening its second location at the Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas on November 9.

TPG tip: United restored its nonstop service between Cleveland and Las Vegas in September, with five flights a week and budget airline Breeze Airways added a daily route between Las Vegas and John Wayne Airport in Orange County.

November is the tail end of hurricane season so the possibilities of one hitting are slim—and there are great deals to be had, and usually, excellent weather. Miches — located on the northeast coast of the Dominican Republic — has been increasing its number of high-end all-inclusive resorts, and it's typically much less crowded than Punta Cana, which is near the airport.

Hilton loyalists can turn Hilton Honors points into an all-inclusive stay at Zemi Miches Punta Cana All-Inclusive Resort, Hilton's first Curio Collection all-inclusive resort in the country. Hyatt has also planted its all-inclusive flag in Miches with two openings: Dreams Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa and Secrets Playa Esmeralda Resort & Spa. At Dreams, families and kids are welcome to enjoy the beautiful beaches, pools, and many restaurants and bars, while Secrets is adults-only.

TPG tip: No matter where you stay, let the hotel arrange your transportation from Punta Cana International Airport for ease and affordability. The transportation area at this airport can be overwhelming, and after a long flight, who doesn't want everything made easy?
