#6199. Southwest Premier Card Review: Is The $149 Mid-Range Card Worth It?

Chase and Southwest have a great portfolio of personal credit cards at three different price points. This is my in-depth review of the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card, the Southwest personal card with a $149 annual fee (which is neither the highest nor lowest annual fee product).

Now is an especially good time to consider this card, both because it’s offering an elevated welcome bonus, and because it’s your last chance to use credit card welcome bonuses to qualify for Southwest’s Companion Pass benefit under the old system.

Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card

Before I get into my Southwest Premier Card review, here’s a broad look at the card and its key features:

In my opinion, here are the pros and cons of the Southwest Airlines Premier Card:

When applying for credit, cards, the welcome bonus, eligibility rules, and fees, are obviously major factors that potential cardmembers consider. So let’s cover those details for the Southwest Premier Card, as the card has a great bonus, nuanced eligibility requirements, and a relatively manageable annual fee.

The Southwest Premier Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus where you can earn 85,000 bonus points after you spend $2,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This is a limited time, elevated offer, as the most recent base offer was for 55,000 points.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So to me, the points from this welcome bonus are worth $1,020, making this a solid welcome offer.

When it comes to Southwest credit card eligibility rules, the Southwest Premier Card isn’t available to anyone who currently has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest Rapid Rewards business credit card.

Beyond the restrictions related to which Southwest cards you have, there are general application rules for Chase cards, including the Chase 5/24 rule, whereby you usually won’t get approved for a Chase credit card if you’ve opened five or more credit card accounts in the past 24 months.

The Southwest Premier Card has a $149 annual fee, and you can add authorized users to the card at no extra cost. Southwest’s personal credit cards have annual fees of $99, $149, and $229, so this is the “middle child” of the Southwest and Chase personal card portfolio.

The Southwest Premier Card has no foreign transaction fees, so you can use it abroad without worrying about extra charges.

In addition to the benefits, one of the main reasons you’ll want to consider picking up a card is because of its return on spending, so you’re sure it aligns with what you’re looking for. In the case of the Southwest Premier Card, it has a limited number of bonus categories, and spending can also help you toward earning elite status with Rapid Rewards. So let’s cover those details.

As far as the Southwest Premier Card’s rewards structure goes, the card offers the following:

It’s good that the card has some bonus categories, though there are ultimately more rewarding cards out there for everyday spending. Based on my valuation of 1.2 cents per point, that’s like a 3.6% return on Southwest purchases, a 2.4% return on grocery stores and restaurants (up to the cap), and a 1.2% return on everything else.

The Southwest Premier Card also lets you earn unlimited Tier Qualifying Points (TQPs) toward Southwest status. Through the end of 2026, you can earn 1,500 TQPs toward A-List status for every $5,000 spent on the card. Starting January 1, 2027, every Southwest credit card will earn 1 TQP per dollar spent, so $35,000 in spending on any of them would get you to Silver status.

A-List is Southwest Airlines’ version of elite status, and offers perks like priority boarding, a 25% points bonus, same-day standby, priority check-in and security lane access, and a dedicated phone number. A-List status ordinarily requires earning 35,000 TQPs in a calendar year, so spending on a Southwest Premier Card could help you earn that. Whether or not that’s worth it depends on how much you’d otherwise fly with Southwest.

Currently, Southwest Rapid Rewards elite status has two levels: A-List and A-List Preferred. Beginning January 1, 2027, though, the program will grow to three tiers, with new names: Silver, Gold, and Platinum. Qualifying for Silver status will require the same 35,000 TQPs needed for A-List, while Gold and Platinum will require 65,000 TQPs and 140,000 TQPs, respectively. I covered these Southwest Rapid Rewards program changes in detail here.

This brings me to another big upcoming change to the Southwest program and how cards like the Southwest Premier Card fit into your strategy — and this is a pretty unwelcome one.

One of the best values in travel is the Southwest Airlines Companion Pass. With a Companion Pass, you can have someone travel with you for the entire year (whether on a cash ticket or award ticket) and just pay taxes and fees for them. This is such an incredible deal and basically doubles the value you can get from flying Southwest.

For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting January 1, 2027, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

This eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only change: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending, won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

This change isn’t specific to the Southwest Premier Card, as it applies to welcome bonuses across all Southwest credit cards. But the good news is that welcome bonuses earned before the end of 2026 do count toward Companion Pass qualification, so now is your last chance to take advantage before this opportunity ends.

I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but I’ll briefly cover how redemptions work.

Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, which means that the value you’ll get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. That said, there are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares.

Basic award fares tend to offer the highest redemption value, and in my experience the best-value Southwest point redemptions are usually for international routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. For instance, I’ve seen Basic awards from Tampa (TPA) to Liberia, Costa Rica (LIR) for 12,000 points and $24.21. The same fare cost $200 in cash, giving you a very strong value of 1.46 cents per point.

One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card offers some benefits that could make the card worth keeping long term. How do the perks compare to Southwest’s lower and higher annual fee cards?

The Southwest Premier Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person. With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card lets you pick a Preferred seat on Southwest, if any are available, starting 48 hours before departure. The cost for a Preferred seat can vary from $28 to nearly $50 depending on the flight, so this perk is another potential money-saver.

Another Southwest Premier Card benefit is early boarding. You’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group. Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last.

On your cardmember anniversary every year, you’ll receive 6,000 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

In other words, 6,000 bonus points get you around $72 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers nearly half of the annual fee right there.

Each year on your Southwest Premier Card cardmember anniversary, you’ll get a 15% promo code that applies to Southwest flights. Just note that this excludes Basic fares.

The Southwest Premier Card offers 25% savings on inflight purchases of Wi-Fi and drinks. Simply pay with your card, and you’ll automatically receive a statement credit for that amount.

The Southwest Premier Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:

You’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

The Southwest Airlines Premier Card is Southwest’s mid-range card, and the $149 annual fee is in line with many other co-branded airline credit cards. The card is offering a fantastic bonus, which is one good reason to consider this product.

On an ongoing basis, the 6,000-point anniversary bonus can get you around $72 worth of airfare. Whether the Southwest Premier Card is worth it in the long run depends on how much you value the other perks like a free checked bag, and whether you plan to use spending on the credit card to qualify for Southwest elite status.

As I mentioned above, the Southwest Premier Card is the mid-range option in Chase’s lineup of Southwest cards. Here’s a look at how it compares to the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more), which is the entry-level option:

If you don’t care about working toward Southwest status through credit card spending and you want to keep your annual fee to a minimum, the Southwest Plus Card is likely a better option for you.

On the other end of the spectrum, there’s the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card, which is the most expensive of the three personal Southwest credit cards. Here’s how it differs from the Southwest Premier Card:

If you fly Southwest all the time and want as many benefits with the airline as possible, the Southwest Priority Card could be the right choice. It’s also the best pick if you want to spend your way toward status before the end of 2026, since it earns TQPs at the fastest rate of the three cards.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. This means that you could earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, and your points will be more flexible (since you can also transfer them to other airlines and hotel programs).

So, should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest Airlines credit card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards credit card?

For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:

On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:

The Southwest Premier Card is a solid mid-range airline credit card. It has a nice welcome bonus, plus ongoing perks that justify the annual fee. However, if you’re not particularly interested in extra perks when you fly Southwest, you’re much better off earning points with Chase Ultimate Rewards and then transferring them to Southwest Rapid Rewards, given that it gives you higher points earning rates and more flexibility.

#6198. United went big on credit cards in 2026. More changes are coming, MileagePlus boss says

Before he ran United Airlines' MileagePlus program, Jarad Fisher was the type of traveler who went "all-in" for elite status.

He read TPG, collected miles and occasionally went on ambitious end-of-year "status runs."

"My wife thought I was nuts," he joked, recalling an epic out-and-back trip to Hawaii 12 years ago — where he never even left the airport — in order to qualify.

Now, Fisher is in charge of United's loyalty program as it undergoes one of its biggest transformations in recent memory.

Ironically, one of his first orders of business was eliminating flight segments as a status metric.

Starting in 2027, "Premier Qualifying Flights" are out. That means United loyalists will no longer be "graded" on how many actual flights they rack up.

Instead, the carrier will rely exclusively on PQPs, which are based on a combination of members' spending, both on flights and on their United credit cards.

United has framed the change as a way to make qualifying for status simpler — though it could make it more challenging for some United flyers.

It will also end the need for eleventh-hour "segment runs" that once had frequent flyers (like Fisher) crisscrossing the country in December to rack up enough elite-qualifying flights.

"That was an old relic," he said, speaking about United's recent changes in an exclusive interview with TPG.

"You're taking seats away from people who actually want to get to a certain destination. It's not great for the environment. It's not a great use of time," he explained. "We thought it made more sense for them to have one, consistent metric."

That's not the only change United has made to MileagePlus in 2026.

Earlier this year, the carrier upended several of its loyalty policies, heavily tilting its program toward members who carry one of its credit cards.

Together, these moves were among the most aggressive any U.S. airline has made to nudge flyers toward its cobranded credit cards.

It's part of a larger strategy Fisher often sums up with this mantra:

"It's good to fly United, it's great to be a MileagePlus member," he said. "But the best way to engage with us is to be a MileagePlus member and actually have one of our cards."

Speaking publicly this year, United's chief commercial officer, Andrew Nocella, has hinted that United's loyalty shakeup isn't done.

It appears some changes may have to wait until the airline can re-negotiate its credit card deal with banking partner Chase.

"While we continue to work under a long-term cobrand contract," Nocella said on an earnings call in April, "We're making changes to what we can control today."

United's current Chase deal is set to run through 2029, according to past TPG reporting.

For now, the carrier has significantly upped the incentives for customers to carry one of its cards in the first place: Over the past year, United's cobranded credit card holders have clearly gained the upper hand in its program.

Fisher said the airline plans to continue adapting the program in ways "that will be more consistent" with that ethos in the coming years.

"And so I think as a function of that, we're looking at not only the core loyalty program, we're looking at our partnerships," he said. "And we're trying to make it so that we will continue to be — not just the best airline loyalty program — but we're really aspiring to be the best loyalty program in the world."

What future changes could MileagePlus members ultimately see when they go to redeem miles, earn on their Lyft rides or enter a United Club?

And Fisher will play a big part in those decisions, after taking the helm of MileagePlus this year with an intriguing pedigree.

Seven years ago, he was heavily involved in the launch of Apple Card.

Before that, he spent time at top rival Delta Air Lines, helping turbocharge its partnership with American Express — which today is the industry's most lucrative tie-up, set to bring Delta $9 billion this year.

That resume has Fisher thinking beyond earn rates and status benchmarks as he looks to build on changes that gave United flyers plenty to digest in 2026.

"We're really trying to think about what will truly help us break away from the pack," he said of the carrier's future plans.

Of course, that's easier said than done in the airline world.

Flight delays are inevitable. Loyal flyers can grow frustrated when they go to book a redemption and are shocked by how many miles they'll need.

Not to mention, complimentary status upgrades don't clear as often as they used to, as first-class seats are increasingly filled by customers who actually paid for their tickets. By the way, balancing paid first-class seats with those long upgrade queues is a dilemma Fisher said the airline is "consistently looking at."

"More folks are paying for [premium seats], which of course is putting pressure on the system," he acknowledged.

But for an airline that has made plenty of waves in recent years — from its on-board internet to its international routes — it's safe to say United won't shy away from trying new things on the loyalty front, either.

And it's a likely bet that customers who carry its credit cards will benefit most.

"If you think about the amount of time people spend with us, and on board our aircraft, we want them to feel known. We want them to feel recognized," he said. "You will continue to see us become even more focused and deliberate about that approach."

#6197. United Airlines Launches New 6-Hour Boeing 737 MAX Nonstop Routes: See Map Now

United Airlines has added two new transcontinental routes from San Francisco International Airport (SFO). It'll operate from its Pacific hub to both Norfolk and Richmond, both of which are in Virginia.

Last month, the carrier disclosed two transcon routes from SFO to Charleston, South Carolina, and Hartford, Connecticut. While Charleston, Norfolk, and Richmond have not previously had United flights from SFO, Hartford has, most recently in 2018.

While United will serve both long domestic routes next year, only two weekly flights will exist on both of them, all on the 166-seat Boeing 737 MAX 8. This configuration has 16 domestic first seats, along with 54 seats in economy plus and 96 seats in main cabin. The schedule, more or less the same for both routes, will allow connectivity to/from various Asia-Pacific destinations. Manila, Seoul, and Tokyo will be especially important.

UA2364: 8:15 AM-4:41 PM (5 hours and 26 minutes)

UA1297: 5:45 PM-8:57 PM (6 hours and 12 minutes)

UA1853: 8:15 AM-4:50 PM (5 hours and 35 minutes)

UA1807: 5:45 PM-9:08 PM (6 hours and 23 minutes)

The Star Alliance member will be the sole operator between SFO and ORF. Cirium Diio shows that it is a brand-new market, with no nonstop services with any airline in the past. It is, therefore, historical in nature. With 43,400 round-trip local passengers, ORF was SFO's tenth-largest unserved domestic market.

SFO to RIC is very different. United will coexist with Breeze Airways, which commenced the long route in May 2022. Running twice-weekly on the Airbus A220-200, it will be the first time the airport pair has had two carriers operating nonstop. Fortunately, both airlines will operate on different days of the week. While United will focus on the local market and some connectivity via SFO, virtually all of Breeze's traffic is point-to-point. With 70,000 local passengers, it was SFO's fifth-largest domestic market that did not have United flights.

While the list of upcoming routes in 2027 will almost certainly increase, the latest information, as of November 2, shows that the following routes will launch. They'll all take off at the end of March, as northern carriers, including United, will switch to summer schedules based on IATA slot seasons on Sunday, March 28, 2027.

The additions join four markets that materialized in 2026 or will do so in the remainder of the year. The first to launch was SFO to Carlsbad, California, on March 29, with two daily services on SkyWest E175s. Flights to Portland International Jetport Airport (PWM), Maine, followed on June 27, with a weekly 737 MAX 8 operation. Both airport pairs are brand-new, which is always great to see. PWM is the longest nonstop domestic service from SFO.

On November 17, United will lift off from SFO to West Palm Beach, with up to a daily MAX 8 service. Then there's SFO to Sapporo, Japan, with three weekly flights on the 787-9. Neither destination has previously been served from SFO. In fact, it'll be the first time that Sapporo has had nonstop flights from the Lower 48. Meanwhile, SFO is West Palm Beach's new longest domestic route.

United is widely expected to return to New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in 2027, having flown there for years until 2015 and again between 2021 and 2022. Clearly, one route will be from SFO, along with Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), presumably all on the so-called A321neo 'Coastliner,' which has 161 seats. It has 50 orders for the equipment.

The airline is seemingly seeking up to 20 slot pairs at JFK, with some probably from JetBlue. While United will not have connectivity via JFK, it'd focus on the enormous local traffic and connectivity via SFO/LAX, especially, of course, to/from Asia-Pacific.

In the current month, United has up to 23 daily flights from SFO/LAX to its Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) hub, from which it is usually quicker to access Manhattan than it is from JFK. It is obviously massively dominant at EWR, which helps with achieving higher yields. The appeal of JFK is to capture a greater share of the considerable market between SFO/LAX and Greater NYC.

#6196. Which Credit Card Should You Use For Marriott Hotel Stays? Here’s The Math

When you’re staying at a Marriott property, what’s the best credit card to use to maximize your return on Marriott hotel spending? Should you use a co-branded Marriott credit card, or are you better off using another credit card offering bonus points on travel? This is a question that comes up every so often, so I’d like to address it in this post…

I’ve written in the past about the best credit cards to use for hotel stays. However, more specifically to Marriott, which credit card should you put all of your Marriott spending on? Let’s take a look at the various approaches that you can take.

Let me start by acknowledging that we all value points currencies differently, so you should apply your own valuation to the math. My below analysis is based on my own valuation of various points currencies.

I also want to emphasize that the credit card you use won’t impact your ability to earn elite qualifying nights, take advantage of elite perks, and accrue the standard points that you can earn with the Marriott Bonvoy program. The credit card rewards offered when paying for your Marriott hotel stay are incremental.

Marriott has co-branded credit cards in the United States that are issued by both American Express and Chase. All of these credit cards with annual fees have the same rewards structure for Marriott spending, as they offer 6x Marriott Bonvoy® Points on all eligible Marriott spending.

This includes cards like the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card (learn more), Marriott Bonvoy Business® American Express® Card (learn more), and Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant® American Express® Card (learn more), just to name a few. Personally, I value Bonvoy points at 0.7 cents each, so to me these cards offer an incremental 4.2% return on that spending.

I think the one thing worth pointing out is that the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy® American Express® Card offers 1,000 Bonvoy bonus points per Marriott stay when paying with the card, in addition to the rewards that you usually earn.

Technically that would be the best co-branded card for Marriott spending, since you earn 6x points, plus 1,000 bonus points per stay. That being said, I’d otherwise consider this to be one of the less compelling Marriott cards in terms of the overall value proposition.

I generally recommend putting most of your spending on cards earning transferable points currencies, given that they offer the most flexible rewards, and also have excellent bonus categories.

I’d argue that the two best cards for hotel spending are the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) and Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more), as they offer 4x transferable points for direct hotel purchases. Since I value Ultimate Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, that’s like a 6.8% return on that spending, which is excellent.

It’s worth noting that there are other cards earning 3x points on hotels, like the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), and I’d value that at a return of 5.1%. Lastly, the Wells Fargo Autograph Journey Card (learn more) actually offers 5x points on hotel purchases, which is excellent, though I don’t value those points as much as other transferable points currencies.

Personally, the Chase Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve Business are my go-to cards for hotel spending. Simply put, I can’t turn down 4x Ultimate Rewards points, in comparison to earning 6x Bonvoy points with the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Amex for my Marriott spending.

The difference in math is just too great, since I value 4x Ultimate Rewards points at way more than 6x Bonvoy points. But this also brings me to a related topic of how points valuations sometimes don’t dictate my consumer behavior. For example, back in the day, the Chase Sapphire Reserve offered 3x Ultimate Rewards points on hotel spending.

So I valued that at offering a 5.1% return, rather than a 4.2% return on a Marriott credit card. Despite that, I’d use a co-branded Marriott card for my Marriott spending. Why? Well, this gets at a consideration that’s hard to factor into my valuation of points. I’m talking about the ease of earning various points currencies.

I can earn transferable points currencies in all kinds of ways, including with my everyday spending. However, there aren’t many ways to efficiently earn Bonvoy points, short of staying at Marriott properties. As I often talk about when sharing my points strategy, there’s merit to collecting points that are harder to earn, even if they’re not the points currency that you necessarily value the most. This was one of those cases, at least for me. However, with the Chase Sapphire Reserve nowadays earning 4x points per dollar spent on hotels, my logic on that has evolved.

Everyone has their own credit card strategy, and at times it can be tough to decide which card is the best for a particular spending category.

In the case of spending at Marriott properties, I’d argue that the Chase Sapphire Reserve and Sapphire Reserve Business are nowadays the most lucrative, given that they offer 4x Ultimate Rewards points on that spending, which I value at a 6.8% return. I’d say that beats the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Amex, offering 6x Bonvoy points, which I value at a 4.2% return.

Which credit card do you use for Marriott hotel spending?

#6194. Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur Opens With 268 Suites And Record Pricing

The Waldorf Astoria brand has been on an impressive growth trajectory in recent times, and has opened several new flagship properties. This Hilton luxury brand has just opened its latest hotel, in Kuala Lumpur. It looks beautiful, but I can’t help but wonder if it will succeed. Let me explain…

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur has opened as of late October 2026. The residential-style, all-suite property features 268 accommodations, ranging in size from 80 square meters (861 square feet) to 745 square meters (8,019 square feet).

The property is set within Kuala Lumpur’s “Golden Triangle” district, and as you’d expect, it’s intended to be an urban retreat with both extensive dining and wellness facilities.

Dining options are headlined by Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s signature market-to-table concepts at JG KL, abc kitchens KL, and The Bar by JG. Then there’s also The Istana (where breakfast is served), Yaari (serving Indian cuisine), and Peacock Alley (the signature Waldorf Astoria bar concept).

The Waldorf Astoria Spa is 2,275 square meters (24,488 square feet), and features La Prairie treatments. Then there’s a fitness center, along with an outdoor pool.

Based on the renderings that have been shared so far, the property looks beautiful, in my opinion.

Kuala Lumpur is one of my favorite hotel markets in the world, in terms of how reasonably priced luxury hotels are, at least by international standards (of course I understand that doesn’t factor in local buying power). The city’s current top hotels, like the Four Seasons and Park Hyatt, can be had for around $300 per night.

With that in mind, what are rates like at the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur? Well, the hotel is trying to set a new pricing record in the city, and not just by a small margin. I see the absolute lowest rate currently being $479 per night, though seasonally rates are $600+. That’s before taxes and fees, for a base suite.

If you’re booking a cash rate, I’d recommend doing so through the Hilton for Luxury program, which offers extra perks when booking through select travel advisors, including breakfast, a hotel credit, an upgrade subject to availability, and more.

For those redeeming Hilton Honors points, the rate seems to be 100,000 points per night, assuming a standard suite is available. At my valuation of 0.5 cents per Hilton point, that’s like “paying” $500 per night to stay here, inclusive of taxes and fees.

When you consider that standard suites are over 860 square feet, that price probably doesn’t seem unreasonable. You’re getting more than twice the space you’d ordinarily get at the city’s top luxury hotels, so it’s not illogical that the pricing would be higher.

If this hotel had 60 accommodations, I’d say there’s probably a market for that, by just chasing the very top end of consumers who value space. But 268 accommodations?! That’s an absolutely massive number of suites to fill at record prices. I mean, this hotel will have more keys than the Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur.

I just can’t imagine the hotel will be able to run any sort of decent occupancy with that pricing, and so many suites to fill. Either I’m wrong, or the hotel will have to lower prices, or will consistently run low occupancy.

The other thing is that if you’re not specifically looking for a suite, it’s really hard to compete with the Park Hyatt Kuala Lumpur, which is also new, and a really stellar property. It also creates intrigue among people, given that it’s one of the world’s highest up hotels.

The Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur is now open. The 268-suite property is setting new records in the city, both for entry level room size, and also for pricing. The property looks beautiful, and the dining options also look top notch. However, filling 268 rooms at rates that are 50%+ higher than any existing option will be a challenge.

What do you make of the Waldorf Astoria Kuala Lumpur? Do you think they’ll be able to get these rates while running decent occupancy?

#6193. United Airlines’ JFK Return Is Imminent: What’s The Strategy, Though?

We know that United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby thinks that one of the carrier’s biggest mistakes in the past was pulling out of New York Kennedy Airport (JFK). He’s committed to changing that, and the airline still seems to think that it’s on track to return to the airport in 2027.

A lot has changed since this was initially a big topic of conversation, including United seemingly no longer being interested in any sort of merger with JetBlue. So with United potentially within a year of returning to JFK, I’d like to talk a bit more about what that could look like, as I’m still not sure I fully understand the strategy.

United obviously has a huge hub at Newark Liberty Airport (EWR), and different airline executives have different takes as to the overlap in demand between Newark and Kennedy.

Through late 2015, United had a relatively small presence at JFK, with a majority of the service consisting of premium transcontinental flights to Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO), with a product that was branded as p.s. The airline operated these flights with specially configured, three cabin Boeing 757-200s.

However, in late 2015, the airline made the decision to end service at JFK, and instead consolidate flights at EWR. The airline was reportedly losing money on these flights, and just couldn’t compete with American and Delta, which both had major hubs there.

Shortly after that decision was made, Kirby joined United, before eventually being appointed CEO. For as long as he has been at United, Kirby has felt that leaving JFK was one of the carrier’s biggest strategic blunders. In 2021, United briefly returned to JFK, operating transcon routes with Boeing 767-300ERs. However, the airline pulled out by 2022, as it couldn’t get permanent slots, and couldn’t scale service in a way that made sense.

Ever since, United has been determined to return to JFK. We know that United wants up to 20 daily slot pairs at the airport, to offer very frequent coast-to-coast service. So, where do things stand? As flagged by JonNYC, United Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella recently went on record to confirm that United is on track to return to JFK in 2027, which is just around the corner.

So, how will United secure the slots needed for service?

United management is generally on top of things when it comes to strategy, and I can make sense of most things. However, I still struggle to fully rationalize the plans for returning to JFK. That’s not to say it doesn’t make sense, or that I’m right, but here’s how I think through this:

On the surface, entering a market as a fourth place player, with limited opportunity to grow, little connectivity on the JFK side, and limited ability to have a great ground experience, seems like it could create a challenge.

United Airlines executives still insist the airline will return to JFK in 2027. This seems to involve getting some number of slots from JetBlue (as part of their partnership), and then possibly acquiring slots from some other carriers. It’s still not entirely clear how this will play out, though last we heard, the goal is to get 20 slot pairs, and aggressively fly to LAX and SFO.

I know Kirby thinks it was a big mistake to leave JFK, though I remain a bit confused by how the airline offering high frequency service from JFK to the West Coast, when the markets are already served by three large carriers, will be lucrative.

How do you see United’s JFK strategy playing out?

#6192. My Atmos Rewards Summit Card Application Approval Experience

The $395 annual fee Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card is the premium credit card of Atmos Rewards, which is the combined loyalty program of Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines.

I’d argue that this is one of the best airline credit cards we’ve seen in a long time, and there are many reasons to pick up this card, from the ability to earn 3x points on foreign purchases, to the Global Companion Awards offered by the card, to the waived partner award booking fees, to the free points sharing, to the Alaska Lounge passes.

Perhaps the most obvious reason to get the Atmos Rewards Summit Card is that it’s offering a limited time welcome bonus, which in and of itself is a reason to apply. Specifically, you can receive 100,000 bonus points and a 25,000-point Global Companion Award with this offer. To qualify, spend $6,000 or more on purchases within the first 90 days of opening your account.

This is in line with the best-ever publicly available welcome offer we’ve seen on the Atmos Rewards Summit Card, and this is exactly the offer with which I applied for the card last year. In this post, I’d like to talk a bit about the rules when it comes to getting approved for the card, and my experience when I applied last year.

Link: Learn more about the Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® Credit Card

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is issued by Bank of America. The good news is that eligibility for this card is unrelated to having any other card from Bank of America, Atmos Rewards, Alaska, or Hawaiian. So you’re eligible for this card (including the welcome bonus) if you have any other card in the portfolio.

For example, if you look at the terms of the Atmos Rewards Summit Card application, you’ll see the following:

This one-time promotion is limited to customers opening a new account in response to this offer and will not apply to requests to convert existing accounts.

That’s great, because it means that anyone who doesn’t yet have this card should be eligible for the bonus. Beyond that, what general restrictions does Bank of America have when it comes to approving people for cards? Here are a couple of common Bank of America restrictions that are often discussed, though let me emphasize that enforcement seems really inconsistent:

Both of these rules are specific to personal cards, and not business cards. Beyond that, neither of those rules seem to be totally consistently enforced, and in particular, that latter policy doesn’t seem consistent at all. For example, I opened more than three new cards in the 12 months before applying, and still ended up being approved.

Bank of America can sometimes be quirky in terms of approvals. I find that with Bank of America, I often get instant approvals with massive credit lines, and then every once in a while, I get random, inexplicable denials. So make of that what you will. If you’re interested in picking up more than one Atmos Rewards card in a day, it’s worth pointing out that you can potentially be approved for two in one day.

What’s the application process like when applying for the Atmos Rewards Summit Card? The online application process is really straightforward, and consists of just one page.

It just asks for personal details — name, date of birth, social security number, address, phone number, income, etc. You’ll also be asked for your Atmos Rewards number, so you’ll want to include that, so that your points are credited to the right account.

The process is even simpler if you already have a Bank of America account, as you’ll be asked to log-in with your account, and then you only have to provide updated income information.

For example, I applied for the card when it launched last year, and was instantly approved, with a pretty big credit line, no less!

Now that I’ve had the Atmos Rewards Summit Card for quite some time, what’s my strategy? I think the first thing to acknowledge is that the welcome bonus on this card is significant. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Atmos Rewards points to be worth 1.5 cents each, so the current 100,000 points plus a 25,000-point Global Companion Award are worth around $1,875 to me. There’s no reason not to give this card a try, and see how it works out, as that’s among the best card welcome bonuses out there.

What about beyond that, though? At a minimum, this is a card that I’ll keep on an ongoing basis, as long as the benefits don’t materially change, even if I don’t spend much on it. The annual 25,000-point Global Companion Award plus waived partner award booking fees more than justify the annual fee for me, given how many awards I book through the Atmos Rewards program, particularly for travel on American (you also get great travel protection with this card, which is useful).

But for the time being, the Atmos Rewards Summit Card is actually a major part of my credit card strategy, and I think there’s an argument to be made for being loyal to Atmos Rewards instead of American AAdvantage:

As I’ve already covered, I’ve actually made the switch from American AAdvantage to Atmos Rewards, and have already earned Platinum status, and am considering going for Titanium. While not specific to the credit card, the fact that award flights count toward elite status is really a selling point of the program.

The Atmos Rewards Summit Card is Bank of America’s premium credit card in the Alaska & Hawaiian Atmos Rewards ecosystem. It’s an incredibly compelling card — it’s worth signing up for given the huge welcome bonus, it’s worth keeping for the ongoing perks, and for many people, it’ll be worth spending money on.

Bank of America can be quirky with approving people for cards, but the good news is that many people should be eligible for this product, given that it’s quite new, and eligibility is unrelated to having other Atmos Rewards, Alaska, or Hawaiian cards. I applied for the card back when it launched, and was instantly approved. I’ve had a good experience so far with this card, and don’t see myself canceling it any time soon.

I’d highly recommend giving this card a try and applying with the current bonus, given the value it offers.

#6191. Air Fares Still ‘Quite Low,’ A4A CEO Says

Air fares have risen about 22% year-over-year, largely due to the surge in jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

But considering the very low-cost environment that prevailed prior to 2026, tickets are still relatively inexpensive, Airlines For America CEO Chris Sununu said this week.

“Airline costs are actually quite low,” Sununu told CBS’ The Takeout. “They’ve risen 22 percent in the last year because of the Iran war, but from all-time lows. So no, overall, flying in the United States is still incredibly affordable.”

“If you want that premium seat, that first class seat, obviously you pay a little more for that,” he continued. “That economy seat is still very affordable.”

Airline ticket prices have risen since February, when the conflict began. The collapse of ultra-low-cost Spirit Airlines in May and major carriers’ shift toward premiumization could also be playing a role.

When pressed by host Major Garrett on reports that U.S. airlines are letting seats go empty instead of lowering prices to effectively discipline the market, Sununu said that was “100 percent” false.

“If a flight is not making money, believe me, it’s been pulled off because jet fuel is so high,” he said. “Instead of three flights a day from Wichita to Green Bay, there’s two flights. So, no, when you get on a flight now, it’s going to be more often than not very very crowded.”

Asked about the FAA’s sweeping air traffic control modernization effort, Sununu was positive and credited Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford with launching the first serious system-wide upgrade in decades.

“For forty years they’ve done nothing,” he said. “And they’ve done more in the last twelve months than they have in the previous forty years. And that is coming as a cynic of Washington, who has seen the political landscape littered with failed infrastructure projects.”

The main benefit for customers, Sununu added, will be efficiency.

“It’s always going to be safe,” he said. “But over the past few years they’ve had to slow the system down, because it is so antiquated, to ensure the safety. But now we get that efficiency back.”

#6189. How Many Flights In One Day? We Tracked A Wideroe Dash 8 For 24 Hours

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

On Wednesday, October 21, a Widerøe Bombardier Dash 8-100 registered LN-WIE flew 17 sectors between eight airports in Arctic Norway. It left Tromsø (TOS) at 04:12 UTC and finished at Lakselv (LKL) at 21:28, spending 8 hours and 34 minutes airborne across an elapsed day of 17 hours and 16 minutes. The shortest flight, Båtsfjord (BJF) to Vadsø (VDS), lasted seven minutes. Five sectors ran under 20 minutes. The aircraft returned to Hammerfest (HFT) five separate times.

None of it exists on commercial merit. These are public service obligation routes, tendered by the Norwegian government and operated under subsidy because no airline would fly them otherwise. Widerøe won all 13 PSO routes in the 2017 tender round, and the Dash 8-100 is the aircraft that makes the arrangement work at 39 seats on short Finnmark runways. Keeping those airframes flying has required De Havilland Canada to certify the type to 160,000 flight cycles, double its original design life and the highest of any commercial aircraft.

On Wednesday, October 21, a Widerøe Dash 8-100 registered LN-WIE operated 17 flights across eight airports in Arctic Norway. The aircraft departed Tromsø Airport (TOS) at 04:12 UTC and arrived at Lakselv Airport (LKL) at 21:28, a span of 17 hours and 16 minutes. We followed the rotation on Simple Flying's Live Flight Tracker, the same approach we took when tracking a Ryanair Boeing 737 through a full day of European short-haul flying.

The two days look nothing alike. LN-WIE spent 8 hours and 34 minutes airborne across its 17 flights, averaging just over 30 minutes per sector. The longest was Tromsø to Kirkenes (KKN) at 1 hour 7 minutes, the only flight of the day to exceed an hour. The shortest was Båtsfjord (BJF) to Vadsø (VDS) at seven minutes. Eleven of the 17 flights lasted 35 minutes or less, and the aircraft completed its first four sectors before 07:30 UTC.

The route pattern is equally unusual. The aircraft arrived at Hammerfest (HFT) five separate times and at Tromsø four, working between those two points and a cluster of smaller airports across Finnmark, Norway's northernmost county. It also reached Alta (ALF), Vardø (VAW), Vadsø, Båtsfjord, Kirkenes and finally Lakselv, where it finished the day rather than returning to where it started. Four of the eight airports were visited more than once. This is not point-to-point flying in any conventional sense. It is one aircraft circling back repeatedly through the same handful of fields, which is a pattern dictated by something other than commercial route planning.

The third sector of the day was Båtsfjord to Vadsø. The aircraft departed at 06:09 UTC and arrived at 06:17. Seven minutes airborne, which is shorter than the taxi time at most major airports. It is the kind of sector that exists nowhere in a conventional airline network, and on this day it was not even unusual.

Four other flights ran under 20 minutes. Vadsø to Båtsfjord in the opposite direction took 10 minutes that evening. Vardø to Vadsø took 11. Kirkenes to Vardø took 15. Hammerfest to Alta took 16. Five of the 17 sectors, nearly a third of the day's flying, lasted under 20 minutes, and together they accounted for 59 minutes of airborne time out of 514. Several were shorter than the turnaround that preceded them, inverting the usual relationship between time airborne and time on the ground.

These sectors are the reason the network exists in this form. The Bombardier Dash 8-100 is the backbone of Widerøe's public service obligation operation in Norway, particularly in the north. The routes connecting Vardø, Vadsø, Båtsfjord and the other Finnmark fields are subsidized by the Norwegian Ministry of Transport and Communications precisely because the distances involved and the populations served do not support commercial air service. The evening sequence makes the logic plain: Kirkenes to Vardø to Vadsø to Båtsfjord, three consecutive sectors totaling 36 minutes airborne, strung together to connect four communities in a single rotation. A seven-minute flight is not an inefficiency in the schedule. It is what the government contracted for.

Air Transat launches Montreal–Istanbul flights, strengthens its Turkish Airlines partnership, and announces five new European routes for 2027.

Across the full rotation, LN-WIE accumulated 8 hours and 34 minutes airborne against an elapsed day of 17 hours and 16 minutes. That leaves 8 hours and 42 minutes between sectors, marginally more time on the ground than in the air. For an aircraft operating 17 flights in a day, the arithmetic is counterintuitive until sector length is taken into account. When half the flights last under 35 minutes, turnaround time becomes the dominant constraint on how many sectors fit into a day.

The turnarounds were quick. The shortest was 18 minutes at Hammerfest, between arriving from Vadsø at 07:26 and departing for Tromsø at 07:44. Several others ran close: 20 minutes at Hammerfest later that morning, 20 minutes at Båtsfjord in the evening, and 22 minutes at Hammerfest, Alta and Vardø. Across the 16 turnarounds, nine were 30 minutes or less, and the median sat at roughly 23 minutes.

The two long stops were both at Tromsø. The aircraft sat for 78 minutes between arriving from Alta at 11:19 and departing for Hammerfest at 12:37, then 62 minutes in the early afternoon before operating to Kirkenes. Those two pauses account for more than two and a half hours of the day's ground time on their own, meaning the remaining 14 turnarounds averaged under half an hour between them. Everywhere else, the pattern held: land, turn, depart. Hammerfest saw the aircraft five times and Tromsø four, with the rotation repeatedly returning to both rather than progressing along a line. The final turnaround of the day, 34 minutes at Tromsø, preceded the 40-minute positioning sector to Lakselv.

None of these flights exist on commercial merit. They operate under public service obligation contracts, under which the Norwegian Ministry of Transport and Communications subsidizes air service on routes that would not otherwise be flown. Widerøe has held those contracts across the regional network, winning all 13 PSO routes in the 2017 tender round after the government determined it wanted a single operator across all subsidized regional routes in the country.

The Dash 8-100 is the aircraft that makes the arrangement work. Dom Sipinski described the type as the backbone of Widerøe's public service obligation operation, noting that Widerøe is not only the largest operator of the Dash 8-100 but the only one running the aircraft to the end of its service life. At 39 seats, the type matches what these communities generate in demand. Widerøe itself is the largest regional airline in Scandinavia, carrying approximately 2.8 million passengers annually across more than 40 domestic and international destinations, operating from a base at Bodø and now part of Norwegian Group.

Widerøe's fleet structure shows how central the smallest type remains. AvioRadar lists 26 Dash 8-100 and -200 aircraft at 39 seats, three Dash 8-300s at 50 seats, 16 Dash 8-400s at 78 seats, and three Embraer E190-E2s at 110 seats. ch-aviation counts 19 Dash 8-100s specifically within a total fleet of 51. Either way, the smallest aircraft in the fleet carries the network that justifies the subsidy. AvioRadar noted that extending the structural life of the Dash 8-100 allows the airline to preserve a network tailored to Norway's geography without prematurely moving to larger aircraft that would undermine the economics of lower-demand routes. Oslo has since opened a new tender covering southern Norway's PSO routes.

Seasonal and year round frequencies are trimmed, forcing travelers to reroute through neighboring airports for connections.

A flight cycle is one takeoff and one landing. On a day like the one LN-WIE flew, the aircraft accumulated 17 of them before midnight, which is where the Dash 8-100's structural problem begins. De Havilland Canada designed the type for 80,000 cycles. Several of Widerøe's aircraft are already well past that figure, because no other operator in the world works the type this hard. The Extended Service Program raised the certified limit to 120,000 cycles. Widerøe went past that too.

In 2022, the airline became the launch customer for Extended Service Program PLUS, which lifts the limit to 160,000 flight cycles. De Havilland Canada states that this gives the Dash 8-100 the highest certified flight-cycle life of any commercial aircraft. Widerøe initially enrolled ten aircraft with options for ten more, and expanded the agreement in 2026 by adding four, bringing the total under ESP+ to 14 with options for six further airframes. It remains the only customer. Dom Sipinski observed that the gap to the second-most-intensive operator of the type is large enough that Widerøe will quite likely remain the only one. The airline also participates in De Havilland Component Solutions, the manufacturer's component support programme, and extended the intervals between A and C checks across its Dash 8-100, -200 and -300 fleets in 2021.

Werner Skaue, Widerøe's Director of Aircraft Trading, framed the decision in operational terms: "The Dash 8-100 remains an important part of our regional network, and ESP+ provides us with a practical and cost-effective way to extend the life of these aircraft while maintaining the safety, reliability and performance on which our operations depend." The alternative is not a newer small turboprop, because none is in production at this size. Extending the airframes Widerøe already owns is the only route to keeping Finnmark's airports connected.

#6188. Report: Alaska to Lay Off 200 Employees

Alaska Air Group, the parent company of Alaska Airlines, Hawaiian Airlines, and Horizon Air, will lay off about 200 workers as financial losses tied to the higher price of jet fuel grow.

The Honolulu Star-Advertiser obtained an email sent to employees Friday morning acknowledging the cuts.

“Despite having the right strategy and strong momentum, fuel prices and geopolitical challenges are putting significant financial pressure on our business,” CEO Ben Minicucci wrote. “If current conditions persist, we could lose as much as $700 million this year, which would be our first adjusted pretax loss outside of the pandemic since 2003.”

According to the Star-Advertiser, 125 workers in Washington state will be laid off, and 48 in Hawaii.

The affected employees will be out of a job Nov. 13, but will continue to receive pay through the end of the year.

Alaska’s leadership said no front-line, non-management positions have been affected, suggesting the eliminated jobs are management-related.

Separately, Hawaiian Airlines CEO Diana Birkett Rakow said in an email to staff that, of the 48 affected positions at Hawaiian, 40 roles will be eliminated entirely, and eight people will be be offered other jobs within the airline.

Birkett Rakow also said that two senior leaders – Jim Landers, head of Hawaii operations, and Shelly Parker, head of guest operations – will retire at the end of the year. Both of their positions will be eliminated following their departure.

A few years ago, on a damp evening in late March in London, I learned the hard way that countries don’t all change their clocks for daylight saving time simultaneously. After ordering a glass of white wine at a cozy bar in Bermondsey, I mindlessly scrolled on my phone while the bartenders chatted about the clocks jumping forward that coming Sunday. I nearly spit out my Chablis.

Back home in New York City, I had already skipped ahead one hour on the second Sunday in March. As I frantically Googled, I learned that in the United Kingdom, the clocks go forward one hour on the last Sunday in March (and back one hour on the last Sunday in October).

Don’t be like me and lose two hours of sleep in one month. When you travel, remember the following to avoid daylight saving time-related snafus and other time zone mistakes — and if you're in the U.S., most states fell back one hour on Sunday, Nov. 1.

The U.K. isn’t the only country that changes its clocks on a different weekend than we do in the U.S. For example, most European countries follow the same calendar as the U.K., moving clocks forward one hour on the last Sunday in March and back one hour on the last Sunday in October.

Generally, when traveling in the spring and fall, it’s always best to check when the country you’re going to falls forward or backward — and also whether that country observes daylight saving time at all. In fact, according to the Pew Research Center, about 66% of the world doesn’t.

Though daylight saving time is commonly observed in North America and Europe, many non-European Union countries in Europe — including Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Iceland, Russia and Turkey — stay on standard time year-round.

In 2023, Egypt became the only country in Africa to change its clocks when it reintroduced daylight saving time for the first time in seven years. Now, each year, its clocks move forward one hour on the last Friday in April and backward one hour on the last Thursday in October.

It’s also worth double-checking these things even if you're traveling within the U.S. In 48 states, daylight saving time runs from the second Sunday in March to the first Sunday in November. Arizona and Hawaii are the outliers that stay on standard time year-round. While it’s less of an issue on an island like Hawaii, Arizona shares enough borders with other states that do observe daylight saving time that it can be problematic.

“Always double-check timing when flying in/out and on road trips through the state,” Becky Blaine, TPG’s newsletter managing editor and former Arizona resident, said. Otherwise, you can risk missing a flight or a reservation.

To keep it simple, remember that Arizona is in the Pacific Daylight Time zone from mid-March to early November, and the rest of the year it’s in the same time zone as other states in Mountain Standard Time.

It’s a similar situation in Canada. Generally, Canada follows the same daylight saving schedule as the U.S., but most of Saskatchewan, the Yukon and some parts of Quebec and British Columbia stay on standard time year-round.

In Australia, daylight saving time starts the first Sunday in October and ends the first Sunday in April in the Australian Capital Territory, New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria; meanwhile, the Northern Territory, Queensland and Western Australia don’t observe it.

Outside of daylight saving time changes, there are some general time zone issues to be aware of while traveling.

In countries as large as the U.S., Canada and Australia, it’s easy to see why there are so many time zones. But Eric Rosen, TPG’s director of travel content, also pointed out that the airport in the Maldives is in a different time zone than some resorts in the tiny island nation.

Technically, the Maldives has only one official time zone: Maldives Time, which is five hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). However, some of the archipelago's private island resorts add an hour to Maldives Time to maximize their guests' evening light.

For example, The St. Regis Maldives Vommuli Resort sets its clock one hour ahead of the official clock to what it calls "Island Time," but also provides guests with butlers who coordinate transfers to and from the airport so nobody accidentally misses a flight.

Before you go to the Maldives, be sure to check if your resort also does this.

Due to its geographic location, the Canadian island of Newfoundland is 90 minutes ahead of Eastern Time instead of just 60 minutes ahead, as in the rest of Atlantic Canada. On a July trip, Nick Ewen, TPG’s editor-in-chief, found this challenging for calendar purposes.

While traveling in Newfoundland, he received an Outlook invitation to a 7:30 p.m. dinner meeting the following week and accepted it without much thought. However, the actual dinner back home in the U.S. started at 6 p.m. — a detail he completely missed until the reminder popped up 15 minutes before. At that point, he realized he would be late.

Other places offset from UTC by 30 minutes include India, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Iran and some states in Australia. Want to be confused even more? Nepal's time zone is offset by 45 minutes due to its geography.

Even when not dealing with half-hour time zones, it can be easy to make similar mistakes when adding events back home to your digital calendar while traveling in a different time zone.

"Last year, I brought my middle son to a birthday party. We were running a few minutes late, but when we arrived, it seemed like the party was almost over," Tarah Chieffi, a senior writer at TPG, said. "While the kids were eating cake, I double-checked my calendar to make sure we had gotten the time right, and it seemed like we had. But then I went to check the invitation, and we had, in fact, arrived one hour late."

Her mistake? When she entered the party into her calendar while traveling, her calendar app defaulted to the time zone she was in and showed her the incorrect time back home.

"Now, I always toggle the time zone to my home time zone if I enter appointments into my calendar while I'm traveling," she said.

"Outlook lets you have up to three time zones showing on the calendar," Madison Blancaflor, a managing editor at TPG, said.

Go to "Settings," then "Calendar," then "Time zones." Then, check the box for "Show second time zone in Day and Week view" underneath your default time zone. If you need a third one, you can also check that box.

It's also important to remember that it's possible to quickly encounter multiple time zones on cruises — especially on transoceanic cruises, where you'll change time zones daily or almost daily. And if you're on a cruise traversing the Pacific Ocean, you could lose an entire day if you cross the international date line, like Clint Henderson, TPG's principal spokesperson, did when he sailed from Seward, Alaska, to Tokyo last year.

Related: I made a rookie travel mistake that nearly cost me $4,000 — here's how I fixed it

Even on shorter cruises, check if you'll have to change time zones. When I was on a five-day Alaska cruise earlier this summer, I changed time zones twice as we moved in and out of Alaska Daylight Time on a round-trip sailing from Vancouver (which was one hour ahead, on Pacific Daylight Time).

Cabin stewards usually leave notes on your bed at turndown to remind you of upcoming time changes. Clint said he had to set his clocks back between one and two hours each night on his cruise. But you can't always rely on your cellphone to display the correct time when it’s in airplane mode and using satellite-based internet. Bring an analog watch or an alarm clock to ground you if you're unsure whether your device will update properly.

However, some cruise ships may ignore time changes at select ports. "I've had that happen on Royal Caribbean ships in the Caribbean, for example, to avoid the ship time changing three days in a row," said Christine Gallipeau, a senior editor on TPG's points and loyalty team. "So if you're doing shore excursions, make sure you know what time the ship is following, as it may not necessarily match the local time."

Related: Can a cruise help with jet lag? The answer might surprise you

When traveling, don’t assume every country or state follows the same daylight-saving-time rules and schedules as where you live, and be mindful of time zone anomalies. Losing or gaining an unexpected hour can lead to lost sleep, arriving late to an event and, worst of all, missed flights.

#6186. Bilt Rent Day Promotion November 2026: Up To $150 Off Hotel, Up To 100% Gift Card Bonus

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus new ways that housing rewards are offered.

There are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With it now being a new month, I’d like to post a reminder of the November 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a gift card redemption bonus and a hotel booking promo code. While there’s no transfer bonus to a travel program, I imagine this will still interest some.

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

Bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

On the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

On November 1, 2026 only, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for gift cards. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:

This same bonus is available for all 125+ gift cards that Bilt Points can be redeemed for. There’s no option to use Bilt Cash to increase your bonus here.

For what it’s worth, ordinarily Bilt points can be redeemed for 0.7 cents each toward gift card purchases. That means a Blue member would be getting 0.875 cents per point of value, while a Platinum member would be getting 1.4 cents per point of value. For me that’s a hard pass, though I suppose for some Platinum members, it could be an interesting way to “cash out” points, if that’s what you’re looking to do.

For the November 2026 Bilt Rent Day promotion, we’re actually seeing an additional offer as well. Bilt members can unlock up to $150 off a hotel stay booked in the Bilt Travel Portal during Rent Week, so it’s available for bookings between 9AM ET on October 28 and 3AM ET on November 2, 2026.

The catch here is that different members are eligible for different offers, so members have to log into their Bilt account, and they will see a targeted chart delineating different savings of up to $150 for hotel bookings. Here are the key details:

On the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for November 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on gift card redemptions, which can get you at most 1.4 cents per point of value. That’s not terribly exciting, in my opinion, but maybe others will appreciate it. The other offer is for up to $150 off a hotel stay booked through the Bilt Travel Portal. There are different offers there that members will be eligible for, so you’ll want to check in the Bilt app to see what you’re targeted for.

Are you taking advantage of the Bilt Rent Day promotion for November 2026?

#6185. American Resumes Service to Haiti After Two-Year Pause

American Airlines on Sunday restarted service to Haiti after a nearly two-year hiatus brought on by gang violence in and around Port-au-Prince.

The carrier is now operating daily nonstop flights between Miami and Cap-Haitien, using Boeing 737 aircraft.

The inaugural flight on Sunday was staffed by an all-Haitian, Creole-speaking crew, the airline said.

“The connection between the United States and Haiti is incredibly meaningful, which is especially true in South Florida,” American Senior Vice President of Miami Operations Juan Carlos Liscano said in a news release. “We know the critical role air service plays in linking countries and communities, so we’re beyond proud to reinstate such a consequential connection for so many.”

U.S. airlines suspended service to and from Haiti in 2024 amid a rise in gang violence. Toussaint Louverture International Airport in Port-au-Prince was temporarily closed after bullets struck aircraft taxiing on the tarmac.

So far, American is the only U.S.-based carrier to have resumed service to the country.

#6184. Transfer Chase Points To IHG With 80% Bonus: Why It’s Not Worth It

Chase Ultimate Rewards has just launched a new transfer bonus to IHG One Rewards. The bonus is for 80%, which on the surface sounds huge. However, even with such a big bonus, I’d still argue this almost certainly isn’t worth it…

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a bonus when you transfer points to IHG One Rewards. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on December 3, 2026, members can receive an 80% bonus when moving points.

Points ordinarily transfer at a 1,000:1,000 ratio, so with this 80% bonus offer, points transfer at a 1,000:1,800 ratio. You can take advantage of this an unlimited number of times. Transfers from Chase Ultimate Rewards to IHG One Rewards are typically instant.

For context, we typically see a transfer bonus from Chase to IHG two or three times per year, and so far the bonuses have been in the range of 50% to 100%. So this 80% bonus is roughly average as far as these bonuses go, and isn’t quite as good as the 100% bonus we saw earlier this year.

An 80% transfer bonus sounds like it could be valuable, since that’s a big percentage bonus. That being said, I still wouldn’t consider this to be a good deal under a vast majority of circumstances.

Why? Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider IHG One Rewards points to be worth 0.5 cents each, while I value Chase Ultimate Rewards points at ~1.7 cents each. Even when you’re getting 1.8 IHG One Rewards points per Ultimate Rewards point, you’re still only getting under one cent of value per Ultimate Rewards point.

I certainly hope that most people are able to redeem their Chase Ultimate Rewards points for well over a penny each, since that’s a really low cash out value.

Even if you value IHG One Rewards points more than I do, the reality is that IHG frequently sells points for 0.5 cents each, so I would instead buy points at that rate. It would be silly to redeem Ultimate Rewards points when you’re only getting one cent of value vs. paying cash.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a new transfer bonus, as you can get an 80% bonus when you move points to IHG One Rewards. While I’m always happy to see a transfer bonus, I’m afraid that this simply isn’t worth it under a vast majority of circumstances.

Transfers to most of Chase’s partners are generally at a 1:1 ratio. While the simplicity of that is nice, the reality is that points have significantly different values, and this creates a few partners that I would never recommend transferring Chase points to.

Anyone have a different take, and see a reason to transfer Chase points to IHG?

#6183. Transfer Chase Points To British Airways, Iberia, Aer Lingus, With 30% Bonus

Chase Ultimate Rewards has just launched its latest airline transfer bonus. Actually, it’s a trio of transfer bonuses, as it’s valid for British Airways Club, Iberia Club, and Aer Lingus AerClub. This is a popular bonus when available, so I think some members will find this to be worthwhile.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is offering a bonus when you transfer points to British Airways Club, Iberia Club, or Aer Lingus AerClub. Between 12AM ET on November 1, 2026, and 11:59PM ET on December 1, 2026, members can receive a 30% bonus when moving points.

A transfer bonus like this seems to be offered an average of once to twice per year, and it’s typically in the range of 20-30%. So the 30% bonus is as good as it gets, and this is the biggest percentage bonus that we’ve seen so far in 2026.

Keep in mind that this bonus covers three different Avios currencies, and on top of that, you can freely transfer Avios between the various “flavors.” When you go to make a transfer, you should immediately see the 30% bonus reflected. Transfers from Ultimate Rewards to these partners are typically instant.

Keep in mind the various Avios currencies also partner with other major transferable points currencies, and we do sometimes see transfer bonuses with other programs as well.

I think there’s value to be had in taking advantage of a 30% bonus on points transfers from Ultimate Rewards to Avios. That’s not because of any one particular redemption opportunity, but rather because of the collective value of the Avios ecosystem.

Back in the day, the best uses of British Airways Avios were for short haul travel on partner airlines, including on Alaska and American. Unfortunately those redemption opportunities have been devalued horribly.

However, lots of great new options using Avios have emerged. For example, I love how Qatar Airways Privilege Club is now an Avios airline, as this opens up some great opportunities:

Anyway, there’s a ton of potential value here, so see my guides to maximizing Avios with British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Aer Lingus Aer Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, and Finnair Plus.

For the next several weeks, you can get a 30% bonus when you convert your Chase Ultimate Rewards points into Avios with British Airways Club, Iberia Club, and Aer Lingus AerClub.

Avios is one of the most useful points currencies out there, especially given across how many airlines you can redeem these rewards. I think for many people, this could be worth a speculative transfer.

#6182. 3 New Routes, 1 New Destination: JetBlue Expands Its Network Today

JetBlue is launching three new nonstop routes today, expanding its network with two services from Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) and another connecting Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI) with San Juan. The new additions bring Columbus back into its network and introduce Indianapolis as an entirely new destination for the airline. All three routes will operate daily using Airbus A320 aircraft.

The launches come amid a significant transformation of JetBlue's network, with Fort Lauderdale recently overtaking New York JFK as its busiest airport. The airline is capitalizing on the demise of Spirit Airlines to expand its South Florida presence, while preparing to introduce additional premium transcontinental services later this month.

JetBlue's latest expansion introduces daily nonstop flights from Fort Lauderdale to Indianapolis International Airport (IND) and John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH). The two new services are part of a broader expansion announced earlier this year, when the airline outlined plans to add 11 destinations from the South Florida airport.

Indianapolis represents the biggest milestone, becoming a new city in JetBlue's network. Columbus, meanwhile, welcomes the carrier back after an absence, giving travelers another option for reaching South Florida. The additions strengthen JetBlue's domestic connectivity from Fort Lauderdale, where the airline has been expanding aggressively throughout 2026. JetBlue CEO, Joanna Geraghty, had the following to say:

"We're building on our already strong foundation by adding more destinations, creating more connections and giving customers even more reasons to choose JetBlue. As Fort Lauderdale's leading airline, we see an opportunity to continue growing together with this community."

The new route from Baltimore to San Juan's Luis Munoz Marin International Airport (SJU) builds on JetBlue's return to Baltimore back in July, when it introduced three daily flights to Fort Lauderdale. The new Puerto Rico service expands its reach from Maryland while reinforcing San Juan's importance within the airline's Caribbean network. Baltimore airport officials welcomed JetBlue's arrival, emphasizing the benefits of additional competition and connectivity.

The Fort Lauderdale expansion has led to it becoming JetBlue's busiest airport by scheduled departures, overtaking its longtime New York JFK Airport (JFK) stronghold. The change illustrates how dramatically the airline's network has shifted toward South Florida. Based on the winter schedule figures highlighted in a recent Simple Flying analysis of JetBlue's network changes, Fort Lauderdale now leads JFK by approximately six daily departures.

The expansion has been accelerated by Spirit Airlines' collapse and JetBlue's changing route network. JetBlue has introduced 15 destinations from Fort Lauderdale while increasing frequencies on existing routes. Its share of scheduled seats at the airport is expected to reach approximately 37% in the fourth quarter, an increase of 14 percentage points year-over-year. Peak daily departures will also exceed 150 this winter.

Crucially, the expansion is also delivering encouraging financial results. During the third quarter, Fort Lauderdale revenue per available seat mile (RASM) increased nearly 15% despite capacity growing by more than 65%. The expansion is also driving increased ancillary revenue, with co-branded credit card acquisitions in the region up 55%. The airline expects the maturing Fort Lauderdale operation to generate further unit revenue improvements as capacity growth moderates.

JetBlue will launch new routes and add more Mint flights from Fort Lauderdale.

JetBlue's next significant Fort Lauderdale launch is scheduled for later this month on November 19, when daily nonstop flights to San Diego International Airport (SAN) begin. The route will feature the airline's premium JetBlue Mint business class, including fully lie-flat seating. This will give the airline a distinct advantage over Southwest Airlines and Alaska Airlines, which also operate the route, by making it the only airline with a lie-flat offering between the two airports.

The San Diego launch is part of a much wider transcontinental push. JetBlue is also adding Mint-equipped flights to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO) this winter, creating its largest-ever Mint schedule from Fort Lauderdale. The airline ultimately plans to offer up to eight daily flights to Los Angeles and three to San Francisco, although these totals include services without Mint.

The premium expansion signals JetBlue's ambition to transform Fort Lauderdale into more than a gateway for leisure travelers heading to Florida and the Caribbean. By adding lie-flat business class capacity on key West Coast routes, the airline hopes to capture higher-yield passengers while differentiating itself from competitors. Combined with today's new domestic and Caribbean routes, the Mint expansion demonstrates how central Fort Lauderdale has become to JetBlue's future growth strategy.
