#6155. American Airlines Spent Years Making Its Cabins Worse—Now It’s Racing To Win Passengers Back From United And Delta

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby says one of his biggest competitive advantages won’t last. Other airlines will catch up with Starlink internet. He says he’s investing anyway, because two or three years is enough time to get passengers to try United, discover other things they like, and move their loyalty and credit card spending. That answers the argument Doug Parker made at American Airlines in 2017 for not investing in product: better products just get copied so can’t offer an enduring advantage. Delta spent nearly two decades showing how investment in the operation, product and employees could work together. United has improved more than any other U.S. airline over the past decade. American has made an impressive amount of progress since its premium pivot roughly 21 months ago. But it’s trying to win back customers while losing money, carrying heavy debt, and with fuel costs up. They’re in a race against time to show results before Wall Street gets impatient. I attended American’s September 2017 media and investor day. The airline’s theory was that competitors would match a better product, leaving corporate culture and employees to differentiate the airline. Take care of employees, who would take care of customers, who would take care of shareholders. (Of course American alienated all three groups.) They didn’t explain how that was going to happen. There were nicer employee facilities coming, help using their health and wellness benefits, and they spent a disproportionate amount of time on company-sponsored weight loss programs. I left without understanding the mission employees were supposed to rally around, or how American would install its workforce with a desire and knowledge to deliver exceptional service. Meanwhile, American was preparing to fly its new domestic interior with less legroom, less padded seats and no seatback screens. At that same media day, they didn’t even think they needed native booking in their mobile app. Sending customers to a mobile website was good enough. A year later, Parker told employees: we work really hard to match our service to our competitors, and they do the same to us. He described watching what competitors put onboard, including meals, to ensure American was comparable. He was surprised by the idea that customers might choose United or Delta because of a different inflight product. In contrast, Richard Anderson became Delta CEO in 2007. Along with Glen Hauenstein and Gil West, he built an airline around keeping its promises to passengers and driving hard bargains with its counterparties. Anderson later explained how much of the advantage came from line maintenance. An older airplane could be reliable if mechanics could work on it where it spent the night, fix recurring problems and have it ready in the morning. Delta also worked toward eliminating involuntary denied boarding. A customer who bought a ticket, arrived on time and followed every instruction shouldn’t be told they weren’t going to travel because the airline had sold too many seats. Finding enough volunteers protected the relationship with that customer. They leaned into seatback screens. Their non-union crews were somewhat friendlier than at competitors. Then Delta made itself relevant in the markets where customers had the most money to spend. The 2011 LaGuardia slot swap with US Airways was one of the great airline asset trades. Parker’s airline gave Delta 132 daily LaGuardia slot pairs in exchange for 42 pairs at Washington National and $66.5 million. Required divestitures reduced Delta’s net gain (they eventually got the slots back that were transferred to WestJet) but it gave them the platform to build the New York business. Delta fleeced Parker. US Airways strengthened Washington, but when it merged with American it had to give up slots there anyway. The combined airline couldn’t keep all of both carriers’ holdings. American – once headquartered in New York – would never be able to position itself in New York the way that Delta had. Delta invested in facilities at LaGuardia, JFK and Los Angeles. That all positioned Delta to overtake American in cobrand credit card spend. I’ve been critical of how much Delta has coasted on that reputation. Its operational advantage isn’t what it was (they’re still a bit more reliable than peers but when things go south they struggle to recover, and no longer go months without a mainline cancel). Their 767s out of New York are arguably the actual worst product across the Atlantic and among those who compete for premium transcon business. And Delta’s success despite weak mileage value shouldn’t have taught competitors to devalue their own programs. Delta offered a better experience – that’s eroding – and had strong positioning in some of the best spend markets, and lack of competition in their other key markets (Atlanta, Upper Midwest, Salt Lake). Kirby took a long time to arrive at his current view. He was president of American when it cut meal service in 2014. Planning for the domestic interior without screens began while he was still there, even though the first aircraft with that interior entered service after he left. He initially carried the same approach to United. They cut full domestic first class meals on flights under four hours outside the dinner window, before customer complaints forced a reversal. They eliminated Polaris wine flights and cocktail carts, then reduced business class staffing by one flight attendant and moved to pre-plated entrees. Some of United’s early product investment was probably overboard – greenlighting most everything when Oscar Munoz came back from medical leave. The later United NEXT commitment to screens, bigger bins and a better domestic cabin, combined with sustained investment in its mobile app, represented a different approach under later Kirby. Most passengers sit in coach. Improving their experience gets them to pay more and builds a reputation that qualifies the airline for their future purchases in business. Even business class passengers internationally are often coach passengers domestically, and bad experiences in domestic form the bulk of a passenger’s opinion when it coms time to buy long haul business. The app is part of the coach product just as well as the premium cabin one. Passengers can manage changes, get help improving their seat assignment and receive clearer explanations when something goes wrong. It gives them more control over their trip. They use it repeatedly, and it’s reason they may hesitate to move their flying elsewhere even after another airline matches the cabin. By 2025, Kirby was explaining a different test for food spending. He told Brian Sumers: Every year we’re going to consciously spend more for customers in a bet that we’ll just win more brand-loyal customers. He couldn’t prove exactly how much additional ticket revenue better food would generate. He was willing to make the investment anyway. The old approach could identify the savings from moving a meal window by 15 minutes, while the revenue lost through a series of small disappointments was much harder to see. United’s network rebuilding started earlier. Kirby restored domestic connectivity that had been cut back under Jeff Smisek, and explicitly explained in October 2017 that better connections would help sell credit cards. If United’s schedule didn’t work for someone, that person wasn’t going to take the card. American went the other way in New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. Retreating made the airline less useful in the country’s most valuable spending markets. Offering a less desirable product alienated customers from spending on the American card. And an airline’s route accounting can miss this. A Chicago customer’s work trips may be what persuade them to get an airline’s card, even if they eventually redeem the miles for Hawaii. Credit the Hawaii flight with all the benefit, cut Chicago because it looks weak, and you lose the spending that generated the miles in the first place. In contrast, aviation watchdog JonNYC shares excerpts attributed to Chief Commercial Officer Andrew Nocella laying out where the airline sees itself: United reached 50% of revenue from Chicago-based passengers in the second quarter of 2026, according to Nocella, and gained share in its other hub cities as well. It expects to largely complete United NEXT’s connectivity goals at its midcontinent hubs by summer 2027. More attention then shifts to coastal gateways and international expansion, including a planned return to New York JFK next year. Premium capacity will grow faster than main cabin capacity as United adds Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft at scale. Comments by Andrew Nocella, shared by JonNYC United’s hubs in some of the best cities for card spend and long haul pre-existed Kirby (and those cities are more contested than other airlines face in their most important hubs). Kirby’s Starlink explanation in his Cheeky Pint interview describes how he plans to accelerate United’s gains. John Collison characterized the opportunity as a two-to-three-year window to win customers, and Kirby agreed. Other airlines will eventually have comparable low Earth orbit connectivity. American, Southwest, Alaska and even Frontier are all adding Starlink (and Southwest expects to complete its install around the time United does). they’re going to try us for Starlink, and they’re going to stay because all the other technology, and everything else is better. A temporary advantage can generate a customer relationship that outlasts it. And the biggest gap will be with Delta, which has committed to Amazon Leo that will maybe start becoming available in 2028, and where they’ve committed only to eventually outfit 500 aircraft. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer. American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience. They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year. They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it. And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship. I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network). American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions. The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now. Delta’s current wifi is generally poor now that demands on the system by giving it away free have overwhelmed available bandwidth. Parker was right that competitors could copy a feature. Copying the feature doesn’t on its own win back the customer.

American is finally reversing course. I first reported its explicit premium pivot in January 2025. In roughly 21 months they’ve changed an extraordinary amount, from better coffee and wine to improved lounges, new business class suites and more attention to the coach experience.

They’ve committed to bringing back domestic seatback screens and adding more first class and extra legroom seats. They’ve announced Starlink installations beginning early next year.

They’ve even instructed employees to stop involuntarily bumping passengers, giving airport leadership more authority to secure volunteers. American is changing what it asks employees to prioritize, and giving them tools to do it.

And Flagship Dining at Los Angeles is finally reopening after more than six years, with access expanded to qualifying business class passengers. It’s a defensive move because Delta’s business class lounge is so much better, and United’s even had been better than American Flagship.

I want this to work. I’ve spent years criticizing American because it had so much potential to be better. They’re making real changes and some customers will come back simply because the airline stops giving them reasons to avoid it. But matching what they already get elsewhere likely isn’t enough – American needs a value proposition for what they deliver to customers that no one else will. That’s Delta’s reliability argument (paired with service and screens that for years others eschewed). That’s United’s Starlink argument (paired with a stronger global network).

American entered the pandemic with heavy debt after spending more than $12 billion on share buybacks under Parker. Borrowing while returning that much cash to shareholders left it weaker than competitors. It has too much debt service, less room to borrow, and less well-positioned to do acquisitions.

The risk is that investors demand results before enough customers have experienced the improvements, or demand cuts to the spending that could produce real results. American’s domestic seatback screens won’t begin arriving on new aircraft until 2028, and the broader fleet project extends into the next decade. It needs the improvements it can deliver sooner to get customers back onboard and spending more before then. The interest and fuel bills are arriving now.

Not until Robert Isom is gone and AA has true leadership will this airline ever recover. Morale is miserable in ALL work groups. Airlines are all alike and it simply comes down to the people that take care of the customers. Whenever I have to fly AA I brace myself for the absolute worst experience. After being scolded asking for a third glass of water during a dinner service in business class I simply have had enough. Like TWA, Braniff, Eastern and Pan Am before them there’s plenty of room in the desert to park planes when it’s all said and done.

I bet NO. We don’t forget the barking dog tapes. They treat passengers like dogs

American’s on time performance and overall reliability remains at the bottom end of the industry peers, slightly above JetBlue. That’s not good.

The fleet is enormous, and a lot of it still flies around in the Parker-era bare bones aesthetic, which is not aging well.

American’s finances are challenged by the buy-backs, yes, and the massive 2011 re-fleet which was needed, but very costly.

American has to work harder in NYC, Chicago, and LA to win back premium customers and position itself not as one that has matched DL and UA but does something a bit better. The wealth on credit card spend in America does not sit in Charlotte or the Sun Belt. It resides in the big blue cities that MAGA hates. Just look at United’s route map and rising premium revenue, and you can see why. It’s hubs are in the right markets.

Delta’s performance in NYC is slipping. Too much flying to Europe is performed on 767-300ERs and 767-400ERs, and A330CEOs that have old, dated cabins. Ground staff at JFK are often rude but Delta still has the ability to find a revenue yield premium like the rest cannot.

Alaska is the winner in the service wars. They have the best employees and give them the authority to do their jobs. That’s not to say that AS hasn’t backslid the last two years but their recent announcement indicated they still get what’s important.

Is that enough to grow to the size of the big three? No not so long as airport slots are constrained. But where they fly Alaska asks for and appears to get a premium which indicates that passengers are willing to pay more to fly with them.

Bigger picture whatever happens the customer is going to see substantial benefits from AA’s change in direction not only when they fly AA but other carriers as well because premium flyers obviously don’t take well to being abused and with loyalty no longer very valuable are much more likely to go with the airline with whom they have had good experiences.

That marginal revenue the airlines have been able to extract by upselling has come at a cost. No longer beholden the carriers have to perform in order to get a passenger’s repeat business.

Ironic but a good outcome for those of us who fly frequently and want more than just a cheap seat.

To respond to another commentator… you’re wrong about Alaska. They absolutely suck. Their Firsr Class food is a joke. And Alaska is already dumbing down Hawaiin Airlines, a once great airline. American will catch up over time. Delta is sliding. Their seats on the a321 Neo in First Class are absolute garbage… there is a metal box for electronics that sits right between the 2 “First Class” seats, severely impeding your legroom. The seats are cheap and you feel like you’re sitting on concrete after a couple of hours. And Delta’s WiFi is pure garbage too.

The US Airways/Doug Parker take over was an unmitigated disaster. The US Air planes right after the merger were horrendous. Charlotte, Phil, PHX are not DFW, MIA, ORD for corporate travel. I get AA was bankrupt and Arpey and Carty before him were not Crandall and Parker had the upper hand of a profitable airline, at that time. Going forward the legacy US AIR team needs to be moved out and bring in fresh blood that can make American Airlines great again.

Bob I agree the box on the floor is terrible and don’t make excuses for it. I’ve not had the same reaction you have to the seats. Are you referring to F or Y?

I haven’t had the same reaction to their food in F. In your opinion how would you say it compares to UA, AA and DL?

It’s not all about ‘systems’. The people at Delta are so friendly and helpful – that can’t be replicated. The 757-400s are being replaced by new planes. That is coming.

Sometimes I fly AA from Heathrow having flown from Boston with BA. The difference in the cabin crews is night and day. The BA staff are sharply dressed, polite, efficient and friendly, while the AA cabin crew look like they have been let out of their nursing homes. Slovenly and sullen are two traits that come to mind. No airline is perfect so as long as I get from A-B safely I’ll put up with cabin crew who couldn’t care less

(Reading the room, whispering to myself… ‘but, I liked the new Flagship Suites’…)

I’m a flight attendant. Employee moral at AA is low. AA expects flight attendants to be punching bags. We even have a lesson in our quarterly training on “how to apologize to passengers”. I no longer tell people that I work for American

Please bring back meals on flights 700+ miles! I’m begging you!

So how does Kirby justify Basic Business where United is very intentionally driving off premium passengers while also destroying loyalty? I’m not an insider but I’d love to hear how alienating premium customers makes your airline more premium.

I don’t want to be rude or mean however it was UNIONS which wanted the so-called “merger” between AA and US. In fact, I remember blogging (back when I used to blog on WordPress.com) about how the APA head was bragging about it and how its going to eventually cost them in the long term.

Horton was doing a fantastic job getting AA back on track – in fact, he was the one who was responsible for the blockbuster aircraft deals with both Boeing and Airbus.

The unions simply didn’t like the way Horton ran AA which is a shame as he’s one of the only people I’ve ever heard who not only was able to get bondholders their 100 cents to the dollar, but didn’t have shareholders wiped out during BK.

As the saying goes, “you reap what you sow”.

As an American Airlines retiree I agree with Texas Fly Girl. When someone asks I tell them I worked for airline and hope they don’t ask which one. It is embarrassing the downfall since the arrival of Parker and the USAIR guys.

I think it’s great to see AA finally realize its mistakes and move towards improvements. Hopefully they figure out ways to actually leapfrog the competition. They need to figure out a way to somehow buy or lease the JetBlue slots and gates at JFK, BOS and LAX. Would be next to impossible given the JetBlue+United partnership, but they need to explore options. Having United with its huge EWR fortress AND with a huge number of JFK slots would put WAY too much power in the hands of one airline.

#6154. Transfer Amex Points To Virgin Atlantic Flying Club With 30% Bonus: Worth It?

The Amex Membership Rewards program has just launched a new 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. While Flying Club is in some ways a niche program, this is a deal that has the potential to offer outsized value, and I’m sure it will interest many people. I’d probably speculatively take advantage of this, except for the fact that I moved a bunch of points last year when there was a 40% transfer bonus.

Between November 2 and November 30, 2026, the American Express Membership Rewards program in the United States is offering a 30% bonus on points transfers to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,300 Flying Club points for every 1,000 Membership Rewards points transferred. Transfers are generally instant.

For context, Amex seems to offer a transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club once or twice per year. The last promotion we saw was over the summer, and this is the second offer so far in 2026. When we do see these offers, they’re typically in the range of 30-40%, so this is on the low side of that range, but could still represent a great deal.

Virgin Atlantic is definitely a frequent flyer program with more niche redemption opportunities. In addition to being able to redeem Flying Club points for travel on Virgin Atlantic, there’s also good value to be had for redemptions on Air New Zealand, All Nippon Airways, and Delta.

In late 2024 we saw Flying Club introduce dynamic award pricing for travel on Virgin Atlantic. While the changes are a mixed bag, what’s exciting is that on the low end, redemptions are cheaper than ever before. It’s now possible to fly one-way Virgin Atlantic Upper Class between the United States and the UK for under 30,000 points, and that’s before a transfer bonus.

Beyond that, Virgin Atlantic has several airline partners, some of which are more lucrative than others. Probably the best use of Flying Club points is for travel in ANA first & business class. You can find the redemption rates below.

Paying 45,000-47,500 Flying Club points for a one-way business class ticket between the United States and Japan is a phenomenal value to start with. Then when you consider the 30% transfer bonus, that means you could be paying significantly fewer Amex points. First class can also be a good deal.

All Nippon Airways’ new first & business class are amazing products as well. The major catch is that availability can be really tough to come by.

Through November 30, 2026, Amex is offering a 30% bonus when you transfer points to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. This is definitely more of a niche program, but with a specific use in mind, there’s a lot of value to be had.

With the 30% bonus, award travel on Virgin Atlantic will be an even better value. There’s also lots of value to booking on partners, ranging from SkyTeam airlines, to Air New Zealand, to All Nippon Airways.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this Amex transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club?

#6153. Hotel Guests Report Mold And Mice—It Still Passed Inspection The Next Day

A mother says mice crawled across her sleeping three-year-old at a Wyndham hotel near the Albany, New York airport. Other residents reported mold, cockroaches and soaked carpets. The hotel passed a county health inspection the next day even though the inspector recorded six violations. The rooms with violations weren’t occupied on the day the inspector arrived and were supposed to be repaired before being rented. We trust hotels to do some very basic things: Change the sheets Clean the bathroom Make sure the door locks And the brand on the hotel is supposed to give you confidence! Baymont by Wyndham Latham Albany Airport markets rooms to travelers. It also houses people placed by county social services. That’s often a good indication… One woman, staying with her nine month old daughter, described cockroaches, mice, mold and bedbugs in some rooms. Other residents described wet carpets and a strong smell. A guest said she’d filmed mice crawling over her sleeping child and had stopped letting the girl sleep in her own bed. There were complaints about mouse droppings and dead flies on a bed, and mold and dead flies in a refrigerator. The County moved some social service clients. Another county with one room there relocated their client as a precaution and suspended use of the hotel. What The Inspection Found Albany County inspected the hotel October 13, finding no public health hazards, but six violations: A removed smoke detector. Three exterior doors that didn’t self-latch. A stained bathroom ceiling tile. Evidence of pests in a room. The plan to fix the rooms before renting them helps explain how the hotel could continue operating, though a missing smoke detector matters even in an empty room. And it seems to me that pests in one room can easily spread. There were earlier maintenance concerns, too. A March 13, 2025 entry in New York’s inspection database notes water stains and possible active leaks at this property. You’re Supposed To Be Able To Rely On A Brand A big part of what a hotel brand sells is confidence that somebody has vetted the property. You know what you’re getting. The hotel may be franchised but it’s supposed to deliver to brand standards. Years ago I covered an Inside Edition investigation that found three of nine hotels tested hadn’t provided completely fresh sheets between guests. The beds were re-made with the previous guest’s used sheets. Then came pandemic promises of enhanced cleaning. Inside Edition went back in 2020, using washable marks visible under ultraviolet light. It reported unchanged bedding at a Hyatt Place and a Hampton Inn in Times Square. At Trump International, the sheets had been changed, but the report said a pillowcase hadn’t. More recently, I covered a Hyatt Place guest who went through three rooms and still wound up with filthy bedding. Hyatt refunded the stay and provided 15,000 points. You’re not supposed to have to even check recent reviews and traveler photos, and pull back the bedding immediately on arrival. I Wouldn’t Let An Airline Choose Where I Sleep, Either I’ve made the same argument about hotels airlines provide during overnight delays. I’ve reported on roaches, floors was so dirty they turned guests’ feet black, and worse. Airlines offering lowest-cost rooms aren’t necessarily delvering places you’d ever want to stay. #6152. Are Authorized Users Eligible For Credit Card Bonuses?

Here’s a topic that seems to cause confusion among some people. If you’re an authorized user on someone else’s credit card, are you eligible for the bonus on that card if you apply outright? The answer is actually pretty straightforward, so let me explain…

Credit cards frequently offer huge upfront welcome offers, whereby you can earn a lot of bonus points for spending a certain amount within a limited timeframe. While there are different credit card application rules for each bank, there are generally restrictions whereby an existing cardmember can’t apply for a card they already have, while also receiving the bonus.

How does that work in the context of authorized users? If you’re the authorized user on someone else’s credit card, can you apply for the card as the primary cardmember and earn the bonus? The answer is universally yes — being an authorized user on someone else’s credit card doesn’t preclude you from applying for that card yourself, and earning the bonus.

When welcome bonus rules talk about existing cardmembers, they’re specifically talking about primary cardmembers, and not authorized users.

You don’t even need to cancel your authorized user card to be able to do this. For example, say you’re an authorized user on your spouse’s Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (learn more), or Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more), or Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more). You could remain an authorized user, and still apply outright and earn the welcome bonus on the card.

For those in relationships, it can sometimes be difficult to decide under which circumstances it makes sense to apply for a card outright, rather than being an authorized user on a spouse’s card (and vice versa). There are pros and cons to each.

The advantage of adding someone as an authorized user is that it minimizes annual fees, since many cards have lower (or no) annual fees for authorized users, compared to the primary cardmembers. Meanwhile the advantages of having both people in a relationship apply for a card outright is that many cards have big welcome bonuses, and on top of that some cards pay for themselves on an ongoing basis.

For more on this topic, see my post on the best credit card strategy for families.

Many credit cards have amazing welcome bonuses, though you’re generally only eligible for them if you don’t already have that card. The good news is that across the board, being an authorized user on someone else’s card still makes you eligible to apply for that card outright and receive the bonus (assuming you’re otherwise eligible for the card).

Therefore this really comes down to deciding for each card whether the economics of applying outright make sense.

Have you ever applied for a credit card on which you’re already an authorized user?

#6149. Passenger Says Delta Flight Attendant Photographed Her Sleeping—‘You Might See It On Facebook’

Tasia Jewel had just arrived in Mexico City and checked into her hotel when she shared the story. She’d been at the Formula One race in Austin, stayed in Texas rather than going home, and was exhausted. She slept for about an hour and a half or so on the roughly three-hour flight.

Then she got to the aircraft door. She says three or four male flight attendants were standing there saying goodbye to passengers. One told her:

Hey, yo friend, I took a picture of you while you were sleeping.

She says the other crewmembers laughed with one adding, “Yeah, she was knocked out.” And the first flight attendant repeated, “You might see it on Facebook.”

Here’s her account, flagged by Paddle Your Own Kanoo:

The woman acknowledges he could have been joking. She also says she hadn’t spoken to him at all on the flight.

My first reaction was that, while Delta has built up its Austin flying, they don’t actually operated Austin – Mexico City. But in a follow-up video she says she flew from Dallas to Atlanta to Mexico City with the flight in question being Delta 602. She says she chose Delta’s Boeing 757 because she didn’t want the Aeromexico Boeing 737 MAX.

And she reports that Delta responded well to her complaint. Her original video caption said she’d filed a complaint. In later replies, she reports a phone call, an apology and an investigation. I guess what matters here was whether there was a fundamental breach or a bad joke. Either way, she says she felt unsafe.

I’ve written about a sleeping passenger who said a man photographed her, where the crew intervened and police met the flight. Here, the person allegedly taking the photos was an employee she was supposed to go to for help.

And last year I covered a flight attendant who caught a passenger secretly filming her and sending her image to someone else. It’s easy to understand why that bothered her. But a passenger can have the same objection when the roles are reversed.

I don’t want a ban on taking pictures inside an aircraft. Passengers need to be able to document how they’re treated. Delta’s customer photography guidance recognizes that people take photos and videos, while asking them to avoid interfering with safety and to be “respectful in your intent” when including employees. Employees ought to show customers that same consideration.

#6148. Buy Choice Privileges Points With 40% Bonus (0.74 Cents Each): Worth It?

Choice Privileges is currently offering a promotion on purchased points, offering up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While this isn’t among the best promotions we’ve seen from the program, it’s still better than no bonus, and there are many situations where you could come out ahead.

Let’s take a look at everything you need to know about this deal, and talk about under what circumstances it makes sense to buy Choice Privileges points. I generally recommend buying points only if you have a short term use in mind, and are sure the math checks out.

Link: Buy Choice Privileges points with a bonus

Between 12AM EDT on November 2 and 11:59PM EDT on November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is offering a sale on purchased points. The accounts I manage show a bonus of up to 40%, which is structured as follows:

Different accounts may very well show different offers, so you’ll want to log into your Choice Privileges account to see what you’re eligible for.

Choice Privileges’ pricing when buying points isn’t linear, and you get a lower cost the more points you purchase, not even factoring in any promotional bonuses or discounts. Before factoring in any bonuses or discounts, the cost to purchase points ranges from 1.28 cents per point (if buying just 1,000 points) to 1.03 cents per point (if buying 180,000 points), and that’s inclusive of taxes and fees.

If you maxed out this promotion, you could purchase a total of 252,000 points (180,000 base points, plus 72,000 bonus points) for $1,854, which is a rate of 0.74 cents per Choice Privileges point.

Note that purchased points will post within 24 hours of completing the transaction, and the points earned don’t count toward Choice Privileges elite status.

Choice Privileges lets you purchase up to 180,000 points per account per calendar year, not factoring in any bonus points.

When Choice offers a promotion on purchased points, it’s typically either a 30-45% discount or a 35-50% bonus. So this 40% bonus is toward the bottom end of that range. Personally, I’d decide on whether to make a purchase more based on if I had an immediate use in mind, rather than the exact cost per point.

Below is a chart with some of the recent promotions we saw from Choice Privileges on buying points, before this one, with the highest bonus amounts offered.

Choice Privileges points purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t generally count as a hotel purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. There is one exception — if you use a co-branded Choice Privileges credit card, then these purchases are rewarded in the same way as hotel spending.

Otherwise, I’d recommend using a card with which you’re trying to reach a minimum spending requirement, or a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending. When in doubt, review which credit cards are best for buying points and miles.

While it doesn’t get much attention in the miles & points world, Choice is a huge hotel group, with over 7,000 properties in 40 countries, representing roughly 570,000 hotel rooms. Choice hotel brands include (among others) Ascend, Cambria, Comfort Inn, Sleep Inn, Quality Inn, Clarion, Rodeway Inn, and more.

The catch is that Choice doesn’t have that many aspirational properties. In general there’s the most value outright purchasing points if you have a premium redemption in mind, given that this is the best way to get outsized value compared to the cost of a stay if paying cash.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have a formal award chart, but award pricing usually ranges from 6,000 to 45,000 points per night. In Asia-Pacific, some properties cost up to 75,000 points per night.

There are definitely some properties where you’ll get outsized value acquiring Choice Privileges points at a discount. For example, Choice has an impressive footprint in Northern Europe, where hotels can otherwise be expensive when paying cash, especially in summer.

Let me just give some examples, and let’s just keep the math easy, to show redemptions where you’re getting well over one cent of value per point (which is way higher than the acquisition cost here). Generally the key is to travel during peak periods, since that’s when you’ll get the most outsized value from your points.

For example, if you wanted to travel to Tromso, Norway, in December (to see the Northern Lights), I see two properties charging $560-620 per night, when you could book them for 40,000-45,000 points per night, getting you very nicely outsized value.

If you wanted to travel to Stockholm, Sweden, in July (summer is popular!), I see two properties charging $420-580 per night, when you could book them for 25,000-30,000 points per night, getting you excellent value.

For an example closer to home, say you wanted to go to Dunedin, Florida, in March. I see a property charging $730 per night, when you could book it for 40,000 points per night, also getting you hugely outsized value.

Let me be clear — you won’t always find outsized value in this way. For example, say you need to spend a night near LAX, where you’ll see properties charging $102-149 per night, when a points redemption requires 20,000-30,000 points per night. Paying cash is the much better value there.

The key is to travel places during peak periods, where the cash rate would be significantly higher than usual, while the points rate isn’t as elevated.

Here’s a fun redemption option with Choice Privileges points. While Choice doesn’t manage these properties, Choice Privileges has a partnership with Preferred Hotels & Resorts, which is a group of over 500 luxury independent properties around the globe.

You can redeem Choice Privileges points for stays here, and the hotels cost anywhere from 25,000 to 118,000 points per night. You can find participating hotels and award costs here, and nowadays you can even book these awards online. There are some participating hotels where you can get significant value redeeming this way, though the recent devaluation sure doesn’t help.

Choice Privileges doesn’t have blackout dates, and points can be redeemed for stays up to 50 weeks in advance, as long as a standard room is available.

Choice Privileges points don’t expire as long as you have at least some account activity once every 18 months. Virtually any activity that involves earning or redeeming points would be considered qualifying for these purposes.

Everyone will value points differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Choice Privileges points to be worth ~0.6 cents each. That’s a conservative valuation, though if you’re strategic you should be able to get lots more value out of your points than that.

Several transferable points currencies have Choice Privileges as a partner:

As you can see, of those transfer partners, Wells Fargo is going to be the most lucrative, followed by Citi, followed by Amex and Capital One.

Through November 26, 2026, Choice Privileges is selling points with up to a 40% bonus, which is an opportunity to buy points for as little as 0.74 cents each. While I wouldn’t recommend speculatively picking up Choice Privileges points at that cost, with a specific and short term use in mind, there could be value with this offer.

Does anyone plan on buying Choice Privileges points?

#6146. Airline Passengers Are Getting Scam Emails With Real Confirmation Numbers—Some Frontier Customers Are Entering Credit Card Details

Frontier Airlines passengers are reporting emails from scammers using their real flight details and confirmation numbers, promising refunds or claiming their bookings haven’t been paid for – and telling them to enter their credit card information to complete purchases or confirm return of funds. Frontier reported an active phishing campaign targeting its customers. That doesn’t tell us where the reservation information came from. A reader sent me a refund email that claims a ticketing error caused duplicate taxes and fees and failed to apply a promotional credit. It promises a full refund after the customer confirms the original payment card. The message even supplies an explanation for why an airline that already charged you supposedly needs your card again: Because the settlement batch for this reservation has already closed, our payment system needs the original payment method confirmed so the refund can be routed back to your card. A closed settlement batch ordinarily means the merchant needs to process a refund rather than void the original transaction. In other words, it’s a made up reason meant to sound plausible. These Emails Are Using Real Reservation Details In a Frontier GoWild! Pass Holders discussion, numerous passengers say they received these emails. Several report that the confirmation numbers matched actual bookings. That includes trips already taken and travel still upcoming. One customer says the supposed refund was about five times what they’d paid. Another reports receiving both versions: a refund offer for a completed trip and a warning that payment hadn’t gone through for an upcoming reservation. A separate Reddit discussion reports the payment problem version, with an email that contained real flight information and confirmation number. Passengers report responding with their credit card numbers. One passenger says they tried several other cards before the site accepted the card originally used to book the flight. And of course a rejection message doesn’t mean the site didn’t collect the card number. Frontier Has Disclosed A Database Incident I wrote in July about a breach affecting 11,482 people. Separately, a security researcher reported that a confirmation number and last name could expose sensitive passenger information through Frontier’s systems. There’s also an October 2 notice from Frontier about a security incident involving its customer care database covering information submitted through its customer care form. They changed the database configuration and are ‘improving monitoring’. Security firm VenariX analyzed leaked samples associated with a group claiming Frontier among its victims. They found booking codes, flight numbers and dates, and evidence pointing to overly broad access permissions on Microsoft customer service portals. This Approach Has Been Used Against Hotel And Cruise Customers I’ve covered hotel scams where the sender knows the guest’s reservation details and uses them to demand payment or card verification. Knowing the hotel, dates and guest’s name makes the message much more persuasive. Norwegian Cruise Line customers reported a similar campaign in October, with messages containing real booking information and demanding payment verification. Norwegian issued its own warning. What To Do If You Received One Frontier won’t email asking you to reconfirm a reservation, re-enter card details, or supply payment information to receive a refund. Check the trip through Frontier directly. Open the app or type the airline’s website address yourself. Use contact information obtained there if something looks wrong. If you entered a card, contact its issuer. Lock it while you report the exposure and arrange a replacement. Include every card you tried, even ones the page said it rejected. Don’t assume leaving before clicking Submit protected the information. Web forms can collect what you type before submission. If you supplied a password, change it through the legitimate site. Change it elsewhere if you reused it. Check the reservation. Make sure the itinerary and contact information remain correct. Frontier’s published instructions say a confirmation code and last name can provide access to changes and cancellations, so changing your frequent flyer password may not close that separate route into a booking. Always check the sender information on an email. That can be spoofed but most scammers don’t go to that level of effort. #6145. Rosewood Beyond Sale: 30% Off Stays, Plus Rosewood Elite Perks

Luxury hotel group Rosewood has just kicked off its best sale of the year, offering savings of up to 30%, and it’s exclusively available through Rosewood Elite travel advisors. If you’ve been considering a stay at a Rosewood, this would be a great time to book.

With the Rosewood Beyond promotion, guests can save 30% off the best available rate when booking a Rosewood property through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. To cover the basics:

In order to take advantage of the Rosewood Beyond sale, you need to book through a Rosewood Elite travel advisor. Ford’s team is happy to help with this, and can be reached at [email protected]. Other travel advisors are welcome to leave their contact details in the comments as well.

Let me emphasize that the 30% discount is off the best available rate, otherwise known as the flexible rate. So you couldn’t get this discount on an advance purchase rate, third or fourth night free rate, etc. So in some situations the savings here won’t be that significant, while in other cases they are huge.

While there are of course some restrictions and blackout dates, this is about as no strings attached as promotions get. The 30% off rate also offers the same flexibility as whatever the flexible rate would be, which of course varies by property.

Since the Rosewood Beyond sale is specifically being offered through Rosewood Elite travel advisors, the good news is that these reservations also unlock additional benefits, including the following:

Rosewood is a really high quality hotel brand, and you can find all the hotels here. If you’re looking for a getaway from the United States, it’s tough to beat the Rosewood Mayakoba, the Rosewood Little Dix Bay, the Rosewood Kona Village, Las Ventanas al Paraiso, etc. Rosewood also has lots of great city hotels, ranging from the Rosewood Hong Kong, to the Rosewood Sao Paulo, to The Carlyle New York.

Rosewood has brought back its biggest promotion of the year, offering 30% off the best available rate. This is valid for bookings confirmed November 3-10, 2026, and for stays through June 30, 2027.

Aside from a small list of excluded properties, this is a pretty straightforward offer that gives you the best deal you’ll find on Rosewood stays. You can even stack this with Rosewood Elite perks, to unlock breakfast, a property credit, a room upgrade, and more.

Just keep in mind that the discount is based on the flexible rate, and not based on any promotional rate you can find.

One of the questions people often ask us is, “How much is a point or mile worth?”

The true answer varies from point to point and person to person. It also depends on your travel goals and how much you maximize a particular loyalty currency. Still, some rewards are worth more than others, and our goal is to give you a sense of how they stack up.

Related: How TPG determines its points and miles valuations

American Express added high-yield savings account deposits as a new Reward Dollars redemption method.

American Express is offering a 30% transfer bonus to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club through Nov. 30 and a 35% transfer bonus to Marriott Bonvoy through Dec. 10.

It also added JetBlue TrueBlue as a transfer partner and announced the transfer ratio for World of Hyatt will worsen on Jan. 1.

Atmos Rewards introduced four new Communities.

Citi and American refreshed two AAdvantage credit cards.

The airline closed its last Pacific Wi-Fi coverage gap and has equipped more than 95% of its fleet for complimentary Wi-Fi. Delta will resume its seasonal Boston-Reykjavik service in 2027.

The airline opened a 54,000-square-foot United Club in Houston and will add service to Bermuda and three San Francisco routes in 2027.

*Calculated using data provided by Points Path.

Members can earn double points at participating hotels through Dec. 31.

Amex and Hilton launched the first Hilton Honors credit card in Canada.

Mereshi Safari Camp Serengeti, Autograph Collection will open soon.

The StandardX Times Square will open in the second half of 2028.

**Calculated using data from Gondola (a free hotel search and direct booking platform for frequent travelers).

Rove has grown from an intriguing newcomer into one of the most valuable transferable rewards programs we track. So, we've decided to add Rove miles to TPG's valuations at 2.05 cents apiece.

That puts Rove on a par with our valuation of Chase Ultimate Rewards points and behind only Bilt Points as the most valuable transferable currencies we track. Using our updated methodology, we considered the value available when redeeming Rove miles, as well as the number and quality of the Rove transfer partners.

Rove now has an impressive 22 transfer partners, including multiple currencies that have traditionally been difficult for U.S. travelers to earn, such as Japan Airlines Mileage Bank and Lufthansa Miles & More. Most transfers are at a 1:1 rate, and the roster also includes TPG favorites Air Canada Aeroplan, Flying Blue, Qantas Frequent Flyer and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

Rove miles are also easy to earn without opening a new credit card. Members can collect miles by booking flights and hotels or shopping online. New members who join through TPG can earn 1,500 bonus miles, then earn another 5,000 miles after making their first hotel booking of more than $500 with code "BRIANKELLY500."

Related: Earning 28 miles per dollar: How a 2-night New York City hotel stay earned me enough miles to fly to Europe using Rove

November's cobranded credit card offer of the month is the Southwest Rapid Rewards personal credit cards, offering welcome bonuses of up to 90,000 Rapid Rewards points. Applicants approved by Dec. 2 can still have their welcome bonus points count toward Companion Pass qualification, even if those points post in 2027.

Here are some of the best welcome offers this month for those seeking a new travel rewards card that earns transferable points or miles.

#6140. Capital One Adds New Airline Partner With 30% Bonus—Book Emirates Business Class Without Fuel Surcharges

All of a sudden Panamanian airline Copa is taking U.S. points transfer programs by storm. Did not have that on my 2026 bingo card! Capital One has added Copa Airlines ConnectMiles as a transfer partner, opening another way to book Emirates business class without fuel surcharges. They’re offering a 30% transfer bonus to launch the partnership, too. But even with that bonus, you’ll get fewer Copa miles than Citi and Rove offer at their regular rates. Beginning November 2, Capital One miles transfer to Copa at 2:1.5. That’s 750 ConnectMiles for every 1,000 Capital One miles. The 30% bonus runs through December 1, 2026, bringing the effective rate to 975 ConnectMiles per 1,000 miles transferred. I like seeing Capital One expand its partner list again. They haven’t done so in a year! I just wish they weren’t quite so tight with the transfer ratio. Citi Added Copa Last Week, Following Rove I covered Rove adding Copa on September 1. Their regular transfer rate is 1:1, and they launched with a 40% bonus through September 30. That meant 1,000 Rove miles became 1,400 Copa miles. Then Citi added ConnectMiles on October 25: Citi Strata Elite, Strata Premier, Prestige and AT&T Access More cardholders receive 1,000 Copa miles per 1,000 ThankYou points. Other eligible ThankYou cards, including the no annual fee Citi Strata, Double Cash and Custom Cash cards, transfer 1,000 points to 700 Copa miles. Here’s how the three programs compare today: Transfer From Copa Miles Per 1,000 Points Rove 1,000 Citi, with an eligible premium card 1,000 Citi, other eligible cards 700 Capital One, regular rate 750 Capital One, with 30% bonus through December 1 975 Capital One’s bonus nearly gets you to 1:1. Transfer 10,000 Capital One miles and receive 9,750 Copa miles during the promotion. Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Copa at 3:1, with the usual 5,000-mile bonus for transferring 60,000 points. That’s 25,000 Copa miles for 60,000 Marriott points. When Rove added Copa, I liked having access to a program that the big U.S. bank currencies didn’t offer. Two months later, Citi and Capital One have followed. Rove’s 40% launch bonus is over, but their ordinary rate still beats Capital One’s promotional rate. The Value In Copa Miles Transfers Copa is a Star Alliance airline based in Panama. Its miles can book United Airlines and other alliance partners, but the redemption I flagged in September was Emirates. Emirates business class from the U.S. to Dubai for 80,000 miles one way, without carrier-imposed surcharges. Taxes and other applicable fees apply. United Airlines premium transcontinental business class for 25,000 miles one way when saver award space is available to Copa. Copa economy awards starting at 15,000 miles one way from its North America 1 region to Panama, Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northern South America. Capital One Now Has 23 Transfer Partners Capital One’s last additions were Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and I Prefer Hotel Rewards on September 23, 2025. It’s been more than a year, so it’s good to see them adding another option. Here’s the complete current list. These are the standard transfer ratios, before temporary bonuses, expressed as Capital One miles to partner miles or points. Transfer Partner Standard Ratio Aeromexico Rewards 1:1 Air Canada Aeroplan 1:1 Air France-KLM Flying Blue 1:1 Avianca LifeMiles 1:1 British Airways Club 1:1 Cathay Pacific Asia Miles 1:1 Copa Airlines ConnectMiles 2:1.5 Emirates Skywards 2:1.5 Etihad Guest 1:1 EVA Air Infinity MileageLands 2:1.5 Finnair Plus 1:1 Japan Airlines Mileage Bank 2:1.5 JetBlue TrueBlue 5:3 Qantas Frequent Flyer 1:1 Qatar Airways Privilege Club 1:1 Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer 1:1 TAP Air Portugal Miles&Go 1:1 Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles 1:1 Virgin Red 1:1 Accor Live Limitless 2:1 Choice Privileges 1:1 I Prefer Hotel Rewards 1:2 Wyndham Rewards 1:1 Capital One manages the economics of its rewards program tightly. They give you 750 Japan Airlines miles per 1,000 Capital One miles, and half as many I Prefer points as Citi offers with its premium cards. Copa is another useful partner, but with a less generous conversion rate. At the regular Copa ratio, earning 2 Capital One miles per dollar on Venture X spending means earning 1.5 Copa miles per dollar. Citi Double Cash earns 2 ThankYou points per dollar on purchases as you buy and pay, and pairing it with an eligible premium ThankYou card gets you 2 Copa miles per dollar. Skift Intelligence is built on a framework designed to track every decision that determines where the next dollar in travel is going. Capital Moves, a new feature updated daily, tracks every notable capital allocation announcement across global travel.

Hotels and aviation accounted for 37 of the 59 capital moves Skift tracked in October, and they tell two different stories.

In hotels, money changed hands, and sellers recycled capital or worked through distress. Pandox sold seven Nordic hotels to pay down debt, receivers sold two Shimao hotels in Hong Kong, and two Indian hotels passed to a new owner through insolvency. Buyers consolidated, from Endeavor’s seven-hotel portfolio around Chicago Midway Airport to Sunday PropTech’s deal for Fletcher’s roughly 170 hotels.

Skift tracked 59 capital moves across travel in October 2026, and hotels and aviation accounted for 37 of them — but the money moved for different reasons. Hotel capital largely changed hands: Pandox sold seven Nordic hotels to pay down debt, receivers sold two Shimao hotels in Hong Kong, two Indian hotels transferred through insolvency, and buyers consolidated portfolios, including Endeavor's seven hotels around Chicago Midway Airport and Sunday PropTech's deal for Fletcher's roughly 170 hotels. Aviation capital went into future capacity and the debt behind it, with Avolon ordering 250 aircraft, Aviation Capital Group ordering 75, and Southwest, IndiGo, and Allegiant lining up financing. Startup funding stayed small — 10 of 17 venture financings were $5 million or less — and the AI money that moved went into infrastructure: connecting AI agents to travel inventory, automating hotel guest messaging, and tracking hotel prices after booking. Booking Holdings' plan to invest up to $100 million in its own AI trip-management startup, Vayo, is contingent on product progress. Consolidation continued in travel technology, with SITA agreeing to two airline and airport technology acquisitions in under two weeks and Duetto buying FLYR's hotel revenue management business.

#6137. American Airlines Philadelphia Flagship Lounge Expected To Double In Size, Taking Over The Admirals Club Next Door

American Airlines’ gorgeous Philadelphia Flagship Lounge may finally get the space it should have had from the start. Lounge staff are reportedly telling passengers it’ll take over the Admirals Club next door around March 2027, essentially doubling the size of the business class lounge before next summer’s transatlantic seasonal peak. That’s the change I called for when the lounge opened. But there’s a potential problem for Admirals Club members since there’s no announced replacement for the club they’d lose. A passenger reports being told by the employee managing Flagship lounge entry that it would expand into the adjoining A West Admirals Club “sometime around next March.” Another commenter says an agent separately told them about expanding to the whole floor (which is the same thing), after they gave up on finding a seat in Flagship and went next door. Officially, an American Airlines spokesperson tells me: Nothing set in stone right now, but we are always evaluating how we can best serve our customers during the summer peak next year. In my original review, I showed the connector behind the check-in desk. There’s already ‘swing space’ that can be opened to either lounge. During my visit it was part of Flagship. These are adjoining spaces with the same beautiful design, and they’re already connected. The dimensions of the spaces are: Flagship: 12,500 square feet, with 200 seats. Admirals Club: 11,000 square feet, with 181 seats. Additional flex space: 1,364 square feet. That’s nearly 25,000 square feet across the complex. Moving the Admirals Club space into Flagship would roughly double its footprint. I quite like this lounge. In the morning and early afternoon, it’s a lovely place to spend time. The trouble comes before the bank of transatlantic departures, when the passengers it’s supposed to serve all arrive at once. A business class lounge needs enough seats for people flying business class. And in the summer from Philadelphia that total grows quite a lot with American’s seasonal services. Things are even worse now that the A West terminal has lost the American Express Centurion Lounge for expansion into the British Airways lounge space, expecting to reopen by the end of 2027. I’ve covered the project taking over the British Airways lounge space below. The British Airways lounge is closed, too. I actually think Flagship was already better than both lounges. It’s just crowded (but not as cramped as Centurion was!). American has been investing more in lounge food. At Dallas recently, I found a better buffet, staffed charcuterie and food ordered by QR code that arrived at my table in four minutes. Philadelphia helped introduce that ordering system, coming after the Soho lounge at JFK which is shared with BA. Philadelphia wasn’t built with a separate Flagship Dining room. Those are operating in Dallas and Miami, and I broke the news that Los Angeles reopens this week. Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden has talked about rethinking Flagship. Delta was the last of the big three to introduce a separate business class lounge, and I think Delta One lounges now offer the strongest overall product. American’s access rules are much more generous, including eligible elites flying coach on qualifying international trips and oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from programs other than American and Alaska even on domestic itineraries. That makes having enough space especially important. American had an Admirals Club in A East. They closed it when these lounges opened in May 2025. I argued then that they should keep A East for Admirals Club members and dedicate A West entirely to Flagship. Under the reported plan, the nearest Admirals Club would instead be B/C. Someone paying for a membership, or carrying the Citi Executive card, would lose access to the beautiful A West club without gaining access to the larger Flagship Lounge. American should take back the A East space as well. Trump is famously a lifelong heterosexual, so many in the media and on the left are confused. Instead, as videos show, they scream with the same laughter they produce when Trump goes on a racist tirade, encourages audience members to commit acts of violence or otherwise showcases his affinity for childish bullying, which remains his main and often sole selling point to his base. He did the same bit with Nicki Minaj, making the rapper-turned-MAGA shill stand up and show off her backside to the crowd at a Michigan rally.Â  As feminists like to remind folks, sexual harassment is about demonstrating power, not lust. Husted is far from the only man Trump ever catcalls. As the New York Times notes, Trump loves making a spectacle out of menâs looks, for the approval of hooting MAGA audiences who get a vicarious thrill from watching Trump say inappropriate things to fellow Republicans, who have no choice but to grin and pretend they enjoy it. Itâs a continuation of the other ways Trump displays his dominance over Republicans with fancy job titles, such as senators and Cabinet officials, by expecting them to flatter him grotesquely on camera or to wear ill-fitting shoes he has âgiftedâ them.Â

None of this should make us feel any sympathy for Husted or other Republicans, who could at any point grow an actual spine and reject Trumpâs abuse. These people grovel for their failing leader in the vain hope that some of his celebrity stardust will rub off on them and boost their political ambitions. Husted is a classic example of the problem now facing Republicans. Like most in his party, he has nothing to offer voters, unless theyâre hyper-rich capitalists seeking deregulation or massive tax cuts. He has no discernible charisma of his own, either. So all thatâs left is leeching onto Trump and hoping his ability to speak to the lizard-brain impulses of bigots will rally enough voters to drag Hustedâs empty pair of pants (and his mediocre ass) across the finish line.Â

All thatâs left is leeching onto Trump and hoping his ability to speak to the lizard-brain impulses of bigots can drag Hustedâs empty pants across the line.

Whatâs funny about all this is that Hustedâs blandness is likely what landed him in the unfortunate spot of getting rhetorically goosed by Trump almost every night. By his own account, Trump knew very little about the Ohio Republican he was there to support at the Youngstown rally, but learned shortly beforehand that Husted played football in college. Trump, whose background is in reality TV, resorted to his tendency to reduce a person to a single defining trait that could fit on a chyron. So even though Hustedâs gridiron career ended decades ago, Trump indulged in lame fantasies about how he thinks a football player should look like, complete with broad shoulders and well-defined glutes.

Likely, it would have ended with one iteration if he hadnât praised Hustedâs ass, which elevated a pedestrian effort to define a candidate into the realm of attention-getting weirdness. But of course that remark got everyoneâs attention, and Trump will reliably return to any bit, no matter how bizarre, as long as it draws eyeballs. So it was that Husted, who was on the verge of being relegated to âFormer College Football Playerâ in the sprawling reality show cast of Trumpâs political orbit, instead became the butt of Trumpâs favorite new joke.

It could be worse, of course. Trump has a similar bit he likes to trot out about Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, the Republican nominee for that stateâs Senate seat. Except instead of being an imaginary muscleman like Husted, Trump has cast Paxton in the role of ugly loser. In nearly every speech where he mentions Paxton, Trump has to talk about how hideous the guy is and how poorly he supposedly dresses.

With both of these GOP candidates, Trumpâs oversimplified, theatrical descriptors donât have much to do with reality. Whatever he once looked like, Husted doesnât really have the athletic build Trump fantasizes about. Paxton is nobodyâs idea of a handsome man, but itâs simply not true that he dresses poorly. There are many terrible things we could say about Paxton, but his wardrobe appears perfectly fine â especially compared to Trump, who seems to believe that wearing enormously oversized suits will hide his ever-expanding bulk. But these two guys are now characters in Trumpâs world, where, as in reality TV shows, individual humans are stripped of all their complexities to be turned into broad, easily consumed caricatures.

Whether heâs inviting the world to stare at these menâs allegedly spectacular rear end or daring them to smile while he calls them ugly, Trump is sending a message: He owns these people. He can define them in reductive, humiliating language, and they have been so hollowed out as human beings that they wonât even defend themselves. Normally, when a leader is both a lame duck and cratering in his approval polls, the way Donald Trump is now, that personâs party will start looking for ways to move on and forge a new identity. Itâs a sign of how empty the Republican Party is that they seem incapable of doing that. They donât just submit to Trumpâs continued abuse, but even keep seeking it out. That must be a miserable experience, but clearly they feel that without him, theyâre nothing at all. Itâs tough to disagree.Â

#6134. Southwest’s New Credit Card Bonuses Offer Up To 90,000 Points Toward Companion Pass—Last Chance Before Rules Change

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

Southwest’s Companion Pass lets someone fly with you for just taxes and fees, even when you redeem points for your own ticket. For someone who flies Southwest with a partner a few times a year, it’s the single best deal in domestic air travel. And the easiest way to earn it is about to disappear.

There’s still a final window to use an 80,000- or 90,000-point credit card initial bonus toward a pass valid through December 31, 2027. You need to apply by December 2, 2026 and get approved. Neither bonus gets you all the way there on its own, but both give you a huge head start.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee. This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation: First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group. You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller. First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares. The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar. I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference. How Close These Bonuses Get You To Companion Pass Under the 2026 rules, earning 135,000 Companion Pass qualifying points in a calendar year gets you the pass for the rest of that year and the following year. Southwest credit card customers receive a 10,000-point qualifying boost, so they effectively need 125,000 more. Priority: 90,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 100,000. You need another 35,000 qualifying points. Plus: 80,000 bonus points plus the 10,000-point boost gets you to 90,000. You need another 45,000 qualifying points. The purchases you make to earn the bonus also earn points. Assuming those purchase points post in 2026, spending the minimum at 1 point per dollar reduces the remaining gap to 32,000 points with Priority or 44,000 with Plus. Bonus category spending and qualifying points you’ve already earned reduce it further. Qualifying flights and eligible partner activity can help fill the gap, too. Check your Companion Pass progress in your account. Once you have the pass, book your own Southwest flight with cash or points and add your designated companion, as long as there’s an available seat. Their taxes and fees start at $5.60 one-way. You can use the benefit repeatedly and change your designated companion up to three times per calendar year. How Optimal Timing Of The Companion Pass Has Changed As I covered in Southwest’s 2027 Rapid Rewards overhaul, unlimited Companion Pass becomes a benefit of the new Platinum elite tier next year. Initial bonuses generally stop helping you qualify. Anniversary points, referral bonuses and extra points from card bonus categories stop counting, too. Southwest’s transition exception preserves the initial bonus for customers who apply by December 2, 2026, are approved, and meet the offer’s requirements. Even if you finish the required spending in early 2027, the bonus can count toward 2026 qualification for a pass ending December 31, 2027. So the old strategy of waiting until January to earn nearly two years of Companion Pass doesn’t work here. A bonus earned under this exception won’t get you a pass through the end of 2028. And Chase’s terms distinguish the initial bonus from ordinary purchase points. Those purchase points must post to your Rapid Rewards account in 2026 to count toward this pass. Spending after your December statement closes generally posts in January. You also want the 10,000-point qualifying boost credited in 2026; Southwest allows up to 30 days after account opening for it to arrive. You still have to meet the initial bonus spending requirement within the first 3 months from account opening. The transition rule doesn’t extend that deadline. If you’re eligible, can handle the required spending, and have a path to the remaining qualifying points, I’d take advantage of this before December 2. The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. It has a $229 annual fee.

This is the premium Southwest co-brand card, really designed for folks who fly the airline. It makes those trips better, and spending helps earn both elite status and Companion Pass®. The travel benefits cover the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation:

First checked bag free. Preferred or Standard seat selection at booking, at no additional charge, when available. Extra Legroom seat upgrades within 48 hours of departure, at no additional charge, when available. Boarding with Group 5 or earlier if another benefit qualifies you for a better group.

You earn 4 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, including flights, inflight purchases and Southwest gift cards; 2 points per dollar at gas stations and restaurants; and 1 point per dollar on other purchases. There are also 7,500 anniversary points each year.

The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (See rates and fees) offers 80,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. Its annual fee is $99. That’s a much lower spending requirement for a bonus that’s only 10,000 points smaller.

First checked bag free for the cardmember and up to 8 additional passengers on the same reservation. Standard seat selection within 48 hours of departure, when available, for the same group of travelers. Group 5 boarding or earlier if you otherwise qualify. 3,000 anniversary points each year, plus a 10% anniversary flight discount code that excludes Basic fares.

The Plus card earns 2 points per dollar on Southwest Airlines® purchases, and 2 points per dollar at gas stations and grocery stores on the first $5,000 in combined purchases per anniversary year. Other purchases earn 1 point per dollar.

I’d choose Plus for the lower cost of getting the bonus. Priority costs $130 more per year, but gives you better seat benefits, 4,500 more anniversary points and a larger initial bonus. For a family that flies Southwest regularly, those seating benefits can easily be worth the difference.

#6132. Flying Around Russia Is Testing Airlines’ Climate Targets

Enter your email for a complimentary article + exclusive offers.

Photo Credit: Airspace Closures Pixabay from Pexels

Avoiding Russia has become a climate problem for airlines heading from Europe to Northeast Asia — and a competitive disadvantage. Finnair, one of the most affected airlines, says it’s committed to its climate goals.

Finnair flights to Northeast Asia now take about a third longer than they did before Russia closed its airspace in 2022, using up more fuel and spewing more emissions.

Russia barred airlines from EU countries and the U.K. from its airspace in retaliation for their bans on Russian carriers after its invasion of Ukraine. Airlines from Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan have largely avoided Russian airspace over safety concerns. This cut off many of the most efficient routes between Europe and Northeast Asia.

On routes between Europe and Northeast Asia, carriers that are barred from or avoid Russian airspace burn 13.8% more fuel per flight than rivals that still fly over it, according to an analysis by Skailark. The firm compared fuel burn on identical routes and aircraft types in 2019 and from March 2025 to June 2026.

The extra fuel burn adds 1.53 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year, or 12% of those flights’ total. Skailark used the Inte

Nearly four years after Russia closed its airspace to EU and UK carriers, the cost is now quantified: airlines barred from or avoiding Russian airspace burn 13.8% more fuel per flight on Europe–Northeast Asia routes than rivals that still overfly Russia, according to an analysis by Skailark comparing identical routes and aircraft types in 2019 and from March 2025 to June 2026. The extra burn adds 1.53 million metric tons of CO2 a year, or 12% of those flights' total emissions. Finnair is the most exposed carrier, with Northeast Asia flights taking 33.2% longer and burning 33.5% more fuel; sustainability VP Riku Aho said company-level gross CO2 emissions are up roughly 10% since 2019, with knock-on effects on fleet, navigation, crew, and aircraft utilization costs. ANA, Japan Airlines, Air France, KLM, and Lufthansa are also among the most affected. Meanwhile carriers from China, the Gulf, and Türkiye that still use Russian airspace are adding European connections — Emirates recently launched Helsinki — while British Airways suspended London–Beijing and Virgin Atlantic dropped Shanghai in 2024. A Lufthansa spokesperson called the situation a structural competitive disadvantage for European carriers. With jet fuel at $4.59 per gallon and the EU's SAF blending mandate underway, Finnair is not planning for Russian airspace to reopen soon.
